Section 1 of 65

Control plane and etcd

7 concepts · about 50 minutes

Kubernetes is a database of desired state (the API server and etcd) plus many small programs that keep reality matching it. Learn that split and the rest of the platform becomes predictable.

Goals
  • Name every control plane and node component and say what it owns
  • Explain how etcd and Raft keep cluster state consistent
  • Describe a controller reconcile loop and why Kubernetes is level driven
1.1

The cluster at a glance

In plain words

A cluster is a control plane that makes decisions and worker nodes that run your containers. You talk only to the control plane, through the API server.

The problem it solves

Running containers across many machines needs one place that knows what should run, where it runs, and what to do when a machine dies. Doing that by hand with SSH does not scale or heal.

What it does

  • The control plane runs kube-apiserver, etcd, kube-scheduler and kube-controller-manager (plus cloud-controller-manager on cloud providers).
  • Each node runs a kubelet, a container runtime and usually kube-proxy and a CNI agent.
  • Everything communicates through the API server; components never talk to each other directly.
  • On managed platforms (EKS, Gardener-managed Kyma) the provider operates the control plane and you only see worker nodes.

First look

bashInspect a cluster
kubectl cluster-info                         # API server and CoreDNS endpoints
kubectl get nodes -o wide                    # nodes, versions, runtime, IPs
kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose' | head   # API server health checks
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -o wide      # system components that run as Pods
kubectl api-resources | head -20             # every kind this cluster serves
Note

On Kyma and EKS you will not see kube-apiserver or etcd as Pods. The provider hosts them outside your nodes.

Check yourself
Which component do kubectl and the kubelet both talk to?

The kube-apiserver. It is the only component that reads and writes etcd.

1.2

The API server

In plain words

The kube-apiserver is a stateless HTTPS server that exposes every Kubernetes object as a REST resource. It is the single gateway to the cluster state.

The problem it solves

If every component read and wrote the data store directly, there would be no common place to enforce identity, permissions, validation and audit.

What it does

  • Authenticates and authorises each request, runs admission, validates and then persists to etcd.
  • Offers list and watch so clients can stream changes instead of polling.
  • Is stateless, so you run several replicas behind a load balancer for availability.
  • Serves built-in APIs and extension APIs (CRDs, aggregated APIs) the same way.

Talk to it directly

bashThe REST API behind kubectl
kubectl get --raw /api/v1/namespaces/default/pods | head -c 300   # raw list call
kubectl get pods -v=8 2>&1 | grep -E 'GET|Response Status' | head -3   # see the HTTP calls
kubectl proxy --port=8001 &                                       # local authenticated proxy
curl -s localhost:8001/apis | head -c 300                         # API groups available
kill %1
1.3

etcd, the state store

In plain words

etcd is a small, strongly consistent key-value database. Every object you create, such as a Deployment or Secret, is a key in etcd with its serialised value.

The problem it solves

The cluster needs one authoritative record that survives restarts and gives every reader the same answer, otherwise two controllers could act on different truths.

What it does

  • Stores objects under keys such as /registry/pods/default/web-0.
  • Supports transactions and revisions, which is what makes watch and optimistic concurrency (resourceVersion) possible.
  • Is sensitive to disk latency, since each write is fsynced. Slow disks cause leader elections and API timeouts.
  • Has a size quota (2 GiB default, 8 GiB suggested maximum). Past the quota it goes read-only until compacted and defragmented.

Back up and inspect

bashetcd snapshot on a self-managed cluster
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  snapshot save /backup/etcd-$(date +%F).db
etcdutl snapshot status /backup/etcd-$(date +%F).db -w table
etcdctl endpoint status --cluster -w table     # leader, DB size, raft index
Careful

A cluster without tested etcd backups has no disaster recovery. On managed services (EKS, Gardener) the provider backs up etcd; Gardener also keeps etcd backups in object storage. Your workload data still needs its own backups, for example Velero.

Check yourself
Why do slow disks hurt the whole cluster?

etcd fsyncs every write. Slow fsync delays commits, heartbeats are missed, leaders change, and the API server times out.

1.4

Raft and quorum

In plain words

Raft is how etcd members agree. One member is the leader, writes go through it, and a write counts only after a majority has stored it.

The problem it solves

With several copies of the data, members could disagree after a crash or network split. Raft guarantees that all members agree on one ordered history.

What it does

  • A quorum is floor(n/2) + 1 members: 2 of 3, 3 of 5.
  • A 3-member cluster survives 1 failure, a 5-member cluster survives 2. Four members tolerate no more than three do, so use odd sizes.
  • Without a quorum etcd refuses writes, so the cluster cannot change, but running Pods keep running because the kubelet works from its local state.
  • More members means slower writes (more acknowledgements), so 3 or 5 is the norm.

Quorum arithmetic

pythonQuorum and failure tolerance
for n in range(1, 8):
    quorum = n // 2 + 1
    print(f"members={n} quorum={quorum} tolerated_failures={n - quorum}")
Check yourself
How many failures does a 5-member etcd tolerate?

Two. Quorum is 3, so 5 - 3 = 2.

1.5

kube-scheduler

In plain words

The scheduler watches for Pods with no node assigned and picks the best node for each one.

The problem it solves

Someone must decide which of hundreds of machines has the room, labels and constraints a Pod needs. Doing it by hand wastes capacity and breaks rules like spreading across zones.

What it does

  • Filters nodes that cannot run the Pod, then scores the remaining ones.
  • Writes the result by creating a binding, which sets spec.nodeName.
  • Never starts containers. The kubelet on the chosen node does that.
  • A Pod with no suitable node stays Pending with a FailedScheduling event explaining why.

See the decision

bashWhy is it Pending
kubectl get pods --field-selector=status.phase=Pending -A
kubectl describe pod web-0 | sed -n '/Events/,$p'     # FailedScheduling reasons
kubectl get events -A --field-selector reason=FailedScheduling --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail
1.6

Controllers and reconcile loops

In plain words

A controller is a loop that compares desired state (the spec) with observed state (the status) and acts to close the gap. It then repeats forever.

The problem it solves

Imperative scripts break when something changes behind their back. A loop that always re-checks reality recovers from crashes, deleted Pods and missed events.

What it does

  • kube-controller-manager bundles dozens of controllers: Deployment, ReplicaSet, Job, Node, EndpointSlice, ServiceAccount and others.
  • Each controller watches objects through an informer (a local cache fed by watch) and puts keys on a work queue.
  • Reconcile is level driven: it looks at current state, not at the event that woke it, so a missed event is harmless.
  • Reconcile must be idempotent. Your own operators and CRD controllers follow the same pattern.

Watch a controller work

bashDelete a Pod and watch it come back
kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:1.27 --replicas=3
kubectl get pods -l app=web -w &
kubectl delete pod -l app=web --wait=false --field-selector=status.phase=Running | head -1
sleep 5; kill %1
kubectl get rs -l app=web -o wide       # ReplicaSet controller restored the count
kubectl delete deployment web
Check yourself
What does level driven mean?

The controller reacts to the current state difference, not to individual events, so lost or duplicated events do not matter.

1.7

Cloud controller manager and managed control planes

In plain words

The cloud-controller-manager holds the code that talks to a cloud provider API: create load balancers, find node metadata and remove nodes whose VM is gone.

The problem it solves

Core Kubernetes should not contain AWS, Azure or Google specific logic. Splitting it out lets providers release on their own schedule.

What it does

  • Its Service controller turns a type: LoadBalancer Service into a cloud load balancer.
  • Its node controller sets zone and instance type labels and deletes Node objects for terminated VMs.
  • In EKS the AWS Load Balancer Controller adds ALB and NLB features on top of this.
  • In Gardener (the base of SAP BTP Kyma) a seed cluster hosts each shoot cluster's control plane, so you never manage etcd or API server nodes.

Check what your nodes report

bashProvider information on nodes
kubectl get nodes -L topology.kubernetes.io/zone,node.kubernetes.io/instance-type
kubectl get node -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.providerID}{"\n"}'

Section 2 of 65

API request flow

8 concepts · about 50 minutes

Every change in Kubernetes is an HTTPS request to the API server. Knowing the stages in order tells you which layer rejected you and why.

Goals
  • Follow a request through authentication, authorisation, admission, validation and persistence
  • Explain resourceVersion, watches and server-side apply
  • Debug a rejected request from its error message
2.1

Resources, groups and versions

In plain words

Every object type has a group, a version and a kind, for example apps/v1 and Deployment. The REST path is built from them.

The problem it solves

Types change over time. Versioned APIs let the project add fields and retire old shapes without breaking existing manifests.

What it does

  • The core group has no name: /api/v1/pods. Others use /apis/apps/v1/deployments.
  • Maturity is encoded in the version: v1 stable, v1beta1 pre-release, v1alpha1 experimental and off by default.
  • Objects are stored in one storage version; the API server converts between served versions.
  • Deprecated versions are removed after announced periods, so run a deprecation check before upgrades.

Explore the API

bashDiscover kinds and fields
kubectl api-resources --api-group=apps -o wide
kubectl api-versions | head
kubectl explain deployment.spec.strategy --recursive | head -30
kubectl get --raw /metrics | grep apiserver_requested_deprecated_apis | head -3
2.2

The request pipeline

In plain words

A write passes through fixed stages: authentication, authorisation, mutating admission, schema validation, validating admission, and finally storage in etcd.

The problem it solves

Without ordered gates, a client could write unvalidated or unauthorised objects. Each stage answers a different question.

What it does

  • Authentication: who are you.
  • Authorisation: may you do this verb on this resource.
  • Mutating admission: change the object, for example inject defaults or sidecars.
  • Validation against the schema, then validating admission: accept or reject the final object.
  • Persistence to etcd. Only then do controllers see it.

Rejections tell you the stage

bashReading errors
kubectl auth whoami                                  # authentication result (1.28+)
kubectl auth can-i create deployments -n shop       # authorisation check
kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f deploy.yaml       # runs the whole pipeline without storing
Tip

--dry-run=server runs admission and validation exactly as a real apply would. --dry-run=client only checks locally and misses webhook and policy rejections.

Check yourself
A request fails with "forbidden". Which stage rejected it?

Authorisation. A 401 means authentication failed; a webhook denial mentions "admission webhook" or a policy name.

2.3

Authentication

In plain words

The API server decides who you are from a credential on the request. It has no user database of its own for people.

The problem it solves

The cluster must identify humans, workloads and nodes without storing passwords. It delegates trust to certificates, tokens and external identity providers.

What it does

  • X.509 client certificates: the common name becomes the user, organisation fields become groups. Used by kubelets and admin kubeconfigs.
  • ServiceAccount tokens: signed JWTs for workloads, normally short lived and projected into Pods.
  • OIDC: the API server trusts an external IdP (for example SAP IAS or Entra ID) and reads username and group claims from the ID token.
  • Webhook token authentication and EKS aws-iam-authenticator or access entries plug in the same way.
  • A request that matches no authenticator becomes system:anonymous or is rejected with 401.

Kubeconfig with OIDC login

yamlkubeconfig user using the kubelogin plugin
apiVersion: v1
kind: Config
clusters:
  - name: dev
    cluster:
      server: https://api.dev.example.com
      certificate-authority-data: LS0tLS1CRUdJTi0tLS0t
contexts:
  - name: dev
    context: {cluster: dev, user: oidc-user}
current-context: dev
users:
  - name: oidc-user
    user:
      exec:
        apiVersion: client.authentication.k8s.io/v1
        command: kubectl
        args:
          - oidc-login
          - get-token
          - --oidc-issuer-url=https://tenant.accounts.example.com
          - --oidc-client-id=kubernetes
        interactiveMode: IfAvailable
2.4

Authorisation

In plain words

After identity is known, authorisers decide whether that identity may perform a verb (get, create, delete) on a resource in a namespace.

The problem it solves

Being logged in must not mean being allowed to do anything. Fine grained rules keep a team out of another team's namespace.

What it does

  • Modes are configured on the API server and checked in order. Node and RBAC are the usual pair; webhook authorisers can be added.
  • The decision is allow, deny or no opinion; if nobody allows, the request is denied.
  • RBAC is purely additive: there are no deny rules.
  • Authorisation sees verbs, resources and names, not the object content. Content rules belong to admission.

Test permissions

bashAsk the authoriser
kubectl auth can-i delete pods -n shop
kubectl auth can-i --list -n shop | head
kubectl auth can-i get secrets -n shop --as=system:serviceaccount:shop:web
2.5

Admission control

In plain words

Admission controllers are plug-ins that inspect or change a request after it is authorised and before it is stored. They apply to create, update and delete, but not to reads.

The problem it solves

RBAC cannot say "no container may run as root" or "every Pod needs a cost label". Admission sees the full object and can enforce such rules.

What it does

  • Mutating controllers run first and may modify the object, for example default StorageClass, Istio sidecar injection, or a Kyverno mutate rule.
  • Validating controllers run after and can only accept or reject.
  • Built-ins include NamespaceLifecycle, LimitRanger, ResourceQuota, ServiceAccount and Pod Security Admission.
  • Your own rules arrive through webhooks, ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (CEL) and policy engines.

Which webhooks are active

bashList admission configuration
kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfigurations
kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations
kubectl get validatingadmissionpolicies,validatingadmissionpolicybindings
Danger

A validating webhook with failurePolicy: Fail that targets kube-system or its own namespace can lock the cluster when the webhook Pod is down. Exclude system namespaces and the webhook itself.

Check yourself
Can a validating webhook modify an object?

No. Only mutating admission can change it; validating can only accept or deny.

2.6

Validation, persistence and optimistic concurrency

In plain words

Every object carries a resourceVersion. An update succeeds only if the version you send is still the current one.

The problem it solves

Two controllers or people editing the same object can overwrite each other's changes silently.

What it does

  • The API server rejects an update with a stale version with 409 Conflict, and the client re-reads and retries.
  • Schema validation rejects unknown or mistyped fields (strict field validation is on by default in kubectl).
  • After a successful write, metadata.generation increases when the spec changes, and controllers record status.observedGeneration to show they have caught up.
  • Deleting with a finalizer sets deletionTimestamp but keeps the object until the finalizer is removed.

See the fields

bashMetadata the server maintains
kubectl create deployment demo --image=nginx:1.27
kubectl get deploy demo -o jsonpath='{.metadata.resourceVersion} gen={.metadata.generation} observed={.status.observedGeneration}{"\n"}'
kubectl scale deploy demo --replicas=2
kubectl get deploy demo -o jsonpath='{.metadata.resourceVersion} gen={.metadata.generation}{"\n"}'
kubectl delete deploy demo
2.7

Watches and informers

In plain words

A watch is a long lived HTTP request that streams changes to objects. Controllers use it instead of polling.

The problem it solves

Polling thousands of objects constantly would overload the API server and react slowly.

What it does

  • A client lists once, remembers the resourceVersion, then watches from that point.
  • If the version is too old (compacted away) the server answers 410 Gone and the client must list again.
  • Informers keep an in-memory cache and share one watch among many handlers, which is why a controller restart costs one list.
  • Watch bookmarks and API Priority and Fairness protect the server from noisy clients.

Try a watch

bashStreaming changes
kubectl get pods -w --output-watch-events    # shows the event type per change
kubectl get --raw '/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods?watch=1&timeoutSeconds=5' | head -c 400
2.8

Server-side apply

In plain words

Server-side apply (SSA) lets the API server track which actor owns which field and merge changes from several actors safely.

The problem it solves

When a controller (such as an HPA setting replicas) and your Git manifest both write the same field, a client-side merge makes them fight.

What it does

  • Each field records a manager in metadata.managedFields.
  • Applying a value another manager owns raises a conflict unless you use --force-conflicts.
  • Removing a field from your manifest removes it from the object only if you owned it.
  • Flux and Argo CD can use SSA. Use kubectl apply --server-side.

Ownership in practice

bashTwo managers on one field
kubectl create deployment demo --image=nginx:1.27 --dry-run=client -o yaml > demo.yaml
kubectl apply --server-side --field-manager=gitops -f demo.yaml
kubectl scale deploy demo --replicas=4            # a different manager now owns replicas
kubectl apply --server-side --field-manager=gitops -f demo.yaml
kubectl get deploy demo --show-managed-fields -o yaml | grep -E 'manager|f:replicas'
kubectl delete deploy demo
Check yourself
Why use SSA with an HPA?

The HPA owns `spec.replicas`; if Git does not set it, SSA leaves the HPA value alone instead of resetting it on every sync.

Section 3 of 65

Nodes, kubelet and the runtime interfaces

6 concepts · about 50 minutes

A node is just a Linux machine with a few agents. The three plug-in interfaces CRI, CNI and CSI are why Kubernetes works the same on EKS, Gardener and bare metal.

Goals
  • Explain what the kubelet does and how it talks to CRI, CNI and CSI
  • Describe node heartbeats, conditions and what happens when a node dies
  • Inspect a node and its container runtime
3.1

The kubelet

In plain words

The kubelet is the agent on every node. It watches the API server for Pods assigned to its node and makes the container runtime match them.

The problem it solves

The scheduler only writes a node name into a Pod. Something local must pull images, mount volumes, start containers, run probes and report status.

What it does

  • Watches Pods with spec.nodeName equal to its node and runs a sync loop for each.
  • Calls the runtime over CRI, the network plugin over CNI (through the runtime) and storage plug-ins over CSI.
  • Runs liveness, readiness and startup probes, and restarts containers per restartPolicy.
  • Reports Pod status, node status and a heartbeat back to the API server.
  • Keeps working from local state if the control plane is briefly unreachable.

Look at a node

bashNode details
kubectl describe node $(kubectl get nodes -o name | head -1 | cut -d/ -f2) | sed -n '1,60p'
kubectl get node -o jsonpath='{.items[0].status.nodeInfo}' | head -c 600
kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/nodes/$(kubectl get nodes -o name | head -1 | cut -d/ -f2)/proxy/healthz"
3.2

CRI and the container runtime

In plain words

The Container Runtime Interface is a gRPC API between the kubelet and a runtime. containerd and CRI-O implement it. Docker Engine support (dockershim) was removed in 1.24.

The problem it solves

Without a standard interface the kubelet would need code for every runtime. CRI lets you swap runtimes without touching Kubernetes.

What it does

  • Two services: RuntimeService (sandboxes and containers) and ImageService (pull, list, remove).
  • A Pod sandbox is created first (the pause container, holding the network namespace); then app containers join it.
  • containerd uses a low level runtime such as runc; a RuntimeClass can select gVisor or Kata for isolation.
  • Use crictl on the node for debugging; docker commands do not see Kubernetes containers.

crictl on a node

bashDebugging at runtime level
crictl ps                       # running containers
crictl pods                     # Pod sandboxes
crictl logs 
crictl images | head
crictl inspectp $(crictl pods -q | head -1) | head -30
Check yourself
Why does every Pod have a pause container?

It owns the shared network namespace so app containers can restart without losing the Pod IP.

3.3

CNI, the Pod network plug-in

In plain words

The Container Network Interface is how the runtime asks a plug-in to give a new Pod sandbox an IP and wire it into the cluster network.

The problem it solves

Kubernetes requires that every Pod can reach every other Pod without NAT, but does not say how. The CNI plug-in does the actual wiring.

What it does

  • The runtime calls the plug-in with ADD when a sandbox starts and DEL when it is removed.
  • The plug-in creates a veth pair, assigns an IP from a Pod CIDR and sets up routes or tunnels.
  • Examples: AWS VPC CNI (Pods get real VPC IPs from ENIs), Calico, Cilium (eBPF), Flannel (overlay).
  • The plug-in also often enforces NetworkPolicy. Flannel alone does not.

Where CNI lives

bashCNI config on a node
ls /etc/cni/net.d/              # network configuration files
ls /opt/cni/bin/                # plug-in binaries
kubectl -n kube-system get ds   # aws-node, calico-node, cilium ...
kubectl get pods -A -o wide | head -5   # Pod IPs
3.4

CSI, the storage plug-in

In plain words

The Container Storage Interface lets storage vendors ship a driver as ordinary Pods, instead of code compiled into Kubernetes.

The problem it solves

In-tree volume code for each cloud bloated Kubernetes and tied storage fixes to Kubernetes releases.

What it does

  • A driver has a controller part (create, delete, snapshot, expand volumes via the cloud API) and a node part (attach, format, mount on the host).
  • Sidecars such as external-provisioner, external-attacher, external-snapshotter and external-resizer translate Kubernetes objects into CSI calls.
  • Examples: ebs.csi.aws.com, efs.csi.aws.com, pd.csi.storage.gke.io.
  • Registered drivers appear as CSIDriver and CSINode objects.

Installed drivers

bashList CSI drivers
kubectl get csidrivers
kubectl get csinodes -o wide
kubectl get storageclass
3.5

Node lifecycle and health

In plain words

Each kubelet renews a Lease object every few seconds and reports node conditions such as Ready, MemoryPressure and DiskPressure.

The problem it solves

The control plane must notice dead nodes and move work off them, but must not panic over a brief network blip.

What it does

  • Leases in kube-node-lease are cheap heartbeats. If none arrives for the grace period (default 40 s) the node controller marks the node Unknown.
  • The controller adds node.kubernetes.io/unreachable taints. Pods tolerate them for 300 s by default before eviction.
  • Under pressure the kubelet evicts Pods itself, lowest QoS first, and taints the node.
  • Cluster autoscalers and Gardener replace machines that stay NotReady.

Conditions and leases

bashNode health
kubectl get lease -n kube-node-lease
kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,READY:.status.conditions[-1].type,STATUS:.status.conditions[-1].status
kubectl describe node worker-1 | grep -A8 Conditions
kubectl get node worker-1 -o jsonpath='{.spec.taints}'
Careful

Stateful Pods are not moved automatically if the node might still be running them. A StatefulSet waits for the Pod to be confirmed gone, to avoid two Pods with the same identity.

3.6

Static Pods, kube-proxy and node add-ons

In plain words

Some Pods are not created through the API. Static Pods are defined by manifest files the kubelet reads from disk. DaemonSets run one agent per node through the API.

The problem it solves

The control plane has to start before the API server exists, and every node needs network and proxy agents.

What it does

  • A static Pod manifest in /etc/kubernetes/manifests is started by the kubelet; the API shows a read-only mirror Pod. kubeadm runs apiserver, etcd and scheduler this way.
  • Node add-ons run as DaemonSets: kube-proxy, CNI agent, log shipper, node exporter, CSI node plugin.
  • The kubelet reserves resources for the system with kubeReserved and systemReserved; allocatable = capacity minus reservations minus eviction thresholds.

Capacity versus allocatable

bashWhat the scheduler can use
kubectl get node worker-1 -o jsonpath='{"capacity: "}{.status.capacity}{"\nallocatable: "}{.status.allocatable}{"\n"}'
kubectl describe node worker-1 | sed -n '/Allocated resources/,/Events/p'
Check yourself
Where does a kubelet find static Pod manifests?

In the directory set by `staticPodPath` in its config, commonly `/etc/kubernetes/manifests`.

← PreviousNext →
Section 4 of 65

Objects, namespaces and extending the API

6 concepts · about 45 minutes

Everything in Kubernetes is an object with the same envelope. Once you read that envelope fluently, any resource, built in or custom, is easy to follow.

Goals
  • Write correct labels, selectors and ownership relations
  • Use namespaces, contexts and finalizers correctly
  • Explain how CRDs extend the API and how rate limiting protects it
4.1

The anatomy of an object

In plain words

Every object has apiVersion, kind, metadata, usually a spec (what you want) and a status (what the controllers observed).

The problem it solves

A uniform shape lets one tool (kubectl, Argo CD, Kyverno) work with thousands of resource types.

What it does

  • metadata holds name, namespace, labels, annotations, uid, ownerReferences and finalizers.
  • You write spec; controllers write status. Status is a separate subresource, so editing it needs different RBAC.
  • Names are unique per kind per namespace; the uid is unique forever.

A complete small object

yamlnamespace.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: shop
  labels:
    team: payments
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: baseline
  annotations:
    owner-email: payments@example.com
4.2

Labels, selectors and annotations

In plain words

Labels are key-value tags used to group objects. Selectors pick objects by those tags. Annotations are free-form metadata that nothing selects on.

The problem it solves

Objects need loose coupling. A Service should find its Pods by what they are, not by fixed names that change on every rollout.

What it does

  • Services, ReplicaSets, NetworkPolicies and PDBs all select by label.
  • Equality selectors: app=web; set based: env in (prod,stage); presence: !canary.
  • Recommended labels: app.kubernetes.io/name, instance, version, component, part-of, managed-by.
  • A Deployment's spec.selector is immutable. A wrong selector overlap between two Deployments causes them to fight over Pods.

Selecting from the CLI

bashLabel queries
kubectl get pods -l 'app=web,env in (prod,stage)' --show-labels
kubectl label pod web-1 canary=true
kubectl label pod web-1 canary-
kubectl get pods -L app,version
kubectl annotate deploy web kubernetes.io/change-cause="bump to 1.27"
4.3

Namespaces

In plain words

Namespaces split one cluster into virtual sub-clusters for names, permissions and quotas.

The problem it solves

Teams and environments sharing a cluster would collide on names and could touch each other's objects.

What it does

  • Namespaced objects: Pods, Services, Deployments, Secrets, Roles. Cluster-scoped: Nodes, PersistentVolumes, StorageClasses, Namespaces, CRDs, ClusterRoles.
  • RBAC, ResourceQuota, LimitRange, NetworkPolicy and Pod Security labels attach at namespace level.
  • Namespaces are not a network or hard security boundary by default. Add NetworkPolicy and quotas.
  • Deleting a namespace deletes everything inside it.
  • Default namespaces: default, kube-system, kube-public, kube-node-lease. On Kyma, kyma-system and istio-system hold platform parts.

Working with namespaces

bashNamespaces and contexts
kubectl api-resources --namespaced=false | head -15
kubectl create namespace shop
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=shop
kubectl config get-contexts
kubectl get all -n shop
Tip

A wrong default namespace in your context is a classic cause of "it works for them". Show it in your shell prompt or use kubectx and kubens.

4.4

Owners, garbage collection and finalizers

In plain words

ownerReferences link a child to its parent. When the parent goes, the garbage collector removes children. Finalizers hold deletion until cleanup is done.

The problem it solves

Deleting a Deployment should remove its ReplicaSets and Pods, and deleting a PVC-bound resource should release external disks first.

What it does

  • Deployment owns ReplicaSets, which own Pods. Deleting the Deployment cascades.
  • Delete modes: background (default), foreground (children first), orphan (children kept).
  • A finalizer in metadata.finalizers keeps the object in Terminating until its controller removes it. A stuck finalizer is the usual reason a namespace hangs in Terminating.

Inspect and unstick

bashOwners and finalizers
kubectl get pod web-abc -o jsonpath='{.metadata.ownerReferences[0].kind}/{.metadata.ownerReferences[0].name}{"\n"}'
kubectl delete deploy web --cascade=orphan      # keep the Pods
kubectl get ns stuck -o jsonpath='{.spec.finalizers}{"\n"}'
kubectl get all,pvc -n stuck                    # find what still blocks deletion
Danger

Removing a finalizer by hand skips the cleanup it guarded and can leak cloud load balancers or disks. Find and fix the controller first.

Check yourself
What does `--cascade=orphan` do?

Deletes the parent but leaves the children running without an owner.

4.5

Custom resources and operators

In plain words

A CustomResourceDefinition (CRD) adds a new kind to the API. A controller for it, often called an operator, reconciles it like any built-in.

The problem it solves

Built-in kinds cannot model everything, such as a database cluster, a certificate or an Istio route. CRDs add domain objects without forking Kubernetes.

What it does

  • The CRD declares group, kind, scope, versions and an OpenAPI schema; the API server then validates and stores instances.
  • Features: status subresource, printer columns, CEL validation rules, conversion webhooks between versions.
  • Kyma itself is built from CRDs such as Kyma, APIRule, Function and module resources.
  • Cert-manager, Gateway API, Argo CD, Karpenter and KEDA are all CRD driven.

A small CRD and instance

yamlcrd.yaml
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: backups.ops.example.com
spec:
  group: ops.example.com
  scope: Namespaced
  names:
    plural: backups
    singular: backup
    kind: Backup
  versions:
    - name: v1
      served: true
      storage: true
      subresources:
        status: {}
      schema:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          type: object
          properties:
            spec:
              type: object
              required: [schedule]
              properties:
                schedule:
                  type: string
                retentionDays:
                  type: integer
                  minimum: 1
            status:
              type: object
              x-kubernetes-preserve-unknown-fields: true
---
apiVersion: ops.example.com/v1
kind: Backup
metadata:
  name: nightly
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"
  retentionDays: 14
Check yourself
Does a CRD alone do anything?

No. It only stores validated data. Behaviour needs a controller that watches the resource.

4.6

API Priority and Fairness, events and audit

In plain words

The API server protects itself from overload by queueing requests per client class, records Events about object changes, and can write an audit log of every request.

The problem it solves

One runaway controller listing all Pods in a loop could starve kubectl and the scheduler.

What it does

  • APF classifies requests into priority levels and flow-queues them; excess requests get HTTP 429 and clients should back off.
  • Events are short lived objects (about one hour) explaining what happened: Scheduled, Pulled, BackOff, FailedMount.
  • Audit policy records who did what at levels None, Metadata, Request, RequestResponse. Managed offerings expose audit logs through their own services.

Reading events and throttling

bashEvents first
kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -20
kubectl events --for pod/web-0 --watch
kubectl get flowschemas,prioritylevelconfigurations
kubectl get --raw /metrics | grep apiserver_flowcontrol_rejected_requests_total | head
← PreviousNext →
Section 5 of 65

Pods, containers and lifecycle

6 concepts · about 50 minutes

The Pod is the smallest unit you deploy. Almost every production incident involves a Pod that did not start, did not become ready, or did not stop cleanly.

Goals
  • Write a complete Pod spec with init containers and sidecars
  • Trace a Pod from Pending to Terminated and explain graceful shutdown
  • Configure liveness, readiness and startup probes without causing outages
5.1

What a Pod is

In plain words

A Pod is one or more containers that share a network identity (one IP), storage volumes and a lifecycle. They are scheduled together onto one node.

The problem it solves

Some processes must run side by side, such as an app and a log shipper or proxy, sharing localhost and files. A Pod groups them as one unit.

What it does

  • Containers in a Pod share the network namespace, so they reach each other on localhost and must use different ports.
  • They can share volumes, and optionally the process namespace (shareProcessNamespace).
  • A Pod is ephemeral and never moves. When a node dies the Pod is replaced by a new one with a new name and IP.
  • You rarely create bare Pods. A controller (Deployment, StatefulSet, Job) owns them.

A complete Pod

yamlpod.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: web
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: web
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: nginx:1.27
      ports:
        - containerPort: 80
      resources:
        requests: {cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi}
        limits: {memory: 256Mi}
      volumeMounts:
        - {name: cache, mountPath: /var/cache/nginx}
  volumes:
    - name: cache
      emptyDir: {}
5.2

Init containers and sidecars

In plain words

Init containers run one after another to completion before the app starts. Native sidecars are init containers marked restartPolicy: Always that keep running beside the app.

The problem it solves

Apps often need setup first, such as waiting for a database, fetching config or running a migration. Mixed into the app image, that setup bloats it and cannot be reused.

What it does

  • Init containers run in order; if one fails the Pod restarts it (per restartPolicy) and the app never starts.
  • A native sidecar (stable since 1.33) starts before the app, stays running, and is stopped after the app on shutdown. This fixes Job Pods that never finished because a sidecar kept running.
  • Both have their own images, so tools like curl or psql stay out of the app image.

Init container and sidecar

yamlinit-sidecar.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  initContainers:
    - name: wait-db
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: ["sh", "-c", "until nc -z db 5432; do sleep 2; done"]
    - name: log-shipper
      image: fluent/fluent-bit:3.1
      restartPolicy: Always
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: ghcr.io/example/api:1.4.2
Note

Native sidecars need Kubernetes 1.29 or later (beta, on by default) and are stable in 1.33. Check your Kyma or EKS version.

5.3

Pod phases and container states

In plain words

A Pod has a phase (Pending, Running, Succeeded, Failed, Unknown) and each container has a state (Waiting, Running, Terminated) with a reason.

The problem it solves

kubectl get pods shows one word. Fixing a problem needs the reason underneath, such as ImagePullBackOff or OOMKilled.

What it does

  • Pending: accepted but not running; unscheduled, pulling images, or waiting for volumes.
  • Running: bound to a node and at least one container is running or starting.
  • Succeeded or Failed: all containers ended; typical for Jobs.
  • Common waiting reasons: ContainerCreating, ImagePullBackOff, CrashLoopBackOff, CreateContainerConfigError.
  • Terminated reasons include Completed, Error and OOMKilled (exit code 137 means SIGKILL).

Find the real reason

bashWhy is the Pod not healthy
kubectl get pod web -o jsonpath='{.status.phase}{"\n"}'
kubectl get pod web -o jsonpath='{range .status.containerStatuses[*]}{.name}{" "}{.state}{" last="}{.lastState}{"\n"}{end}'
kubectl describe pod web | sed -n '/Events/,$p'
kubectl logs web --previous            # logs of the crashed instance
Check yourself
Exit code 137 means what?

The process was killed by SIGKILL, most often by the OOM killer (check for reason OOMKilled) or after the grace period ended.

5.4

Probes

In plain words

Probes are health checks the kubelet runs against a container. Startup says it has booted, readiness says it can take traffic, liveness says it is not stuck.

The problem it solves

A running process is not always a working one. Without probes, Kubernetes would send traffic to an app still warming up, or leave a deadlocked process running forever.

What it does

  • Readiness failure removes the Pod from Service endpoints but does not restart it.
  • Liveness failure restarts the container. Keep it cheap and independent of dependencies.
  • Startup disables the other two until it passes, which suits slow starting apps without a long initialDelaySeconds.
  • Mechanisms: httpGet, tcpSocket, exec and grpc.

Three probes together

yamlprobes.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: ghcr.io/example/api:1.4.2
      ports:
        - {name: http, containerPort: 8080}
      startupProbe:
        httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: http}
        periodSeconds: 5
        failureThreshold: 30
      readinessProbe:
        httpGet: {path: /ready, port: http}
        periodSeconds: 5
        failureThreshold: 3
      livenessProbe:
        httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: http}
        periodSeconds: 10
        timeoutSeconds: 2
        failureThreshold: 3
Danger

A liveness probe that calls the database turns a database blip into a restart storm of every Pod. Liveness checks only the process itself.

Check yourself
The app needs 90 seconds to start. Which probe handles that?

A startup probe, for example periodSeconds 5 with failureThreshold 30 allows 150 seconds before liveness takes over.

5.5

Graceful termination

In plain words

When a Pod is deleted, Kubernetes sends SIGTERM, waits up to terminationGracePeriodSeconds (default 30), then sends SIGKILL.

The problem it solves

Dropping a Pod in the middle of requests causes errors during every rollout and scale-down.

What it does

  • Deletion sets deletionTimestamp. Two things happen in parallel: the Pod is removed from endpoints, and the kubelet runs the preStop hook then sends SIGTERM.
  • Endpoint removal and SIGTERM race, so load balancers may still send traffic for a moment. A short preStop sleep covers that.
  • The app should stop accepting new connections, finish in-flight work and exit before the grace period ends.
  • PID 1 must forward or handle SIGTERM, otherwise the app is killed only at the deadline.

Drain-friendly container

yamlgraceful.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: nginx:1.27
      lifecycle:
        preStop:
          sleep:
            seconds: 10
5.6

Restart policy, CrashLoopBackOff and image pulls

In plain words

restartPolicy decides what the kubelet does when a container exits. Repeated failures cause growing waits, shown as CrashLoopBackOff.

The problem it solves

A broken container must not hammer the node, but a transient crash should recover on its own.

What it does

  • Always (default for Deployments), OnFailure and Never (used by Jobs).
  • Backoff starts at 10 s and doubles to a 5 minute maximum, reset after 10 minutes of success.
  • ImagePullBackOff comes from a wrong tag, missing registry credentials (imagePullSecrets) or rate limits.
  • imagePullPolicy defaults to IfNotPresent, or Always when the tag is latest or missing. Prefer immutable tags or digests.

Debug helpers

bashEphemeral debug container
kubectl logs web -c app --previous
kubectl debug -it web --image=busybox:1.36 --target=app    # shares the app process namespace
kubectl debug node/worker-1 -it --image=busybox:1.36        # shell on a node
kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=web

Section 6 of 65

ReplicaSets, Deployments and rollouts

6 concepts · about 45 minutes

Deployments are the default way to run stateless apps. Understanding the ReplicaSet underneath makes rollouts, rollbacks and stuck deployments readable.

Goals
  • Explain how Deployments, ReplicaSets and Pods relate
  • Tune rolling update surge and unavailability and roll back safely
  • Choose between rolling, blue green and canary releases
6.1

ReplicaSets

In plain words

A ReplicaSet keeps a fixed number of identical Pods running. If a Pod disappears it creates another.

The problem it solves

Bare Pods are not replaced when a node fails or someone deletes them.

What it does

  • Uses a label selector to count its Pods and adopts matching ones.
  • Creates Pods from spec.template and names them <replicaset>-<random>.
  • It has no upgrade logic. You rarely use it directly; Deployments create one ReplicaSet per version.

See the chain

bashDeployment to Pods
kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:1.26 --replicas=3
kubectl get deploy,rs,pods -l app=web
kubectl get rs -l app=web -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.ownerReferences[0].name}{"\n"}'
6.2

Deployments

In plain words

A Deployment manages ReplicaSets to move your app from one version to another in a controlled way.

The problem it solves

Updating an app by replacing all Pods at once causes downtime, and fixing a bad release by hand is slow.

What it does

  • Changing spec.template (image, env, resources) creates a new ReplicaSet and scales it up while the old one scales down.
  • Keeps revisionHistoryLimit (default 10) old ReplicaSets for rollback.
  • Changing only replicas does not create a new revision.
  • kubectl rollout status reports progress and progressDeadlineSeconds (default 600) marks it failed when stuck.

A production Deployment

yamldeployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
  labels:
    app: web
spec:
  replicas: 3
  revisionHistoryLimit: 5
  progressDeadlineSeconds: 300
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: nginx:1.27
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: {path: /, port: 80}
          resources:
            requests: {cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi}
            limits: {memory: 256Mi}
6.3

Rolling update tuning

In plain words

maxSurge is how many extra Pods may exist during a rollout. maxUnavailable is how many may be missing. Both accept a number or a percentage.

The problem it solves

Too aggressive a rollout drops capacity; too cautious a one is slow or blocked by quota.

What it does

  • Defaults are 25% for both. For 4 replicas that is 1 surge and 1 unavailable.
  • maxUnavailable: 0 with maxSurge: 1 never reduces capacity but needs room for one extra Pod.
  • A new Pod counts as available only after readiness passes (plus minReadySeconds). Without a readiness probe a bad version rolls out fully.
  • Recreate strategy stops all old Pods first; use it when two versions cannot coexist (for example a single-writer volume).

Roll, watch, undo

bashRollout commands
kubectl set image deployment/web web=nginx:1.27.1
kubectl rollout status deployment/web --timeout=120s
kubectl rollout history deployment/web
kubectl rollout undo deployment/web                 # back one revision
kubectl rollout undo deployment/web --to-revision=2
kubectl rollout restart deployment/web              # new Pods, same spec
kubectl rollout pause deployment/web                # batch several edits
Check yourself
Why might a rollout with a broken image never finish yet cause no outage?

New Pods fail readiness so they never count as available, and with maxUnavailable limits the old Pods stay. The rollout stalls at the progress deadline.

6.4

Blue green and canary releases

In plain words

Blue green runs two full versions and switches traffic at once. A canary sends a small share of traffic to the new version first.

The problem it solves

Rolling updates mix versions with no control over who sees the new one and give weak rollback signals.

What it does

  • Blue green: two Deployments, one Service. Change the Service selector (or route) to flip, flip back to roll back. Costs double capacity.
  • Canary with plain Kubernetes: two Deployments behind one Service; share is proportional to Pod counts, which is coarse.
  • Precise canary: weighted routes in Gateway API, Istio (used by Kyma) or Argo Rollouts and Flagger, with metric-based promotion.

Weighted routing with Gateway API

yamlcanary-route.yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: shared-gateway
  hostnames: ["shop.example.com"]
  rules:
    - backendRefs:
        - {name: web-stable, port: 80, weight: 90}
        - {name: web-canary, port: 80, weight: 10}
Release strategy
OptionRolling update
Choose whenstateless apps with compatible versions
Avoid whenbreaking schema or API changes
OptionBlue green
Choose wheninstant switch and instant rollback
Avoid whencapacity is tight
OptionCanary
Choose whenrisky changes you want to measure
Avoid whenyou have no metrics to judge success
6.5

Scaling, labels and Deployment pitfalls

In plain words

kubectl scale changes replicas. Most Deployment trouble comes from a few repeating mistakes.

The problem it solves

Small spec errors silently produce outages or stuck rollouts.

What it does

  • Selector is immutable; to change it you recreate the Deployment.
  • Do not set replicas in Git when an HPA manages them, otherwise every sync resets it.
  • Use immutable image tags or digests, never latest, so a rollout equals a spec change.
  • Set requests, a readiness probe and a PodDisruptionBudget on every production Deployment.
  • ConfigMap changes do not restart Pods; roll them with a hash annotation or tools like Reloader.

Quick checks

bashIs the Deployment healthy
kubectl get deploy web -o jsonpath='{.status}' | head -c 400
kubectl describe deploy web | grep -E 'Replicas|Strategy|Conditions' -A4
kubectl get deploy -A -o json | grep -c '"image": ".*:latest"'   # count of latest tags
6.6

Progress, availability and PodDisruptionBudgets

In plain words

A Deployment reports conditions Progressing and Available. A PodDisruptionBudget limits how many Pods voluntary actions such as drains may remove.

The problem it solves

During node upgrades, a drain could evict every replica of a service at the same moment.

What it does

  • Available is true when at least replicas - maxUnavailable Pods are ready.
  • A PDB (minAvailable or maxUnavailable) is honoured by the eviction API, so kubectl drain waits instead of breaking the service.
  • A PDB does not protect against node crashes or kubectl delete pod.
  • A PDB with minAvailable equal to replicas blocks drains forever; leave room for one Pod.

A PDB

yamlpdb.yaml
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  maxUnavailable: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
← PreviousNext →
Section 7 of 65

StatefulSets and DaemonSets

6 concepts · about 45 minutes

Stateless Pods are interchangeable. Databases, queues and per-node agents are not, and they need controllers built for that.

Goals
  • Explain stable identity, ordered rollout and per Pod storage in a StatefulSet
  • Write a headless Service and volumeClaimTemplates
  • Use DaemonSets for node agents and understand their update behaviour
7.1

Why StatefulSets exist

In plain words

A StatefulSet runs Pods with a stable name, a stable network identity and their own persistent disk, which survive rescheduling.

The problem it solves

A Deployment gives random names and shared templates. A database replica must know it is db-1, keep its own data and be reachable by a predictable DNS name.

What it does

  • Pods are named <set>-0, <set>-1 and so on.
  • Each Pod gets its own PVC from volumeClaimTemplates; the same PVC reattaches when the Pod is recreated.
  • Pods are created in order 0..N-1 and removed in reverse (the default OrderedReady policy). Parallel skips the ordering.
  • A headless Service (clusterIP: None) gives each Pod DNS db-0.db.shop.svc.

Headless Service and StatefulSet

yamlstatefulset.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: db
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  selector:
    app: db
  ports:
    - {name: pg, port: 5432}
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: db
spec:
  serviceName: db
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: db
  updateStrategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      partition: 0
  persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy:
    whenDeleted: Retain
    whenScaled: Retain
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: db
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: postgres
          image: postgres:16
          env:
            - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef: {name: db-secret, key: password}
          ports:
            - {name: pg, containerPort: 5432}
          volumeMounts:
            - {name: data, mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data}
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata:
        name: data
      spec:
        accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
        storageClassName: gp3
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 20Gi
7.2

StatefulSet updates and failure behaviour

In plain words

StatefulSets update Pods one at a time from the highest ordinal down, waiting for each to be Ready.

The problem it solves

Clustered databases need a quorum. Replacing all members at once, or running two Pods with the same identity, can corrupt data.

What it does

  • partition: N updates only ordinals at or above N, a built-in canary: lower it step by step.
  • OnDelete updates only when you delete Pods yourself.
  • If a node vanishes, the Pod stays Terminating or Unknown. Kubernetes will not start a duplicate until the old one is confirmed gone, preserving at-most-one semantics.
  • Scaling down keeps PVCs unless persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy says Delete. Disks cost money; clean up deliberately.

Staged update

bashCanary a StatefulSet
kubectl patch sts db -p '{"spec":{"updateStrategy":{"rollingUpdate":{"partition":2}}}}'
kubectl set image sts/db postgres=postgres:16.4         # only db-2 updates
kubectl rollout status sts/db
kubectl patch sts db -p '{"spec":{"updateStrategy":{"rollingUpdate":{"partition":0}}}}'
kubectl get pvc -l app=db
Tip

For production databases prefer an operator (CloudNativePG, Percona, Zalando) over a hand-written StatefulSet. It encodes failover, backups and upgrades that the StatefulSet does not know about.

Check yourself
What does `partition: 2` on a 3-replica StatefulSet do?

Only db-2 receives the new template; db-0 and db-1 stay on the old revision.

7.3

DaemonSets

In plain words

A DaemonSet runs one Pod on every node, or on every node that matches a selector.

The problem it solves

Node-level agents, such as log collectors, metrics exporters, CNI and CSI node plug-ins, must be on each machine, including ones added later by autoscaling.

What it does

  • New nodes get the Pod automatically; removed nodes drop it.
  • Use nodeSelector or affinity to target a subset (for example GPU nodes).
  • Add tolerations so it runs on tainted nodes, as agents usually should.
  • RollingUpdate replaces Pods node by node with maxUnavailable (default 1); OnDelete is manual.
  • Set a priorityClassName such as system-node-critical for essential agents and keep requests small.

A log agent

yamldaemonset.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: log-agent
  namespace: logging
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: log-agent
  updateStrategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 10%
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: log-agent
    spec:
      priorityClassName: system-node-critical
      tolerations:
        - operator: Exists
      containers:
        - name: agent
          image: fluent/fluent-bit:3.1
          resources:
            requests: {cpu: 50m, memory: 64Mi}
            limits: {memory: 128Mi}
          volumeMounts:
            - {name: varlog, mountPath: /var/log, readOnly: true}
      volumes:
        - name: varlog
          hostPath:
            path: /var/log
7.4

Choosing the right workload controller

In plain words

Each controller models a different promise about identity, ordering and completion.

The problem it solves

Using a Deployment for a database, or a StatefulSet for a stateless API, brings unnecessary risk or complexity.

What it does

  • Deployment: interchangeable replicas, fast rollouts.
  • StatefulSet: stable identity and per-Pod storage.
  • DaemonSet: one per node.
  • Job and CronJob: run to completion.
  • ReplicaSet and bare Pods: only for experiments or custom controllers.
Workload controller
OptionDeployment
Choose whenweb apps, APIs, workers
Avoid whenyou need a stable hostname or own disk
OptionStatefulSet
Choose whendatabases, brokers, quorum systems
Avoid whenthe app is stateless
OptionDaemonSet
Choose whenlog, metric, network, storage agents
Avoid whenyou want N replicas anywhere
OptionJob
Choose whenbatch, migrations
Avoid whenit must run forever
7.5

Operating StatefulSets safely

In plain words

Most StatefulSet incidents are storage related: a Pod bound to a disk in one zone, or a volume that cannot attach.

The problem it solves

An EBS volume lives in one availability zone. If the Pod is rescheduled to another zone it stays Pending.

What it does

  • Use a StorageClass with volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer so the disk is created in the zone where the Pod lands.
  • Spread replicas over zones with topology spread so one zone failure leaves quorum.
  • Expand volumes by editing the PVC (if the class allows expansion); the StatefulSet template itself cannot be changed, delete it with --cascade=orphan and recreate it to change volumeClaimTemplates.
  • Always add a PDB so drains cannot take quorum below the safe number.

Diagnose a stuck Pod

bashPending StatefulSet Pod
kubectl describe pod db-0 | sed -n '/Events/,$p'
kubectl get pvc data-db-0 -o wide
kubectl get pv $(kubectl get pvc data-db-0 -o jsonpath='{.spec.volumeName}') -o jsonpath='{.spec.nodeAffinity}'
kubectl get volumeattachments
7.6

Headless Services and Pod DNS

In plain words

A headless Service has no virtual IP. Its DNS name returns the individual Pod IPs, and each StatefulSet Pod gets its own record.

The problem it solves

Cluster members and clients sometimes need to reach a specific replica (the primary, or peer number two), not a random one behind a load balancer.

What it does

  • db.shop.svc.cluster.local returns all ready Pod IPs as A records.
  • db-0.db.shop.svc.cluster.local returns only that Pod, valid as long as the StatefulSet's serviceName is db.
  • publishNotReadyAddresses: true lets peers find each other before they are Ready, which clustered databases need to bootstrap.
  • Pod IPs change on reschedule; the DNS name stays stable.

Test the records

bashResolve from inside the cluster
kubectl run dns --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- nslookup db-0.db.shop.svc.cluster.local
kubectl run dns --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- nslookup db.shop.svc.cluster.local
← PreviousNext →
Section 8 of 65

Jobs and CronJobs

5 concepts · about 35 minutes

Not everything runs forever. Migrations, reports, backups and batch pipelines are finite work that Kubernetes can retry and clean up.

Goals
  • Run finite work with retries, parallelism and cleanup
  • Write a CronJob with safe concurrency and deadlines
  • Debug Jobs that never finish or run twice
8.1

Jobs

In plain words

A Job creates Pods and keeps retrying until a set number of them finish successfully.

The problem it solves

A bare Pod that fails once stays failed, and a Deployment would restart a finished task forever.

What it does

  • restartPolicy must be OnFailure or Never.
  • completions is how many successes are needed, parallelism how many Pods run at once.
  • backoffLimit (default 6) caps retries with exponential delay; activeDeadlineSeconds caps total runtime.
  • ttlSecondsAfterFinished deletes the finished Job and its Pods, otherwise they stay for log inspection.

A migration Job

yamljob.yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: db-migrate
spec:
  backoffLimit: 3
  activeDeadlineSeconds: 600
  ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 3600
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: migrate
          image: ghcr.io/example/api:1.4.2
          command: ["./migrate", "--up"]
8.2

Parallel and indexed Jobs

In plain words

Jobs can split work across many Pods, either with a shared queue or with each Pod getting a fixed index.

The problem it solves

Processing a thousand files in one Pod is slow. Starting a thousand separate Jobs is untidy.

What it does

  • Indexed completion mode gives each Pod JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX (0 to completions-1) so it picks its slice.
  • completions: 10 with parallelism: 3 runs three at a time until ten succeed.
  • Work queue pattern: leave completions unset; Pods pull from a queue and the Job ends when one succeeds and all have exited.
  • podFailurePolicy can fail the Job at once on a given exit code or ignore disruptions such as preemption.

Indexed Job

yamlindexed-job.yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: shard-process
spec:
  completionMode: Indexed
  completions: 10
  parallelism: 3
  backoffLimitPerIndex: 1
  maxFailedIndexes: 2
  podFailurePolicy:
    rules:
      - action: FailJob
        onExitCodes:
          operator: In
          values: [42]
      - action: Ignore
        onPodConditions:
          - type: DisruptionTarget
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: worker
          image: busybox:1.36
          command: ["sh", "-c", "echo processing shard $JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX"]
Check yourself
How does a Pod know which slice to process?

In Indexed mode it reads the `JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX` environment variable.

8.3

CronJobs

In plain words

A CronJob creates a Job on a schedule written in cron syntax.

The problem it solves

Recurring tasks like backups or cleanups need a scheduler that is part of the cluster and not tied to one server.

What it does

  • schedule uses five-field cron, in the controller manager's time zone unless timeZone is set (stable since 1.27).
  • concurrencyPolicy: Allow (default), Forbid skips if the last run is still going, Replace stops the old one.
  • startingDeadlineSeconds lets a missed run start late; without it, a missed run is skipped.
  • successfulJobsHistoryLimit and failedJobsHistoryLimit keep a few Jobs for debugging.

Nightly backup

yamlcronjob.yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: nightly-backup
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"
  timeZone: Etc/UTC
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
  startingDeadlineSeconds: 900
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  failedJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      backoffLimit: 2
      activeDeadlineSeconds: 3600
      ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 86400
      template:
        spec:
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
          containers:
            - name: backup
              image: ghcr.io/example/backup:2.1
              args: ["--target", "s3://backups/shop"]
8.4

Operating Jobs

In plain words

Jobs are easy to write and hard to observe. Know the commands that show why they stall.

The problem it solves

A CronJob that silently stopped producing Jobs is only noticed when the backup is needed.

What it does

  • Jobs are at-least-once. Your task must be idempotent because a Pod can run twice.
  • Suspend a CronJob with spec.suspend: true during maintenance.
  • Trigger a one-off run with kubectl create job --from=cronjob/NAME.
  • A CronJob that missed more than 100 schedules stops and logs an error, which needs a fix and a manual run.
  • Alert on kube_job_failed and on time since the last success (kube-state-metrics).

Commands

bashRun and inspect
kubectl create job manual-backup --from=cronjob/nightly-backup
kubectl get jobs,pods -l job-name=manual-backup
kubectl logs job/manual-backup
kubectl patch cronjob nightly-backup -p '{"spec":{"suspend":true}}'
kubectl wait --for=condition=complete job/manual-backup --timeout=300s
Careful

Forbid concurrency with a Job that hangs blocks all future runs. Always set activeDeadlineSeconds.

Check yourself
Why must Job code be idempotent?

Kubernetes guarantees at least once, not exactly once; retries or overlapping runs can repeat work.

8.5

Batch at scale with queues

In plain words

For large batch loads, Kubernetes Jobs combine with queueing and quotas so one team cannot starve the rest.

The problem it solves

Thousands of Jobs submitted together overwhelm the scheduler and autoscaler and block other workloads.

What it does

  • Kueue admits Jobs against quotas and queues them until capacity exists.
  • Set suspend: true on Jobs so a queue controller starts them when ready.
  • Use PriorityClasses so batch work yields to services via preemption.
  • Run batch on a spot or preemptible node pool with a toleration so costs stay low.
  • Prefer Argo Workflows, Tekton or Airflow when you need dependency graphs between steps.

Suspended Job for a queue

yamlqueued-job.yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: nightly-report
  labels:
    kueue.x-k8s.io/queue-name: team-a
spec:
  suspend: true
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      tolerations:
        - {key: workload, operator: Equal, value: batch, effect: NoSchedule}
      containers:
        - name: report
          image: busybox:1.36
          command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 5"]
          resources:
            requests: {cpu: "1", memory: 512Mi}

Section 9 of 65

Services and kube-proxy

6 concepts · about 50 minutes

Pod IPs are temporary. A Service gives a set of Pods one stable address and load balances across the healthy ones.

Goals
  • Choose the right Service type and write its manifest
  • Explain how kube-proxy implements ClusterIPs in iptables, IPVS and nftables modes
  • Read EndpointSlices to debug a Service with no traffic
9.1

The Kubernetes network model

In plain words

Every Pod gets its own IP. Any Pod can reach any other Pod directly without NAT, and nodes can reach all Pods.

The problem it solves

Without a simple flat model, applications would need port mapping and address translation logic.

What it does

  • The CNI plug-in implements Pod to Pod routing (overlay, routed or cloud-native VPC addresses).
  • Services add a stable virtual IP on top; NetworkPolicy restricts the flat network.
  • Four traffic types: container to container (localhost), Pod to Pod, Pod to Service, external to Service.
  • On EKS with the VPC CNI each Pod IP is a VPC address, so IP exhaustion in subnets is a real limit.

See addresses

bashPod and node IPs
kubectl get pods -A -o wide | head
kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{" "}{.spec.podCIDR}{"\n"}{end}'
kubectl cluster-info dump | grep -m2 -E 'service-cluster-ip-range|cluster-cidr'
9.2

Service types

In plain words

A Service picks Pods with a label selector and exposes them in one of four ways: ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer or ExternalName.

The problem it solves

Clients need one durable address, whether inside the cluster, on node ports or on the internet.

What it does

  • ClusterIP (default): virtual IP reachable only inside the cluster.
  • NodePort: also opens a port (30000 to 32767) on every node.
  • LoadBalancer: also asks the cloud to create an external load balancer.
  • ExternalName: a DNS CNAME to an outside name, no proxying.
  • Headless (clusterIP: None): no virtual IP; DNS returns Pod IPs.

ClusterIP and LoadBalancer

yamlservices.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web-public
  annotations:
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-type: external
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-nlb-target-type: ip
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  loadBalancerClass: service.k8s.aws/nlb
  externalTrafficPolicy: Local
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
    - {name: https, port: 443, targetPort: 8080}
Note

The annotations above are for the AWS Load Balancer Controller. Other clouds and Kyma use different annotations, so check the provider documentation.

Check yourself
Which port is `port` and which is `targetPort`?

`port` is what clients call on the Service; `targetPort` is the container port receiving traffic.

9.3

How kube-proxy implements a Service

In plain words

kube-proxy runs on each node and programs the kernel so that traffic to a Service IP is redirected to one of its Pod IPs. It does not carry traffic itself in the common modes.

The problem it solves

A virtual IP exists on no interface. Something must translate it to a real Pod on every node, and keep up as Pods come and go.

What it does

  • Watches Services and EndpointSlices and rewrites kernel rules (DNAT) on change.
  • iptables mode (default for a long time): chains of rules with random probability; lookup cost grows linearly with Services.
  • IPVS mode: kernel load balancer with hash tables and algorithms like round robin and least connection; scales better.
  • nftables mode: newer, faster rule updates; GA in Kubernetes 1.33.
  • Some CNIs (Cilium) replace kube-proxy with eBPF.

Inspect the rules

bashOn a node
kubectl -n kube-system get cm kube-proxy -o jsonpath='{.data.config\.conf}' | grep mode
iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES -n | head
ipvsadm -Ln | head            # when mode is ipvs
nft list table ip kube-proxy | head   # when mode is nftables
conntrack -L | head
Check yourself
Why do conntrack table limits matter?

NAT'd connections are tracked per flow; a full table drops new connections, often seen as random timeouts under load.

9.4

EndpointSlices

In plain words

An EndpointSlice lists the IPs, ports and readiness of Pods behind a Service. The old single Endpoints object is replaced by sharded slices.

The problem it solves

One Endpoints object for a Service with thousands of Pods had to be rewritten and shipped to every node on each change.

What it does

  • Each slice holds up to 100 endpoints by default, so a change only updates one small object.
  • Each endpoint has conditions ready, serving and terminating, plus topology hints (zone, node).
  • The EndpointSlice controller creates them from the Service selector; kube-proxy and service meshes consume them.
  • A Service with no slices or no ready endpoints is the first thing to check when traffic fails.

Debug a Service

bashService has no traffic
kubectl get svc web -o wide
kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web
kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web -o jsonpath='{range .items[*].endpoints[*]}{.addresses}{" ready="}{.conditions.ready}{"\n"}{end}'
kubectl get pods -l app=web --show-labels      # do the labels match the selector
Tip

Empty endpoints almost always mean the selector does not match the Pod labels, or readiness is failing. Check these before suspecting the network.

9.5

Traffic policies and session behaviour

In plain words

Traffic policies control which endpoints a Service may use: any, only local to the node, or preferring the same zone.

The problem it solves

Cross-zone traffic costs money and adds latency, and node-to-node hops hide the real client IP.

What it does

  • externalTrafficPolicy: Local sends external traffic only to Pods on the receiving node, preserves the client source IP and avoids a hop. Nodes without Pods fail the load balancer health check.
  • internalTrafficPolicy: Local does the same for in-cluster callers.
  • trafficDistribution: PreferClose (beta in 1.31, GA in 1.33) prefers endpoints in the caller's zone; falls back if none are healthy.
  • sessionAffinity: ClientIP pins a client to one Pod for a time; it is crude, prefer app level sessions.

Zone aware routing

yamlzone-aware-service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  selector:
    app: api
  trafficDistribution: PreferClose
  ports:
    - {port: 80, targetPort: 8080}
9.6

Debugging Service connectivity

In plain words

A methodical order finds a broken Service quickly: Pod, selector, endpoints, port, DNS, policy.

The problem it solves

"Connection refused" and timeouts mean different things, and guessing wastes hours.

What it does

  • Connection refused: reached something, nothing listening on that port (wrong targetPort).
  • Timeout: packets dropped, usually NetworkPolicy, security group, or no endpoints.
  • Could not resolve host: DNS or wrong namespace in the name.
  • Test from a throw-away Pod in the same namespace and compare Pod IP, Service IP and DNS name.

Layered test

bashCurl each layer
kubectl run net --rm -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot --restart=Never -- bash
# inside the shell
curl -sv http://10.0.2.9:8080/healthz      # Pod IP
curl -sv http://web.shop.svc/healthz       # service DNS
nslookup web.shop.svc

Section 10 of 65

DNS and service discovery

6 concepts · about 35 minutes

Almost every connection in a cluster begins with a DNS lookup. DNS problems look like random application failures, so know how it works.

Goals
  • Explain Service and Pod DNS names and the search path
  • Understand ndots and why it multiplies lookups
  • Tune CoreDNS and NodeLocal DNSCache
10.1

Cluster DNS names

In plain words

CoreDNS answers names for Services and Pods inside the cluster domain, cluster.local by default.

The problem it solves

Hard coding IPs breaks as soon as a Pod restarts. Names give stable discovery.

What it does

  • Service: <svc>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local returns the ClusterIP (or the Pod IPs for headless).
  • Pod: <ip-with-dashes>.<namespace>.pod.cluster.local.
  • StatefulSet Pod: <pod>.<svc>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local.
  • SRV records exist for named ports: _http._tcp.web.shop.svc.cluster.local.
  • Within the same namespace the short name web works; across namespaces use web.shop.

What the Pod sees

bashPod resolver config
kubectl exec deploy/web -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
kubectl run dns --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- nslookup kubernetes.default
kubectl get svc -n kube-system kube-dns
10.2

ndots and the search path

In plain words

options ndots:5 means any name with fewer than five dots is first tried with each search domain appended, before being tried as is.

The problem it solves

This makes short names convenient but turns a lookup of api.example.com into several wasted queries that all fail with NXDOMAIN first.

What it does

  • Default search list: <ns>.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local plus any node domain.
  • Looking up api.example.com (2 dots) tries three or more cluster suffixes before the real name; with A and AAAA that is many queries.
  • Fixes: use a trailing dot (api.example.com.), set a lower ndots in dnsConfig, or use NodeLocal DNSCache.
  • Also lower dependence on external names that fail slowly.

Set ndots for a Pod

yamldnsconfig.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: client
spec:
  dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
  dnsConfig:
    options:
      - name: ndots
        value: "2"
      - name: single-request-reopen
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: ["sleep", "3600"]
Check yourself
Why is `api.example.com.` with a trailing dot faster?

It is a fully qualified name, so the resolver skips the search list.

10.3

CoreDNS configuration

In plain words

CoreDNS is a plug-in based DNS server configured by a Corefile in a ConfigMap. Each plug-in does one job: cluster zone, cache, forward, health.

The problem it solves

You may need to forward a corporate domain to an internal resolver, or rewrite names.

What it does

  • The kubernetes plug-in serves the cluster zone from the API.
  • forward . /etc/resolv.conf sends everything else to the node's resolvers.
  • cache 30 caches answers; errors, log, prometheus :9153 help observability.
  • Add stub zones for private domains, then restart CoreDNS.
  • On Kyma and EKS CoreDNS is managed; customisations may use a supported coredns-custom ConfigMap or add-on config. Check the platform docs.

Add a stub zone

yamlcoredns-stub.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: coredns-custom
  namespace: kube-system
data:
  corp.server: |
    corp.example.com:53 {
        errors
        cache 30
        forward . 10.20.0.2 10.20.0.3
    }
Note

The coredns-custom name and the import mechanism depend on the platform (AKS and Gardener use it; vanilla CoreDNS needs an import line in the Corefile). Verify yours before applying.

10.4

DNS scale and NodeLocal DNSCache

In plain words

Heavy lookup traffic can overload CoreDNS and conntrack. NodeLocal DNSCache runs a caching agent on every node.

The problem it solves

UDP DNS through NAT hits conntrack races that cause five second timeouts, and a few CoreDNS Pods become a bottleneck.

What it does

  • Pods query a link-local address on their own node; cache hits return immediately, misses go upstream over TCP.
  • Run enough CoreDNS replicas, spread across zones, and consider cluster-proportional-autoscaler to scale them with node count.
  • Watch coredns_dns_request_duration_seconds and coredns_dns_responses_total{rcode="SERVFAIL"}.

Check health

bashCoreDNS status
kubectl -n kube-system get deploy coredns
kubectl -n kube-system logs deploy/coredns --tail=20
kubectl -n kube-system top pods -l k8s-app=kube-dns
kubectl -n kube-system get ds node-local-dns
10.5

Debugging DNS

In plain words

DNS failures show as timeouts, NXDOMAIN or slow requests. Separate the layers: Pod resolver, CoreDNS, upstream.

The problem it solves

Applications report "unknown host" without saying whether the name, the server or the network is wrong.

What it does

  • Run nslookup and dig from a debug Pod, in the same namespace and with the same dnsPolicy.
  • NXDOMAIN: wrong name or namespace. SERVFAIL: upstream problem. Timeout: NetworkPolicy blocking UDP/TCP 53 egress to CoreDNS, or CoreDNS down.
  • A default-deny egress policy must explicitly allow DNS.
  • Alpine (musl) images resolve slightly differently from glibc; test in the real image when it matters.

Commands

bashTest from a debug Pod
kubectl run dig --rm -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot --restart=Never -- bash
# inside
dig web.shop.svc.cluster.local +short
dig @10.96.0.10 example.com +time=2 +tries=1
dig +search web.shop
10.6

ExternalDNS and public names

In plain words

ExternalDNS watches Services, Ingresses and Gateway routes and creates matching records in Route 53, Cloud DNS or similar.

The problem it solves

Hand-editing public DNS for every new hostname is slow and drifts from what the cluster serves.

What it does

  • Reads the external-dns.alpha.kubernetes.io/hostname annotation or the host in an Ingress or HTTPRoute.
  • Creates A, AAAA or CNAME records pointing at the load balancer, and owns them with TXT markers.
  • --policy=upsert-only prevents deletions; --txt-owner-id separates clusters sharing a zone.
  • On Kyma the API Gateway module and Gardener DNS management serve a similar purpose for default domains.

Annotation example

yamlsvc-dns.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web-public
  annotations:
    external-dns.alpha.kubernetes.io/hostname: shop.example.com
    external-dns.alpha.kubernetes.io/ttl: "300"
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
    - {port: 443, targetPort: 8080}
