Section 11 of 65

Ingress and Gateway API

7 concepts · about 50 minutes

Services expose ports. Real applications need hostnames, paths, TLS and routing rules. Ingress and Gateway API describe those, and a controller makes them real.

Goals
  • Route external HTTP traffic with Ingress and understand what a controller does
  • Model roles and routes with the Gateway API
  • Choose between Ingress and Gateway API and terminate TLS with cert-manager
11.1

Why L7 routing

In plain words

A LoadBalancer Service gives one external IP per Service at layer 4. Layer 7 routing shares one entry point among many apps by reading the HTTP host and path.

The problem it solves

One cloud load balancer per Service is costly and gives no host or path routing, TLS handling or redirects.

What it does

  • One load balancer or proxy receives all traffic and forwards by Host header and URL path.
  • TLS can be terminated once at the edge.
  • The routing rules are Kubernetes objects, so they are version controlled and reviewed.
  • The object alone does nothing; a controller (NGINX, Envoy, Istio, an ALB controller) must be installed.

See what is installed

bashClasses in the cluster
kubectl get ingressclass
kubectl get gatewayclass
kubectl get ingress,gateway,httproute -A
11.2

Ingress

In plain words

An Ingress is a single object with host and path rules pointing to Services, handled by the controller named in ingressClassName.

The problem it solves

You need basic web routing that works on any cluster with minimal configuration.

What it does

  • Rules: host, path, pathType (Prefix, Exact, ImplementationSpecific) and backend Service and port.
  • tls section references a Secret holding the certificate.
  • Everything beyond that (rewrites, timeouts, auth, rate limits) is controller-specific annotations, which makes manifests non-portable.
  • The NGINX community Ingress controller was retired by its maintainers (best-effort maintenance ended in March 2026), so plan migration to a maintained controller or Gateway API.

An Ingress with TLS

yamlingress.yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: shop
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
    - hosts: [shop.example.com]
      secretName: shop-tls
  rules:
    - host: shop.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /api
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service: {name: api, port: {number: 80}}
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service: {name: web, port: {number: 80}}
Check yourself
Why can the same Ingress YAML behave differently on two clusters?

Annotations and defaults belong to the controller, and each controller interprets them differently.

11.3

Ingress controllers

In plain words

The controller watches Ingress objects and configures a proxy. Some run a proxy inside the cluster; some program a cloud load balancer.

The problem it solves

Choosing wrongly gives the wrong features, cost or failure modes.

What it does

  • In-cluster proxy (NGINX, Traefik, HAProxy, Envoy based): one LoadBalancer Service in front, flexible, you operate it.
  • Cloud native (AWS Load Balancer Controller): creates an ALB per Ingress (or per group), traffic goes straight to Pod IPs with target-type: ip.
  • Mesh gateways (Istio, used by Kyma): Envoy with richer policies.
  • Use ingress.group.name on AWS to share one ALB among Ingresses and save cost.

ALB Ingress on EKS

yamlalb-ingress.yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: shop-alb
  annotations:
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/scheme: internet-facing
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-type: ip
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/group.name: shared
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/listen-ports: '[{"HTTPS":443}]'
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/certificate-arn: arn:aws:acm:eu-west-1:111122223333:certificate/example
spec:
  ingressClassName: alb
  rules:
    - host: shop.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service: {name: web, port: {number: 80}}
11.4

Gateway API model

In plain words

Gateway API splits routing into role-based objects: GatewayClass (the implementation), Gateway (listeners, owned by the platform team) and routes (owned by app teams).

The problem it solves

Ingress mixes infrastructure, security and app routing in one object and leans on annotations. Platform and app teams need separate ownership and a portable standard.

What it does

  • GatewayClass names a controller, like StorageClass does for storage.
  • Gateway defines listeners (port, protocol, hostname, TLS) and which namespaces may attach (allowedRoutes).
  • HTTPRoute, GRPCRoute, TLSRoute, TCPRoute attach to a Gateway through parentRefs.
  • Native features: header matching, redirects, rewrites, traffic weights, mirroring. Cross-namespace references need a ReferenceGrant.
  • The core API (gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1) is GA; some route kinds remain in the experimental channel.

Gateway and route

yamlgateway.yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: shared-gateway
  namespace: infra
spec:
  gatewayClassName: istio
  listeners:
    - name: https
      port: 443
      protocol: HTTPS
      hostname: "*.example.com"
      tls:
        mode: Terminate
        certificateRefs:
          - name: wildcard-example-com
      allowedRoutes:
        namespaces:
          from: Selector
          selector:
            matchLabels:
              gateway-access: "true"
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: shop
  namespace: shop
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: shared-gateway
      namespace: infra
  hostnames: ["shop.example.com"]
  rules:
    - matches:
        - path: {type: PathPrefix, value: /api}
          headers:
            - {name: x-tenant, value: acme}
      backendRefs:
        - {name: api, port: 80}
    - filters:
        - type: RequestRedirect
          requestRedirect: {scheme: https, statusCode: 301}
      matches:
        - path: {type: PathPrefix, value: /old}
Check yourself
Which object lets a team in namespace shop use a Gateway in namespace infra?

The Gateway's `allowedRoutes` must permit that namespace; the HTTPRoute then names the Gateway in `parentRefs`.

11.5

Ingress versus Gateway API

In plain words

Ingress is frozen: still supported, but no new features. Gateway API is the successor and where new routing capabilities land.

The problem it solves

Teams ask which to use for new work and how to migrate.

What it does

  • Prefer Gateway API for new clusters when your controller supports it (Istio, Envoy Gateway, Cilium, NGINX Gateway Fabric, GKE and AWS Gateway controllers).
  • Keep Ingress where it works and migration offers no gain.
  • The ingress2gateway tool converts many Ingress objects into Gateway resources.
  • Check controller conformance reports rather than assuming a feature exists.
Which API
OptionIngress
Choose whensimple HTTP routing on an existing controller
Avoid whenyou need weights, header routing or shared Gateways
OptionGateway API
Choose whenmulti-team platforms, canaries, non-HTTP routes
Avoid whenyour controller lacks conformance for the features you need

Migration helper

bashConvert Ingress to Gateway objects
ingress2gateway print --providers ingress-nginx --all-namespaces > gateway-objects.yaml
kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f gateway-objects.yaml
11.6

TLS and cert-manager

In plain words

cert-manager requests certificates from an issuer (Let's Encrypt, a private CA, Vault, AWS PCA) and keeps them renewed as Kubernetes Secrets.

The problem it solves

Manual certificate handling expires at the worst moment.

What it does

  • Issuer and ClusterIssuer describe the CA; Certificate asks for a certificate and names the Secret to store it.
  • ACME HTTP-01 proves control through a temporary route; DNS-01 uses a DNS record and supports wildcards.
  • Ingress annotation or Gateway listener annotation lets cert-manager create the Certificate automatically.
  • It renews by default at two thirds of the lifetime. Monitor certmanager_certificate_expiration_timestamp_seconds.

Issuer and Certificate

yamlcert-manager.yaml
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: letsencrypt
spec:
  acme:
    server: https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
    email: platform@example.com
    privateKeySecretRef:
      name: letsencrypt-account-key
    solvers:
      - dns01:
          route53:
            region: eu-west-1
---
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata:
  name: shop
  namespace: shop
spec:
  secretName: shop-tls
  dnsNames: ["shop.example.com"]
  issuerRef:
    name: letsencrypt
    kind: ClusterIssuer
11.7

Kyma APIRule and Istio gateways

In plain words

Kyma exposes workloads with its own APIRule custom resource, which creates Istio VirtualService and optional authentication rules behind the Kyma gateway.

The problem it solves

On Kyma you rarely install an ingress controller, so you need to know the platform's native way to publish a service.

What it does

  • The Kyma API Gateway module manages an Istio ingress gateway and a default domain.
  • An APIRule selects a Service, host and rules (access strategies such as JWT, or no_auth for public paths).
  • You can alternatively write Istio Gateway and VirtualService, or Gateway API where the module supports it. Check your Kyma release notes, since the APIRule API version has changed (v1beta1 to v2).
  • Identity usually comes from SAP IAS or XSUAA via JWT validation or an OAuth2 proxy.

Inspect Kyma exposure

bashKyma gateways
kubectl get apirules -A
kubectl get gateways.networking.istio.io -A
kubectl get virtualservices -A
kubectl get kyma default -n kyma-system -o jsonpath='{.status.modules}'
Note

APIRule field names differ between versions. Run kubectl explain apirule.spec --api-version=gateway.kyma-project.io/v2 on your cluster to see the live schema.

Section 12 of 65

CNI choices, load balancers and egress

5 concepts · about 40 minutes

Below Services and Ingress sits the real network. IP planning, load balancer behaviour and egress paths decide whether the cluster scales and stays reachable.

Goals
  • Compare overlay, routed and VPC native Pod networking
  • Place cloud load balancers correctly with target types and health checks
  • Control and troubleshoot egress traffic
12.1

Pod networking models

In plain words

CNI plug-ins connect Pods in one of three ways: an overlay tunnel, plain routing, or addresses taken directly from the cloud network.

The problem it solves

The choice affects IP consumption, performance, observability and how firewalls see Pod traffic.

What it does

  • Overlay (VXLAN, Geneve; Flannel, Calico, Cilium): Pod IPs are private to the cluster; needs encapsulation and sets a smaller MTU.
  • Routed (Calico BGP): no encapsulation, routes advertised to the network.
  • VPC native (AWS VPC CNI, Azure CNI): Pods get real VPC IPs; firewalls and security groups see Pods, but subnets can run out of addresses.
  • Prefix delegation on the AWS VPC CNI assigns /28 blocks per ENI to raise Pod density.

Check IP headroom

bashEKS Pod IP usage
kubectl -n kube-system get ds aws-node -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].env}' | head -c 600
kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,PODS:.status.allocatable.pods
aws ec2 describe-subnets --subnet-ids subnet-0abc --query 'Subnets[].AvailableIpAddressCount'
12.2

Cloud load balancers

In plain words

A type: LoadBalancer Service or an Ingress makes a controller create a cloud load balancer. How it reaches Pods depends on the target type.

The problem it solves

Traffic can take extra hops, lose the client IP or fail health checks if the load balancer and Service settings disagree.

What it does

  • Instance targets send to NodePorts, then kube-proxy forwards to a Pod. An extra hop, and externalTrafficPolicy: Local affects health.
  • IP targets (VPC CNI) send straight to Pod IPs, skipping kube-proxy. Readiness gates keep Pods out of rotation until registered.
  • NLB (layer 4) keeps source IP and is fast; ALB (layer 7) adds host routing, WAF and OIDC authentication.
  • Pod readiness gates (elbv2.k8s.aws/pod-readiness-gate-inject) avoid dropped traffic during rollouts.

Namespace readiness gate

yamlreadiness-gate-namespace.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: shop
  labels:
    elbv2.k8s.aws/pod-readiness-gate-inject: enabled
Check yourself
Why use IP targets rather than instance targets with the VPC CNI?

Traffic reaches Pods directly: one less hop, true source IP kept, and no dependence on NodePort and kube-proxy.

12.3

Egress and NAT

In plain words

Egress is traffic leaving the cluster. By default Pods reach the internet through the node's route, usually a NAT gateway, so all Pods share a few source IPs.

The problem it solves

Partners may whitelist your IP, and unexpected outbound connections are a data exfiltration risk.

What it does

  • On clouds the node subnet's NAT gateway sets the visible source IP; one NAT per zone avoids cross-zone cost.
  • Private endpoints (VPC endpoints for S3, ECR) keep traffic off NAT and reduce cost.
  • NetworkPolicy egress rules and DNS-aware policies (Cilium FQDN policy) restrict destinations.
  • Istio egress gateway funnels outbound mesh traffic through a fixed point; Kyma can use it for stable egress identity.

Find your egress IP

bashWhat IP do outside systems see
kubectl run egress --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- curl -s https://checkip.amazonaws.com
12.4

MTU, hairpin and common network faults

In plain words

Some failures only appear with large packets, specific paths or when a Pod calls its own Service.

The problem it solves

"Works for small requests, hangs for big ones" wastes days if you do not suspect MTU.

What it does

  • Overlay adds headers, so inner MTU must be lower than the node MTU (for example 1450 on a 1500 network). A mismatch breaks large TLS handshakes silently.
  • Hairpin: a Pod calling its own Service IP needs the CNI to loop back; most do it correctly.
  • Conntrack exhaustion shows nf_conntrack: table full in node logs.
  • Cross-node failures with healthy same-node traffic point to security groups, firewall, or blocked overlay ports (UDP 4789, 8472, 6081).

Probe MTU and path

bashFrom a debug Pod
kubectl run net --rm -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot --restart=Never -- bash
# inside
ping -M do -s 1400 10.0.2.9      # do not fragment; lower the size until it passes
ip link show eth0 | grep mtu
tracepath 10.0.2.9
12.5

Service mesh and network observability preview

In plain words

A mesh adds a proxy to each Pod (or node) to supply mTLS, retries and metrics without app changes. eBPF tools show flows without a mesh.

The problem it solves

You cannot see or secure service-to-service traffic from the Service object alone.

What it does

  • Istio and Linkerd use sidecars or ambient mode (Istio) with per-node ztunnel for L4 mTLS and optional waypoint proxies for L7.
  • Kyma ships an Istio module, so sidecar injection is a namespace label (istio-injection=enabled).
  • Cilium Hubble and Retina show flow level visibility based on eBPF.
  • A mesh costs CPU, memory and operational complexity; adopt it for a clear need such as mTLS everywhere.

Enable sidecars in a namespace

bashLabel a namespace for Istio injection
kubectl label namespace shop istio-injection=enabled
kubectl rollout restart deployment -n shop        # Pods must be recreated
kubectl get pods -n shop -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{" "}{.spec.containers[*].name}{"\n"}{end}'
← PreviousNext →
Section 13 of 65

ConfigMaps and Secrets

6 concepts · about 45 minutes

Configuration should live outside the image. Kubernetes gives two objects for it and several patterns for delivering it to a container.

Goals
  • Inject configuration as environment variables and files and know the update behaviour of each
  • Explain what a Secret protects and what it does not
  • Bring secrets in from AWS and Vault with External Secrets or CSI
13.1

ConfigMaps

In plain words

A ConfigMap stores non-secret configuration as key-value pairs or whole files.

The problem it solves

Baking config into images forces a rebuild per environment and mixes code with settings.

What it does

  • Keys hold short values or full file contents. Size limit about 1 MiB.
  • Consume as environment variables, command arguments, or files in a volume.
  • immutable: true forbids edits, protects against accidental change and reduces API server load.
  • Namespaced; a Pod can only use ConfigMaps from its own namespace.

ConfigMap and its use

yamlconfigmap.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: web-config
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: info
  FEATURE_X: "true"
  app.properties: |
    cache.ttl=60
    pool.size=10
immutable: false
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: nginx:1.27
      envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: web-config
      volumeMounts:
        - name: cfg
          mountPath: /etc/app
          readOnly: true
  volumes:
    - name: cfg
      configMap:
        name: web-config
        items:
          - {key: app.properties, path: app.properties}
13.2

How config updates reach a Pod

In plain words

Environment variables are fixed at container start. Files from a ConfigMap volume are refreshed by the kubelet, but only when you do not use subPath.

The problem it solves

Changing a ConfigMap and seeing nothing happen is a classic surprise.

What it does

  • Env vars: change requires a Pod restart.
  • Volume mounts: updated eventually (kubelet sync period plus cache, typically up to a minute or so). The app must reread the file.
  • subPath mounts never update.
  • To force a rollout on change, put a hash of the config into a Pod template annotation (Helm checksum/config) or use a reloader controller.

Roll on change

bashRestart after config change
kubectl create configmap web-config --from-literal=LOG_LEVEL=debug --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
kubectl rollout restart deployment/web
kubectl exec deploy/web -- env | grep LOG_LEVEL
Check yourself
You changed a ConfigMap used via envFrom and nothing changed. Why?

Environment variables are read when the container starts; restart the Pods.

13.3

Secrets

In plain words

A Secret holds sensitive values such as passwords, tokens and keys. It is used like a ConfigMap but with tighter handling.

The problem it solves

Passwords in manifests or images leak through Git, registries and logs.

What it does

  • Values are base64 encoded, which is encoding, not encryption. Anyone with get secret permission reads them.
  • Types: Opaque, kubernetes.io/tls, kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson, kubernetes.io/basic-auth, kubernetes.io/service-account-token.
  • Mounted Secrets are held in memory (tmpfs) on the node, not written to disk.
  • Prefer file mounts over env vars: env values appear in crash dumps, docker inspect style tools and child processes.

Create and use

bashSecret commands
kubectl create secret generic db-secret --from-literal=password='S3cr3t!' -n shop
kubectl get secret db-secret -n shop -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d; echo
kubectl create secret tls shop-tls --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key -n shop
kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred --docker-server=ghcr.io --docker-username=bot --docker-password="$TOKEN"
Danger

Never commit a Secret manifest to Git, even base64 encoded. Use Sealed Secrets, SOPS or an external secret store.

13.4

Protecting Secrets in the cluster

In plain words

Secrets need encryption at rest in etcd, tight RBAC and audit.

The problem it solves

Anyone who can read etcd or has broad get secrets rights can read every password in the cluster.

What it does

  • Encryption at rest through an EncryptionConfiguration on the API server, ideally with a KMS provider (AWS KMS, Google KMS). EKS supports envelope encryption with a KMS key; Gardener enables etcd encryption by default.
  • Limit get, list and watch on Secrets. list also returns the values.
  • Avoid wildcard Roles on secrets.
  • Audit access and rotate on suspicion.

Check encryption is on

bashEKS envelope encryption
aws eks describe-cluster --name prod --query 'cluster.encryptionConfig'
kubectl auth can-i list secrets -A --as=system:serviceaccount:shop:web
13.5

External Secrets Operator

In plain words

External Secrets Operator (ESO) reads secrets from a cloud store such as AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault or HashiCorp Vault and creates ordinary Kubernetes Secrets from them.

The problem it solves

Real secrets belong in a managed store with rotation and audit, while apps still expect a Kubernetes Secret.

What it does

  • A SecretStore or ClusterSecretStore defines the connection and auth (IRSA or Pod Identity on EKS, no static keys).
  • An ExternalSecret maps remote keys to the target Secret and a refreshInterval.
  • Git holds only the references, never the values.
  • Changes upstream propagate on the next refresh; pair with a reloader to restart Pods.

ExternalSecret

yamlexternalsecret.yaml
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ClusterSecretStore
metadata:
  name: aws-sm
spec:
  provider:
    aws:
      service: SecretsManager
      region: eu-west-1
      auth:
        jwt:
          serviceAccountRef:
            name: eso
            namespace: external-secrets
---
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: db-secret
  namespace: shop
spec:
  refreshInterval: 1h
  secretStoreRef:
    name: aws-sm
    kind: ClusterSecretStore
  target:
    name: db-secret
  data:
    - secretKey: password
      remoteRef:
        key: prod/shop/db
        property: password
Note

Use the API version your installed ESO release serves (v1 in recent releases, v1beta1 earlier). Check with kubectl api-resources | grep external-secrets.

Check yourself
Why is IRSA or Pod Identity better than an access key Secret for ESO?

The pod gets short-lived credentials tied to a role, so no long-lived key is stored in the cluster.

13.6

Secrets Store CSI driver, Sealed Secrets and SOPS

In plain words

Three other patterns: mount secrets straight from a store as files, encrypt secrets so they can live in Git, or decrypt them in the pipeline.

The problem it solves

Teams doing GitOps want secrets versioned like other config, or want secrets never stored as Kubernetes Secrets at all.

What it does

  • Secrets Store CSI driver mounts values from a provider (AWS, Vault, Azure) as a volume at Pod start. It can also sync to a Kubernetes Secret.
  • Sealed Secrets encrypts with a cluster public key into a SealedSecret that only the in-cluster controller decrypts. Safe in Git, bound to the cluster and namespace.
  • SOPS (with age or KMS) encrypts values in YAML files; Flux and Argo CD plug-ins decrypt at apply time.
  • Vault Agent / injector or Vault Secrets Operator for dynamic credentials with leases.

Secrets Store CSI volume

yamlsecretproviderclass.yaml
apiVersion: secrets-store.csi.x-k8s.io/v1
kind: SecretProviderClass
metadata:
  name: aws-db
  namespace: shop
spec:
  provider: aws
  parameters:
    objects: |
      - objectName: "prod/shop/db"
        objectType: "secretsmanager"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: api
  namespace: shop
spec:
  serviceAccountName: api
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: ghcr.io/example/api:1.4.2
      volumeMounts:
        - {name: secrets, mountPath: /mnt/secrets, readOnly: true}
  volumes:
    - name: secrets
      csi:
        driver: secrets-store.csi.k8s.io
        readOnly: true
        volumeAttributes:
          secretProviderClass: aws-db

Section 14 of 65

Pod configuration patterns

5 concepts · about 35 minutes

Beyond ConfigMaps and Secrets there are several ways to hand a Pod information and to set guard rails on how much a namespace may consume.

Goals
  • Use the Downward API, projected volumes and service account tokens correctly
  • Apply namespace defaults and limits with LimitRange and ResourceQuota
  • Keep configuration declarative and reloadable
14.1

The Downward API

In plain words

The Downward API lets a container read facts about its own Pod, such as its name, namespace, IP, labels and resource limits, without calling the API server.

The problem it solves

Apps often need their identity for logging, metrics labels or clustering, and giving them API access just for that is excessive.

What it does

  • fieldRef exposes metadata.name, metadata.namespace, status.podIP, spec.nodeName, labels and annotations.
  • resourceFieldRef exposes requests and limits, useful for sizing JVM heaps or worker counts.
  • Available as env vars or as files in a downwardAPI volume (labels update live in files).

Example

yamldownward.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: whoami
  labels:
    app: whoami
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: ["sh", "-c", "env | grep -E 'POD|NODE|MEM'; sleep 3600"]
      resources:
        limits: {memory: 256Mi}
      env:
        - name: POD_NAME
          valueFrom: {fieldRef: {fieldPath: metadata.name}}
        - name: POD_IP
          valueFrom: {fieldRef: {fieldPath: status.podIP}}
        - name: NODE_NAME
          valueFrom: {fieldRef: {fieldPath: spec.nodeName}}
        - name: MEM_LIMIT
          valueFrom: {resourceFieldRef: {containerName: app, resource: limits.memory}}
14.2

Projected volumes and service account tokens

In plain words

A projected volume combines several sources (ServiceAccount token, ConfigMap, Secret, Downward API) into one directory. Bound service account tokens are short lived and audience scoped.

The problem it solves

Old ServiceAccount token Secrets never expired, so a leaked one worked forever.

What it does

  • Since 1.24 Pods receive an automatically rotated token (about one hour, refreshed by the kubelet) tied to the Pod, valid only while the Pod exists.
  • A projected token can have a custom audience, for example sts.amazonaws.com (IRSA) or a Vault audience.
  • Set automountServiceAccountToken: false for Pods that never call the API.
  • Tokens are JWTs: inspect the claims with any JWT decoder to see audience, subject and expiry.

Custom audience token

yamlprojected-token.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  serviceAccountName: api
  automountServiceAccountToken: false
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: ghcr.io/example/api:1.4.2
      volumeMounts:
        - {name: aws-token, mountPath: /var/run/secrets/aws, readOnly: true}
  volumes:
    - name: aws-token
      projected:
        sources:
          - serviceAccountToken:
              audience: sts.amazonaws.com
              expirationSeconds: 3600
              path: token
Check yourself
Why prefer a projected token to a token Secret?

It expires, is rotated automatically, is bound to the Pod and is scoped to an audience.

14.3

ResourceQuota

In plain words

A ResourceQuota caps the total resources and object counts a namespace may use.

The problem it solves

One team can consume the whole cluster or create a million ConfigMaps if nothing limits them.

What it does

  • Limits sums of requests.cpu, requests.memory, limits.*, storage per class, and counts such as pods, services.loadbalancers, persistentvolumeclaims.
  • When a quota covers compute, every Pod must set those values (or get them from a LimitRange) or it is rejected.
  • Exceeding the quota rejects creation at admission with a clear 403 message.
  • scopes such as PriorityClass apply different quotas to different priorities.

Namespace quota

yamlquota.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: team-a
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "20"
    requests.memory: 64Gi
    limits.memory: 96Gi
    pods: "100"
    persistentvolumeclaims: "20"
    requests.storage: 500Gi
    services.loadbalancers: "2"
14.4

LimitRange

In plain words

A LimitRange sets default, minimum and maximum resources for containers in a namespace.

The problem it solves

Developers forget requests and limits, which breaks scheduling and quotas, or request absurd amounts.

What it does

  • default is applied as limit and defaultRequest as request when a container omits them.
  • min and max reject outliers; maxLimitRequestRatio caps overcommit.
  • Applies to containers, Pods and PVCs.
  • Defaults are a safety net, not a substitute for sizing each service from measurements.

Defaults

yamllimitrange.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: defaults
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Container
      defaultRequest: {cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi}
      default: {memory: 512Mi}
      max: {cpu: "4", memory: 8Gi}
Check yourself
A namespace has a CPU quota but a Pod without CPU requests is rejected. Fix?

Add requests to the Pod or a LimitRange with `defaultRequest`.

14.5

Declarative configuration and immutable infrastructure

In plain words

Treat every manifest as code in Git, applied by a controller, and avoid hand edits to live objects.

The problem it solves

kubectl edit in production causes drift that nobody can review, reproduce or roll back.

What it does

  • GitOps tools (Argo CD, Flux) compare Git with the cluster and reconcile; drift is shown or reverted.
  • kubectl diff -f previews changes; kubectl apply --server-side --dry-run=server validates.
  • kubeconform or kubectl --dry-run=server in CI catches schema errors; kube-linter and kyverno test catch policy errors.
  • Use kubectl get -o yaml only to inspect; strip status, managedFields and resourceVersion before re-applying.

CI validation

bashValidate manifests before merge
kubeconform -strict -summary -ignore-missing-schemas manifests/
kubectl diff -f manifests/ ; test $? -le 1       # 0 no diff, 1 diff found, >1 error
kubectl apply --server-side --dry-run=server -f manifests/

Section 15 of 65

Volumes, PersistentVolumes and StorageClasses

6 concepts · about 50 minutes

Containers are disposable, data is not. Kubernetes separates the request for storage (PVC) from the supply of it (PV and StorageClass).

Goals
  • Pick the right volume type and access mode
  • Explain static and dynamic provisioning and binding modes
  • Resize, reclaim and debug persistent storage
15.1

Volume types

In plain words

A volume is a directory made available to containers in a Pod. Its lifetime and backing storage depend on the type.

The problem it solves

A container's filesystem disappears on restart, and containers in a Pod often need to share files.

What it does

  • emptyDir: scratch space that lives as long as the Pod; medium: Memory uses tmpfs.
  • hostPath: a node directory. Powerful and risky; avoid except for node agents.
  • configMap, secret, projected, downwardAPI: config as files.
  • persistentVolumeClaim: durable storage that outlives the Pod.
  • csi inline and ephemeral generic volumes: per-Pod volumes from a StorageClass that are deleted with the Pod.

Scratch space with a size limit

yamlemptydir.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: scratch
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: ["sleep", "3600"]
      resources:
        limits: {ephemeral-storage: 1Gi}
      volumeMounts:
        - {name: tmp, mountPath: /tmp}
  volumes:
    - name: tmp
      emptyDir:
        sizeLimit: 500Mi
15.2

PersistentVolume and PersistentVolumeClaim

In plain words

A PV is a piece of storage in the cluster. A PVC is a user's request for storage of a size and access mode. Kubernetes binds one PVC to one matching PV.

The problem it solves

Developers should ask for "20 GiB, read-write" without knowing about EBS volume IDs or NFS servers.

What it does

  • PV is cluster-scoped, usually created automatically; PVC is namespaced.
  • Binding is one-to-one and exclusive. A bound PV cannot serve another claim.
  • The Pod references only the PVC name.
  • Phases: PV Available, Bound, Released, Failed; PVC Pending, Bound, Lost.

Claim and use

yamlpvc.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: data
spec:
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
  storageClassName: gp3
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 20Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: db
spec:
  containers:
    - name: pg
      image: postgres:16
      volumeMounts:
        - {name: data, mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data}
  volumes:
    - name: data
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: data
15.3

Access modes

In plain words

Access modes say how many nodes may use a volume and whether they may write: ReadWriteOnce, ReadOnlyMany, ReadWriteMany, ReadWriteOncePod.

The problem it solves

Two Pods writing the same block device on different nodes corrupts the filesystem.

What it does

  • RWO: one node at a time (several Pods on that node may share it). Typical for EBS and block disks.
  • RWOP: exactly one Pod in the cluster (stable in 1.29). Safest for single-writer databases.
  • ROX: many nodes read only.
  • RWX: many nodes write; needs a shared filesystem such as EFS, NFS, CephFS or Azure Files.
  • A Deployment with 3 replicas and one RWO PVC runs fine on one node but stalls on a rollout across nodes with Multi-Attach errors.
Access mode
OptionRWOP
Choose whena database that must have a single writer
Avoid whenseveral replicas must share files
OptionRWO
Choose whenblock disk for one Pod or one node
Avoid whenreplicas on different nodes need the same data
OptionRWX
Choose whenshared uploads or content
Avoid whenyou need low latency block performance
Check yourself
Why does a Deployment with an RWO PVC fail rolling updates across nodes?

The new Pod lands on another node while the volume is still attached to the old one: Multi-Attach error. Use Recreate, a StatefulSet, or RWX.

15.4

StorageClasses and dynamic provisioning

In plain words

A StorageClass describes a kind of storage (type, IOPS, encryption) and the CSI driver that creates it on demand when a PVC names the class.

The problem it solves

Pre-creating disks for every request is slow and manual.

What it does

  • A PVC with storageClassName triggers the provisioner, which creates the disk and the PV automatically.
  • volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer delays creation until a Pod is scheduled, so the disk is made in the right zone.
  • allowVolumeExpansion: true allows growing a PVC later.
  • reclaimPolicy Delete removes the disk with the PVC; Retain keeps it.
  • One class can be the default (annotation storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class).

EBS gp3 class

yamlstorageclass.yaml
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: gp3
  annotations:
    storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"
provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com
parameters:
  type: gp3
  encrypted: "true"
  iops: "3000"
  throughput: "125"
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
allowVolumeExpansion: true
reclaimPolicy: Delete
15.5

Reclaim, resize and static PVs

In plain words

What happens to data when a claim goes away, how to grow a disk, and how to adopt an existing one.

The problem it solves

Deleting a PVC can destroy production data, and running out of space is common.

What it does

  • Delete: PV and disk removed with the PVC. Retain: PV becomes Released with data intact; an admin must clean and reuse it.
  • Production databases usually use a class with Retain, or snapshots plus backups.
  • Expand by editing spec.resources.requests.storage upward on the PVC; shrinking is not supported. Many CSI drivers resize online; the filesystem grows after a Pod restart if needed.
  • Static PV: create a PV pointing at an existing disk, then a PVC with volumeName.

Commands

bashResize and inspect
kubectl patch pvc data -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"50Gi"}}}}'
kubectl get pvc data -w
kubectl describe pvc data | grep -A5 Conditions
kubectl patch pv pvc-1234 -p '{"spec":{"persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy":"Retain"}}'
kubectl get pv
Careful

Setting Retain on the PV before deleting a PVC is the cheapest data-loss insurance. Do it before risky operations like namespace cleanup.

15.6

Debugging storage

In plain words

Storage failures show up as Pods stuck in ContainerCreating or PVCs stuck in Pending.

The problem it solves

Without a method, you look in the wrong layer: Pod, PVC, PV, driver or cloud.

What it does

  • PVC Pending: no matching class, provisioner down, quota exceeded, or WaitForFirstConsumer waiting for a Pod.
  • Pod ContainerCreating with FailedAttachVolume: volume still attached elsewhere, or node limit on attachments reached.
  • FailedMount: filesystem error, wrong permissions, missing NFS target.
  • Permission denied on write: set securityContext.fsGroup so volume files get the right group.

Investigate

bashStorage triage
kubectl describe pod db | sed -n '/Events/,$p'
kubectl describe pvc data
kubectl get volumeattachments
kubectl -n kube-system logs deploy/ebs-csi-controller -c csi-provisioner --tail=30
kubectl get events --field-selector reason=ProvisioningFailed -A

Section 16 of 65

Snapshots, cloning and backup

5 concepts · about 35 minutes

A volume is not a backup. This lesson shows the tools Kubernetes provides for point-in-time copies, and what they still do not cover.

Goals
  • Take and restore CSI VolumeSnapshots
  • Clone volumes and tune volume performance
  • Plan application consistent backup with Velero
16.1

VolumeSnapshots

In plain words

A VolumeSnapshot is a point-in-time copy of a PVC, created by the CSI driver using the storage system's snapshot feature.

The problem it solves

You need a fast, cheap restore point before an upgrade or migration, without copying data through the Pod.

What it does

  • Three objects: VolumeSnapshotClass (driver settings), VolumeSnapshot (namespaced request), VolumeSnapshotContent (cluster-scoped result).
  • The snapshot CRDs and the snapshot controller must be installed; EKS and Gardener add-ons usually provide them.
  • Snapshots are crash consistent unless the application is quiesced first.
  • Snapshots on EBS are stored in S3 and are incremental, but they remain inside the same account unless copied.

Take a snapshot

yamlsnapshot.yaml
apiVersion: snapshot.storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: VolumeSnapshotClass
metadata:
  name: ebs-snap
driver: ebs.csi.aws.com
deletionPolicy: Retain
---
apiVersion: snapshot.storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: VolumeSnapshot
metadata:
  name: data-pre-upgrade
spec:
  volumeSnapshotClassName: ebs-snap
  source:
    persistentVolumeClaimName: data
16.2

Restore and clone

In plain words

You restore by creating a new PVC whose dataSource is a snapshot. A clone does the same from another PVC.

The problem it solves

Testing a migration or recovering from corruption needs a fresh volume populated from known data.

What it does

  • The new PVC must be the same or larger size and same namespace as the source snapshot.
  • Restores always create a new volume; they never rewind the old one.
  • Cloning (dataSource.kind: PersistentVolumeClaim) needs driver support and the same StorageClass.
  • Switch the application to the new PVC (new StatefulSet claim or Deployment edit) after verifying data.

Restore PVC

yamlrestore-pvc.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: data-restored
spec:
  storageClassName: gp3
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 20Gi
  dataSource:
    apiGroup: snapshot.storage.k8s.io
    kind: VolumeSnapshot
    name: data-pre-upgrade
Check yourself
Does restoring a snapshot overwrite the original volume?

No. It creates a new volume; you then point the workload at it.

16.3

Application consistent backups

In plain words

A snapshot taken while a database writes may need crash recovery on restore. Quiescing or using native dumps gives clean copies.

The problem it solves

Crash-consistent copies of databases can be unusable or lose recent transactions.

What it does

  • Prefer the database's own tools: pg_dump or pg_basebackup, WAL archiving to object storage, mysqldump, or an operator's backup resource.
  • Use pre and post hooks (Velero hooks, fsfreeze) when relying on volume snapshots.
  • Test restores on a schedule; an untested backup is a hope.
  • HANA, as used with Kyma, has its own backup tooling; use that for data consistency.

Backup CronJob using pg_dump

yamlpgdump-cronjob.yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: pg-dump
spec:
  schedule: "30 1 * * *"
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      activeDeadlineSeconds: 3600
      template:
        spec:
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
          containers:
            - name: dump
              image: postgres:16
              command: ["sh", "-c", "pg_dump -h db -U app shop | gzip > /backup/shop-$(date +%F).sql.gz"]
              env:
                - name: PGPASSWORD
                  valueFrom:
                    secretKeyRef: {name: db-secret, key: password}
              volumeMounts:
                - {name: backup, mountPath: /backup}
          volumes:
            - name: backup
              persistentVolumeClaim:
                claimName: backup-pvc
16.4

Velero

In plain words

Velero backs up Kubernetes objects and volume data to object storage, and restores them into the same or another cluster.

The problem it solves

Snapshots cover disks only. After a cluster loss you also need Deployments, Services, Secrets and CRDs.

What it does

  • Backup saves selected namespaces and resources to an S3 bucket; volumes via CSI snapshots or file-system backup (Kopia).
  • Schedule runs backups with a TTL; Restore recreates objects, optionally into a different namespace.
  • Used for cluster migration, DR and namespace recovery.
  • It does not replace GitOps: Git is the source for manifests, Velero for state and stateful data.

Schedule

yamlvelero-schedule.yaml
apiVersion: velero.io/v1
kind: Schedule
metadata:
  name: daily-shop
  namespace: velero
spec:
  schedule: "0 3 * * *"
  template:
    includedNamespaces: ["shop"]
    snapshotMoveData: true
    ttl: 720h
16.5

Ephemeral storage, local volumes and performance

In plain words

Containers also use node disk through logs, writable layers and emptyDir. Local SSDs and instance stores give speed without durability.

The problem it solves

A chatty Pod fills the node disk and gets evicted, or a database on network storage is slower than expected.

What it does

  • Set requests and limits for ephemeral-storage; exceeding the limit evicts the Pod.
  • Kubelet eviction triggers on nodefs.available and imagefs.available thresholds.
  • Local PVs (local volume type) and CSI local drivers (TopoLVM, Local Path) give NVMe speed but pin the Pod to a node and lose data with the node.
  • EBS gp3 lets you set IOPS and throughput independently of size; check VolumeQueueLength and throttling metrics when latency rises.

Watch node disk

bashDisk pressure
kubectl describe node worker-1 | grep -E 'DiskPressure|ephemeral-storage'
kubectl top pods --containers -A | head
kubectl get pods -A -o json | grep -c Evicted

Section 17 of 65

Requests, limits and QoS

6 concepts · about 50 minutes

Resource settings are the contract between your Pod and the scheduler, the kubelet and the Linux kernel. Most mysterious latency and restarts trace back to them.

Goals
  • Size requests and limits and explain what each one does in the kernel
  • Explain CPU throttling and OOM kills
  • Predict QoS class and eviction order
17.1

Requests and limits

In plain words

A request is what the scheduler reserves for a container. A limit is the ceiling the kernel enforces at run time.

The problem it solves

Without requests the scheduler packs Pods blindly. Without limits one noisy Pod can starve its neighbours.

What it does

  • The scheduler adds up requests of Pods on a node and compares with the node's allocatable; limits are ignored for placement.
  • CPU is measured in cores (500m is half a core); memory in bytes (256Mi).
  • CPU is compressible: over the limit you are slowed down. Memory is incompressible: over the limit you are killed.
  • Requests are also the basis for HPA utilisation percentages and for quota.

Container resources

yamlresources.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/example/api:1.4.2
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 250m
              memory: 512Mi
            limits:
              memory: 512Mi
17.2

CPU throttling

In plain words

A CPU limit is enforced with the CFS quota: in each 100 ms period the container may use only limit x 100 ms of CPU time, then it is paused until the next period.

The problem it solves

A container with a 1-core limit can still show low average CPU but suffer long latency, because bursts hit the cap within a period.

What it does

  • A multi-threaded app with a limit of 1 CPU and 4 busy threads uses its quota in 25 ms and stalls for 75 ms.
  • Metric container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total / container_cpu_cfs_periods_total shows the throttled share.
  • Many teams set CPU requests but no CPU limits, so spare CPU can be used and the request still guarantees a share; memory requests equal limits. This is a trade-off, not a rule: limits are needed for fairness in shared tenancy and some compliance regimes.
  • Runtimes must see the limit: modern JVM and Go (1.25+) respect cgroup limits; older Go needs GOMAXPROCS set (automaxprocs).

Measure throttling

promqlPromQL for throttling
# percentage of periods throttled per container
sum by (pod, container) (rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total[5m]))
  / sum by (pod, container) (rate(container_cpu_cfs_periods_total[5m]))
# actual use versus request
sum by (pod) (rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total[5m]))
Tip

Alert on sustained throttling above about 25 percent for latency-sensitive services, then raise the limit or remove it, rather than only raising the request.

Check yourself
Why can a service be throttled at 20 percent average CPU?

Throttling is decided per 100 ms period; short bursts across many threads can exhaust the quota while the average stays low.

17.3

Memory limits and OOM kills

In plain words

Exceeding the memory limit makes the kernel's OOM killer terminate the container's process. Kubernetes shows OOMKilled and exit code 137.

The problem it solves

Memory cannot be slowed down like CPU, so the only enforcement is killing.

What it does

  • Page cache and mapped files count toward the cgroup. Reclaimable cache is dropped first; anonymous memory is not.
  • Set memory request equal to limit for predictable behaviour and QoS Guaranteed (if CPU also matches).
  • JVM: set -XX:MaxRAMPercentage (for example 75) so heap plus off-heap fits the limit. Node.js: --max-old-space-size.
  • Swap is off by default; limited swap support exists for Burstable Pods, so do not assume it.
  • Node-level memory pressure causes kubelet eviction (graceful), different from a container OOM kill.

Confirm an OOM kill

bashFind OOM kills
kubectl get pod api-7d9 -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState.terminated}{"\n"}'
kubectl top pod api-7d9 --containers
kubectl describe pod api-7d9 | grep -E 'OOMKilled|Exit Code|Limits' -A2
kubectl get events -A --field-selector reason=OOMKilling
17.4

QoS classes and eviction order

In plain words

Kubernetes labels each Pod Guaranteed, Burstable or BestEffort from its requests and limits, and uses it to decide who dies first under pressure.

The problem it solves

When a node runs out of memory, someone must be removed. The order should protect important Pods.

What it does

  • Guaranteed: every container has CPU and memory requests equal to limits. Lowest OOM score.
  • Burstable: at least one request or limit set, but not Guaranteed.
  • BestEffort: nothing set at all. First to be killed.
  • Kubelet eviction ranks Pods by whether they exceed requests, then priority, then usage above request. Within the kernel OOM killer, oom_score_adj follows QoS.

Read the class

bashQoS of running Pods
kubectl get pods -A -o custom-columns=NS:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,QOS:.status.qosClass | sort -k3 | head -20
kubectl get pod api-7d9 -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}{"\n"}'
Check yourself
A Pod has memory requests equal to limits but only a CPU request. QoS?

Burstable. Guaranteed needs requests equal to limits for both CPU and memory in every container.

17.5

Right-sizing, in-place resize and PriorityClass

In plain words

Good numbers come from measurement. Newer Kubernetes can resize a running Pod, and PriorityClass says which Pods matter more.

The problem it solves

Guessing requests wastes money (too high) or causes evictions and throttling (too low).

What it does

  • Measure P95 or P99 usage over a representative window; set request near typical usage plus headroom, memory limit above peak.
  • Tools: VPA in recommendation mode, Goldilocks, Kubecost, Prometheus queries.
  • In-place Pod resize (resizePolicy, beta and on by default from 1.33) changes CPU and memory of a running container without recreation.
  • PriorityClass gives integer priority; the scheduler can preempt lower priority Pods to place a higher one. preemptionPolicy: Never prevents preempting others.

Priority classes

yamlpriorityclass.yaml
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: business-critical
value: 100000
globalDefault: false
description: Customer facing services
---
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: batch-low
value: 1000
preemptionPolicy: Never
description: Batch work that yields to services
17.6

Node pressure, eviction and allocatable

In plain words

Each node reserves resources for the OS and kubelet and evicts Pods before the machine runs out of memory or disk.

The problem it solves

If Pods can use all RAM, the kubelet and kernel starve and the whole node fails instead of one Pod.

What it does

  • Allocatable = capacity - kube-reserved - system-reserved - eviction threshold.
  • Hard thresholds (for example memory.available<100Mi) trigger immediate eviction; soft thresholds wait a grace period.
  • Under pressure the node gets conditions MemoryPressure, DiskPressure, PIDPressure and a NoSchedule taint.
  • Evicted Pods end in Failed with reason Evicted; clean them with a periodic job since they linger.

Inspect node accounting

bashWhat is allocated
kubectl describe node worker-1 | sed -n '/Allocated resources/,/Events/p'
kubectl top nodes
kubectl get pods -A --field-selector=status.phase=Failed | grep Evicted | head
← PreviousNext →
Section 18 of 65

The scheduler in depth

6 concepts · about 45 minutes

The scheduler is a pipeline of plugins. Knowing the stages lets you read FailedScheduling messages and pick the right constraint for each job.

Goals
  • Explain the scheduling cycle and its plugin extension points
  • Use nodeSelector, node affinity and Pod affinity correctly
  • Use taints, tolerations and priority to place and protect workloads
18.1

Scheduling cycle and plugins

In plain words

For each Pod the scheduler runs a queue, a filter phase, a score phase and a bind phase. Each phase is made of plugins you can enable, disable or weight.

The problem it solves

Fixed placement logic cannot suit batch, GPU, stateful and multi-tenant clusters all at once.

What it does

  • Extension points: PreFilter, Filter, PostFilter (preemption), PreScore, Score, Reserve, Permit, Bind.
  • Built-in plugins include NodeResourcesFit, NodeAffinity, TaintToleration, PodTopologySpread, InterPodAffinity, VolumeBinding, ImageLocality.
  • Profiles in KubeSchedulerConfiguration allow several schedulers behaviours; Pods choose with schedulerName.
  • On managed control planes you cannot change the default scheduler config, but you can run a second scheduler (for example Volcano, Kueue's integration or a bin-packing one).

Read a scheduling failure

bashTypical message
kubectl describe pod api-7d9 | grep -A3 FailedScheduling
# 0/6 nodes are available: 2 Insufficient cpu, 3 node(s) had untolerated taint {dedicated: gpu},
# 1 node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector.
kubectl get events -A --field-selector reason=FailedScheduling | tail
Check yourself
What does a message listing counts per reason tell you?

Every node was rejected by one of those filters, so the Pod stays Pending until one reason is resolved.

18.2

nodeSelector and node affinity

In plain words

nodeSelector picks nodes by exact labels. Node affinity adds operators, required versus preferred rules and weights.

The problem it solves

Workloads need particular hardware or location: GPU nodes, a zone, an architecture, a spot pool.

What it does

  • nodeSelector: simple AND of key=value.
  • requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution: hard rule; Pod stays Pending if no node matches.
  • preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution: soft rule with weight 1 to 100.
  • Operators: In, NotIn, Exists, DoesNotExist, Gt, Lt.
  • "IgnoredDuringExecution" means running Pods are not moved if labels later change.
  • Well-known labels: topology.kubernetes.io/zone, kubernetes.io/arch, node.kubernetes.io/instance-type, karpenter.sh/capacity-type.

Arm64 on-demand preference

yamlnode-affinity.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: batch-arm
spec:
  affinity:
    nodeAffinity:
      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
        nodeSelectorTerms:
          - matchExpressions:
              - {key: kubernetes.io/arch, operator: In, values: [arm64]}
      preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
        - weight: 80
          preference:
            matchExpressions:
              - {key: karpenter.sh/capacity-type, operator: In, values: [spot]}
  containers:
    - name: job
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: ["sleep", "60"]
18.3

Pod affinity and anti-affinity

In plain words

Pod affinity attracts a Pod toward nodes (or zones) that already run certain other Pods. Anti-affinity repels it.

The problem it solves

You may want a cache beside its app, or want replicas of one service on different nodes for failure isolation.

What it does

  • Uses a labelSelector plus a topologyKey (kubernetes.io/hostname for node, topology.kubernetes.io/zone for zone).
  • Required anti-affinity across hostnames means at most one replica per node; scaling beyond node count leaves Pods Pending.
  • Evaluation cost grows with cluster size; prefer topology spread constraints for even spreading at scale.
  • matchLabelKeys (stable in recent releases) ties the rule to a rollout's pod-template-hash, so old and new ReplicaSets do not block each other.

Spread replicas across nodes

yamlanti-affinity.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api
    spec:
      affinity:
        podAntiAffinity:
          preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
            - weight: 100
              podAffinityTerm:
                topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
                labelSelector:
                  matchLabels:
                    app: api
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/example/api:1.4.2
18.4

Taints and tolerations

In plain words

A taint on a node repels Pods. A toleration on a Pod lets it ignore a matching taint. Taints keep unwanted Pods out; they do not attract.

The problem it solves

Special nodes (GPU, spot, control plane) should not receive ordinary Pods, and a failing node should shed its workloads.

What it does

  • Effects: NoSchedule (new Pods blocked), PreferNoSchedule (soft) and NoExecute (also evicts running Pods, optionally after tolerationSeconds).
  • Taint a node: kubectl taint nodes n1 dedicated=gpu:NoSchedule; remove with a trailing -.
  • Control plane nodes carry node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule.
  • The node lifecycle controller adds node.kubernetes.io/not-ready and unreachable taints.
  • For dedicated pools combine a taint (keep others out) with node affinity (pull yours in).

GPU Pod

yamltoleration.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: trainer
spec:
  tolerations:
    - {key: dedicated, operator: Equal, value: gpu, effect: NoSchedule}
    - {key: node.kubernetes.io/unreachable, operator: Exists, effect: NoExecute, tolerationSeconds: 60}
  nodeSelector:
    pool: gpu
  containers:
    - name: train
      image: ghcr.io/example/trainer:2.0
      resources:
        limits:
          nvidia.com/gpu: 1
Check yourself
Does a toleration make a Pod go to the tainted node?

No. It only permits it. Add node affinity or a selector to attract it.

18.5

Topology spread constraints

In plain words

Topology spread constraints keep Pods evenly distributed across zones, nodes or any label domain, within an allowed difference called maxSkew.

The problem it solves

Without spreading, the scheduler may put all replicas in one zone, and a zone outage takes the service down.

What it does

  • topologyKey names the domain, maxSkew the largest allowed difference between the fullest and emptiest domain.
  • whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule is hard; ScheduleAnyway is soft.
  • minDomains forces use of at least that many domains; nodeAffinityPolicy and nodeTaintsPolicy control which nodes count.
  • Combine zone (hard, skew 1) with hostname (soft) for strong availability.
  • Spreading only applies at scheduling time; rebalance with the Descheduler or rollout restarts.

Spread across zones and nodes

yamltopology-spread.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  replicas: 6
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      topologySpreadConstraints:
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
          labelSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: web
          matchLabelKeys: [pod-template-hash]
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
          whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
          labelSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: web
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: nginx:1.27
18.6

PodDisruptionBudgets and node maintenance

In plain words

Voluntary disruptions (drain, upgrade, autoscaler scale-down) go through the Eviction API, which respects PodDisruptionBudgets. Involuntary ones (crash, hardware) do not.

The problem it solves

An upgrade that drains nodes can remove all replicas of a service in a minute.

What it does

  • PDB sets minAvailable or maxUnavailable for a selected set of Pods.
  • kubectl drain cordons the node, evicts Pods through the API and waits when a PDB blocks.
  • unhealthyPodEvictionPolicy: AlwaysAllow lets drains evict Pods that are not Ready, so a broken app cannot block an upgrade.
  • Drains stuck for hours usually mean a PDB with zero allowed disruptions or a Pod with a local emptyDir needing --delete-emptydir-data.
  • On Gardener-managed Kyma, node rolling follows the worker pool's maxSurge and maxUnavailable and respects PDBs; always uncordon and verify afterwards if you drain manually.

PDB and drain

yamlpdb-api.yaml
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  unhealthyPodEvictionPolicy: AlwaysAllow
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
bashSafe drain
kubectl get pdb -A
kubectl drain worker-1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --timeout=10m
kubectl get node worker-1                  # SchedulingDisabled
kubectl uncordon worker-1                  # always restore afterwards

Section 19 of 65

Pod autoscaling with HPA, VPA and KEDA

6 concepts · about 50 minutes

Autoscaling adds copies of a Pod (horizontal) or resizes it (vertical). Each has rules that cause surprises if ignored.

Goals
  • Compute HPA replicas from the formula and configure behaviour
  • Choose between HPA, VPA and KEDA for a workload
  • Scale on custom, external and event metrics
19.1

Metrics for autoscaling

In plain words

Autoscalers read metrics through three APIs: resource metrics from metrics-server, custom metrics about Kubernetes objects, and external metrics from outside the cluster.

The problem it solves

Scaling on CPU only misses queue depth, request rate or latency, which are often better signals.

What it does

  • metrics.k8s.io: CPU and memory per Pod, served by metrics-server (also powers kubectl top).
  • custom.metrics.k8s.io: per-object metrics, provided by an adapter such as Prometheus Adapter.
  • external.metrics.k8s.io: values like SQS length or Kafka lag, provided by an adapter such as KEDA.
  • Without metrics-server, HPA shows <unknown> for targets.

Check metrics

bashIs metrics-server healthy
kubectl get apiservices | grep metrics
kubectl top nodes
kubectl top pods -n shop --sort-by=cpu
kubectl get --raw "/apis/metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1/namespaces/shop/pods" | head -c 300
19.2

The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler

In plain words

The HPA changes replicas of a Deployment or StatefulSet to keep a metric near a target.

The problem it solves

Load varies, and fixed replica counts are either wasteful or too small for peaks.

What it does

  • Formula: desired = ceil(current replicas x current metric / target metric). Example: 4 replicas at 90% CPU with target 60% gives ceil(4 x 90/60) = 6.
  • CPU utilisation is relative to the request, so missing requests break HPA.
  • It evaluates every 15 s by default, ignores a 10% tolerance band, and uses the highest result when several metrics are given.
  • Do not set replicas in Git for an HPA-managed workload.
  • Not for scale to zero (HPA minimum is 1 unless the alpha HPAScaleToZero feature gate is enabled).

Compute the formula

pythonHPA replica calculation
import math
def desired(current, metric, target, tolerance=0.1):
    ratio = metric / target
    return current if abs(ratio - 1) <= tolerance else math.ceil(current * ratio)
print(desired(4, 90, 60))   # scale up
print(desired(6, 62, 60))   # inside tolerance
print(desired(10, 20, 60))  # scale down
Check yourself
Why does HPA need CPU requests on the Pods?

Utilisation is measured as a percentage of the request; without one there is nothing to compare against.

19.3

HPA behaviour and a full manifest

In plain words

The behavior section controls how fast the HPA may scale up or down and how long it waits before scaling down.

The problem it solves

Without limits, noisy metrics cause flapping and aggressive scale-down removes capacity before load truly drops.

What it does

  • scaleUp and scaleDown each have policies (Pods or Percent per period) and stabilizationWindowSeconds.
  • Defaults: scale down waits 300 s using the highest recommendation in the window; scale up has no window and can double or add 4 Pods per 15 s.
  • selectPolicy: Max | Min | Disabled.
  • Multiple metrics (CPU, memory, custom) are allowed.

HPA v2

yamlhpa.yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: api
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 30
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target: {type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 60}
    - type: Pods
      pods:
        metric: {name: http_requests_per_second}
        target: {type: AverageValue, averageValue: "100"}
  behavior:
    scaleUp:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0
      policies:
        - {type: Percent, value: 100, periodSeconds: 15}
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 600
      policies:
        - {type: Percent, value: 10, periodSeconds: 60}
19.4

Vertical Pod Autoscaler

In plain words

The VPA watches real usage and recommends, or applies, better CPU and memory requests for a workload.

The problem it solves

Developers guess requests wrongly, and usage drifts with each release.

What it does

  • Components: recommender, updater and admission controller.
  • updateMode: Off (recommendations only), Initial (set at Pod creation), Recreate or Auto (evict and recreate with new values; newer versions can resize in place).
  • Do not use VPA and HPA on the same CPU or memory metric; HPA on custom metrics plus VPA is fine.
  • Start with Off and use the output to set requests in Git.
  • It is an add-on, not part of core Kubernetes; EKS and Gardener offer it as an add-on or extension.

Recommendation only

yamlvpa.yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling.k8s.io/v1
kind: VerticalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  targetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: api
  updatePolicy:
    updateMode: "Off"
  resourcePolicy:
    containerPolicies:
      - containerName: "*"
        minAllowed: {cpu: 50m, memory: 64Mi}
        maxAllowed: {cpu: "2", memory: 4Gi}
bashRead the advice
kubectl describe vpa api | sed -n '/Recommendation/,$p'
19.5

KEDA, event-driven scaling

In plain words

KEDA scales workloads on events such as queue length, Kafka lag, cron schedules or Prometheus queries, including down to zero.

The problem it solves

HPA alone cannot scale to zero or read most external systems directly.

What it does

  • A ScaledObject references a Deployment and one or more triggers; KEDA creates and manages an HPA for 1..N and handles 0<->1 itself.
  • ScaledJob creates Jobs per event batch for long tasks.
  • 60+ scalers: AWS SQS, Kafka, RabbitMQ, Prometheus, Cron, HTTP (add-on).
  • TriggerAuthentication references credentials or pod identity so secrets stay out of triggers.
  • Used for workers where idle cost should be nil, and for burst processing.

Scale on queue length

yamlscaledobject.yaml
apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: TriggerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: aws-pod-identity
  namespace: shop
spec:
  podIdentity:
    provider: aws
---
apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata:
  name: worker
  namespace: shop
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    name: worker
  minReplicaCount: 0
  maxReplicaCount: 50
  cooldownPeriod: 300
  triggers:
    - type: aws-sqs-queue
      authenticationRef:
        name: aws-pod-identity
      metadata:
        queueURL: https://sqs.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/111122223333/orders
        queueLength: "20"
        awsRegion: eu-west-1
Pod autoscaler
OptionHPA
Choose whenCPU or request-rate scaling of web services
Avoid whenyou need scale to zero or external queues
OptionKEDA
Choose whenqueues, streams, schedules, scale to zero
Avoid whenplain CPU scaling is enough
OptionVPA (Off mode)
Choose whenfinding correct requests
Avoid whenyou want it to restart Pods during peak hours
19.6

Autoscaling pitfalls

In plain words

Most autoscaling incidents come from slow starts, missing limits on dependencies or fighting controllers.

The problem it solves

Autoscalers react after load arrives; slow Pod startup means users already felt the spike.

What it does

  • Readiness delay: new Pods take time to be ready, so keep a minReplicas buffer for the typical spike.
  • Scaling a stateless tier can overload the database; cap maxReplicas or use connection pooling.
  • Metrics lag (scrape interval, 15 s HPA loop) adds delay of up to a minute.
  • Pending Pods from HPA need the Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter to add nodes, adding minutes more.
  • Pre-warm with minReplicas, small image sizes, startupProbe tuned, and overprovisioning Pods (low-priority placeholders).

Watch an HPA

bashHPA diagnostics
kubectl get hpa api -w
kubectl describe hpa api | sed -n '/Conditions/,$p'
kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.kind=HorizontalPodAutoscaler

Section 20 of 65

Node autoscaling with Cluster Autoscaler and Karpenter

5 concepts · about 40 minutes

Pod autoscalers create Pods; something must create machines for them. Node autoscalers watch for Pods that cannot be placed and for nodes that are underused.

Goals
  • Explain how node autoscalers react to Pending Pods and idle nodes
  • Compare Cluster Autoscaler and Karpenter
  • Configure a Karpenter NodePool and protect nodes from disruption
20.1

What node autoscalers do

In plain words

A node autoscaler adds nodes when Pods are Pending for lack of capacity and removes nodes that are empty or can be consolidated.

The problem it solves

Fixed-size clusters are either too small at peak or too expensive off peak.

What it does

  • Trigger: a Pod with Unschedulable condition that would fit on a new node.
  • Scale down: nodes below utilisation threshold (or emptied by consolidation) are drained and removed, respecting PDBs and annotations.
  • Pods that block removal: no controller owner, local storage, restrictive PDBs, safe-to-evict: false or karpenter.sh/do-not-disrupt.
  • On Gardener and Kyma the worker pool minimum and maximum and the Gardener-managed cluster autoscaler do this for you.

Is the autoscaler acting

bashAutoscaler signals
kubectl -n kube-system logs deploy/cluster-autoscaler --tail=30 | grep -E 'Scale-up|Scale-down|NotTriggerScaleUp'
kubectl get pods -A --field-selector=status.phase=Pending
kubectl get nodes -L topology.kubernetes.io/zone -L karpenter.sh/nodepool
20.2

Cluster Autoscaler

In plain words

Cluster Autoscaler (CA) scales pre-defined node groups (AWS Auto Scaling Groups, Gardener worker pools, managed node groups) up and down.

The problem it solves

You want elasticity but keep strict control over instance types through the groups you define.

What it does

  • Works per node group: it picks a group whose template node would fit the pending Pod, and raises its desired size.
  • Scale-down after nodes are underused (utilisation below 50% of requests by default) for 10 minutes.
  • Expanders (random, least-waste, priority) choose between groups.
  • Each group is a single instance shape, so many shapes need many groups. This is the main weakness.
  • Zone-bound volumes require one node group per zone so the CA can add a node in the right zone.

Annotations that guide CA

yamlca-annotations.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: long-job
  annotations:
    cluster-autoscaler.kubernetes.io/safe-to-evict: "false"
spec:
  containers:
    - name: job
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: ["sleep", "3600"]
20.3

Karpenter

In plain words

Karpenter creates nodes directly from the pending Pods' needs, choosing instance types and sizes on the fly, without pre-defined node groups.

The problem it solves

Node groups limit instance variety and scale slowly through the ASG API, leaving capacity wasted.

What it does

  • Watches unschedulable Pods, batches them, and picks the cheapest instance types that satisfy requests, affinities, topology spread and taints.
  • A NodePool sets constraints (architecture, capacity type spot or on-demand, instance families, limits, taints); an EC2NodeClass sets AWS specifics (AMI family, subnets, security groups, IAM role).
  • Consolidation replaces or removes nodes to reduce cost (WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized), respecting PDBs and budgets.
  • Disruption budgets and expireAfter control node rotation, which also keeps AMIs fresh.
  • AWS-native (EKS) with a provider for Azure; not used by Gardener, which has its own autoscaler.

NodePool and EC2NodeClass

yamlkarpenter.yaml
apiVersion: karpenter.sh/v1
kind: NodePool
metadata:
  name: general
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      nodeClassRef:
        group: karpenter.k8s.aws
        kind: EC2NodeClass
        name: default
      requirements:
        - {key: karpenter.sh/capacity-type, operator: In, values: [spot, on-demand]}
        - {key: kubernetes.io/arch, operator: In, values: [amd64, arm64]}
        - {key: karpenter.k8s.aws/instance-category, operator: In, values: [c, m, r]}
      expireAfter: 720h
  limits:
    cpu: "500"
  disruption:
    consolidationPolicy: WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized
    consolidateAfter: 1m
    budgets:
      - nodes: "10%"
---
apiVersion: karpenter.k8s.aws/v1
kind: EC2NodeClass
metadata:
  name: default
spec:
  amiFamily: AL2023
  amiSelectorTerms:
    - alias: al2023@latest
  role: KarpenterNodeRole-prod
  subnetSelectorTerms:
    - tags: {karpenter.sh/discovery: prod}
  securityGroupSelectorTerms:
    - tags: {karpenter.sh/discovery: prod}
Note

al2023@latest follows new AMIs automatically. Pin an AMI alias version in production and promote it through environments.

Check yourself
How does Karpenter differ from CA?

It selects instance types from Pod requirements and creates nodes directly, rather than resizing fixed node groups.

20.4

Consolidation and disruption safety

In plain words

Cost optimisation means moving Pods. Make that safe with PDBs, budgets and do-not-disrupt markers.

The problem it solves

Aggressive consolidation during business hours can restart critical workloads.

What it does

  • Each voluntary node removal drains with the Eviction API, so PDBs apply.
  • Budgets can restrict disruptions by count and by schedule (for example none during weekdays 9 to 17).
  • karpenter.sh/do-not-disrupt: "true" on a Pod or node blocks voluntary removal.
  • Spot interruptions give a 2 minute warning; handle SIGTERM fast and use terminationGracePeriodSeconds below that.
  • Keep critical system Pods on a small on-demand pool with a taint.

Scheduled budget

yamldisruption-budget.yaml
apiVersion: karpenter.sh/v1
kind: NodePool
metadata:
  name: business-hours-safe
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      nodeClassRef:
        group: karpenter.k8s.aws
        kind: EC2NodeClass
        name: default
      requirements:
        - {key: karpenter.sh/capacity-type, operator: In, values: [on-demand]}
  disruption:
    consolidationPolicy: WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized
    budgets:
      - nodes: "0"
        schedule: "0 8 * * mon-fri"
        duration: 10h
      - nodes: "20%"
20.5

Capacity planning and cost

In plain words

Autoscaling finds machines; you still decide the shape of the fleet, how much headroom to hold and where the money goes.

The problem it solves

Clusters often run at 20 to 30 percent real utilisation because requests are inflated.

What it does

  • Compare requested versus used CPU and memory; the gap is waste.
  • Use spot instances for stateless and batch work with PDBs and multiple instance types; keep a baseline on-demand.
  • Overprovision with low-priority pause Pods so burst traffic lands on ready nodes; they are preempted at once.
  • Show cost per namespace or label with OpenCost or Kubecost.
  • Right-size first, then consolidate, then buy commitments.

Headroom placeholder

yamloverprovision.yaml
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: overprovision
value: -10
globalDefault: false
description: Placeholder Pods that yield to real workloads
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: overprovision
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: overprovision
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: overprovision
    spec:
      priorityClassName: overprovision
      containers:
        - name: pause
          image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.10
          resources:
            requests: {cpu: "1", memory: 2Gi}
