Section 21 of 65

RBAC and identity for workloads

6 concepts · about 50 minutes

RBAC answers one question: may this identity do this verb on this resource. Most clusters are over-permissioned because RBAC is written once and never reviewed.

Goals
  • Write least privilege Roles and bindings and test them
  • Use ServiceAccounts and cloud identity (IRSA, Pod Identity) for workloads
  • Audit and reduce excess permissions
21.1

RBAC building blocks

In plain words

Four objects: Role (permissions in a namespace), ClusterRole (cluster-wide or reusable permissions), RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding (attach a role to subjects).

The problem it solves

Giving everyone cluster-admin is easy and dangerous. You need a way to grant exactly what a person or workload requires.

What it does

  • A rule lists apiGroups, resources, optional resourceNames and verbs (get, list, watch, create, update, patch, delete, deletecollection).
  • Subjects are User, Group or ServiceAccount. Users and groups come from authentication (OIDC claims, certificates).
  • A RoleBinding can reference a ClusterRole but still limits it to its own namespace, a good way to reuse view or edit.
  • RBAC is additive and has no deny.

A least privilege Role

yamlrbac.yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: deploy-manager
  namespace: shop
rules:
  - apiGroups: ["apps"]
    resources: ["deployments"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "patch"]
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["pods", "pods/log"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: shop-devs
  namespace: shop
subjects:
  - kind: Group
    name: oidc:shop-developers
    apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: deploy-manager
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
21.2

ClusterRoles, aggregation and built-ins

In plain words

Kubernetes ships cluster-admin, admin, edit and view. Aggregated ClusterRoles let CRDs add themselves to them with labels.

The problem it solves

Writing a role per team from nothing is slow, and new CRDs would otherwise be invisible to view or edit.

What it does

  • view: read most objects except Secrets. edit: read and write most objects including Secrets. admin: edit plus RBAC within a namespace. cluster-admin: everything.
  • Label a ClusterRole with rbac.authorization.k8s.io/aggregate-to-view: "true" to include it into view automatically; operators use this.
  • edit can read Secrets, so it can effectively reach any ServiceAccount token-bearing identity in that namespace. Treat it as privileged.
  • Never bind system:authenticated or system:anonymous to broad roles.

Reuse a built-in in one namespace

bashBind view to a group
kubectl create rolebinding auditors --clusterrole=view --group=oidc:auditors -n shop
kubectl get clusterrole view -o yaml | head -30
kubectl get clusterrolebinding -o wide | grep cluster-admin
Check yourself
Why is `edit` risky?

It can read Secrets, including tokens and passwords used by other workloads in the namespace.

21.3

ServiceAccounts

In plain words

A ServiceAccount is the identity of a workload inside Kubernetes. Pods run as one and use it to call the API.

The problem it solves

Pods that share the namespace default ServiceAccount share permissions, so one compromise spreads.

What it does

  • Create one ServiceAccount per workload and bind only the rights it needs.
  • The default ServiceAccount should have no bindings; set automountServiceAccountToken: false if the app never calls the API.
  • The username is system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name>.
  • Tokens are short lived and bound to the Pod. For external callers use kubectl create token for a time-limited token.

Workload identity manifest

yamlserviceaccount.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: reader
  namespace: shop
automountServiceAccountToken: true
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: configmap-reader
  namespace: shop
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["configmaps"]
    resourceNames: ["web-config"]
    verbs: ["get", "watch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: reader-binding
  namespace: shop
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: reader
    namespace: shop
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: configmap-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
21.4

Cloud identity for Pods

In plain words

Pods call AWS, Azure or Google APIs by exchanging their Kubernetes token for short-lived cloud credentials, with no stored keys.

The problem it solves

Access keys in Secrets are long lived, copied around and rarely rotated.

What it does

  • IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts): the cluster's OIDC provider is trusted by IAM; a ServiceAccount annotation names the role, and the AWS SDK exchanges the projected token for credentials.
  • EKS Pod Identity: an agent on nodes delivers credentials; association is created with the EKS API, no per-cluster OIDC trust edits.
  • Always scope the role to one service, and the trust policy to one namespace and ServiceAccount.
  • Azure Workload Identity and GKE Workload Identity use the same federated token model.
  • On Kyma, SAP BTP service bindings and IAS-based app identity play a similar role for BTP services.

IRSA ServiceAccount

yamlirsa.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: uploader
  namespace: shop
  annotations:
    eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/shop-uploader
bashPod Identity association
aws eks create-pod-identity-association \
  --cluster-name prod --namespace shop --service-account uploader \
  --role-arn arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/shop-uploader
Check yourself
What does the IAM trust policy for IRSA limit?

Which OIDC subject (namespace and ServiceAccount) can assume the role.

21.5

Testing and auditing RBAC

In plain words

You can ask the API server what an identity may do, and use tools to find dangerous or unused permissions.

The problem it solves

Permissions accumulate. Without checks, a leaked token has more power than anyone intended.

What it does

  • kubectl auth can-i VERB RESOURCE --as=USER -n NS and --list.
  • Escalation rights to watch: create pods (can mount Secrets and run privileged), get/list secrets, impersonate, escalate, bind on roles, create serviceaccounts/token, wildcard *.
  • Tools: kubectl-who-can, rbac-lookup, rakkess, KubiScan, Kubescape and Trivy for RBAC findings.
  • Review cluster-admin bindings quarterly; expire access via short-lived OIDC sessions rather than long-lived certificates.

Commands

bashAudit permissions
kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:shop:reader -n shop
kubectl auth can-i create pods --as=system:serviceaccount:shop:reader -n shop
kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json | grep -B3 -A10 '"name": "cluster-admin"' | head -40
kubectl who-can get secrets -n shop
kubectl rakkess --as system:serviceaccount:shop:reader -n shop
Danger

create pods in a namespace is close to get secrets, because a Pod can mount any Secret there. Count it as a privileged permission.

21.6

Kubernetes access for people

In plain words

Humans should reach clusters through your identity provider with short sessions and group-based roles, not shared kubeconfigs with client certificates.

The problem it solves

A kubeconfig with an admin certificate never expires and cannot be revoked per person.

What it does

  • OIDC with your IdP (Astra Connect, SAP IAS, Entra ID, Okta): groups in the token map to ClusterRoleBindings.
  • EKS: access entries and access policies map IAM principals to Kubernetes permissions; the older aws-auth ConfigMap is deprecated.
  • Kyma: cluster access via kubeconfig with OIDC (kubelogin) against SAP IAS or similar; use groups rather than named users.
  • Break-glass: a separate, audited, short-lived admin path.
  • Impersonation (--as) is itself a privilege, so grant it narrowly.

EKS access entry

bashGrant a group read access on EKS
aws eks create-access-entry --cluster-name prod \
  --principal-arn arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/platform-readonly
aws eks associate-access-policy --cluster-name prod \
  --principal-arn arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/platform-readonly \
  --policy-arn arn:aws:eks::aws:cluster-access-policy/AmazonEKSViewPolicy \
  --access-scope type=cluster

Section 22 of 65

Pod security

5 concepts · about 45 minutes

A container is a Linux process with isolation, not a virtual machine. Pod security reduces what a compromised process can do to the node and to its neighbours.

Goals
  • Write a hardened securityContext
  • Apply Pod Security Standards with namespace labels
  • Explain capabilities, seccomp, AppArmor and user namespaces
22.1

securityContext

In plain words

securityContext sets user, group, filesystem, capability and privilege options on a Pod or container.

The problem it solves

By default containers often run as root with a writable filesystem and many kernel capabilities, which makes breakouts easier.

What it does

  • runAsNonRoot: true with runAsUser refuses to start a container whose user is root.
  • allowPrivilegeEscalation: false blocks setuid binaries gaining privileges.
  • readOnlyRootFilesystem: true forces writes into explicit volumes.
  • capabilities: drop: ["ALL"] then add back only what is needed (for example NET_BIND_SERVICE).
  • seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault filters dangerous syscalls.
  • fsGroup sets group ownership of mounted volumes.

Hardened Deployment

yamlhardened.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api
    spec:
      automountServiceAccountToken: false
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 10001
        runAsGroup: 10001
        fsGroup: 10001
        seccompProfile:
          type: RuntimeDefault
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/example/api:1.4.2
          securityContext:
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
            capabilities:
              drop: ["ALL"]
          volumeMounts:
            - {name: tmp, mountPath: /tmp}
      volumes:
        - name: tmp
          emptyDir: {}
22.2

Pod Security Standards

In plain words

Three built-in policy levels define what a Pod may do: privileged (anything), baseline (blocks known escalations) and restricted (current hardening best practice).

The problem it solves

PodSecurityPolicy was removed in 1.25. You still need a simple, built-in guard rail.

What it does

  • Baseline forbids host namespaces, privileged containers, most host paths and dangerous capabilities.
  • Restricted adds non-root, no privilege escalation, drop ALL capabilities (only NET_BIND_SERVICE may be added), seccomp RuntimeDefault or Localhost, and limited volume types.
  • Applied per namespace by the built-in Pod Security Admission controller.
  • Standards check Pods, and Pod templates in workload objects are checked for warnings.

Enforce per namespace

yamlpsa-namespace.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: shop
  labels:
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version: latest
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: restricted
Check yourself
What are the three Pod Security Admission modes?

`enforce` rejects violations, `audit` records them in the audit log, `warn` shows a warning to the user.

22.3

Rolling out Pod Security safely

In plain words

Start with warn and audit, fix what they report, then enforce.

The problem it solves

Turning on enforce for existing namespaces breaks workloads that run as root.

What it does

  • Label the namespace with warn and audit first and run kubectl label --dry-run=server to see what would fail.
  • Use AdmissionConfiguration for cluster defaults and exemptions (for example system namespaces); on managed clusters check what the provider already sets.
  • Existing running Pods are not killed by enforce; new ones are rejected.
  • For exceptions use a dedicated namespace with a weaker level, not a weaker cluster default.

Dry run

bashWhat would break
kubectl label --dry-run=server --overwrite ns shop pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted
kubectl label ns shop pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=restricted --overwrite
kubectl get ns --show-labels | grep pod-security
22.4

Capabilities, seccomp and AppArmor

In plain words

Linux splits root power into capabilities, filters syscalls with seccomp and confines files and network with AppArmor or SELinux.

The problem it solves

Even a non-root process can be dangerous with extra capabilities, and a root process in a container is only as safe as the kernel filters around it.

What it does

  • Capabilities like NET_ADMIN, SYS_ADMIN, SYS_PTRACE allow network, mount and process control; avoid them.
  • RuntimeDefault seccomp blocks around 40+ rarely-needed syscalls with little compatibility cost; custom Localhost profiles can be generated from observed behaviour (Security Profiles Operator).
  • AppArmor is set via securityContext.appArmorProfile (stable in 1.31); SELinux via seLinuxOptions on supporting distributions.
  • privileged: true removes almost all isolation; only node-level agents should use it.

AppArmor and seccomp

yamlapparmor-seccomp.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: confined
spec:
  securityContext:
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault
    appArmorProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: ["sleep", "3600"]
      securityContext:
        allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
        capabilities:
          drop: ["ALL"]
22.5

Isolation beyond defaults

In plain words

When tenants are untrusted, add stronger boundaries: sandboxed runtimes, user namespaces or dedicated nodes.

The problem it solves

Containers share the host kernel; a kernel bug can cross the boundary.

What it does

  • RuntimeClass selects a sandboxing runtime such as gVisor or Kata Containers (microVM) for specific Pods.
  • User namespaces (hostUsers: false, stable in 1.33) map container root to an unprivileged host UID, shrinking the impact of a breakout.
  • Dedicated node pools with taints for sensitive workloads; no shared nodes between trust levels.
  • Avoid hostNetwork, hostPID, hostIPC and hostPath; do not mount the container runtime socket.

Sandboxed Pod

yamlruntimeclass.yaml
apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
kind: RuntimeClass
metadata:
  name: gvisor
handler: runsc
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: untrusted
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor
  hostUsers: false
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: ["sleep", "3600"]
← PreviousNext →
Section 23 of 65

NetworkPolicy and segmentation

4 concepts · about 40 minutes

By default every Pod can talk to every other Pod. NetworkPolicy turns the flat network into a set of allowed paths.

Goals
  • Write default deny and allow rules for ingress and egress
  • Explain selectors, namespaces, ipBlock and how rules combine
  • Verify policies and know the limits of the standard API
23.1

How NetworkPolicy works

In plain words

A NetworkPolicy selects Pods and lists which traffic is allowed to or from them. Once a Pod is selected by any policy for a direction, everything not allowed in that direction is denied.

The problem it solves

A compromised Pod in one namespace can scan and attack every other Pod in the cluster.

What it does

  • Needs a CNI that enforces policy (Calico, Cilium, AWS VPC CNI with network policy enabled, Antrea). With a plain Flannel the object is accepted and does nothing.
  • podSelector chooses the protected Pods; policyTypes says Ingress, Egress or both.
  • Policies are additive allow lists; there is no deny rule. Order does not matter.
  • Allows are by Pod labels, namespace labels and IP blocks, and by port and protocol.

Default deny for a namespace

yamldefault-deny.yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: shop
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: ["Ingress", "Egress"]
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-dns
  namespace: shop
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: ["Egress"]
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
          podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              k8s-app: kube-dns
      ports:
        - {protocol: UDP, port: 53}
        - {protocol: TCP, port: 53}
Careful

Default-deny egress without a DNS allow rule breaks every lookup. Add the DNS policy in the same change.

23.2

Allowing application traffic

In plain words

Add small allow policies per tier: frontend to API, API to database, ingress controller to frontend.

The problem it solves

Deny-all alone stops the application working. You must declare the real call graph.

What it does

  • from and to entries are OR'd; within one entry namespaceSelector and podSelector together are AND'd.
  • Select the Ingress controller or mesh gateway namespace so external traffic can reach front-end Pods.
  • Use ipBlock with except for external CIDRs; Pod IPs are not matched by ipBlock in most implementations.
  • Name ports, and keep policies next to the workload manifests so they change together.

API tier policy

yamlallow-api.yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: api-allow
  namespace: shop
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  policyTypes: ["Ingress", "Egress"]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: web
      ports:
        - {protocol: TCP, port: 8080}
  egress:
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: db
      ports:
        - {protocol: TCP, port: 5432}
    - to:
        - ipBlock:
            cidr: 0.0.0.0/0
            except: ["169.254.169.254/32", "10.0.0.0/8"]
      ports:
        - {protocol: TCP, port: 443}
Check yourself
In one `from` item you list namespaceSelector and podSelector together. AND or OR?

AND: the Pod must match both. Separate list items are OR.

23.3

Testing and observing policies

In plain words

Policies are easy to get wrong and fail silently. Test with real traffic and observe drops.

The problem it solves

A typo in a label silently opens or closes a path.

What it does

  • Run a temporary Pod with the same labels as the caller and curl the target; also test a forbidden path.
  • Cilium Hubble and Calico flow logs show allowed and denied flows; AWS VPC CNI writes policy decision logs when enabled.
  • Tools: netpol-analyzer, Cilium's network policy editor, kubectl describe networkpolicy.
  • Include policy tests in CI against a kind cluster with Calico or Cilium.

Probe

bashPositive and negative test
kubectl -n shop run t1 --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --labels=app=web --restart=Never -- curl -s -m 3 http://api:8080/healthz
kubectl -n shop run t2 --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl --labels=app=other --restart=Never -- curl -s -m 3 http://api:8080/healthz
kubectl -n shop describe networkpolicy api-allow
hubble observe --namespace shop --verdict DROPPED --last 20
23.4

Limits of NetworkPolicy and extended policies

In plain words

The standard API is layer 3 and 4 only. Larger needs use CNI-specific or newer APIs.

The problem it solves

You may need to allow by DNS name, apply cluster-wide defaults or add explicit denies.

What it does

  • No FQDN rules, no HTTP path rules, no logging, and no cluster-scoped policy in the base API.
  • Cilium CiliumNetworkPolicy and Calico GlobalNetworkPolicy add FQDN, L7, deny and ordered rules.
  • The upstream AdminNetworkPolicy and BaselineAdminNetworkPolicy APIs (network-policy-api project, still alpha) add cluster-scoped allow, deny and default behaviour.
  • A service mesh adds identity-based AuthorizationPolicy (Istio) at L7 with mTLS, used in Kyma.

Istio AuthorizationPolicy

yamlauthorizationpolicy.yaml
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: api-from-web
  namespace: shop
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
    - from:
        - source:
            principals: ["cluster.local/ns/shop/sa/web"]
      to:
        - operation:
            methods: ["GET", "POST"]
            paths: ["/orders/*"]

Section 24 of 65

Admission webhooks and policy engines

5 concepts · about 50 minutes

RBAC says who may act. Admission policy says what a request may contain. This is where you enforce labels, resource limits, trusted registries and security settings.

Goals
  • Write ValidatingAdmissionPolicy rules in CEL
  • Explain webhook configuration, failure policy and safe operation
  • Compare Kyverno and OPA Gatekeeper and write one policy in each
24.1

Admission webhooks

In plain words

A webhook admission controller sends the request to an HTTPS service you run. The service answers allow, deny or a patch.

The problem it solves

Built-in admission cannot know your organisation's rules.

What it does

  • MutatingWebhookConfiguration and ValidatingWebhookConfiguration list rules (operations, resources), the service, failurePolicy, timeoutSeconds and selectors.
  • The API server calls the webhook with an AdmissionReview and expects an answer within the timeout (default 10 s, max 30 s).
  • failurePolicy: Fail blocks requests if the webhook is down; Ignore lets them through.
  • namespaceSelector, objectSelector and matchConditions (CEL) narrow what is sent.
  • Webhook servers need a trusted TLS certificate, usually via cert-manager caBundle injection.

Webhook configuration

yamlwebhook-config.yaml
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingWebhookConfiguration
metadata:
  name: policy-check
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/inject-ca-from: policy/policy-webhook
webhooks:
  - name: pods.policy.example.com
    admissionReviewVersions: ["v1"]
    sideEffects: None
    timeoutSeconds: 5
    failurePolicy: Fail
    clientConfig:
      service:
        name: policy-webhook
        namespace: policy
        path: /validate
    rules:
      - apiGroups: [""]
        apiVersions: ["v1"]
        operations: ["CREATE", "UPDATE"]
        resources: ["pods"]
    namespaceSelector:
      matchExpressions:
        - {key: kubernetes.io/metadata.name, operator: NotIn, values: [kube-system, policy]}
Danger

Exclude kube-system and the webhook's own namespace. A Fail webhook that blocks its own Pods can prevent the cluster from recovering.

24.2

ValidatingAdmissionPolicy with CEL

In plain words

ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (VAP) runs validation rules written in CEL inside the API server, with no webhook service. It is stable since 1.30.

The problem it solves

Webhooks need a service, certificates and high availability just to check one field.

What it does

  • A ValidatingAdmissionPolicy holds matchConstraints, validations (CEL expressions with messages) and optional variables.
  • A ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding applies it to namespaces with an action: Deny, Warn or Audit.
  • paramKind lets a policy read thresholds from a CRD or ConfigMap, so one policy serves many teams.
  • Fast, in-process and fail-safe: no network call.
  • A MutatingAdmissionPolicy equivalent is newer and less widely available; check your version.

Require resource limits and a team label

yamlvap.yaml
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-team-and-memory-limit
spec:
  failurePolicy: Fail
  matchConstraints:
    resourceRules:
      - apiGroups: ["apps"]
        apiVersions: ["v1"]
        operations: ["CREATE", "UPDATE"]
        resources: ["deployments"]
  validations:
    - expression: "has(object.metadata.labels) && 'team' in object.metadata.labels"
      message: "Deployment must have a team label"
    - expression: >-
        object.spec.template.spec.containers.all(c,
        has(c.resources) && has(c.resources.limits) && 'memory' in c.resources.limits)
      message: "Every container needs a memory limit"
---
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding
metadata:
  name: require-team-and-memory-limit
spec:
  policyName: require-team-and-memory-limit
  validationActions: ["Deny"]
  matchResources:
    namespaceSelector:
      matchLabels:
        policy: enforced
Check yourself
Why use VAP before writing a webhook?

It runs inside the API server, needs no service or certificates and cannot be down.

24.3

Kyverno

In plain words

Kyverno is a Kubernetes-native policy engine whose policies are plain YAML. It can validate, mutate, generate and verify images.

The problem it solves

Writing Rego or webhook servers is a barrier for platform teams that think in Kubernetes manifests.

What it does

  • ClusterPolicy or the newer ValidatingPolicy, MutatingPolicy and related CEL-based policies in current releases; check the API available in your installed version.
  • Rule types: validate (block or audit), mutate (add defaults), generate (create NetworkPolicy or quota for each new namespace), verifyImages (signature checks).
  • validationFailureAction: Audit reports to PolicyReports without blocking, useful for rollout.
  • kyverno test and the CLI let you run policies in CI against manifests.

Disallow latest tag and generate a default deny

yamlkyverno.yaml
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: disallow-latest-tag
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  background: true
  rules:
    - name: no-latest
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds: ["Pod"]
      validate:
        message: "Images must use a pinned tag, not latest."
        pattern:
          spec:
            containers:
              - image: "!*:latest"
---
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-netpol
spec:
  rules:
    - name: generate-deny
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds: ["Namespace"]
      generate:
        apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
        kind: NetworkPolicy
        name: default-deny
        namespace: "{{request.object.metadata.name}}"
        synchronize: true
        data:
          spec:
            podSelector: {}
            policyTypes: ["Ingress"]
24.4

OPA Gatekeeper

In plain words

Gatekeeper enforces policies written in Rego through ConstraintTemplates (the logic) and Constraints (where and how it applies).

The problem it solves

Organisations that already use OPA for other systems want one policy language across them.

What it does

  • A ConstraintTemplate defines a new CRD and its Rego; a Constraint is an instance that carries parameters.
  • enforcementAction: deny, warn or dryrun.
  • Audit controller scans existing objects and lists violations on the constraint status.
  • Config sync can replicate resources into OPA for cross-object checks.
  • Compared with Kyverno: more flexible logic and shared language with Conftest in CI, but a steeper learning curve and no built-in generate.

Required labels constraint

yamlgatekeeper.yaml
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: k8srequiredlabels
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: K8sRequiredLabels
      validation:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          type: object
          properties:
            labels:
              type: array
              items:
                type: string
  targets:
    - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh
      rego: |
        package k8srequiredlabels
        violation[{"msg": msg}] {
          required := input.parameters.labels[_]
          not input.review.object.metadata.labels[required]
          msg := sprintf("missing required label: %v", [required])
        }
---
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: K8sRequiredLabels
metadata:
  name: ns-must-have-team
spec:
  enforcementAction: deny
  match:
    kinds:
      - apiGroups: [""]
        kinds: ["Namespace"]
  parameters:
    labels: ["team"]
Policy engine
OptionValidatingAdmissionPolicy
Choose whensimple field checks with no extra install
Avoid whenyou need mutate, generate or cross-resource lookups
OptionKyverno
Choose whenKubernetes teams who want YAML policies and generation
Avoid whenyou require a single language shared with non-Kubernetes OPA
OptionGatekeeper
Choose whencomplex logic and shared Rego across systems
Avoid whenyour team does not want to learn Rego
24.5

Operating policy safely

In plain words

Policies are production code. Roll them out in stages, test them and watch the webhooks.

The problem it solves

A new deny rule can stop deployments across the company on a Friday.

What it does

  • Start in Audit or Warn, read the reports, fix owners, then enforce.
  • Exempt system namespaces and the policy engine itself; use matchConditions to narrow scope.
  • Run the policy engine with multiple replicas, PDB, anti-affinity and a high priority class; monitor webhook latency and failures (apiserver_admission_webhook_rejection_count).
  • Version policies in Git, test with kyverno test or gator verify, and ship via GitOps.
  • Provide clear messages: tell developers exactly how to fix the rejection.

Test commands

bashPolicy in CI
kyverno test ./policies
kyverno apply ./policies --resource ./manifests/deploy.yaml
gator verify ./gatekeeper-tests
kubectl get policyreport -A
kubectl get constraints

Section 25 of 65

Image policy, supply chain and runtime security

6 concepts · about 50 minutes

Securing the cluster starts before the Pod: which image runs, who built it and what it contains. It continues after the Pod starts: what it actually does.

Goals
  • Enforce trusted registries, digests and signatures at admission
  • Use SBOMs and vulnerability scanning in the delivery path
  • Detect runtime threats with eBPF tools and audit logs
25.1

Image provenance and registries

In plain words

Pull only from registries you control, reference images by digest, and keep the build chain trustworthy.

The problem it solves

Mutable tags such as 1.0 or latest can point to different content tomorrow, and public images can be tampered with or typosquatted.

What it does

  • Use a private registry (ECR, Harbor, Artifactory) as the only allowed source, with a pull-through cache for public images.
  • Reference by digest: image: ghcr.io/example/api@sha256:.... Tags are for humans; digests are for production.
  • Build from minimal base images (distroless, Chainguard, Alpine) to shrink attack surface.
  • imagePullSecrets or node IAM (ECR) gives pull access; never embed registry passwords in images.

Restrict registries

yamlallowed-registries.yaml
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: allowed-registries
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
    - name: only-internal-registry
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds: ["Pod"]
      validate:
        message: "Images must come from 111122223333.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com."
        pattern:
          spec:
            containers:
              - image: "111122223333.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/*"
25.2

Signing and verification

In plain words

Signing proves who built an image and that it has not changed. Admission verifies the signature before the Pod runs.

The problem it solves

Network access to a registry is not proof the image came from your pipeline.

What it does

  • Cosign (Sigstore) signs images and attestations; keyless mode uses short-lived certificates tied to the CI identity (OIDC) and records in a transparency log (Rekor).
  • Sign in CI after build and scan: cosign sign IMAGE@DIGEST.
  • Verify in the cluster with Kyverno verifyImages, Sigstore policy-controller or Ratify (on Azure and others).
  • Attestations (SLSA provenance, SBOM, vulnerability scan result) can also be required.

Verify signatures

yamlverify-images.yaml
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: verify-signed-images
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  webhookTimeoutSeconds: 30
  rules:
    - name: cosign-keyless
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds: ["Pod"]
      verifyImages:
        - imageReferences: ["ghcr.io/example/*"]
          mutateDigest: true
          attestors:
            - entries:
                - keyless:
                    issuer: https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
                    subject: https://github.com/example/*
                    rekor:
                      url: https://rekor.sigstore.dev
Check yourself
What does `mutateDigest: true` give you?

Admission rewrites the tag to the verified digest, so the Pod runs exactly what was verified.

25.3

SBOMs and vulnerability scanning

In plain words

An SBOM lists every package in an image. Scanners compare that list against vulnerability databases.

The problem it solves

You cannot patch what you cannot see, and new CVEs appear after an image has shipped.

What it does

  • Generate SBOMs with Syft or BuildKit attestations; scan with Trivy, Grype or registry-native scanning (ECR Inspector).
  • Scan in CI (fail on critical, fixable findings) and continuously in the registry or cluster (Trivy Operator creates VulnerabilityReport objects).
  • Prioritise reachable and fixable vulnerabilities; use VEX statements to record not-affected decisions.
  • Rebuild base images on a schedule so patches flow without code changes.

Scan and generate

bashTrivy and Syft
trivy image --severity CRITICAL,HIGH --ignore-unfixed --exit-code 1 ghcr.io/example/api:1.4.2
syft ghcr.io/example/api:1.4.2 -o spdx-json > sbom.spdx.json
cosign attest --predicate sbom.spdx.json --type spdxjson ghcr.io/example/api@sha256:0123
trivy k8s --report summary --namespace shop
kubectl get vulnerabilityreports -n shop
25.4

Runtime security

In plain words

Runtime tools watch what containers actually do and alert on unexpected behaviour: shells in containers, unexpected network calls, writes to sensitive files.

The problem it solves

Admission controls cannot stop an attack that exploits a running, correctly signed application.

What it does

  • Falco (eBPF) applies rules to syscalls: "shell spawned in container", "read of /etc/shadow", "outbound connection to unexpected IP". Alerts go to SIEM or chat.
  • Tetragon and Tracee (eBPF) add process lineage and can enforce (kill) on policy.
  • Cilium Hubble shows network flows; GuardDuty EKS Runtime Monitoring provides a managed agent on AWS.
  • Combine with read-only root filesystem and dropped capabilities so fewer attacks succeed at all.

Custom Falco rule

yamlfalco-rule.yaml
- rule: Shell in app container
  desc: A shell started inside a production container
  condition: >
    evt.type in (execve, execveat) and evt.dir=<
    and container.id != host
    and proc.name in (bash, sh, zsh)
    and k8s.ns.name = "shop"
  output: >
    Shell in container (user=%user.name pod=%k8s.pod.name ns=%k8s.ns.name
    cmd=%proc.cmdline image=%container.image.repository)
  priority: WARNING
  tags: [container, shell]
25.5

Audit logs and detection

In plain words

Kubernetes audit logs record every API request: who, what, when and the result. They are the main record for investigations.

The problem it solves

After an incident you must answer who read the Secret or changed the Deployment.

What it does

  • Audit policy sets level per resource: None, Metadata, Request, RequestResponse. Log Secrets at Metadata so values are not stored in logs.
  • Managed services ship audit logs to their own sinks (EKS to CloudWatch Logs, Gardener to the shoot's logging stack). Enable it and set retention.
  • Useful detections: exec into Pods, creation of privileged Pods or ClusterRoleBindings, access by anonymous or unusual users, Secret reads by non-system identities.
  • Forward to a SIEM and alert on high-risk verbs.

Enable and query on EKS

bashEKS audit logging
aws eks update-cluster-config --name prod \
  --logging '{"clusterLogging":[{"types":["api","audit","authenticator"],"enabled":true}]}'
aws logs start-query --log-group-name /aws/eks/prod/cluster \
  --start-time $(date -d '-1 hour' +%s) --end-time $(date +%s) \
  --query-string 'fields @timestamp, user.username, verb, objectRef.resource | filter verb = "create" and objectRef.subresource = "exec"'
25.6

A layered security checklist

In plain words

No single control is enough. Combine identity, admission, network and runtime layers and verify them regularly.

The problem it solves

Teams add one tool, feel safe and leave gaps elsewhere.

What it does

  • Identity: OIDC for humans, least privilege RBAC, no long-lived keys, cloud identity for Pods.
  • Config: Pod Security restricted, secrets from a store, encryption at rest.
  • Network: default deny, mesh mTLS, egress control.
  • Supply chain: private registry, signed digests, scans, SBOMs.
  • Runtime and ops: eBPF detection, audit logs, patched nodes through regular node rotation, benchmark scans (CIS with kube-bench, Kubescape).

Benchmark scans

bashPosture checks
kubescape scan framework nsa --namespace shop
kube-bench run --targets node
trivy k8s --compliance k8s-pss-restricted-0.1 --report summary cluster

Section 26 of 65

Helm fundamentals

6 concepts · about 45 minutes

Raw manifests repeat themselves across environments. Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes. It bundles manifests as a templated chart, fills them with values, and tracks every install as a release you can upgrade and roll back.

Goals
  • Explain charts, releases and repositories and how Helm stores release state
  • Lay out a chart and read the values precedence rules
  • Install, upgrade, roll back and inspect a release from the command line
26.1

Charts, releases and repositories

In plain words

A chart is a folder of templated Kubernetes YAML plus default settings. A release is one installed copy of a chart in a cluster, with a name you choose. A repository is a place that serves charts, either a classic HTTP index or an OCI registry.

The problem it solves

Installing a database, an ingress controller or your own service by hand means dozens of YAML files that differ slightly per environment. Copying and editing them leads to drift, and there is no single command to undo a bad change.

What it does

  • The same chart can be installed many times under different release names and namespaces.
  • Helm 3 and later has no server component. The helm client talks to the API server using your kubeconfig, so it has exactly your RBAC permissions.
  • Each upgrade creates a new numbered revision, which is what makes rollback possible.

Finding and using a chart

bashRepositories and search
helm repo add ingress-nginx https://kubernetes.github.io/ingress-nginx
helm repo update                                  # refresh the local index cache
helm search repo ingress-nginx --versions | head  # available chart versions
helm show chart ingress-nginx/ingress-nginx | head -20
helm show values ingress-nginx/ingress-nginx > default-values.yaml   # every knob and its default
Check yourself
Does Helm need a controller running in the cluster?

No. Helm 3 and later is client-only and stores release state in the cluster as Secrets.

What is the difference between a chart and a release?

A chart is the package; a release is one named installation of it with a specific values set.

26.2

Anatomy of a chart

In plain words

A chart is a directory with a fixed layout. Chart.yaml describes it, values.yaml holds defaults, and templates/ holds the YAML with placeholders.

The problem it solves

Without a convention every team would organise packages differently, and tooling such as linting, packaging and dependency resolution could not work.

What it does

  • Chart.yaml has version (the chart version) and appVersion (the version of the software inside). They are independent.
  • templates/_helpers.tpl holds reusable named templates. Files starting with an underscore render no object.
  • templates/NOTES.txt is printed after install. charts/ holds dependencies. values.schema.json can validate input.
  • crds/ holds CRDs that are installed once and never upgraded or deleted by Helm.

A minimal Chart.yaml and values.yaml

yamlChart.yaml
apiVersion: v2
name: shop-api
description: Shop API service
type: application
version: 0.3.0          # chart version, bump on every chart change
appVersion: "1.8.2"     # application image version
kubeVersion: ">=1.28.0-0"
yamlvalues.yaml
replicaCount: 2
image:
  repository: registry.example.com/shop/api
  tag: ""               # empty means use Chart.appVersion
  pullPolicy: IfNotPresent
service:
  port: 80
resources:
  requests: {cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi}
  limits: {memory: 256Mi}
ingress:
  enabled: false
  host: shop.example.com
bashScaffold a new chart
helm create shop-api        # generates a working example chart
helm lint shop-api --strict # warnings become errors
helm package shop-api       # produces shop-api-0.3.0.tgz
26.3

Values and their precedence

In plain words

Values are the inputs to a chart. The chart ships defaults; you override them with files or command-line flags. Later sources win over earlier ones.

The problem it solves

One chart must serve dev, staging and production with different replica counts, hostnames and sizes, without editing the chart.

What it does

  • Lowest to highest priority is the chart's values.yaml, then parent chart values, then each -f file in order, then --set flags.
  • Maps merge key by key. Lists are replaced whole, not merged, which surprises people.
  • --set a.b=c sets nested keys, --set-string forces a string, --set-file reads a value from a file.
  • Keep one values file per environment in version control and avoid long --set chains.

Per environment files

yamlvalues-prod.yaml
replicaCount: 4
image:
  tag: "1.8.2"
ingress:
  enabled: true
  host: shop.prod.example.com
resources:
  requests: {cpu: 500m, memory: 512Mi}
  limits: {memory: 512Mi}
bashApply layered values
helm upgrade --install shop ./shop-api -n shop --create-namespace \
  -f values.yaml -f values-prod.yaml --set image.tag=1.8.3
helm get values shop -n shop            # only what you overrode
helm get values shop -n shop --all      # computed values including defaults
Careful

--reuse-values keeps the previous release's overrides but ignores new chart defaults, so a chart upgrade can silently miss new settings. Prefer passing the same -f files every time.

26.4

Templates and built-in objects

In plain words

Templates are YAML files with Go template expressions in double braces. Helm gives them objects such as .Values, .Release and .Chart to read.

The problem it solves

Plain YAML cannot change a name, a replica count or an image tag from one install to the next. Templates make one file produce many correct variants.

What it does

  • .Values holds merged input. .Release.Name, .Release.Namespace, .Release.IsInstall and .Release.IsUpgrade describe the install.
  • .Chart.Name, .Chart.AppVersion come from Chart.yaml. .Capabilities.KubeVersion shows the cluster version.
  • {{ .Values.x | quote }} pipes a value through a function. {{- ... -}} trims surrounding whitespace.
  • nindent and toYaml are the usual way to insert a block with the right indentation.

A Deployment template

yamltemplates/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-api
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: shop-api
    app.kubernetes.io/instance: {{ .Release.Name }}
    app.kubernetes.io/version: {{ .Chart.AppVersion | quote }}
spec:
  replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/instance: {{ .Release.Name }}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app.kubernetes.io/instance: {{ .Release.Name }}
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag | default .Chart.AppVersion }}"
          imagePullPolicy: {{ .Values.image.pullPolicy }}
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          resources:
            {{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 12 }}
Tip

Always render before you install. helm template shop ./shop-api -f values-prod.yaml | kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f - validates the output against the real API server.

26.5

Install, upgrade, rollback

In plain words

helm upgrade --install is the one idempotent command for CI: it installs if the release is missing and upgrades otherwise. Every change makes a new revision, and helm rollback returns to an earlier one.

The problem it solves

A failed deployment must not leave the application half updated with no way back, and pipelines need a single repeatable command.

What it does

  • --wait blocks until Pods and Deployments are ready; --timeout bounds it. --atomic rolls back automatically if the wait fails, and implies --wait.
  • helm history lists revisions with status such as deployed, failed or superseded.
  • helm rollback NAME REVISION creates a new revision that reapplies an old manifest.
  • helm uninstall removes the objects; --keep-history retains the release record.

Commands

bashRelease lifecycle
helm upgrade --install shop ./shop-api -n shop --create-namespace \
  -f values-prod.yaml --atomic --timeout 5m
helm list -n shop                          # releases and their status
helm history shop -n shop                  # revisions
helm rollback shop 3 -n shop --wait        # go back to revision 3
helm uninstall shop -n shop
Check yourself
What does --atomic do on failure?

It rolls the release back to the previous revision and returns a non-zero exit code.

Why can a rollback of a Helm release not undo a database migration?

Helm only reapplies old manifests; it knows nothing about data changes made by the application.

26.6

Where release state lives and how to inspect it

In plain words

Helm stores each revision as a Secret in the release namespace, named sh.helm.release.v1.NAME.vN. It contains the chart, the values and the rendered manifest, compressed.

The problem it solves

When a release is stuck in pending-upgrade or the live cluster differs from what you think you deployed, you need to see what Helm believes.

What it does

  • helm get manifest shows what Helm applied; compare it with kubectl get -o yaml to find manual edits.
  • helm get hooks, helm get notes and helm status show the rest of the record.
  • A release stuck in a pending-* state (for example after a killed CI job) blocks further upgrades with "another operation is in progress". Roll back or delete the stuck revision Secret.
  • Old revisions are pruned according to --history-max, which defaults to 10.

Inspecting

bashSee what Helm knows
kubectl get secret -n shop -l owner=helm        # one Secret per revision
helm status shop -n shop
helm get manifest shop -n shop | head -40
helm get manifest shop -n shop | kubectl diff -f -   # drift between Helm and the cluster
helm rollback shop 4 -n shop                    # recover a release stuck in pending-upgrade
Note

Do not edit Helm-owned objects by hand. The next upgrade may overwrite the edit, or fail on a conflict. Change the values and upgrade instead.

Section 27 of 65

Helm templating in depth and dependencies

6 concepts · about 45 minutes

Basic substitution gets you far, but real charts need optional objects, repeated blocks and shared helpers. This section covers the template features you meet in production charts.

Goals
  • Use conditionals, loops, named templates and validation helpers in templates
  • Compose charts with dependencies, subcharts and library charts
  • Validate input with a values schema and test a release
27.1

Conditionals, with and range

In plain words

Templates can include a block only when a condition holds (if), loop over a list or map (range), and change the current scope (with).

The problem it solves

Not every install wants an Ingress, a HorizontalPodAutoscaler or a ServiceMonitor. One chart has to switch parts on and off and render a variable number of items.

What it does

  • {{- if .Values.ingress.enabled }} ... {{- end }} wraps a whole object so it is skipped when disabled.
  • range repeats a block for every item. Inside it . is the current item, so use $ to reach the root context.
  • with runs the block only if the value is non-empty and rebinds . to it.
  • Empty string, 0, false, empty list and empty map are all false.

Optional Ingress with a loop

yamltemplates/ingress.yaml
{{- if .Values.ingress.enabled }}
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}
spec:
  ingressClassName: {{ .Values.ingress.className }}
  rules:
    {{- range .Values.ingress.hosts }}
    - host: {{ .name | quote }}
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: {{ $.Release.Name }}
                port:
                  number: {{ $.Values.service.port }}
    {{- end }}
{{- end }}
27.2

Named templates and _helpers.tpl

In plain words

A named template is a reusable snippet defined with define and called with include. The convention is to keep them in templates/_helpers.tpl.

The problem it solves

Names, labels and selectors must be identical across a Deployment, a Service and a PodDisruptionBudget. Copying them invites a typo that breaks a selector.

What it does

  • {{ define "shop.labels" }} ... {{ end }} declares it; {{ include "shop.labels" . | nindent 4 }} uses it and lets you pipe the result.
  • Prefix names with the chart name, because template names are global across a chart and its subcharts.
  • Prefer include over template, since only include returns a string that can be piped.
  • helm create generates fullname, labels and selectorLabels helpers you can keep.

Helpers

yamltemplates/_helpers.tpl
{{- define "shop.name" -}}
{{- default .Chart.Name .Values.nameOverride | trunc 63 | trimSuffix "-" -}}
{{- end }}

{{- define "shop.selectorLabels" -}}
app.kubernetes.io/name: {{ include "shop.name" . }}
app.kubernetes.io/instance: {{ .Release.Name }}
{{- end }}

{{- define "shop.labels" -}}
helm.sh/chart: {{ .Chart.Name }}-{{ .Chart.Version }}
{{ include "shop.selectorLabels" . }}
app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: {{ .Release.Service }}
{{- end }}
Note

The 63 character truncation matters. Many Kubernetes names and all label values are limited to 63 characters, so long release names fail at install time without it.

27.3

Validation with required, fail and schema

In plain words

You can make a chart refuse bad input early: required stops rendering when a value is missing, fail stops with your message, and values.schema.json validates the whole values tree.

The problem it solves

Without validation, a missing hostname renders an empty string, the install succeeds, and the failure appears later as a confusing runtime error.

What it does

  • {{ required "image.repository is required" .Values.image.repository }} aborts with that message.
  • values.schema.json is JSON Schema. Helm checks it on install, upgrade, lint and template.
  • additionalProperties: false catches misspelled keys, which otherwise are silently ignored.

A small schema

jsonvalues.schema.json
{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#",
  "type": "object",
  "required": ["image"],
  "properties": {
    "replicaCount": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1},
    "image": {
      "type": "object",
      "required": ["repository"],
      "properties": {
        "repository": {"type": "string", "minLength": 1},
        "tag": {"type": "string"}
      }
    }
  }
}
27.4

Dependencies and subcharts

In plain words

A chart can depend on other charts, such as PostgreSQL or Redis. They are declared in Chart.yaml, downloaded into charts/, and configured through a section of your values named after the dependency.

The problem it solves

An application usually needs supporting services. Re-implementing them in your own chart is wasteful, and installing them separately breaks the "one command" promise.

What it does

  • helm dependency update resolves versions, writes Chart.lock and downloads archives; helm dependency build restores exactly what the lock says.
  • condition: postgresql.enabled lets users turn a dependency off, for example when they use a managed database.
  • Values under the key postgresql: go to the subchart; values under global: reach every chart.
  • alias lets you include the same chart twice under different names.

Declaring a dependency

yamlChart.yaml
apiVersion: v2
name: shop
version: 1.2.0
appVersion: "2.0.0"
dependencies:
  - name: postgresql
    version: "15.x.x"
    repository: oci://registry-1.docker.io/bitnamicharts
    condition: postgresql.enabled
  - name: redis
    version: "19.x.x"
    repository: oci://registry-1.docker.io/bitnamicharts
    condition: redis.enabled
bashResolve and build
helm dependency update ./shop     # writes Chart.lock and fills charts/
helm dependency build ./shop      # reproducible, uses Chart.lock
helm template shop ./shop --set postgresql.enabled=false | grep -c '^kind:'
27.5

Library charts and chart tests

In plain words

A library chart (type: library) contains only named templates and renders nothing by itself. Other charts depend on it to share conventions. Chart tests are Pods marked as tests that helm test runs against an installed release.

The problem it solves

Fifty microservices each carrying a copy of the same Deployment template drift apart. And a successful install says only that objects were created, not that the service works.

What it does

  • A library chart exposes helpers such as mylib.deployment; consumers call them with include.
  • A test is a template in templates/tests/ with the annotation helm.sh/hook: test. It passes when the Pod exits 0.
  • helm test RELEASE runs them and reports; keep them small, such as one HTTP call to the Service.

A smoke test

yamltemplates/tests/test-connection.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: shop-test-connection
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": test
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
    - name: wget
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: ["wget", "-qO-", "http://shop:80/healthz"]
bashRun it
helm test shop -n shop --logs
27.6

Debugging a template

In plain words

When rendering fails or produces odd YAML, you inspect the rendered output instead of guessing. helm template and --debug show what Helm would send.

The problem it solves

Template errors mention line numbers in generated text, and indentation mistakes produce valid-looking YAML that means something different.

What it does

  • helm template NAME CHART -f values.yaml renders locally without a cluster. --show-only templates/ingress.yaml renders one file.
  • helm install --dry-run=server --debug renders and validates against the API server, including admission webhooks.
  • helm lint --strict catches common mistakes. toYaml plus nindent mismatches are the most frequent cause of errors.
  • --validate on helm template checks the output against cluster API versions.

Commands

bashRender and validate
helm lint ./shop --strict -f values-prod.yaml
helm template shop ./shop -f values-prod.yaml --show-only templates/ingress.yaml
helm template shop ./shop -f values-prod.yaml | kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f -
helm install shop ./shop -n shop --dry-run=server --debug 2>&1 | tail -30
Check yourself
Why use include instead of template for a labels helper?

include returns a string, so you can pipe it to nindent; template writes directly and cannot be piped.

Where do subchart values go in the parent values file?

Under a key with the subchart name, for example postgresql, or under global to reach all charts.

Section 28 of 65

Helm hooks, diff, OCI charts and delivery

6 concepts · about 45 minutes

A release is more than apply. Databases must migrate, changes should be reviewed before they land, and charts need a trusted home. This section covers hooks, previewing, OCI registries and how Helm fits into delivery.

Goals
  • Run migrations and checks with hooks and know their deletion policies
  • Preview changes with helm diff and publish charts to an OCI registry
  • Choose between pipeline driven Helm and GitOps controllers
28.1

Hooks

In plain words

A hook is a manifest in a chart that Helm runs at a chosen moment of the release lifecycle, such as before an upgrade, instead of treating it as a normal part of the release.

The problem it solves

A database migration must finish before the new Pods start, and a cleanup Job must run after an uninstall. Plain manifests are applied together with no ordering.

What it does

  • Marked by the annotation helm.sh/hook with values such as pre-install, post-install, pre-upgrade, post-upgrade, pre-delete, post-delete, pre-rollback, post-rollback and test.
  • Helm waits for hook Jobs and Pods to complete; a failed pre-upgrade hook stops the upgrade.
  • helm.sh/hook-weight orders hooks of the same kind (lower first, as strings of integers).
  • Hook objects are not part of the release, so helm uninstall does not remove them unless you set a delete policy.

A migration hook

yamltemplates/migrate-job.yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: shop-migrate
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": pre-install,pre-upgrade
    "helm.sh/hook-weight": "0"
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": before-hook-creation,hook-succeeded
spec:
  backoffLimit: 1
  activeDeadlineSeconds: 600
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: migrate
          image: registry.example.com/shop/api:1.8.3
          command: ["./migrate", "up"]
28.2

Hook delete policies and pitfalls

In plain words

Delete policies decide when Helm removes a hook object. Without one, a completed Job from the last run remains and the next run fails with "already exists".

The problem it solves

Hooks are the most common source of stuck pipelines: leftover Jobs, hooks waiting on resources that do not exist yet, and migrations that are not safe to run twice.

What it does

  • before-hook-creation (default) deletes the old object before a new one is made. hook-succeeded and hook-failed delete after the outcome.
  • Keep failed hooks (omit hook-failed) so you can read the Pod logs.
  • A pre-install hook runs before the release's other resources exist, so it cannot use a ServiceAccount or ConfigMap from the same chart unless that is also a hook with a lower weight.
  • Make migrations idempotent and backwards compatible, because a rollback does not undo them.

Diagnosing a stuck hook

bashFind the hook Job and its logs
helm get hooks shop -n shop | head -30
kubectl get jobs,pods -n shop -l job-name=shop-migrate
kubectl logs -n shop job/shop-migrate --tail=50
kubectl delete job shop-migrate -n shop     # remove a leftover before retrying
Careful

Hooks run in a helm upgrade --wait pipeline with the pipeline's timeout. A migration that takes 20 minutes needs a matching --timeout, or Helm marks the release failed while the Job continues.

28.3

helm diff and safe upgrades

In plain words

helm diff is a plugin that renders the new revision and shows what would change compared with the live release, in the same style as kubectl diff.

The problem it solves

Reading a values file tells you what you intended, not what will change in the cluster. A chart bump can alter dozens of objects you never mentioned.

What it does

  • Install with helm plugin install https://github.com/databus23/helm-diff.
  • helm diff upgrade RELEASE CHART -f values.yaml prints a coloured diff; --detailed-exitcode returns 2 when there are changes, which is useful in CI.
  • --suppress-secrets hides Secret content from logs.
  • Pair it with helm template | kubectl diff -f - to also compare against edits made outside Helm.

In CI

bashDiff gate
helm plugin install https://github.com/databus23/helm-diff
helm diff upgrade shop ./shop -n shop -f values-prod.yaml --suppress-secrets --detailed-exitcode
echo "exit=$?"     # 0 no change, 1 error, 2 changes found
28.4

OCI charts and registries

In plain words

Helm can store charts in any OCI registry (ECR, Harbor, GHCR, Artifact Registry), the same place you keep container images. A chart is addressed as oci://registry/path/name.

The problem it solves

Classic HTTP chart repositories need an index.yaml to be rebuilt and hosted. Teams already operate an image registry with auth, replication and retention, and want one system for both.

What it does

  • helm push chart.tgz oci://REGISTRY/PATH publishes; the chart name and version become the repository and tag.
  • helm install shop oci://REGISTRY/PATH/shop --version 1.2.0 pulls and installs. There is no helm repo add step.
  • helm registry login stores credentials. For Amazon ECR, pipe aws ecr get-login-password into it.
  • Pin the exact --version; OCI charts also support pulling by digest.

Amazon ECR example

bashPush and install from ECR
REG=123456789012.dkr.ecr.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com
aws ecr get-login-password --region eu-west-1 | helm registry login --username AWS --password-stdin "$REG"
aws ecr create-repository --repository-name charts/shop     # ECR needs the repo first
helm package ./shop                                           # shop-1.2.0.tgz
helm push shop-1.2.0.tgz oci://$REG/charts
helm install shop oci://$REG/charts/shop --version 1.2.0 -n shop
28.5

Signing, provenance and post-renderers

In plain words

You can sign a chart so consumers verify it was not altered, and you can pipe Helm's rendered output through a program (a post-renderer) before it is applied.

The problem it solves

Charts from third parties can change underneath you, and sometimes you must patch a chart you do not own, for example to add a label or a securityContext it does not expose.

What it does

  • helm package --sign creates a .prov file with a PGP signature; helm verify and --verify check it. Many teams instead sign OCI artifacts with cosign.
  • --post-renderer ./script receives rendered YAML on standard input and returns changed YAML on standard output. A common script runs kustomize build.
  • This is a clean bridge between Helm and Kustomize for charts you cannot modify.

A kustomize post-renderer

bashpost-render.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
cat > all.yaml                      # rendered chart arrives on stdin
kustomize build .                   # kustomization.yaml lists all.yaml plus patches
bashUse it
chmod +x post-render.sh
helm upgrade --install ingress ingress-nginx/ingress-nginx -n ingress --post-renderer ./post-render.sh
28.6

Helm in pipelines and GitOps

In plain words

Two common models exist. In pipeline driven delivery your CI runs helm upgrade. In GitOps a controller in the cluster (Argo CD or Flux) watches Git and applies the chart itself.

The problem it solves

Credentials for the cluster should not live in a CI system forever, and the live state should always match a reviewed source.

What it does

  • Pipeline model is simple and gives you hooks, --atomic and test steps natively; the pipeline needs cluster credentials, ideally short lived through OIDC.
  • Argo CD renders charts with helm template and applies the result itself. Helm hooks are mapped onto Argo sync hooks, and there is no Helm release object. Flux's helm-controller does keep a real Helm release.
  • Either way, pin chart versions and keep values in Git.
Choosing a delivery model
OptionPipeline helm upgrade
Choose whena small number of clusters and a team new to GitOps
Avoid whenmany clusters or a need for continuous drift correction
OptionFlux HelmRelease
Choose whenyou want real Helm releases with GitOps pull
Avoid whenyou need rich UI and app of apps views
OptionArgo CD Application
Choose whenyou want a UI, multi cluster and sync waves
Avoid whenyou rely on helm test or helm list showing the release
Check yourself
Why add before-hook-creation to a migration Job?

Otherwise the Job from the previous run still exists and the next hook fails with already exists.

What does helm diff --detailed-exitcode return when changes exist?

Exit code 2.

Section 29 of 65

Kustomize bases and overlays

6 concepts · about 40 minutes

Kustomize is built into kubectl (kubectl apply -k). Instead of templating, it takes valid YAML as a base and applies declared changes on top in overlays. Every input and output is plain Kubernetes YAML.

Goals
  • Explain how Kustomize customises plain YAML without templates
  • Build a base and per environment overlays
  • Use generators, name prefixes, images and replacements
29.1

What Kustomize is

In plain words

Kustomize reads a kustomization.yaml that lists resources and the changes to apply to them, then prints the final manifests. The original files are never modified.

The problem it solves

Helm templates are powerful but hide the YAML behind logic. Teams that only need "same app, different replicas and image per environment" want to keep readable YAML and avoid a template language.

What it does

  • kubectl kustomize DIR (or kustomize build DIR) renders; kubectl apply -k DIR renders and applies.
  • No variables or loops. Changes are expressed as patches, transformers and generators.
  • The standalone kustomize binary is often newer than the version embedded in kubectl.

Smallest example

yamlkustomization.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
namespace: shop
resources:
  - deployment.yaml
  - service.yaml
commonLabels:
  app.kubernetes.io/part-of: shop
bashRender and apply
kubectl kustomize . | head -30       # preview the output
kubectl apply -k . --dry-run=server  # validate against the API server
kubectl diff -k .                    # what would change
kubectl apply -k .
Note

commonLabels also rewrites selectors, and selectors of a Deployment are immutable. For labels on metadata only, use the newer labels: field with includeSelectors: false.

29.2

Bases and overlays

In plain words

A base holds the shared manifests. An overlay is another directory whose kustomization.yaml points at the base and adds environment-specific changes.

The problem it solves

Copying the whole manifest set per environment duplicates everything and the copies drift. You want one source and small differences.

What it does

  • Overlays reference a base in resources: by relative path or a remote Git URL pinned to a tag.
  • Overlays can stack: base, then overlays/prod, then overlays/prod-eu.
  • The directory structure is the convention, not a requirement.

An overlay

yamloverlays/prod/kustomization.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
namespace: shop-prod
namePrefix: prod-
resources:
  - ../../base
  - hpa.yaml
images:
  - name: registry.example.com/shop/api
    newTag: "1.8.3"
replicas:
  - name: api
    count: 5
bashBuild each environment
kubectl kustomize overlays/dev
kubectl kustomize overlays/prod | grep -E 'kind:|replicas:|image:'
29.3

The base manifests

In plain words

The base is ordinary, valid YAML that could be applied by itself. It uses no placeholders.

The problem it solves

A base that only works after substitution cannot be validated, linted or tested on its own.

What it does

  • The base lists its files in its own kustomization.yaml.
  • Keep names generic (api) and let overlays add prefixes, namespaces and labels.
  • Defaults in the base should be safe for the smallest environment.

Base files

yamlbase/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: registry.example.com/shop/api:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          resources:
            requests: {cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi}
            limits: {memory: 256Mi}
yamlbase/kustomization.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
resources:
  - deployment.yaml
  - service.yaml
29.4

Image, replica, namespace and name transformers

In plain words

Built-in transformers change common fields everywhere they appear: image tags, replica counts, namespace, name prefix and suffix, labels and annotations.

The problem it solves

CI needs to set a new image tag after every build. Editing YAML with sed is fragile; Kustomize does it structurally.

What it does

  • images: replaces name with newName or newTag or digest in Pod specs of all workload kinds.
  • replicas: sets the count for named Deployments or StatefulSets.
  • namespace: sets the namespace on all namespaced objects; namePrefix and nameSuffix rename and also fix up references (for example a ConfigMap name used by a Deployment).
  • kustomize edit set image NAME=NAME:TAG updates the file for you.

Commands

bashSet a tag from CI
cd overlays/prod
kustomize edit set image registry.example.com/shop/api=registry.example.com/shop/api:1.8.4
kustomize edit set namespace shop-prod
git diff --stat
Check yourself
Why not change the image with sed?

sed matches text; Kustomize edits the right field in every workload structurally and keeps the YAML valid.

29.5

ConfigMap and Secret generators

In plain words

A generator creates a ConfigMap or Secret from files or literals and adds a hash of the content to its name. When the content changes, the name changes, and every workload that references it is updated and rolled.

The problem it solves

Pods do not restart when a ConfigMap changes. People add manual annotations or restart by hand to pick up new config.

What it does

  • configMapGenerator and secretGenerator accept files, literals and envs.
  • The generated name is suffixed such as app-config-7g8d5k2b9f. References in the same kustomization are rewritten.
  • behavior: merge or replace lets an overlay change a generated map from the base.
  • generatorOptions.disableNameSuffixHash: true turns hashing off if something outside needs the plain name.

Generators

yamlkustomization.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
resources:
  - deployment.yaml
configMapGenerator:
  - name: app-config
    literals:
      - LOG_LEVEL=info
      - FEATURE_X=false
  - name: nginx-conf
    files:
      - nginx.conf
generatorOptions:
  labels:
    generated: "true"
Careful

Do not put real secrets in a secretGenerator committed to Git. Use External Secrets, Sealed Secrets or SOPS, and let Kustomize only reference the resulting Secret name.

29.6

Replacements and vars

In plain words

replacements copy a value from one field of one object into fields of other objects, for example a hostname defined once and used in an Ingress and a ConfigMap.

The problem it solves

Kustomize has no variables, but the same value (a domain, a service name) often has to appear in several places and must stay consistent.

What it does

  • A replacement has a source (object, fieldPath) and targets (select objects, list fieldPaths).
  • It replaces the deprecated vars feature, which should not be used for new work.
  • options.delimiter and index replace a part of a string such as one segment of a hostname.

Example

yamlkustomization.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
resources:
  - configmap.yaml
  - ingress.yaml
  - deployment.yaml
replacements:
  - source:
      kind: ConfigMap
      name: site
      fieldPath: data.domain
    targets:
      - select:
          kind: Ingress
          name: shop
        fieldPaths:
          - spec.rules.0.host
      - select:
          kind: Deployment
          name: api
        fieldPaths:
          - spec.template.spec.containers.[name=api].env.[name=PUBLIC_HOST].value
← PreviousNext →
Section 30 of 65

Kustomize patches, components and Helm together

6 concepts · about 40 minutes

Patching is where Kustomize earns its keep. This section covers the two patch styles, reusable components, inflating Helm charts, and how to decide between the tools.

Goals
  • Write strategic merge and JSON 6902 patches with targets
  • Package optional features as components
  • Choose between Helm and Kustomize and combine them
30.1

Strategic merge patches

In plain words

A strategic merge patch is a partial manifest. You write only the fields you want to change, with enough identity (kind and name) to find the target, and Kustomize merges it in.

The problem it solves

You need to change one field, such as a memory limit, in the base without copying the whole Deployment.

What it does

  • Lists of containers merge by the name key, so a patch naming container api updates just that container.
  • Setting a value to null deletes a field; $patch: delete removes a whole object.
  • patches: with path or inline patch and an optional target selector is the current syntax. patchesStrategicMerge is deprecated.

Patch file

yamloverlays/prod/kustomization.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
resources:
  - ../../base
patches:
  - path: resources-patch.yaml
    target:
      kind: Deployment
      name: api
yamloverlays/prod/resources-patch.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          resources:
            requests: {cpu: 500m, memory: 1Gi}
            limits: {memory: 1Gi}
30.2

JSON 6902 patches

In plain words

A JSON patch is an explicit list of operations (add, remove, replace) on paths in the document. It is precise and works on any object, including custom resources.

The problem it solves

Strategic merge relies on schema knowledge. For CRDs, or when you must change one list item by index or remove a field, you need exact control.

What it does

  • Each operation has op, path and for add or replace a value.
  • List items are addressed by index (/spec/template/spec/containers/0/args/- appends).
  • Inline patches in kustomization.yaml keep small changes next to the target selection.
  • Selectors can match by kind, name, labelSelector or annotationSelector, including regular expressions for names.

Inline JSON patch

yamlkustomization.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
resources:
  - ../../base
patches:
  - target:
      kind: Deployment
      name: api
    patch: |-
      - op: add
        path: /spec/template/spec/containers/0/args/-
        value: --log-format=json
      - op: replace
        path: /spec/replicas
        value: 4
      - op: remove
        path: /spec/template/spec/containers/0/ports/0
30.3

Components

In plain words

A component is a reusable bundle of resources and patches for an optional feature. Overlays opt in by listing it under components:.

The problem it solves

Several overlays need the same optional feature, such as a monitoring sidecar or a PodDisruptionBudget, but not all of them. Copying patches between overlays repeats work.

What it does

  • A component's kustomization.yaml has kind: Component and apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1alpha1.
  • It is applied after the resources of the overlay, so it can patch them.
  • Overlays then differ only by which components they include.

A component

yamlcomponents/pdb/kustomization.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component
resources:
  - pdb.yaml
yamloverlays/prod/kustomization.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
resources:
  - ../../base
components:
  - ../../components/pdb
  - ../../components/hpa
30.4

Remote bases and the helmCharts generator

In plain words

A kustomization can use a Git repository as a base, and can inflate a Helm chart into plain YAML so you can patch it.

The problem it solves

Third-party software ships as a Helm chart or a Git repository, and you need to adjust it without forking.

What it does

  • Remote base: github.com/org/repo//path?ref=v1.2.3. Always pin ref to a tag or commit.
  • helmCharts: renders a chart (name, repo, version, releaseName, namespace, valuesInline) during build. Run with kustomize build --enable-helm.
  • Patches then apply to the rendered output, which is the same bridge a Helm post-renderer provides.
  • Helm hooks and release tracking are lost; Kustomize only emits YAML.

Example

yamlkustomization.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
helmCharts:
  - name: ingress-nginx
    repo: https://kubernetes.github.io/ingress-nginx
    version: 4.11.3
    releaseName: ingress
    namespace: ingress
    valuesInline:
      controller:
        replicaCount: 3
patches:
  - target:
      kind: Deployment
      name: ingress-ingress-nginx-controller
    patch: |-
      - op: add
        path: /spec/template/spec/priorityClassName
        value: system-cluster-critical
bashBuild
kustomize build --enable-helm . | kubectl apply --server-side -f -
30.5

Helm or Kustomize

In plain words

They solve different problems. Helm packages and distributes software with logic and a release lifecycle. Kustomize adapts YAML you own for several environments without logic.

The problem it solves

Teams pick one tool for everything, then fight it: complicated templates for simple overlays, or large patch sets for software that is really configurable.

What it does

  • Use Helm to consume third-party software and to publish software to others.
  • Use Kustomize for your own apps across dev, staging and prod when differences are small.
  • Combine them: Helm for the vendor chart, Kustomize for last-mile patches, a GitOps tool to apply.
  • Both must be reviewed as rendered output; render in CI and diff.
Picking a tool
OptionHelm
Choose whenyou install vendor software or ship your app to many users
Avoid whenthe only difference is replicas and image tag per environment
OptionKustomize
Choose whenyou own the YAML and need per environment overlays
Avoid whenyou need hooks, conditionals or a distributable package
OptionHelm plus Kustomize
Choose whenyou must patch a chart you cannot change
Avoid whena plain values override already does the job
30.6

Validating rendered output

In plain words

Whatever generates your YAML, the final result should be checked before it reaches the cluster: schema validity, policy rules and live diff.

The problem it solves

A typo in a patch path may still render valid YAML that is silently wrong, such as a limit that was not applied.

What it does

  • kubectl apply --dry-run=server checks against the real API, including admission webhooks.
  • kubeconform validates against Kubernetes JSON schemas offline and can include CRD schemas.
  • kubectl diff shows the effect on live objects. Policy tools such as Kyverno CLI or conftest can enforce rules in CI.
  • Check that your patch really landed by grepping the rendered output for the changed value.

Commands

bashCI validation
for env in dev staging prod; do
  kustomize build overlays/$env > /tmp/$env.yaml
  kubeconform -strict -summary -ignore-missing-schemas /tmp/$env.yaml
done
kubectl diff -f /tmp/prod.yaml || test $? -eq 1   # diff exits 1 when differences exist
Check yourself
How do overlays opt in to optional features?

By listing components in the components field of their kustomization.

Which patch style works well on a custom resource?

A JSON 6902 patch, because it needs no schema knowledge.
