Section 31 of 65

Observability signals in Kubernetes

7 concepts · about 45 minutes

Troubleshooting starts with signals the cluster already produces. This section covers where Kubernetes records state, events, resource usage and logs before you add any extra tooling.

Goals
  • Read status, conditions and events to learn why an object is unhealthy
  • Use metrics-server and kubectl top and know what they do not show
  • Collect container logs and know the logging architecture options
31.1

Status, conditions and describe

In plain words

Every object has a spec (what you asked for) and a status (what the controller observed). Conditions are named true or false facts inside status, such as Ready or PodScheduled, each with a reason and message.

The problem it solves

"It does not work" is not actionable. You need the controller's own explanation, which is almost always written into status.

What it does

  • kubectl describe shows status, conditions and the related events in one view.
  • kubectl get -o yaml shows the raw status, including containerStatuses with lastState (why the previous container died).
  • kubectl get -o jsonpath or custom-columns extracts one field across many objects.
  • kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready blocks until a condition is met, useful in scripts.

Reading status

bashWhere to look first
kubectl describe pod api-7d9f8c-x2k4p -n shop | sed -n '/Conditions/,$p'
kubectl get pod api-7d9f8c-x2k4p -n shop -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState}{"\n"}'
kubectl get pods -n shop -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,PHASE:.status.phase,NODE:.spec.nodeName,RESTARTS:.status.containerStatuses[0].restartCount
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod -l app=api -n shop --timeout=120s
Check yourself
Where do you find why the previous container instance died?

In status.containerStatuses[].lastState.terminated, which shows reason, exit code and timestamps.

31.2

Events

In plain words

Events are short records created by the scheduler, kubelet and controllers: "Scheduled", "Pulling image", "FailedMount", "BackOff". They explain what happened to an object.

The problem it solves

Status says the state, but not the sequence. A Pod that is Pending was refused for a specific reason, and that reason is only in an event.

What it does

  • Events are namespaced objects with a short retention, about one hour by default. Look early or ship them to storage.
  • kubectl events (stable since 1.26) sorts and filters better than kubectl get events.
  • Types are Normal and Warning. Filter on warnings first.
  • Tools such as the kubernetes-event-exporter forward events to logs or alerting.

Querying events

bashEvents that matter
kubectl events -n shop --types=Warning                       # warnings only
kubectl events -n shop --for pod/api-7d9f8c-x2k4p            # one object
kubectl events -A --types=Warning --watch                    # live view across the cluster
kubectl get events -n shop --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -20
31.3

metrics-server and kubectl top

In plain words

metrics-server is a small add-on that collects current CPU and memory use from each kubelet and exposes it through the Metrics API. kubectl top and the HorizontalPodAutoscaler read it.

The problem it solves

You need a quick answer to "which Pod or node is using the most CPU or memory right now" without installing a full monitoring stack.

What it does

  • Provides only the latest sample (about 15 to 60 seconds old), not history. For history use Prometheus.
  • Memory shown is the working set, which is what the kernel considers for OOM kills.
  • Required for HPA on CPU and memory. EKS does not install it by default; Gardener-managed clusters such as Kyma commonly provide it.
  • If kubectl top says "Metrics API not available", check the metrics-server Deployment and the APIService.

Commands

bashResource usage now
kubectl top nodes
kubectl top pods -n shop --sort-by=memory
kubectl top pod api-7d9f8c-x2k4p -n shop --containers
kubectl get apiservice v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io           # Available must be True
kubectl get --raw /apis/metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1/nodes | head -c 400
31.4

Container logs

In plain words

Containers write to standard output and standard error. The container runtime stores those streams as files on the node, and kubectl logs reads them through the kubelet.

The problem it solves

When a Pod misbehaves you need its output, including from the instance that just crashed, without logging into the node.

What it does

  • kubectl logs POD -c CONTAINER reads the current instance, --previous reads the last terminated one, -f follows, --since=10m and --tail=100 limit output.
  • -l app=api --all-containers --prefix reads many Pods at once; add --max-log-requests if you exceed the default of 5.
  • The kubelet rotates files (containerLogMaxSize 10Mi and containerLogMaxFiles 5 by default), so old logs vanish with the Pod or the node.
  • Logs of a deleted Pod are gone unless a collector shipped them.

Commands

bashReading logs
kubectl logs deploy/api -n shop --tail=100
kubectl logs api-7d9f8c-x2k4p -n shop --previous            # the crashed instance
kubectl logs -l app=api -n shop --all-containers --prefix --since=15m --max-log-requests=10
kubectl logs api-7d9f8c-x2k4p -n shop -c istio-proxy        # a sidecar
Check yourself
Why does kubectl logs --previous matter for CrashLoopBackOff?

The current container may have just restarted and be empty; the useful error is in the previous instance.

31.5

Cluster-level logging architecture

In plain words

Kubernetes itself does not store logs long term. A log agent runs on every node as a DaemonSet, reads the container log files, adds Pod labels and sends them to a backend.

The problem it solves

Pods are disposable. When one is evicted or a node is replaced, its logs disappear exactly when you need them.

What it does

  • Node agents: Fluent Bit, Vector, Promtail or Grafana Alloy, Filebeat. A DaemonSet needs only read access to /var/log.
  • Backends: Loki, Elasticsearch or OpenSearch, CloudWatch Logs (EKS with Fluent Bit or the CloudWatch Observability add-on), SAP Cloud Logging on BTP.
  • Emit structured JSON logs with a request ID; metadata enrichment adds namespace, Pod and labels.
  • Sidecar log agents are only needed when an app writes to files instead of stdout.

A Fluent Bit DaemonSet skeleton

yamllog-agent.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: log-agent
  namespace: logging
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: log-agent
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: log-agent
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: log-agent
      tolerations:
        - operator: Exists
      containers:
        - name: fluent-bit
          image: cr.fluentbit.io/fluent/fluent-bit:3.1
          resources:
            requests: {cpu: 50m, memory: 64Mi}
            limits: {memory: 128Mi}
          volumeMounts:
            - name: varlog
              mountPath: /var/log
              readOnly: true
      volumes:
        - name: varlog
          hostPath:
            path: /var/log
31.6

Metrics and the Prometheus model

In plain words

Prometheus pulls numeric time series from HTTP endpoints. In Kubernetes it discovers targets through the API, so new Pods are scraped automatically.

The problem it solves

kubectl top shows now. Capacity planning, alerting and finding a slow leak need history.

What it does

  • Core sources: kubelet and cAdvisor (container CPU and memory), kube-state-metrics (object state such as restarts and Pod phase), node-exporter (host), and your own /metrics.
  • The Prometheus Operator adds ServiceMonitor and PodMonitor CRDs that declare what to scrape. kube-prometheus-stack bundles all of this.
  • Useful signals: container_memory_working_set_bytes, kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total, kube_pod_status_phase, container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total.
  • Managed options: Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus, Container Insights, SAP Cloud Logging and Dynatrace on BTP.

Declaring a scrape

yamlservicemonitor.yaml
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: ServiceMonitor
metadata:
  name: api
  namespace: shop
  labels:
    release: kube-prometheus-stack
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  endpoints:
    - port: http
      path: /metrics
      interval: 30s
Note

The release label must match what your Prometheus selects. A ServiceMonitor that never appears in targets is usually a label mismatch.

31.7

Probes, API health and control plane signals

In plain words

Readiness, liveness and startup probes tell the kubelet about application health. Separately, the API server exposes /readyz and /livez, and control plane components expose metrics.

The problem it solves

A running process is not necessarily working. Traffic should only reach Pods that are ready, and hung processes should be restarted.

What it does

  • A failing readiness probe removes the Pod from Service endpoints without restarting it. A failing liveness probe restarts the container. Startup probe delays the other two for slow starters.
  • Probe failures appear as events (Unhealthy) and show in describe.
  • kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose' lists API server checks.
  • On managed control planes (EKS, Gardener) you cannot reach the scheduler or controller manager directly; use the provider's control plane logging and API server metrics.

Commands

bashHealth endpoints
kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose' | tail -15
kubectl get --raw='/livez'
kubectl get endpoints api -n shop -o wide            # only ready Pods are listed
kubectl get endpointslices -n shop -l kubernetes.io/service-name=api
Check yourself
A Pod is Running but receives no traffic. Which probe is likely failing?

The readiness probe; the Pod is removed from the Service endpoints.

← PreviousNext →
Section 32 of 65

Troubleshooting playbook, Pod startup and runtime

6 concepts · about 50 minutes

Most Kubernetes incidents fall into a small set of patterns. This playbook starts with a method and then walks through each pattern with the commands to confirm it and the usual fix.

Goals
  • Follow a repeatable method to find the layer that is failing
  • Diagnose Pending, CrashLoopBackOff, ImagePullBackOff, OOMKilled and evictions with exact commands
  • Fix the cause rather than restart the symptom
32.1

The troubleshooting method

In plain words

Work from the outside in and from the object to its owner: is it scheduled, is it started, is it ready, is it reachable. Each stage has its own evidence.

The problem it solves

Random restarts and kubectl delete pod hide the cause and the problem returns. A fixed order avoids guesswork and keeps you from changing three things at once.

What it does

  • Stage 1, scheduling: Pod phase Pending, event FailedScheduling.
  • Stage 2, start: image pull, volume mount, container create (ImagePullBackOff, ContainerCreating, CreateContainerConfigError).
  • Stage 3, run: process exits or is killed (CrashLoopBackOff, OOMKilled).
  • Stage 4, ready and reachable: readiness probe, Service endpoints, DNS, NetworkPolicy.
  • Always check what changed: a rollout, a node event, a quota, a new policy.

First five commands

bashAlways start here
kubectl get pods -n shop -o wide                              # phase, restarts, node
kubectl describe pod POD -n shop | tail -25                   # conditions and events
kubectl events -n shop --for pod/POD
kubectl logs POD -n shop --previous --tail=50
kubectl rollout history deploy/api -n shop                    # what changed recently
Check yourself
Why start with events rather than logs for a Pending Pod?

A Pending Pod has not started, so it has no logs. The scheduler explains itself in events.

32.2

Pending Pods

In plain words

A Pod stays Pending when no node can run it yet. The scheduler tells you the reason in a FailedScheduling event.

The problem it solves

New Pods never start, a rollout stalls, or the cluster autoscaler does not add nodes.

What it does

  • Insufficient cpu or Insufficient memory: requests exceed free capacity. Reduce requests or add nodes.
  • node(s) had untolerated taint: add a toleration or use a different pool.
  • didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector: labels on nodes do not exist.
  • pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims: the PVC is pending (see storage).
  • exceeded quota appears when the Deployment cannot create a Pod at all; look at ReplicaSet events instead.
  • A topology spread or anti-affinity rule that cannot be satisfied also leaves Pods Pending.

Commands

bashWhy is it Pending
kubectl get pods -n shop --field-selector=status.phase=Pending
kubectl describe pod POD -n shop | grep -A8 -i 'events'
kubectl describe nodes | grep -A6 'Allocated resources'      # requests already placed
kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,TAINTS:.spec.taints
kubectl get resourcequota,limitrange -n shop
kubectl describe rs -n shop -l app=api | tail -15            # quota errors show on the ReplicaSet
Tip

Requests, not actual usage, decide scheduling. A node at 10% CPU use can be "full" if the sum of requests is high. Compare kubectl top nodes with the Allocated resources output.

32.3

ImagePullBackOff and ErrImagePull

In plain words

The kubelet could not download the container image. It retries with an increasing delay, which is the BackOff in the name.

The problem it solves

The Pod is scheduled but never starts, and the rollout stalls on the new ReplicaSet.

What it does

  • Read the exact error in describe: manifest unknown (tag does not exist), unauthorized or denied (credentials), no such host or timeout (network or DNS), toomanyrequests (registry rate limit).
  • Private registry: create a docker-registry Secret and reference it in imagePullSecrets, or attach it to the ServiceAccount.
  • On EKS with ECR the node role needs AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryReadOnly; ECR tokens are handled by the kubelet credential provider. Cross-account ECR needs a repository policy.
  • Check the architecture: an arm64-only image on amd64 nodes fails differently (exec format error) after pulling.

Commands

bashPull failures
kubectl describe pod POD -n shop | grep -E 'Failed|Back-off|image' 
kubectl get pod POD -n shop -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].image}{"\n"}'
kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred -n shop \
  --docker-server=registry.example.com --docker-username=ci --docker-password="$REG_TOKEN"
kubectl patch serviceaccount default -n shop -p '{"imagePullSecrets":[{"name":"regcred"}]}'
kubectl debug node/NODE -it --image=busybox:1.36 -- nslookup registry.example.com
32.4

CrashLoopBackOff

In plain words

The container starts, exits, and the kubelet restarts it with a delay that doubles from 10 seconds up to 5 minutes. CrashLoopBackOff is a symptom, never a cause.

The problem it solves

The application never becomes stable. Restart counts rise and the rollout does not complete.

What it does

  • First get the exit code: kubectl get pod -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState.terminated}'. 1 is an application error, 137 is SIGKILL (often OOM or failed liveness), 143 is SIGTERM, 126 / 127 mean command not executable or not found.
  • Read logs --previous. Typical causes are missing config or Secret values, an unreachable dependency at startup, bad command or args, and a liveness probe that kills a slow starter.
  • If there are no logs, the process may fail before logging; use kubectl debug with a copy that overrides the command.
  • A Pod that exits 0 under a Deployment also loops, since Deployments expect long running processes.

Commands

bashDiagnose a crash loop
kubectl get pod POD -n shop -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState.terminated}{"\n"}'
kubectl logs POD -n shop --previous --tail=80
kubectl describe pod POD -n shop | grep -E 'Liveness|Readiness|Startup|Restart Count'
kubectl debug POD -n shop -it --copy-to=api-debug --container=api -- sh   # copy with a shell instead of the app
kubectl delete pod api-debug -n shop
32.5

OOMKilled and memory limits

In plain words

When a container uses more memory than its limit, the kernel's OOM killer ends it. Kubernetes records Reason: OOMKilled with exit code 137.

The problem it solves

The Pod restarts at seemingly random times, and logs end abruptly with no error.

What it does

  • Confirm with lastState.terminated.reason. The cause can be a leak, a limit set too low, or runtime settings such as the JVM heap not matching the container limit.
  • Memory is incompressible, unlike CPU, which is throttled. Set the memory limit equal to the request for predictable behaviour and Guaranteed or Burstable QoS.
  • The limit counts page cache and tmpfs (emptyDir with medium: Memory) too, not just heap.
  • Use the working set metric, not RSS, when sizing. VPA in recommendation mode helps pick numbers.
  • A node level OOM (the node ran out of memory) is different: the kernel kills by score and the kubelet may evict Pods first.

Commands

bashConfirm and size
kubectl get pod POD -n shop -o jsonpath='{range .status.containerStatuses[*]}{.name}{" "}{.lastState.terminated.reason}{" "}{.lastState.terminated.exitCode}{"\n"}{end}'
kubectl top pod POD -n shop --containers
kubectl get pod POD -n shop -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}{"\n"}'
kubectl describe node NODE | grep -A3 -i 'oom\|MemoryPressure'
yamlRight sized memory
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  containers:
    - name: api
      image: registry.example.com/shop/api:1.8.3
      env:
        - name: JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
          value: "-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70"
      resources:
        requests: {cpu: 250m, memory: 768Mi}
        limits: {memory: 768Mi}
32.6

Evictions and node pressure

In plain words

When a node runs low on memory, disk or process IDs, the kubelet evicts Pods to protect the node. Evicted Pods show status Failed with reason Evicted.

The problem it solves

Pods vanish from a node with no deployment change, and Evicted Pods pile up in the namespace.

What it does

  • Conditions: MemoryPressure, DiskPressure, PIDPressure on the node. A pressured node also gets a taint, so new Pods avoid it.
  • Eviction order favours Pods that exceed their requests and have low priority; Guaranteed Pods are last.
  • ephemeral-storage requests and limits protect against logs and emptyDir filling the disk.
  • Evicted Pods are replaced by their controller; the old objects are leftovers (clean up with a field selector).
  • This differs from preemption (scheduler removes lower priority Pods to place a higher one) and from API-initiated eviction during drain.

Commands

bashFind and clean evictions
kubectl describe node NODE | grep -E 'Conditions' -A8
kubectl get pods -A --field-selector=status.phase=Failed | grep Evicted | head
kubectl get pod POD -n shop -o jsonpath='{.status.reason}{" "}{.status.message}{"\n"}'
kubectl delete pods -n shop --field-selector=status.phase=Failed
kubectl top node NODE
Check yourself
Which resource is incompressible, CPU or memory?

Memory. CPU is throttled; memory over the limit causes an OOM kill.

Why do Guaranteed Pods survive evictions longest?

Their requests equal their limits, so they never use more than they asked for, which is the first eviction criterion.

← PreviousNext →
Section 33 of 65

Troubleshooting playbook, network, nodes and storage

6 concepts · about 50 minutes

Pod level problems are only half of the playbook. The other half is connectivity, node health and storage, where the cause is rarely in the Pod you are looking at.

Goals
  • Trace a failing connection from Pod to Service to endpoints to DNS to policy
  • Diagnose NotReady nodes and PVCs stuck in Pending or Terminating
  • Use kubectl debug with ephemeral containers and node debugging
33.1

Service has no endpoints

In plain words

A Service forwards to the Pods that match its selector and are Ready. If the endpoint list is empty, connections fail even though Pods are running.

The problem it solves

connection refused or timeouts when calling a Service name, while the Pods look healthy.

What it does

  • Compare kubectl get svc -o yaml selector with Pod labels. A single mismatched label gives zero endpoints.
  • Check targetPort matches the container port the process listens on, and that the process binds 0.0.0.0, not 127.0.0.1.
  • Pods failing readiness are excluded; see them as notReadyAddresses.
  • Test inside the cluster, not from your laptop, to separate application from exposure problems.

Commands

bashCheck the chain
kubectl get svc api -n shop -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector}{" "}{.spec.ports}{"\n"}'
kubectl get pods -n shop --show-labels
kubectl get endpointslices -n shop -l kubernetes.io/service-name=api -o wide
kubectl get pods -n shop -l app=api -o wide        # same selector as the Service
kubectl run curl --rm -it --restart=Never -n shop --image=curlimages/curl:8.8.0 -- curl -sv http://api/healthz
33.2

DNS failures

In plain words

Pods resolve names through CoreDNS. Names look like service.namespace.svc.cluster.local, and short names work through search domains in the Pod's /etc/resolv.conf.

The problem it solves

Applications report no such host, intermittent timeouts of five seconds, or slow lookups.

What it does

  • First prove DNS rather than assume: resolve the name from a Pod, then resolve an external name.
  • Check CoreDNS Pods and logs in kube-system; look at their CPU throttling and restarts.
  • ndots:5 makes external names try several search domains first, causing extra queries. Use fully qualified names with a trailing dot or lower ndots through dnsConfig.
  • Intermittent failures often come from a NetworkPolicy blocking egress to port 53, a node level conntrack issue, or an overloaded CoreDNS. NodeLocal DNSCache reduces load.
  • On EKS, CoreDNS is a managed add-on; scale it through add-on config or an autoscaler.

Commands

bashProve DNS
kubectl run dns --rm -it --restart=Never -n shop --image=registry.k8s.io/e2e-test-images/agnhost:2.47 -- nslookup api.shop.svc.cluster.local
kubectl exec POD -n shop -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns -o wide
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns --tail=30
kubectl top pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
kubectl get cm coredns -n kube-system -o jsonpath='{.data.Corefile}'
yamlReduce ndots for one workload
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: api-dns
spec:
  dnsConfig:
    options:
      - name: ndots
        value: "2"
  containers:
    - name: api
      image: registry.example.com/shop/api:1.8.3
33.3

NetworkPolicy blocking traffic

In plain words

If a Pod is selected by a NetworkPolicy, only traffic that a policy allows can reach it (ingress) or leave it (egress). A missing allow rule looks exactly like a network fault: timeouts, not refusals.

The problem it solves

A new default deny policy is applied and half the application stops working, including DNS lookups and calls to the metrics scraper.

What it does

  • List policies in both namespaces involved; check policyTypes and whether egress DNS (UDP and TCP 53 to kube-dns) is allowed.
  • Remember a connection needs allowance at both ends: egress from the source and ingress at the destination.
  • A timeout suggests policy or routing; connection refused suggests nothing is listening or the Service has no endpoints.
  • Cilium users can see decisions with Hubble (hubble observe --verdict DROPPED); Calico has flow logs.

Commands and a DNS egress allow

bashInspect policies
kubectl get networkpolicy -A
kubectl describe networkpolicy -n shop
kubectl get pod POD -n shop --show-labels                      # does a policy select it
kubectl run nettest --rm -it --restart=Never -n shop --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- nc -zv api 80
yamlallow-dns-egress.yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-dns-egress
  namespace: shop
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: ["Egress"]
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
          podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              k8s-app: kube-dns
      ports:
        - {protocol: UDP, port: 53}
        - {protocol: TCP, port: 53}
33.4

Nodes in NotReady

In plain words

A node is NotReady when the kubelet stops reporting healthy to the control plane. After a grace period the node gets taints and its Pods are evicted.

The problem it solves

Workloads stop being scheduled to a node, or Pods on it go Unknown or Terminating.

What it does

  • Read node Conditions and events: Ready, MemoryPressure, DiskPressure, PIDPressure, NetworkUnavailable.
  • Causes: kubelet or container runtime stopped, node out of disk or memory, CNI failure, lost network to the API server, instance terminated.
  • Debug the node with kubectl debug node/NAME and chroot /host; then systemctl status kubelet, journalctl -u kubelet, crictl ps.
  • The node lifecycle controller adds node.kubernetes.io/not-ready and unreachable taints; Pods tolerate them for 300 seconds by default.
  • On managed clusters prefer replacing the node (EKS node group, Gardener worker pool, Karpenter) over repairing it, after capturing evidence.

Commands

bashInvestigate a node
kubectl get nodes -o wide
kubectl describe node NODE | sed -n '/Conditions/,/Addresses/p'
kubectl get lease NODE -n kube-node-lease -o jsonpath='{.spec.renewTime}{"\n"}'
kubectl debug node/NODE -it --image=busybox:1.36
# inside the debug container, the node filesystem is at /host
chroot /host systemctl status kubelet --no-pager
chroot /host journalctl -u kubelet --since "30 min ago" | tail -30
chroot /host crictl ps | head
Careful

Do not delete a NotReady node object from the API to "fix" it unless you know the instance is gone. For StatefulSets with attached volumes, force-deleting Pods on an unreachable node risks two writers on one volume.

33.5

PVC stuck Pending or Terminating

In plain words

A PersistentVolumeClaim is Pending until a volume is bound to it. A claim or Pod stuck in Terminating usually waits on a finalizer, a mount or a detach.

The problem it solves

Stateful Pods stay Pending, or a deleted namespace never finishes deleting.

What it does

  • Pending PVC: describe pvc shows the provisioner message. Typical causes: no default StorageClass, wrong class name, access mode unsupported, quota, or WaitForFirstConsumer binding where the claim waits for a Pod to be scheduled.
  • Zone mismatch: an EBS volume lives in one AZ; the Pod must be scheduled in that zone. Topology aware binding avoids this.
  • Multi-Attach error: a ReadWriteOnce volume is still attached to another node. Wait for detach or check the old Pod.
  • Terminating PVC is protected by kubernetes.io/pvc-protection while a Pod uses it. Stuck namespaces typically wait on custom resources with finalizers.
  • CSI problems show in the driver Pods (ebs-csi-controller) logs.

Commands

bashStorage checks
kubectl get pvc,pv -n shop
kubectl describe pvc data-db-0 -n shop | tail -15
kubectl get storageclass
kubectl get volumeattachments | head
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l app=ebs-csi-controller -c csi-provisioner --tail=30
kubectl get namespace shop -o jsonpath='{.spec.finalizers}{" "}{.status.conditions}{"\n"}'
Check yourself
Why does a PVC stay Pending with WaitForFirstConsumer?

Binding is delayed until a Pod using it is scheduled, so the volume is created in the right zone. It is normal until a consumer exists.

33.6

kubectl debug and ephemeral containers

In plain words

kubectl debug adds a temporary container with your tools to a running Pod, or makes a modified copy of a Pod, or opens a shell on a node.

The problem it solves

Production images are often minimal or distroless, with no shell, curl or tcpdump. You still need to look inside the Pod's network and process space.

What it does

  • Ephemeral container: kubectl debug -it POD --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=api shares the network namespace, and with --target the process namespace, of the container. It cannot be removed until the Pod ends.
  • Copy: --copy-to=NAME clones the Pod; --container plus a new command or --set-image changes it. The original is unharmed.
  • Node: kubectl debug node/NAME -it --image=... runs a Pod on that node with the host filesystem at /host.
  • Needs RBAC on pods/ephemeralcontainers. Pod Security restricted may block node debug profiles; use --profile= options (general, baseline, restricted, netadmin, sysadmin) as appropriate.

Commands

bashDebug recipes
kubectl debug -it api-7d9f8c-x2k4p -n shop --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=api -- bash
kubectl debug api-7d9f8c-x2k4p -n shop -it --copy-to=api-dbg --set-image=api=busybox:1.36 -- sh
kubectl debug node/ip-10-0-1-23.eu-west-1.compute.internal -it --image=busybox:1.36 --profile=sysadmin
kubectl get pod api-7d9f8c-x2k4p -n shop -o jsonpath='{.spec.ephemeralContainers[*].name}{"\n"}'
kubectl delete pod api-dbg -n shop

Section 34 of 65

Upgrade strategy, version skew and deprecated APIs

6 concepts · about 45 minutes

Kubernetes ships a minor release about every four months and supports roughly the latest three. Staying current is routine work, not an event. This section covers how to plan upgrades so they stay boring.

Goals
  • Plan an upgrade around the release cadence and version skew rules
  • Find and fix deprecated API usage before it breaks
  • Prepare a checklist and rollback position for a control plane upgrade
34.1

Release cadence and support windows

In plain words

Kubernetes releases a new minor version (1.33, 1.34, 1.35 and so on) about three times a year. The community supports the newest three minor versions with patches. Managed services add their own windows.

The problem it solves

A cluster left on one version falls out of security patches, add-ons stop supporting it, and a long jump later is risky because many changes arrive at once.

What it does

  • Upstream patch support is around 14 months per minor version. EKS standard support is 14 months, then paid extended support for a further 12 months. Gardener offers a version to Kyma and other shoots for a limited time and expires older ones, forcing an update.
  • Always check the release notes "Urgent upgrade notes" and "Deprecation" sections for the target version.
  • Plan a recurring slot, such as one minor upgrade per quarter, rather than reacting to end of life.
  • Verify the exact supported versions in the provider console or CLI instead of relying on memory.

Checking what is available

bashVersions you can use
kubectl version                                                # client and server versions
kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,KUBELET:.status.nodeInfo.kubeletVersion
aws eks describe-cluster --name shop --query 'cluster.version' --output text
aws eks describe-cluster-versions --query 'clusterVersions[].{v:clusterVersion,s:status}' --output table
34.2

Version skew rules

In plain words

Components of a cluster may run different minor versions, but only within strict limits. You upgrade the control plane first, then nodes, then clients.

The problem it solves

Upgrading in the wrong order, or skipping minors, breaks API compatibility between the kubelet, the API server and your tools.

What it does

  • kube-apiserver: with several API servers (HA), they may differ by at most one minor.
  • kubelet: may be up to three minor versions older than the API server (since 1.28) but never newer.
  • kube-proxy: same as kubelet. controller-manager and scheduler: up to one minor older than the API server.
  • kubectl: within one minor of the API server, either side.
  • You cannot skip control plane minors; go 1.32 to 1.33 to 1.34. Nodes may be upgraded later and can skip within the allowed skew, though upgrading them every time is simpler.
Check yourself
Can a kubelet be newer than the API server?

No. The kubelet must not be newer than the kube-apiserver.

Can you jump from 1.31 straight to 1.34 on the control plane?

No. Control plane upgrades go one minor version at a time.

34.3

Deprecated and removed APIs

In plain words

Kubernetes deprecates API versions (for example policy/v1beta1 PodDisruptionBudget) and later removes them. Manifests using a removed version stop applying, and controllers that still call it fail.

The problem it solves

An upgrade succeeds but the next deploy, or a Helm chart, fails with "no matches for kind" because the old API version no longer exists.

What it does

  • Stable APIs follow a deprecation policy: GA versions are supported for at least twelve months or three releases after a replacement is announced; beta versions for about nine months.
  • Objects stored in the cluster are migrated automatically to the new storage version, but your manifests, charts and operators are not.
  • Warning headers appear in kubectl output ("... is deprecated in v1.xx, unavailable in v1.yy"). The metric apiserver_requested_deprecated_apis shows who still calls them.
  • Check the deprecated API migration guide for the target version before every upgrade.

Finding usage on a live cluster

bashWhat still calls removed APIs
kubectl get --raw /metrics | grep apiserver_requested_deprecated_apis | head
kubectl get --raw /metrics | grep 'apiserver_requested_deprecated_apis{' | grep 'removed_release="1.3'
kubectl api-resources --verbs=list -o name | head -20
kubectl convert -f old-ingress.yaml --output-version networking.k8s.io/v1   # needs the kubectl-convert plugin
34.4

Scanning with pluto and kubent

In plain words

pluto and kube-no-trouble (kubent) scan manifests, Helm releases or a live cluster and report API versions that are deprecated or removed in a given Kubernetes version.

The problem it solves

Reading release notes by hand will miss something. You want a CI check that fails when a manifest will not work on the next version.

What it does

  • pluto detect-files -d manifests/ --target-versions k8s=v1.37.0 scans files in a directory.
  • pluto detect-helm --target-versions k8s=v1.37.0 reads releases installed through Helm, which is where hidden old versions live because the release Secret stores the old manifest.
  • pluto detect-all-in-cluster scans several sources in the live cluster.
  • kubent inspects the cluster and Helm 3 releases and uses the cluster version to guess the target.
  • Exit codes are non-zero when findings exist, so they fit CI gates. Rendered Helm output can also go through pluto detect -.

Commands

bashPre-upgrade scan
kustomize build overlays/prod | pluto detect - --target-versions k8s=v1.37.0
pluto detect-helm --target-versions k8s=v1.37.0 -o wide
pluto detect-files -d ./manifests --target-versions k8s=v1.37.0
kubent --target-version 1.37
Note

Pass the version you really plan to move to. Confirm the flag spelling with pluto detect-helm --help, because option names have changed between releases.

34.5

Pre-upgrade checklist

In plain words

A short, written checklist turns an upgrade from a risky event into a repeatable procedure.

The problem it solves

Upgrades fail from avoidable causes: an add-on that does not support the new version, PodDisruptionBudgets that block drains, a lack of free capacity, or no recent backup.

What it does

  • Compatibility: CNI, CSI, CoreDNS, ingress controller, service mesh, cert-manager, operators and policy engines support the target version.
  • APIs: scans above are clean; Helm chart versions are current.
  • Capacity: enough spare CPU and memory, IP addresses in subnets (EKS), and quota so surge nodes and drained Pods fit.
  • Availability: at least 2 replicas for important workloads and sensible PDBs; no single-replica StatefulSet with a maxUnavailable: 0 PDB.
  • Backups: etcd is managed on EKS and Gardener, so back up your data: Velero or volume snapshots, plus manifests in Git.
  • Observability: dashboards and alerts are open during the window; a rollback or abort criterion is written down.

Commands

bashReadiness checks
kubectl get pdb -A -o custom-columns=NS:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,ALLOWED:.status.disruptionsAllowed
kubectl get pods -A --field-selector=status.phase!=Running,status.phase!=Succeeded
kubectl get nodes
kubectl top nodes
kubectl get deploy,sts -A -o custom-columns=NS:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,REPLICAS:.spec.replicas | awk '$3==1'
34.6

Upgrading the control plane

In plain words

The control plane is upgraded as one operation by the provider. You start it, wait, and verify. For self-managed clusters, kubeadm upgrade does the same steps on each control plane node.

The problem it solves

If the API server is replaced badly, nothing can be managed. Providers do it with rolling replacement so the API stays available, but the operation is one-way: control plane minor upgrades cannot be reversed.

What it does

  • EKS: aws eks update-cluster-version (or Terraform). The API server remains available. Add-ons are upgraded separately through managed add-on versions.
  • Gardener (and Kyma on BTP): change kubernetes.version in the Shoot spec through the dashboard, gardenctl or the Kyma environment. Gardener rolls control plane first, then worker pools according to the maintenance window.
  • kubeadm: kubeadm upgrade plan, then kubeadm upgrade apply v1.37.x on the first control plane node, kubeadm upgrade node on the others, then upgrade kubelet packages.
  • Verify with kubectl version, component health, and a test deployment.

Commands

bashEKS control plane
aws eks update-cluster-version --name shop --kubernetes-version 1.37
aws eks describe-update --name shop --update-id UPDATE_ID --query 'update.status'
aws eks list-addons --cluster-name shop
aws eks describe-addon-versions --addon-name coredns --kubernetes-version 1.37 --query 'addons[0].addonVersions[0].addonVersion'
aws eks update-addon --cluster-name shop --addon-name coredns --addon-version vX.Y.Z-eksbuild.N
← PreviousNext →
Section 35 of 65

Node upgrades, drain and PodDisruptionBudgets

7 concepts · about 45 minutes

Nodes are replaced far more often than control planes. The skill is to move workloads off a node without breaking availability, using drain, eviction and PodDisruptionBudgets together.

Goals
  • Drain a node safely and explain what a PodDisruptionBudget protects
  • Choose between in-place, surge and blue-green node pool upgrades
  • Diagnose a drain that never finishes
35.1

Cordon, drain and the eviction API

In plain words

Cordon marks a node unschedulable. Drain cordons and then asks every Pod on the node to leave using the Eviction API, which respects PodDisruptionBudgets and graceful shutdown.

The problem it solves

Simply shutting a node down kills its Pods abruptly. Services drop requests and StatefulSet members vanish without warning.

What it does

  • kubectl drain NODE --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data evicts all Pods except DaemonSet Pods and warns about local data.
  • Evicted Pods are recreated by their controller on other nodes; bare Pods are not recreated and block drain unless --force.
  • Each eviction sends SIGTERM and waits terminationGracePeriodSeconds before SIGKILL.
  • Use --timeout, and --disable-eviction only in emergencies because it bypasses PDBs.
  • Always kubectl uncordon NODE after maintenance on a node you keep.

Commands

bashMaintenance on one node
kubectl cordon node-3
kubectl drain node-3 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --timeout=300s
kubectl get pods -A -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=node-3
# do the maintenance, then
kubectl uncordon node-3
kubectl get nodes
Careful

On Gardener-managed clusters such as Kyma, reconciliation can reset node state. Check that cordoned nodes are uncordoned afterwards, and prefer replacing nodes through the worker pool instead of long manual maintenance.

35.2

PodDisruptionBudgets

In plain words

A PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) limits how many Pods of a set can be down because of voluntary disruptions such as drain. It does not stop crashes or node failures.

The problem it solves

A drain or autoscaler could evict all replicas of a service at once, causing an outage that nobody intended.

What it does

  • Set either minAvailable or maxUnavailable (not both), as a number or percentage, with a label selector.
  • The Eviction API refuses an eviction that would break the budget, returning 429, and drain retries.
  • status.disruptionsAllowed shows how many Pods may be evicted right now.
  • unhealthyPodEvictionPolicy: AlwaysAllow lets drain evict Pods that are not ready, which prevents stuck drains with crashing Pods (stable since 1.31).

A PDB

yamlpdb.yaml
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: api
  namespace: shop
spec:
  maxUnavailable: 1
  unhealthyPodEvictionPolicy: AlwaysAllow
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
bashInspect budgets
kubectl get pdb -n shop
kubectl describe pdb api -n shop | grep -E 'Allowed|Current|Desired'
Tip

A PDB with minAvailable equal to the replica count (or maxUnavailable: 0) blocks every drain. That is the most common reason an upgrade hangs.

35.3

Why a drain hangs

In plain words

A drain finishes only when every evictable Pod has left. A single blocker keeps it waiting forever unless you set a timeout.

The problem it solves

An upgrade pipeline hangs on one node, nodes stay cordoned, and capacity shrinks.

What it does

  • PDB with zero allowed disruptions: scale up, loosen the PDB, or fix the unhealthy Pod.
  • Single replica with minAvailable: 1: add a replica, or accept a short outage with a documented exception.
  • Pod not terminating: a finalizer, a stuck volume detach, or an app ignoring SIGTERM; check the grace period.
  • Replacement cannot schedule: no capacity, topology constraints, or a PVC pinned to another zone.
  • Bare Pod or local storage: needs --force or --delete-emptydir-data.

Diagnose

bashFind the blocker
kubectl drain node-3 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --timeout=120s 2>&1 | tail -5
kubectl get pdb -A -o custom-columns=NS:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,ALLOWED:.status.disruptionsAllowed
kubectl get pods -A -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=node-3 | grep -v DaemonSet
kubectl get pods -A --field-selector=status.phase=Pending
kubectl get pod POD -n shop -o jsonpath='{.metadata.finalizers}{" "}{.metadata.deletionTimestamp}{"\n"}'
Check yourself
What does a PDB protect against?

Voluntary disruptions through the Eviction API, such as drain and autoscaler scale down. It does not prevent crashes or node failure.

35.4

Graceful shutdown for Pods

In plain words

When a Pod is deleted, it is removed from Service endpoints and the container receives SIGTERM at roughly the same time. A preStop hook and terminationGracePeriodSeconds give the app time to finish.

The problem it solves

During drains and rollouts, in-flight requests fail because the app stops immediately, or because load balancers still send traffic to a Pod that is shutting down.

What it does

  • Endpoint removal and SIGTERM are asynchronous; traffic can still arrive for a few seconds. A preStop sleep of 5 to 10 seconds, or app-level draining, hides this race.
  • The app must handle SIGTERM: stop accepting, finish requests, close connections, then exit. Shell wrappers that do not forward signals break this.
  • The grace period (30 s default) includes preStop time. Raise it for slow jobs.
  • Native sleep lifecycle action exists in newer releases, so distroless images do not need a shell for the preStop.

Manifest

yamlgraceful-deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
  namespace: shop
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: registry.example.com/shop/api:1.8.3
          lifecycle:
            preStop:
              sleep:
                seconds: 10
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8080}
35.5

Node upgrade strategies

In plain words

Nodes are upgraded either in place (update software on the same machine), by rolling replacement (new nodes join, old ones drain and leave), or by blue-green node pools.

The problem it solves

Mutating long-lived nodes accumulates drift and risk. Replacing them is cleaner but needs spare capacity and tolerant workloads.

What it does

  • Surge (rolling replacement): create up to N extra nodes with the new version first, then drain old ones. EKS managed node groups use maxUnavailable or percentage settings; Gardener worker pools use maxSurge and maxUnavailable.
  • Blue-green pool: create a new node group or pool, cordon and drain the old, delete it. Easy to roll back until the old pool is gone.
  • In-place (kubeadm, self-managed): fastest for small clusters, hardest to undo.
  • Karpenter: set drift or expire policies and a new AMI selector; nodes are replaced within disruption budgets.
  • Prefer immutable images and regular rotation, even without a Kubernetes upgrade, to pick up OS patches.
Strategy
OptionSurge rolling replacement
Choose whenthe default for managed node groups and Gardener pools
Avoid whenzero spare capacity or quota for extra nodes
OptionBlue-green pool
Choose whenbig version jumps, new OS or instance family, easy rollback
Avoid whenIP space or quota is tight
OptionIn place
Choose whensmall self-managed clusters you can rebuild
Avoid whenproduction where a failed node upgrade must be reversible

Commands

bashEKS managed node group
aws eks update-nodegroup-config --cluster-name shop --nodegroup-name general \
  --update-config maxUnavailablePercentage=33
aws eks update-nodegroup-version --cluster-name shop --nodegroup-name general
kubectl get nodes -L eks.amazonaws.com/nodegroup,topology.kubernetes.io/zone -w
35.6

Node rotation and Gardener notes

In plain words

Nodes should be rotated regularly, not only on Kubernetes upgrades. Gardener (the system under Kyma and SAP's managed Kubernetes) does this through maintenance windows and worker pool settings.

The problem it solves

Old nodes miss OS security updates and carry drift. Unplanned rotation during business hours causes disruption.

What it does

  • A Gardener Shoot has a maintenance section with a time window and flags to auto update Kubernetes patch versions and machine image versions. Machine image updates replace nodes, so the window decides when workloads move.
  • Worker pools define minimum, maximum, maxSurge, maxUnavailable, zones, and machine type; pools can be changed without touching others.
  • Run workloads with 2 or more replicas, topology spread across zones, PDBs and graceful shutdown, so any rotation looks like a normal rollout.
  • Verify the live Shoot spec in your landscape before relying on field names; they differ by Gardener version.

Commands

bashWatch a rotation
kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,VERSION:.status.nodeInfo.kubeletVersion,OS:.status.nodeInfo.osImage,AGE:.metadata.creationTimestamp
kubectl get events -A --field-selector reason=NodeNotSchedulable --watch
kubectl get pods -A -o wide | grep -v Running
kubectl get pdb -A
Check yourself
Why spread replicas across zones and nodes?

So a drain or node loss removes only some replicas and the PDB can still allow evictions.

35.7

After the upgrade, verify and roll back

In plain words

After each step you verify cluster health with a short, fixed set of commands. Rolling back means undoing what you can: node pools, add-ons and manifests. The control plane version cannot be downgraded.

The problem it solves

Problems found hours later are hard to attribute. Without a stop rule you keep going on a degraded cluster.

What it does

  • Check API server health, node versions and readiness, system Pods, and deprecated API metrics, then run a smoke test deployment and your synthetic checks.
  • Compare alert rates and error budget against the pre-upgrade baseline.
  • Rollback options: keep old node pool until the soak ends; pin add-on versions so you can revert them; revert application manifests in Git.
  • For a failed control plane upgrade on a managed service, the provider normally handles it; open a support case early. Recovering from a bad state without a downgrade path is why you test in a non-production cluster first.

Post-upgrade checks

bashSmoke commands
kubectl version
kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose' | tail -5
kubectl get nodes -o wide
kubectl get pods -n kube-system
kubectl get pods -A --field-selector=status.phase!=Running,status.phase!=Succeeded
kubectl run smoke --rm -it --restart=Never --image=busybox:1.36 -- nslookup kubernetes.default
kubectl get --raw /metrics | grep apiserver_requested_deprecated_apis | head

Section 36 of 65

Cluster lifecycle on EKS and Gardener

6 concepts · about 40 minutes

A cluster is not a pet. This section covers the full life of a cluster: creation as code, add-on management, the differences between EKS and Gardener/Kyma, backups, and replacing a cluster rather than repairing it.

Goals
  • Describe how clusters are created, scaled, replaced and retired as code
  • Manage EKS add-ons and Gardener shoots without drifting from Git
  • Plan backups and disaster recovery for what the provider does not protect
36.1

Clusters as code

In plain words

Create clusters from declarative definitions (Terraform, eksctl, Gardener Shoot manifests, Crossplane) stored in Git, not by clicking in a console.

The problem it solves

A hand-built cluster cannot be reproduced after a disaster, reviewed before a change, or compared with staging.

What it does

  • Separate layers: network and account, the cluster and node pools, platform add-ons, and applications. Each has its own state and change rhythm.
  • Terraform with the AWS EKS module or eksctl for EKS; a Shoot custom resource applied to the Gardener garden cluster for Gardener; the Kyma runtime is provisioned through the BTP cockpit, CLI or Terraform provider.
  • Platform add-ons (ingress, cert-manager, external-dns, policy engine, monitoring) are installed by GitOps so a new cluster converges to the same state.

An eksctl definition

yamlcluster.yaml
apiVersion: eksctl.io/v1alpha5
kind: ClusterConfig
metadata:
  name: shop
  region: eu-west-1
  version: "1.37"
managedNodeGroups:
  - name: general
    instanceType: m6i.large
    minSize: 3
    maxSize: 9
    desiredCapacity: 3
    availabilityZones: ["eu-west-1a", "eu-west-1b", "eu-west-1c"]
    updateConfig:
      maxUnavailablePercentage: 33
addons:
  - name: vpc-cni
  - name: coredns
  - name: kube-proxy
  - name: aws-ebs-csi-driver
iam:
  withOIDC: true
bashCreate and connect
eksctl create cluster -f cluster.yaml
aws eks update-kubeconfig --name shop --region eu-west-1
kubectl get nodes
36.2

EKS managed add-ons

In plain words

EKS can install and upgrade core components (VPC CNI, CoreDNS, kube-proxy, EBS CSI driver, Pod Identity agent) as managed add-ons with versions that are tested against each Kubernetes version.

The problem it solves

Core add-ons are easy to forget during an upgrade. An outdated CoreDNS or CNI breaks after a control plane upgrade or misses fixes.

What it does

  • aws eks describe-addon-versions lists versions compatible with a Kubernetes version; update-addon upgrades with a conflict resolution mode (OVERWRITE, PRESERVE).
  • Custom configuration goes in the add-on's configurationValues JSON, so Terraform can own it instead of drifting through kubectl edit.
  • Upgrade add-ons right after the control plane and before the nodes, following the version guidance in the EKS documentation.

Commands

bashInspect and upgrade an add-on
aws eks describe-addon-versions --addon-name vpc-cni --kubernetes-version 1.37 \
  --query 'addons[0].addonVersions[0:3].addonVersion'
aws eks describe-addon --cluster-name shop --addon-name coredns --query 'addon.{v:addonVersion,s:status}'
aws eks update-addon --cluster-name shop --addon-name coredns --addon-version vX.Y.Z-eksbuild.N --resolve-conflicts PRESERVE
36.3

Gardener shoots and Kyma runtimes

In plain words

Gardener manages Kubernetes clusters called shoots. A shoot's control plane runs as Pods in another cluster (the seed), and workers run in your infrastructure account. The Kyma runtime on SAP BTP is a Gardener shoot with Kyma modules enabled.

The problem it solves

Operating control planes, OS images and node rotation yourself is expensive. Gardener makes them declarative and automated.

What it does

  • The Shoot spec holds kubernetes.version, provider.workers[] (machine type, minimum, maximum, maxSurge, maxUnavailable, zones), networking, maintenance and hibernation.
  • Hibernation scales workers to zero to save cost for non-production clusters.
  • In Kyma, you manage modules (Istio, Serverless, API Gateway, Telemetry and others) through the Kyma custom resource; your workloads run on the shoot like any Kubernetes cluster.
  • Typical access is through a kubeconfig from the BTP cockpit or the kubectl oidc-login plugin; verify which context you are on before every command.

Verify context safely

bashKnow where you are
kubectl config get-contexts
kubectl config current-context
kubectl get nodes -L topology.kubernetes.io/zone,node.kubernetes.io/instance-type
kubectl get kyma -A 2>/dev/null | head       # present only on Kyma runtimes
kubectl get namespace kyma-system
36.4

Add-on inventory and GitOps for platform components

In plain words

Keep one list of everything that runs in kube-system and platform namespaces, with version and owner, and install it from Git with a GitOps controller.

The problem it solves

Without an inventory you cannot answer "what must I upgrade before moving to 1.37?" and new clusters differ subtly from old ones.

What it does

  • Pin chart versions in Git; renovate or similar tooling opens pull requests for updates.
  • Use an app of apps (Argo CD) or Flux Kustomizations so one commit bootstraps a new cluster.
  • Group by wave: CRDs and CNI first, then controllers (cert-manager, ingress), then policies, then apps.
  • Record the supported Kubernetes range per add-on in the repository README.

Flux bootstrap sketch

yamlclusters/prod/platform.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1
kind: Kustomization
metadata:
  name: platform
  namespace: flux-system
spec:
  interval: 10m
  path: ./platform/overlays/prod
  prune: true
  sourceRef:
    kind: GitRepository
    name: fleet
  healthChecks:
    - apiVersion: apps/v1
      kind: Deployment
      name: ingress-nginx-controller
      namespace: ingress
36.5

Backup and disaster recovery

In plain words

The provider protects the control plane and etcd. You protect your application data, your manifests and your ability to rebuild.

The problem it solves

Deleted namespaces, corrupt volumes or a lost region cannot be fixed by the cloud provider. A backup that was never restored is only a hope.

What it does

  • Manifests: Git is the backup of desired state. Data: CSI VolumeSnapshots, cloud snapshots (EBS), database native backups.
  • Velero backs up cluster objects and volume snapshots to object storage and restores them into the same or another cluster.
  • Define RPO (how much data you can lose) and RTO (how long recovery may take) per application, then test a restore on a schedule.
  • Remember secrets and keys: restoring encrypted Secrets also needs the key or external secrets source.

Velero schedule

yamlvelero-schedule.yaml
apiVersion: velero.io/v1
kind: Schedule
metadata:
  name: daily-shop
  namespace: velero
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"
  template:
    includedNamespaces: ["shop"]
    snapshotVolumes: true
    ttl: 168h0m0s
bashRestore drill
velero backup get
velero restore create --from-backup daily-shop-20261031020000 --namespace-mappings shop:shop-restore
velero restore describe daily-shop-20261031020000-20261031100000 --details
36.6

Replace rather than repair

In plain words

For major changes, build a new cluster beside the old one and move traffic, instead of mutating the old one in place.

The problem it solves

In-place upgrades of control plane, CNI or networking mode cannot always be undone, and drifted clusters accumulate surprises.

What it does

  • Blue-green clusters: create cluster B from the same code with the new version, deploy through GitOps, test, then move traffic using DNS weights or a global load balancer.
  • Works best for stateless services; stateful data needs replication or a planned cutover.
  • Costs temporary double capacity but gives a complete rollback path: point DNS back.
  • Decommission only after a soak, and remove DNS records, load balancers and volumes to avoid orphans.
Upgrade or replace
OptionIn-place upgrade
Choose whenroutine minor upgrades with good test coverage
Avoid whenyou also change CNI mode, IP family or other one-way settings
OptionBlue-green cluster
Choose whenlarge changes, risky add-on swaps, compliance rebuilds
Avoid whenyou cannot move stateful data or afford double capacity
Check yourself
Who backs up your application data on EKS?

You do. AWS operates the control plane and etcd, but volumes and databases need your own snapshots or backups.

Section 37 of 65

Service mesh concepts and data planes

6 concepts · about 40 minutes

A service mesh moves common network features (encryption, retries, traffic splitting, telemetry) out of every application and into the platform. It is powerful and not free, so the first question is whether you need one.

Goals
  • Explain what a service mesh adds and what it costs
  • Compare sidecar and ambient data planes
  • Choose between Istio, Linkerd and Cilium for a given need
37.1

What a service mesh does

In plain words

A mesh adds a managed layer between your services. A data plane handles the traffic; a control plane configures it. Applications keep making ordinary HTTP or gRPC calls.

The problem it solves

Each team re-implements TLS between services, retries, timeouts and metrics in a different library and language. Security teams cannot prove that internal traffic is encrypted.

What it does

  • mTLS: automatic encryption and service identity between workloads, with certificate rotation.
  • Traffic management: retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, weighted routing for canaries, fault injection.
  • Observability: request rate, errors and latency for every service pair without code changes, plus tracing headers.
  • Authorisation: allow or deny calls by workload identity, method and path.

Is a mesh needed

bashQuestions to answer with data
kubectl get pods -A | wc -l                                  # how many workloads
kubectl get svc -A | wc -l                                   # how many services talk to each other
kubectl get networkpolicy -A | wc -l                         # existing segmentation
Tip

If you only need ingress TLS, a few retries in code and NetworkPolicy, you do not need a mesh. Adopt one for a concrete requirement such as mandatory internal mTLS, progressive delivery or cross-cluster traffic.

37.2

The sidecar model

In plain words

In the classic design, a proxy container (Envoy for Istio, linkerd2-proxy for Linkerd) is injected into every Pod. Traffic in and out of the application container passes through it.

The problem it solves

The network features must apply to unmodified applications in any language, at the Pod boundary.

What it does

  • A mutating webhook injects the sidecar when a namespace or Pod carries the injection label or annotation. Traffic is redirected by iptables rules set by an init container or a CNI plugin.
  • Each Pod carries its own proxy, so CPU and memory overhead scale with Pod count, and each proxy adds latency in both directions.
  • Sidecars must start before the app and stop after it; ordering problems cause connection errors on start and shutdown. Native sidecar containers (restartable init containers, stable since 1.33) address this.
  • Changing the mesh version means restarting Pods to pick up the new proxy.

Enable injection for a namespace

yamlnamespace-injected.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: shop
  labels:
    istio-injection: enabled
bashCheck the sidecar
kubectl label namespace shop istio-injection=enabled --overwrite
kubectl rollout restart deploy -n shop            # existing Pods need a restart
kubectl get pods -n shop -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{" "}{.spec.containers[*].name}{"\n"}{end}'
37.3

The ambient model

In plain words

Istio ambient mode removes per-Pod sidecars. A small agent on each node (ztunnel) handles L4 features such as mTLS and identity. Optional waypoint proxies per namespace or service handle L7 features like HTTP routing.

The problem it solves

Sidecars cost resources on every Pod, couple the mesh lifecycle to application restarts, and add friction for jobs and short-lived Pods.

What it does

  • ztunnel (a Rust DaemonSet) provides mTLS, L4 authorisation and telemetry for all Pods on a node, using the HBONE tunnel protocol.
  • Waypoint proxies (Envoy) are deployed only where L7 policy is required, and are managed through the Kubernetes Gateway API.
  • Enrol a namespace with the label istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient; no Pod restart is needed.
  • Ambient reached general availability in Istio 1.24. Check the current documentation for supported platforms and CNI interplay.

Enrol a namespace

bashAmbient enrolment
istioctl install --set profile=ambient
kubectl label namespace shop istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient
istioctl ztunnel-config workloads | head
kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l app=ztunnel -o wide
37.4

Istio, Linkerd and Cilium compared

In plain words

Three popular meshes make different trade-offs. Istio has the broadest features, Linkerd aims for simplicity and a small footprint, and Cilium builds networking, policy and optional mesh features on eBPF.

The problem it solves

Choosing by popularity leads to a heavy mesh where a light one would do, or a light one that lacks a feature you must have.

What it does

  • Istio: Envoy based, rich traffic and security policy (VirtualService, DestinationRule, AuthorizationPolicy, Gateway API), sidecar or ambient. The mesh behind Kyma's Istio module.
  • Linkerd: its own Rust micro-proxy, automatic mTLS by default, small CRD surface. Stable releases from the open source project are not distributed as binaries by Buoyant after 2024, so verify how you source them and their licence.
  • Cilium: CNI with eBPF dataplane, NetworkPolicy and CiliumNetworkPolicy, Hubble observability, transparent encryption (WireGuard or IPsec), and service mesh features using node level Envoy.
  • Do not run two meshes on the same workloads.
Picking one
OptionIstio
Choose whenyou need rich L7 traffic control, a Kyma/SAP integrated mesh or multi cluster
Avoid whenthe team cannot invest in operating it
OptionLinkerd
Choose whenyou want mTLS and golden metrics with the least complexity
Avoid whenyou need advanced routing and extension points
OptionCilium
Choose whenyou already use it as CNI and want policy plus flow visibility
Avoid whenyou need the broad L7 feature set of Envoy meshes
OptionNo mesh
Choose whenfew services, ingress TLS and NetworkPolicy are enough
Avoid whencompliance requires mTLS everywhere
37.5

Costs and failure modes

In plain words

A mesh adds a new moving part on the path of every request. Know the overhead and the typical failure modes before you enable it.

The problem it solves

Teams enable a mesh and then see higher latency, higher bills, unexplained 503s and upgrade outages, with no one who understands the proxy layer.

What it does

  • Resources: sidecar proxies use memory and CPU per Pod; measure with kubectl top pod --containers. Ambient reduces but does not remove this.
  • Latency: each hop adds a small amount of time; verify p99 against your SLO.
  • Failure modes: sidecar not ready at app start, 503 UC or NR responses from misconfigured routes, certificate or clock problems, jobs that never finish because the sidecar keeps running, and control plane outage freezing config pushes (existing traffic keeps flowing).
  • Operations: the mesh version must be upgraded in step with Kubernetes; canary the control plane and then data plane.

Measure before and after

bashOverhead and health
kubectl top pod -n shop --containers | sort -k4 -h | tail
istioctl analyze -n shop                               # config validation
istioctl proxy-status                                  # are proxies in sync with the control plane
kubectl logs deploy/api -n shop -c istio-proxy --tail=20
Check yourself
Does an Istio control plane outage stop traffic between running Pods?

No. Proxies keep the last configuration they received. New or changed config and new Pods are affected.

37.6

Adopting a mesh step by step

In plain words

Introduce a mesh gradually: observe first, then secure, then add traffic features, one namespace at a time.

The problem it solves

Turning on strict mTLS and sidecars everywhere on day one breaks the services that talk to non-mesh clients and databases.

What it does

  • Start with a non-critical namespace and permissive mTLS, which accepts both plain and mTLS traffic.
  • Watch dashboards (request success rate, latency, mTLS percentage), then move to strict mode.
  • Add policy (AuthorizationPolicy) from a default deny with explicit allows, similar to NetworkPolicy.
  • Handle special cases: Jobs, databases, and traffic from outside the mesh through an ingress gateway.

PeerAuthentication in steps

yamlpeerauthentication.yaml
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: shop
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: PERMISSIVE     # change to STRICT after every client is in the mesh
← PreviousNext →
Section 38 of 65

Istio traffic management and security

6 concepts · about 45 minutes

Istio is the mesh you are most likely to meet on Kyma. This section covers the resources you will actually write and how to debug them.

Goals
  • Route and split traffic with Gateway API and Istio resources
  • Enforce mTLS and workload authorisation
  • Debug a mesh with istioctl and proxy logs
38.1

Gateways for ingress

In plain words

A gateway is an Envoy proxy at the edge of the mesh that accepts external traffic. You configure it with the Kubernetes Gateway API (Gateway, HTTPRoute) or Istio's own Gateway and VirtualService.

The problem it solves

Traffic from outside needs TLS termination, host and path routing, and the same policy and telemetry as internal calls.

What it does

  • Gateway API is the portable model; Istio implements it with gatewayClassName: istio. Istio's own resources remain widely used, and Kyma's API Gateway module builds on Istio.
  • A Gateway defines listeners (port, hostname, TLS); an HTTPRoute attaches to it and routes by host, path or header to backend Services.
  • TLS certificates come from Secrets, often created by cert-manager.

Gateway API example

yamlgateway.yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: public
  namespace: shop
spec:
  gatewayClassName: istio
  listeners:
    - name: https
      port: 443
      protocol: HTTPS
      hostname: shop.example.com
      tls:
        mode: Terminate
        certificateRefs:
          - name: shop-tls
      allowedRoutes:
        namespaces:
          from: Same
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: shop
  namespace: shop
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: public
  hostnames: ["shop.example.com"]
  rules:
    - matches:
        - path:
            type: PathPrefix
            value: /api
      backendRefs:
        - name: api
          port: 80
38.2

Weighted routing and canaries

In plain words

Traffic can be split between versions by percentage, independent of the number of Pods. This allows a canary release that sends 5 percent of requests to the new version.

The problem it solves

With plain Services, traffic share follows Pod counts, so a 5 percent canary needs 20 Pods. And there is no quick way to shift traffic back.

What it does

  • Gateway API: backendRefs with weight in an HTTPRoute.
  • Istio native: DestinationRule defines subsets by Pod label (version: v2); VirtualService routes weights to subsets.
  • Header matching sends internal testers to the new version while the public stays on the old one.
  • Progressive delivery tools (Argo Rollouts, Flagger) automate weight steps and rollback from metrics.

Weighted HTTPRoute

yamlcanary-route.yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: api-canary
  namespace: shop
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: public
  rules:
    - backendRefs:
        - name: api-v1
          port: 80
          weight: 95
        - name: api-v2
          port: 80
          weight: 5
38.3

Retries, timeouts and circuit breaking

In plain words

The mesh can enforce time limits, retry failed calls, and eject unhealthy backends, so these policies are consistent for all services.

The problem it solves

Without limits, a slow dependency makes every caller slow, and uncoordinated retries in many layers multiply load on a struggling service (a retry storm).

What it does

  • Per-route timeout and retries (attempts, perTryTimeout, retryOn) in a VirtualService.
  • DestinationRule.trafficPolicy.connectionPool limits connections and pending requests; outlierDetection ejects hosts after consecutive 5xx errors.
  • Retry only idempotent operations, and keep total attempts small. Total time must fit inside the caller's own timeout.

VirtualService and DestinationRule

yamlresilience.yaml
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: api
  namespace: shop
spec:
  hosts: ["api"]
  http:
    - route:
        - destination:
            host: api
      timeout: 5s
      retries:
        attempts: 2
        perTryTimeout: 2s
        retryOn: 5xx,connect-failure
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: api
  namespace: shop
spec:
  host: api
  trafficPolicy:
    connectionPool:
      http:
        http1MaxPendingRequests: 100
    outlierDetection:
      consecutive5xxErrors: 5
      interval: 10s
      baseEjectionTime: 30s
38.4

mTLS and PeerAuthentication

In plain words

Istio gives every workload a certificate based identity (a SPIFFE ID built from namespace and service account) and encrypts traffic between proxies. PeerAuthentication controls whether plain traffic is still accepted.

The problem it solves

Internal traffic is plain text by default, and any compromised Pod can read or forge calls to other services.

What it does

  • Modes: PERMISSIVE (accept both), STRICT (mTLS only), DISABLE. Set mesh-wide in the root namespace, or per namespace or workload.
  • Certificates are issued by istiod and rotated automatically (24 hours by default).
  • Identity is the service account, so give each workload its own ServiceAccount.
  • Check the effective mode with istioctl x describe pod and look for mTLS on the connection.

Strict mode

yamlstrict-mtls.yaml
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: shop
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT
38.5

AuthorizationPolicy

In plain words

An AuthorizationPolicy allows or denies requests based on who is calling (identity or namespace), where it goes (host, method, path) and request attributes such as headers or JWT claims.

The problem it solves

mTLS proves who is calling, but it does not decide whether the call is allowed. Without policy, every workload in the mesh can call every other.

What it does

  • Like NetworkPolicy, once any ALLOW policy selects a workload, requests that match no ALLOW are denied. An empty policy spec: {} in a namespace denies everything.
  • Evaluation order: CUSTOM, then DENY, then ALLOW.
  • principals refer to identities (cluster.local/ns/shop/sa/web), while namespaces match caller namespaces.
  • L7 rules (path, method) need a sidecar or, in ambient mode, a waypoint proxy; L4 rules work with ztunnel.

Allow only the web frontend

yamlauthz-api.yaml
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: api-allow-web
  namespace: shop
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
    - from:
        - source:
            principals: ["cluster.local/ns/shop/sa/web"]
      to:
        - operation:
            methods: ["GET", "POST"]
            paths: ["/api/*"]
38.6

Debugging Istio

In plain words

Most mesh problems are configuration mismatches or startup ordering. Istio ships tools that compare what you wrote with what each proxy actually received.

The problem it solves

A route does nothing, requests return 503 with a cryptic flag, or one namespace behaves differently, and the Envoy configuration is large and unreadable.

What it does

  • istioctl analyze validates configuration and flags typical mistakes (a missing gateway, a host that matches nothing).
  • istioctl proxy-status shows whether each proxy is synced with istiod; istioctl proxy-config routes|clusters|listeners POD shows what a proxy knows.
  • Envoy access logs show response flags such as UH (no healthy upstream), UF (upstream connection failure), NR (no route), URX (retry limit).
  • On Kyma, the Istio module is managed: change mesh-wide settings through the Istio custom resource, not by editing the installed control plane.

Commands

bashMesh triage
istioctl analyze -A
istioctl proxy-status
istioctl proxy-config routes deploy/api -n shop
istioctl proxy-config clusters deploy/api -n shop | grep -i api
kubectl logs deploy/api -n shop -c istio-proxy --tail=30
kubectl get peerauthentication,authorizationpolicy,virtualservice,destinationrule -A
Check yourself
What does an empty AuthorizationPolicy do?

It selects all workloads in the namespace with no allow rules, so it denies all requests.

Which Istio resource limits connections and ejects failing hosts?

DestinationRule, through connectionPool and outlierDetection.
