Section 39 of 65

Linkerd, Cilium and operating a mesh

5 concepts · about 35 minutes

Istio is not the only option. This section shows how Linkerd and Cilium solve the same problems differently and how to run any mesh without surprises.

Goals
  • Describe how Linkerd and Cilium implement mesh features
  • Use Hubble and mesh telemetry to see service traffic
  • Upgrade and troubleshoot a mesh safely
39.1

Linkerd in practice

In plain words

Linkerd injects a lightweight Rust proxy into each Pod and enables mTLS and golden metrics (success rate, request rate, latency) with no extra configuration.

The problem it solves

You want encryption and basic observability between services quickly, without learning dozens of CRDs.

What it does

  • Enrol workloads with the annotation linkerd.io/inject: enabled on a namespace or Pod template.
  • linkerd check validates the installation; linkerd viz adds a metrics dashboard and linkerd viz stat prints live success rate and latency.
  • Policy uses Server and AuthorizationPolicy resources; traffic splitting uses Gateway API HTTPRoute.
  • The control plane identity trust anchor certificate must be rotated before it expires; automate it with cert-manager.

Enrol a namespace

yamllinkerd-namespace.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: shop
  annotations:
    linkerd.io/inject: enabled
bashCheck and observe
linkerd check
kubectl rollout restart deploy -n shop
linkerd viz stat deploy -n shop
linkerd viz tap deploy/api -n shop        # live requests; needs permission
39.2

Cilium as CNI and mesh

In plain words

Cilium uses eBPF programs in the Linux kernel to route packets, enforce NetworkPolicy and observe traffic. It can replace kube-proxy and offers mesh features without a sidecar per Pod.

The problem it solves

iptables based networking becomes slow with many Services, and standard NetworkPolicy cannot filter by DNS name or HTTP path.

What it does

  • CiliumNetworkPolicy adds L7 rules (HTTP methods and paths), DNS-name egress rules (toFQDNs), and identity based selection.
  • Hubble gives flow visibility: who talked to whom, what was allowed or dropped, DNS and HTTP metadata.
  • Transparent encryption between nodes with WireGuard or IPsec; optional mutual authentication through SPIFFE.
  • On EKS you can run Cilium in place of or chained with the VPC CNI; this is a deliberate design choice made at cluster creation.

Policy with a DNS name

yamlcilium-fqdn.yaml
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: api-egress
  namespace: shop
spec:
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  egress:
    - toEndpoints:
        - matchLabels:
            io.kubernetes.pod.namespace: kube-system
            k8s-app: kube-dns
      toPorts:
        - ports:
            - port: "53"
              protocol: ANY
          rules:
            dns:
              - matchPattern: "*"
    - toFQDNs:
        - matchName: api.payments.example.com
      toPorts:
        - ports:
            - port: "443"
              protocol: TCP
39.3

Seeing traffic with Hubble

In plain words

Hubble records network flows with Kubernetes identity (namespace, Pod, labels) and the policy verdict for each, so you can answer "why is this connection dropped" directly.

The problem it solves

Debugging NetworkPolicy by guesswork is slow. You need to see the actual dropped packets and which policy decided.

What it does

  • hubble observe streams flows; filter by namespace, Pod, verdict (FORWARDED, DROPPED), protocol and HTTP status.
  • hubble status and cilium status check agents; the Hubble UI draws a service map.
  • Flows are kept in a ring buffer on each node, so they are for live debugging, not long-term audit. Export to storage for history.

Commands

bashFind drops
cilium status --wait
hubble observe --namespace shop --verdict DROPPED --last 50
hubble observe --from-pod shop/web-0 --to-service shop/api --protocol http
hubble observe --namespace shop --type policy-verdict
39.4

Observing the mesh with metrics and traces

In plain words

Proxies emit uniform metrics for every service pair and propagate trace headers. Prometheus scrapes the metrics; a tracing backend receives spans.

The problem it solves

Without the mesh each service exposes different metrics, if any, and tracing is missing for services nobody instrumented.

What it does

  • Golden signals per workload: request rate, error rate, latency percentiles, bytes.
  • Tracing needs the application to forward trace headers (W3C traceparent or B3). The proxy cannot join spans without them.
  • Keep label cardinality under control; per-path labels can explode the number of time series.
  • Kyma ships a Telemetry module that configures pipelines for logs, traces and metrics towards your backend.

Useful queries

promqlPromQL for mesh traffic
# request rate per destination service (Istio standard metrics)
sum(rate(istio_requests_total{reporter="destination"}[5m])) by (destination_service_name)

# error ratio
sum(rate(istio_requests_total{reporter="destination",response_code=~"5.."}[5m]))
  / sum(rate(istio_requests_total{reporter="destination"}[5m]))

# p99 latency
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(istio_request_duration_milliseconds_bucket{reporter="destination"}[5m])) by (le, destination_service_name))
39.5

Upgrading and troubleshooting a mesh

In plain words

Treat the mesh as a platform component with its own upgrade process: control plane first, then data plane, in a canary fashion.

The problem it solves

A mesh upgrade that restarts every Pod at once, or a control plane version that does not support your Kubernetes version, takes down the traffic layer.

What it does

  • Check the compatibility table of the mesh against the target Kubernetes version before a cluster upgrade.
  • Istio revision based upgrade: install a second control plane revision (istioctl install --set revision=1-24-0), move a namespace by changing its istio.io/rev label, restart workloads, then remove the old revision. Ambient ztunnel upgrades per node.
  • Linkerd: upgrade CRDs, then control plane, then restart workloads to pick up the new proxy.
  • Alert on proxy out of sync, certificate expiry, and control plane restarts.
  • If the mesh breaks traffic during an incident, the fastest mitigation is removing injection and restarting the affected workload, which is why you rehearse it.

Commands

bashRevision switch
istioctl install --set revision=1-24-0 -y
kubectl label namespace shop istio-injection- istio.io/rev=1-24-0 --overwrite
kubectl rollout restart deploy -n shop
istioctl proxy-status | head
kubectl get pods -n shop -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{" "}{.metadata.annotations.sidecar\.istio\.io/status}{"\n"}{end}' | head -3
Check yourself
Why must apps forward trace headers when a mesh is present?

The proxy creates spans per hop but cannot know which inbound request caused an outbound call unless the application passes the trace context along.

Section 40 of 65

Namespaces, quotas and LimitRange

6 concepts · about 45 minutes

Multi-tenancy means several teams or customers share one cluster. The cluster is cheaper and simpler to run, but you must prevent tenants from starving or harming each other. The namespace is where that starts.

Goals
  • Use namespaces as the unit of tenancy and know what they do not isolate
  • Cap a tenant with ResourceQuota and set defaults with LimitRange
  • Onboard a team with a repeatable namespace template
40.1

Tenancy models

In plain words

There is a range from "everyone in one cluster" to "one cluster per tenant". Namespaces give soft isolation inside a cluster. Separate clusters give hard isolation.

The problem it solves

Too little isolation lets one team's mistake or compromise affect others. Too much (a cluster per team) multiplies cost and operations.

What it does

  • Soft multi-tenancy (trusted teams in one company): namespaces plus RBAC, quotas, NetworkPolicy and Pod Security.
  • Hard multi-tenancy (untrusted tenants): separate clusters, or virtual clusters with dedicated nodes and sandboxed runtimes.
  • Kubernetes shares the control plane, the kernel on each node (unless sandboxed) and cluster-scoped resources such as CRDs between tenants in a cluster.
  • Decide the model from the trust level and compliance needs, not from convenience.
Which model
OptionNamespace per team
Choose wheninternal teams who share a trust boundary
Avoid whentenants that must not share a kernel or API server
OptionVirtual cluster
Choose whenteams need their own CRDs, cluster admin and CI environments
Avoid whenstrict kernel level isolation is required
OptionCluster per tenant
Choose whenregulation, noisy or hostile tenants, different versions
Avoid whenyou cannot afford the operations overhead
40.2

Namespaces

In plain words

A namespace is a named scope inside a cluster. Most objects (Pods, Services, Secrets, ConfigMaps, Roles) live in exactly one namespace, and names must be unique only within it.

The problem it solves

Without scoping, every object name in the cluster would need to be unique, and permissions or limits could not be given to one team only.

What it does

  • Cluster-scoped objects (Nodes, PersistentVolumes, StorageClasses, CRDs, ClusterRoles, Namespaces themselves) are not namespaced; kubectl api-resources --namespaced=false lists them.
  • Namespaces are the attachment point for RBAC RoleBindings, ResourceQuota, LimitRange, NetworkPolicy and Pod Security labels.
  • They do not isolate network traffic by themselves, and a Service in one namespace is reachable from another as svc.ns.
  • Deleting a namespace deletes everything in it. Protect production namespaces with RBAC and admission policy.
  • Every namespace has the automatic label kubernetes.io/metadata.name, handy for selectors.

Commands

bashExplore scope
kubectl api-resources --namespaced=true | head -12
kubectl api-resources --namespaced=false | head -12
kubectl get ns --show-labels
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=shop       # default namespace for kubectl
40.3

ResourceQuota

In plain words

A ResourceQuota caps the total resources a namespace may consume or create: CPU and memory requests and limits, storage, and counts of objects.

The problem it solves

One team deploys a runaway job or too many replicas and takes all the capacity from everyone else. Or a mistaken loop creates thousands of objects and burdens the API server.

What it does

  • requests.cpu, requests.memory, limits.cpu, limits.memory: totals across all Pods in the namespace.
  • requests.storage, persistentvolumeclaims, per StorageClass quotas, and object counts such as pods, services, services.loadbalancers, count/deployments.apps.
  • When compute quota is set, every Pod must specify requests and limits for those resources, or be rejected; a LimitRange can supply defaults.
  • scopes and scopeSelector apply quota to a subset, such as Pods of a PriorityClass.
  • Exceeding quota rejects creation at the API (HTTP 403 exceeded quota). For Deployments the error appears on the ReplicaSet events.

A team quota

yamlquota.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: team-a
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "8"
    requests.memory: 16Gi
    limits.memory: 24Gi
    persistentvolumeclaims: "10"
    requests.storage: 200Gi
    services.loadbalancers: "1"
    count/deployments.apps: "30"
bashUsage versus limit
kubectl describe resourcequota team-a -n team-a
kubectl get resourcequota -A
40.4

LimitRange

In plain words

A LimitRange sets default requests and limits for containers that do not specify any, and minimum and maximum values per container, Pod or PersistentVolumeClaim.

The problem it solves

Quota demands requests on every Pod, so teams that forget get rejections. And without a maximum one container can claim a whole node.

What it does

  • default sets limits and defaultRequest sets requests for containers that omit them.
  • min and max reject containers outside the range; maxLimitRequestRatio limits the gap between request and limit.
  • Applied at admission time; it does not change running Pods.
  • Choose defaults that are safe, such as a small request and a memory limit equal to the request.

Defaults and bounds

yamllimitrange.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: defaults
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Container
      defaultRequest:
        cpu: 100m
        memory: 128Mi
      default:
        memory: 256Mi
      max:
        cpu: "2"
        memory: 4Gi
    - type: PersistentVolumeClaim
      max:
        storage: 50Gi
Check yourself
Why do Pods get rejected after you add a compute ResourceQuota?

Quota requires every Pod to declare requests and limits for the quota'd resources. Add them or provide a LimitRange with defaults.

40.5

Priority classes and fairness

In plain words

When capacity is short, PriorityClass decides which Pods may preempt others. API Priority and Fairness protects the API server from one noisy client.

The problem it solves

Critical services must not wait behind batch jobs, and one tenant's controller must not saturate the API server for everybody.

What it does

  • A PriorityClass gives a Pod an integer priority. The scheduler may evict lower priority Pods to place a higher one (preemption). preemptionPolicy: Never disables evicting others.
  • Restrict who may use high priorities with a quota scoped to PriorityClass, or an admission policy; otherwise every team marks their Pods critical.
  • API Priority and Fairness (FlowSchema, PriorityLevelConfiguration) queues API requests fairly per user or service account; check apiserver_flowcontrol_* metrics when controllers are throttled.

Priority classes

yamlpriorityclasses.yaml
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: business-critical
value: 100000
globalDefault: false
description: Customer facing services
---
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: batch
value: 1000
preemptionPolicy: Never
description: Batch jobs that must not displace others
40.6

A namespace template for onboarding

In plain words

Create tenant namespaces from one template so every team gets the same guardrails: labels, quota, LimitRange, default-deny NetworkPolicy, Pod Security level and RBAC.

The problem it solves

Hand-made namespaces differ. Some lack quota, some lack policy, and nobody can tell which is correct.

What it does

  • Keep the template in Git as a Helm chart or Kustomize base, and apply it per tenant through GitOps.
  • Labels carry ownership and cost metadata (team, cost-center, env) that cost tools use later.
  • Bind a team group (from your identity provider) to the edit ClusterRole in its namespace, not cluster-admin.
  • Tools such as Capsule or the Hierarchical Namespace Controller automate this pattern; plain GitOps works too.

Template

yamltenant-namespace.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: team-a
  labels:
    team: team-a
    cost-center: "cc-1042"
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: baseline
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: team-a-edit
  namespace: team-a
subjects:
  - kind: Group
    name: oidc:team-a
    apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
roleRef:
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: edit
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-ingress
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: ["Ingress"]
bashVerify the tenant
kubectl auth can-i create deployments -n team-a --as-group oidc:team-a --as someone
kubectl auth can-i create clusterrolebindings --as-group oidc:team-a --as someone
← PreviousNext →
Section 41 of 65

Hierarchical tenancy, vcluster and node isolation

5 concepts · about 40 minutes

Namespaces are flat. Real organisations are not. This section covers tools that add hierarchy, virtual clusters for stronger separation, and node-level isolation.

Goals
  • Model teams and sub-teams with hierarchical namespaces or Capsule
  • Explain how vcluster gives each tenant a virtual control plane
  • Isolate noisy or untrusted workloads on dedicated nodes or sandboxed runtimes
41.1

Hierarchical namespaces and Capsule

In plain words

Organisations have teams that contain sub-teams. Tools such as the Hierarchical Namespace Controller (HNC) and Capsule let you group namespaces under a tenant and propagate policy from parent to children.

The problem it solves

With flat namespaces, giving a team ten namespaces means ten copies of RoleBindings, quotas and policies, and drift between them.

What it does

  • HNC adds parent and child relationships, and propagates selected objects (Roles, RoleBindings, NetworkPolicies) down the tree. Its development has slowed; check the project status before adopting.
  • Capsule defines a Tenant custom resource owning many namespaces, with a shared quota, allowed StorageClasses and registries, and owners who may create namespaces within limits without cluster admin rights.
  • Alternatives: Kyverno or Argo CD ApplicationSets generating the same objects into every namespace of a team.

Capsule tenant

yamlcapsule-tenant.yaml
apiVersion: capsule.clastix.io/v1beta2
kind: Tenant
metadata:
  name: team-a
spec:
  owners:
    - name: oidc:team-a
      kind: Group
  namespaceOptions:
    quota: 5
  resourceQuotas:
    scope: Tenant
    items:
      - hard:
          requests.cpu: "16"
          requests.memory: 32Gi
  storageClasses:
    allowed:
      - gp3
41.2

Virtual clusters with vcluster

In plain words

vcluster runs a complete Kubernetes API server (and its own data store) as Pods inside a namespace of a host cluster. The tenant gets a kubeconfig for the virtual cluster, where they are cluster admin.

The problem it solves

Teams need cluster-level rights (install CRDs, create namespaces, run operators) but a real cluster per team is too costly and slow to create.

What it does

  • A syncer copies workload objects such as Pods and Services from the virtual cluster to the host namespace, where they actually run on shared nodes.
  • Tenants see only their own namespaces and CRDs; the host sees ordinary Pods in one namespace with name suffixes.
  • Creating one takes seconds, so they suit CI per pull request, ephemeral dev environments and platform teams offering self-service.
  • The isolation is at the API level only. Pods still share the host kernel unless combined with dedicated nodes or sandboxing. Check the current vcluster documentation for the distribution and options.

Commands

bashCreate and use a vcluster
vcluster create team-a --namespace vcluster-team-a
vcluster connect team-a --namespace vcluster-team-a        # switches kubeconfig context
kubectl get ns                                              # only the virtual cluster's namespaces
kubectl create ns demo && kubectl create deploy web --image=nginx:1.27 -n demo
vcluster disconnect
kubectl get pods -n vcluster-team-a                         # the synced Pod on the host
vcluster delete team-a --namespace vcluster-team-a
Note

Put a ResourceQuota on the host namespace. The virtual cluster's own quotas are advisory for the tenant, but the host quota is the hard limit.

41.3

Dedicated nodes with taints and affinity

In plain words

Reserve nodes for a tenant or workload class by tainting them and adding a matching toleration and node selector to that tenant's Pods.

The problem it solves

Noisy batch jobs slow latency sensitive services, and compliance may require that a tenant's Pods never share a node with others.

What it does

  • Taint repels all Pods that do not tolerate it; node labels with nodeSelector or affinity attract the right Pods. You need both to make a pool exclusive.
  • Enforce the toleration and selector with a mutating policy (Kyverno or a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy plus defaults), otherwise tenants can omit them.
  • On EKS use managed node groups or Karpenter NodePools per tenant; on Gardener use separate worker pools with labels and taints.
  • Dedicated nodes cost more through lower packing efficiency; use them only where needed.

Manifest

yamldedicated-pool.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: billing
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: billing
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: billing
    spec:
      nodeSelector:
        tenant: team-a
      tolerations:
        - key: tenant
          operator: Equal
          value: team-a
          effect: NoSchedule
      containers:
        - name: billing
          image: registry.example.com/team-a/billing:2.1.0
bashPrepare the nodes
kubectl label node node-5 tenant=team-a
kubectl taint node node-5 tenant=team-a:NoSchedule
kubectl get nodes -L tenant
41.4

Sandboxed runtimes and stronger isolation

In plain words

Containers share the host kernel. For untrusted code, a RuntimeClass can select a sandbox (gVisor, Kata Containers, Firecracker based) that puts a smaller kernel or a micro VM between the workload and the host.

The problem it solves

A kernel exploit in one container can reach every other container on the node. Running arbitrary customer code needs a stronger boundary than namespaces and cgroups.

What it does

  • RuntimeClass maps a name to a runtime handler configured on the node, and Pods opt in with runtimeClassName.
  • Sandboxes add overhead and may not support every syscall or device; test your workload.
  • Combine with Pod Security restricted, NetworkPolicy, dedicated nodes and no service account token.
  • On EKS, Fargate gives a micro VM per Pod; on Gardener, availability of sandboxed runtimes depends on the worker image and extensions, so verify with your provider.

RuntimeClass

yamlruntimeclass.yaml
apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
kind: RuntimeClass
metadata:
  name: gvisor
handler: runsc
scheduling:
  nodeSelector:
    sandbox: gvisor
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: untrusted-job
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor
  automountServiceAccountToken: false
  containers:
    - name: job
      image: registry.example.com/team-a/runner:1.0
41.5

Fair sharing with Kueue and noisy neighbours

In plain words

Beyond quotas, batch-heavy clusters use a queueing system such as Kueue to admit jobs by tenant share, and Pod-level controls to limit noisy neighbours.

The problem it solves

A hard quota either wastes idle capacity or lets a tenant starve others once the cluster is full. Batch jobs need fair, queued admission, not instant failure.

What it does

  • Kueue adds ClusterQueue, LocalQueue and ResourceFlavor. Tenants submit Jobs to their LocalQueue; Kueue admits them when quota is available and can borrow unused capacity from other queues within a cohort.
  • Noisy neighbours also come from CPU throttling, shared disks, and network. Use requests that reflect reality, topology spread, and Guaranteed QoS for latency sensitive Pods.
  • Set ephemeral-storage limits and PID limits to stop single Pods from exhausting node resources.

Queue sketch

yamlkueue.yaml
apiVersion: kueue.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: ClusterQueue
metadata:
  name: team-a
spec:
  namespaceSelector:
    matchLabels:
      team: team-a
  cohort: shared
  resourceGroups:
    - coveredResources: ["cpu", "memory"]
      flavors:
        - name: default
          resources:
            - name: cpu
              nominalQuota: 16
            - name: memory
              nominalQuota: 64Gi
---
apiVersion: kueue.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: LocalQueue
metadata:
  name: main
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  clusterQueue: team-a
Check yourself
Do taints alone make a node pool exclusive?

No. A taint repels other Pods, but the tenant's Pods also need a node selector or affinity so they do not land on shared nodes.

Does vcluster isolate the kernel?

No. It isolates the API. Pods still share the host kernel unless you add dedicated nodes or a sandboxed runtime.

← PreviousNext →
Section 42 of 65

Cost allocation and FinOps on Kubernetes

5 concepts · about 40 minutes

A node bill does not say which team spent what. Cost allocation maps cloud spend onto namespaces, labels and workloads so teams can see and own their costs.

Goals
  • Explain why Kubernetes cost is hard to attribute and how requests drive it
  • Measure cost per namespace and team with OpenCost or Kubecost
  • Reduce waste with right-sizing, autoscaling, spot and scheduling
42.1

Why cost is hard to attribute

In plain words

You pay for nodes, disks, load balancers and network traffic. Pods share those. Allocation rules decide how a node's price is split among the Pods that ran on it.

The problem it solves

Finance sees a single EC2 and EBS bill, teams see none, and idle capacity is nobody's fault. Without visibility nobody reduces waste.

What it does

  • A common model: a Pod's cost is the greater of its CPU/memory request and its actual usage, priced by the node's hourly rate. Idle node capacity is shown separately.
  • Shared costs (control plane fee, monitoring, ingress, system namespaces) are split by a rule: evenly or proportional to usage.
  • Costs outside nodes: persistent volumes, load balancers, NAT gateway and cross-AZ traffic, managed services.
  • Requests are the lever: oversized requests reserve capacity you pay for even if unused.

Quick estimate by hand

bashWhere requests are high
kubectl get pods -A -o custom-columns=NS:.metadata.namespace,CPU:.spec.containers[*].resources.requests.cpu,MEM:.spec.containers[*].resources.requests.memory | head -20
kubectl top pods -A --sort-by=cpu | head -10
kubectl describe nodes | grep -A8 'Allocated resources' | head -30
42.2

Labels and tagging for cost

In plain words

Consistent labels on namespaces and workloads (and tags on cloud resources) are what let tools attribute cost to a team.

The problem it solves

Without ownership labels, 30 percent of spend ends up in "unallocated" and nobody acts on it.

What it does

  • Standardise a small set: team, cost-center, app, env. Enforce with admission policy (Kyverno or ValidatingAdmissionPolicy) so objects without them are rejected.
  • Label namespaces (inherit at tenant level) and workloads (for shared namespaces).
  • On EKS, activate cost allocation tags in AWS Billing, and use split cost allocation data to see Pod-level cost in the Cost and Usage Report.
  • Apply the same tags to volumes and load balancers through StorageClass parameters or controller annotations.

Enforce labels

yamlrequire-labels.yaml
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-team-label
spec:
  failurePolicy: Fail
  matchConstraints:
    resourceRules:
      - apiGroups: ["apps"]
        apiVersions: ["v1"]
        operations: ["CREATE", "UPDATE"]
        resources: ["deployments"]
  validations:
    - expression: "has(object.metadata.labels) && 'team' in object.metadata.labels"
      message: "Deployments must have a team label"
---
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding
metadata:
  name: require-team-label
spec:
  policyName: require-team-label
  validationActions: ["Deny"]
42.3

OpenCost and Kubecost

In plain words

OpenCost is the open source CNCF project that calculates Kubernetes cost from Prometheus metrics and cloud price lists. Kubecost is a commercial product built on the same engine, adding history, alerts and multi-cluster views.

The problem it solves

You need numbers per namespace, label and workload without building a data pipeline of your own.

What it does

  • Installs in a cluster, reads node, Pod and PV metrics from Prometheus, and prices them with provider APIs or custom prices (useful on-prem).
  • API and UI show allocation by namespace, controller, label, Pod, with idle and shared cost separated.
  • The allocation API: /allocation/compute?window=7d&aggregate=namespace.
  • Check the current Helm chart and licence terms of each project before choosing; capabilities of the free tier change over time.

Install and query

bashOpenCost
helm repo add opencost https://opencost.github.io/opencost-helm-chart
helm upgrade --install opencost opencost/opencost -n opencost --create-namespace
kubectl port-forward -n opencost svc/opencost 9003:9003 &
curl -s "http://localhost:9003/allocation/compute?window=7d&aggregate=namespace" | python3 -m json.tool | head -40
42.4

Showback and chargeback

In plain words

Showback reports cost to teams for awareness. Chargeback actually bills their budget. Start with showback.

The problem it solves

Teams do not change behaviour until they see their own numbers regularly and in terms they understand.

What it does

  • Publish a monthly and weekly report per team: total, trend, efficiency (usage versus request), and top workloads.
  • Define an efficiency metric: used divided by requested. A team at 20 percent is paying for four times what it uses.
  • Treat shared costs transparently; explain the rule once.
  • Set budgets and alerts (AWS Budgets by tag, Kubecost alerts) rather than surprise end-of-month reviews.

Efficiency from Prometheus

promqlCPU request efficiency per namespace
sum by (namespace) (rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{container!=""}[7d]))
  /
sum by (namespace) (kube_pod_container_resource_requests{resource="cpu"})
42.5

Reducing cost safely

In plain words

After you can see cost, reduce it in order of safety: remove waste, right-size, then change purchasing and scheduling.

The problem it solves

Cutting blindly causes outages. Waste removal first gives the largest savings with least risk.

What it does

  • Remove: unused namespaces, orphaned PVCs and load balancers, idle dev clusters (hibernate Gardener shoots, scale node groups to zero at night).
  • Right-size: use VPA recommendations, kubectl top, and efficiency reports to lower requests; keep memory limit equal to request.
  • Autoscale: HPA/KEDA for Pods and Karpenter or Cluster Autoscaler for nodes with consolidation of underused nodes.
  • Purchase: spot instances for fault tolerant workloads with PDBs and graceful shutdown; Savings Plans for the stable baseline.
  • Bin-pack: fewer larger nodes pack better but reduce failure isolation; balance with topology spread.

Orphans and idle objects

bashFind waste
kubectl get pvc -A --no-headers | awk '{print $1, $2, $3}' | head
kubectl get pv -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,STATUS:.status.phase,CLAIM:.spec.claimRef.name | grep Released
kubectl get svc -A --field-selector spec.type=LoadBalancer
kubectl get deploy -A -o custom-columns=NS:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,REPL:.spec.replicas | awk '$3==0'
Check yourself
Why can a Pod with low CPU usage still cost a lot?

Cost is based on reserved requests, so an oversized request holds node capacity whether or not the Pod uses it.

Section 43 of 65

CRDs and custom resources

6 concepts · about 45 minutes

Kubernetes is an API platform. Everything from Pods to cert-manager Certificates is an object in the same API server. CustomResourceDefinitions let you add your own object types and use them with kubectl, RBAC and GitOps like built-in ones.

Goals
  • Explain how a CustomResourceDefinition extends the Kubernetes API
  • Write a CRD with a validated schema, printer columns and a status subresource
  • Version, validate and safely upgrade CRDs
43.1

What a CRD is

In plain words

A CustomResourceDefinition (CRD) teaches the API server a new object type. After you apply it, you can create, read and watch objects of that kind. A CRD stores data only; behaviour comes from a controller.

The problem it solves

You want to describe higher level things (a database, a certificate, a tenant) in YAML and manage them with the same tools as everything else, instead of a separate system with its own API and access control.

What it does

  • The CRD defines group, kind, scope (Namespaced or Cluster), versions and a schema. The API server then serves REST endpoints for it, with storage in etcd, RBAC, watch and audit for free.
  • The objects are called custom resources (CRs). Delete the CRD and all its CRs are deleted.
  • Names: plural.group, for example databases.data.example.com.
  • kubectl api-resources and kubectl explain work on CRDs.

Looking at CRDs

bashExplore CRDs on a cluster
kubectl get crd | head -20
kubectl get crd certificates.cert-manager.io -o jsonpath='{.spec.versions[*].name}{"\n"}'
kubectl api-resources --api-group=cert-manager.io
kubectl explain certificate.spec.issuerRef
kubectl get crd | wc -l                          # Kyma and Istio add dozens
43.2

Writing a CRD

In plain words

A CRD names the type, lists versions, and gives an OpenAPI v3 schema describing allowed fields.

The problem it solves

Without a schema anyone could store any shape of data in your resource, and typos like replcias would be silently accepted.

What it does

  • spec.versions[].schema.openAPIV3Schema defines types, required fields, enums, minimum and maximum, and defaults.
  • Exactly one version has storage: true.
  • additionalPrinterColumns choose what kubectl get shows, such as phase and age.
  • subresources.status enables a separate /status endpoint so controllers update status without touching spec; scale lets kubectl scale and HPA work.
  • Structural schemas are required: every field needs a type; use x-kubernetes-preserve-unknown-fields sparingly.

A Database CRD

yamldatabase-crd.yaml
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: databases.data.example.com
spec:
  group: data.example.com
  scope: Namespaced
  names:
    kind: Database
    listKind: DatabaseList
    plural: databases
    singular: database
    shortNames: ["db"]
  versions:
    - name: v1
      served: true
      storage: true
      subresources:
        status: {}
      additionalPrinterColumns:
        - name: Engine
          type: string
          jsonPath: .spec.engine
        - name: Phase
          type: string
          jsonPath: .status.phase
        - name: Age
          type: date
          jsonPath: .metadata.creationTimestamp
      schema:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          type: object
          required: ["spec"]
          properties:
            spec:
              type: object
              required: ["engine", "storageGB"]
              properties:
                engine:
                  type: string
                  enum: ["postgres", "mysql"]
                version:
                  type: string
                  default: "16"
                storageGB:
                  type: integer
                  minimum: 1
                  maximum: 1000
            status:
              type: object
              properties:
                phase:
                  type: string
                observedGeneration:
                  type: integer
                  format: int64
43.3

Custom resources in use

In plain words

Once the CRD exists, you create objects of the new kind like any other manifest and manage them with the usual commands.

The problem it solves

Users need a simple, declarative interface. They should say what they want, not how it is built.

What it does

  • kubectl apply -f database.yaml creates the CR; validation runs at admission and errors come back immediately.
  • kubectl get db, describe, edit, delete all work. kubectl get db -o yaml shows both spec and status.
  • RBAC applies per resource and verb on the group, for example databases in data.example.com.
  • Because they are API objects, they work with Helm, Kustomize and GitOps without special handling.

Example

yamlorders-db.yaml
apiVersion: data.example.com/v1
kind: Database
metadata:
  name: orders
  namespace: shop
spec:
  engine: postgres
  version: "16"
  storageGB: 50
bashUse it
kubectl apply -f database-crd.yaml
kubectl wait --for=condition=Established crd/databases.data.example.com --timeout=30s
kubectl apply -f orders-db.yaml
kubectl get db -n shop
kubectl apply -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: data.example.com/v1
kind: Database
metadata:
  name: bad
  namespace: shop
spec:
  engine: oracle
  storageGB: 0
YAML
Check yourself
What happens to existing custom resources if you delete their CRD?

They are all deleted, because the API no longer knows the type.

43.4

Validation rules with CEL

In plain words

Beyond schema types, CRDs can carry CEL (Common Expression Language) rules that check relations between fields, evaluated by the API server.

The problem it solves

Some constraints are not expressible with types: "storage may only grow", "if replicas > 1 then highAvailability must be true". Putting these in a webhook adds an extra service to run.

What it does

  • x-kubernetes-validations holds rules with rule (the expression) and message.
  • self is the object at that schema level; oldSelf enables transition rules that compare to the previous value on update.
  • Rules run inside the API server, so no network call, no webhook availability risk, and they are cost-limited to prevent abuse.
  • GA since 1.29.

Rules inside the schema

yamlcel-fragment.yaml
spec:
  type: object
  properties:
    storageGB:
      type: integer
      x-kubernetes-validations:
        - rule: "self >= oldSelf"
          message: "storage can only grow"
    replicas:
      type: integer
    highAvailability:
      type: boolean
  x-kubernetes-validations:
    - rule: "self.replicas == 1 || self.highAvailability"
      message: "highAvailability must be true when replicas is above 1"
43.5

Versions and conversion

In plain words

A CRD can serve several versions (v1alpha1, v1beta1, v1) of the same type. The API converts between them, while only one version is stored in etcd.

The problem it solves

APIs evolve. You must change field names or structure without breaking existing users or stored objects.

What it does

  • served: true makes a version available; storage: true marks the stored one; deprecated: true adds a warning header.
  • Conversion strategy None only changes apiVersion, which is fine if schemas are identical. Webhook calls a conversion webhook for real structural changes.
  • To retire an old version: migrate stored objects (storage version migration), set served: false, then remove it from status.storedVersions after migrating.
  • Follow Kubernetes naming: alpha may break, beta is mostly stable, v1 is a commitment.

Commands

bashWhich versions are stored
kubectl get crd databases.data.example.com -o jsonpath='{.status.storedVersions}{"\n"}'
kubectl get crd databases.data.example.com -o jsonpath='{range .spec.versions[*]}{.name}{" served="}{.served}{" storage="}{.storage}{"\n"}{end}'
kubectl get databases.v1.data.example.com -A       # request a specific version explicitly
43.6

Installing and upgrading CRDs safely

In plain words

CRDs are cluster-wide and shared by everyone. Their lifecycle needs more care than ordinary workload manifests.

The problem it solves

Helm does not upgrade or delete CRDs in a chart's crds/ folder. A CRD upgrade applied late or never leads to controllers expecting fields the API drops.

What it does

  • Install CRDs before the CRs and controllers. In GitOps, use sync waves or a separate Kustomization that other layers depend on.
  • Use server-side apply (kubectl apply --server-side) for big CRDs; client-side apply fails because the last-applied annotation exceeds 262144 bytes.
  • Many projects ship CRDs as a separate chart or a manifest file; follow their upgrade notes for each release.
  • Never delete a CRD to "refresh" it; that deletes all data of that type.
  • Back up custom resources (Velero) before CRD changes.

Commands

bashApply big CRDs
kubectl apply --server-side --force-conflicts -f https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/releases/download/v1.16.2/cert-manager.crds.yaml
kubectl get crd -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,CREATED:.metadata.creationTimestamp | sort -k2 | tail -5
kubectl get crd -l app.kubernetes.io/instance=cert-manager
Careful

Deleting a CRD cascades to every custom resource of that type, including ones created by other teams. Treat kubectl delete crd like dropping a database table.

Section 44 of 65

Controllers and the operator pattern

6 concepts · about 45 minutes

A CRD is only data. A controller watches that data and makes the world match it. A controller that encodes the operational knowledge of a specific application is called an operator.

Goals
  • Describe the reconcile loop and why controllers are level triggered
  • Explain the operator pattern and when to use or avoid it
  • Read the anatomy of a controller built with controller-runtime
44.1

The reconcile loop

In plain words

A controller repeatedly compares desired state (spec) with observed state (the real world) and takes actions to reduce the difference. It does not react to events as commands; it re-evaluates the whole situation.

The problem it solves

Systems fail partway, events get lost, controllers restart. A design based on "do exactly what this event says" breaks. You need something that converges to the right state from any starting point.

What it does

  • Level triggered, not edge triggered: events only say "look at object X again". The reconciler reads current state and decides what to do, so missing an event is harmless.
  • Reconcile must be idempotent: running it ten times gives the same result as once.
  • Work arrives through a work queue with rate limiting and retries with backoff. Failed reconciles are requeued.
  • Built-in controllers (Deployment, ReplicaSet, Job) work exactly this way.

See controllers at work

bashObserve a built-in controller
kubectl create deploy demo --image=nginx:1.27 --replicas=3
kubectl delete pod -l app=demo --wait=false      # the controller notices the difference
kubectl get pods -l app=demo -w
kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.kind=ReplicaSet | tail -5
kubectl delete deploy demo
Check yourself
Why should a reconciler not assume it sees every event?

Controllers are level triggered: events can be coalesced, dropped or replayed after restart. The reconciler must derive its actions from current state.

44.2

Informers, caches and the work queue

In plain words

Controllers do not poll the API server. An informer opens a watch, keeps a local cache of objects, and notifies handlers when something changes.

The problem it solves

Hundreds of controllers each listing all Pods every second would overwhelm the API server.

What it does

  • The first step is a list (initial sync), then a watch stream of changes, resumed by resourceVersion.
  • Reads in the reconciler come from the local cache (cheap, slightly stale); writes go to the API server.
  • Handlers enqueue object keys; duplicates collapse, so a burst of 50 changes causes one reconcile.
  • Because the cache can be stale, writes use resourceVersion for optimistic concurrency. A conflict error means: re-read and retry.

Cost on the API server

bashWatch API traffic
kubectl get --raw /metrics | grep '^apiserver_registered_watchers' | head
kubectl get --raw /metrics | grep 'apiserver_request_total' | grep 'verb="WATCH"' | head -5
kubectl get --raw '/apis/data.example.com/v1/namespaces/shop/databases?watch=1&timeoutSeconds=5'
44.3

The operator pattern

In plain words

An operator is a CRD plus a controller that automates the operational tasks a skilled human would do for a particular application: install, configure, back up, upgrade, fail over.

The problem it solves

Stateful software (databases, message brokers, search clusters) needs more than a Deployment. Someone must initialise replicas, promote a new primary, resize volumes and run upgrades in the right order.

What it does

  • You declare kind: PostgresCluster with instances and backup schedule; the operator creates StatefulSets, Services, Secrets and CronJobs and keeps them healthy.
  • Examples: cert-manager, Prometheus Operator, CloudNativePG, Strimzi (Kafka), Argo CD, Crossplane, Istio operator.
  • Capability levels range from basic install through upgrades, lifecycle and backup, up to auto-tuning.
  • Operators are powerful but are privileged software: review their RBAC and treat their upgrades as platform changes.
Operator or something simpler
OptionOperator
Choose whenstateful or complex software with ordered lifecycle steps
Avoid whena stateless app a Deployment and Helm chart can run
OptionHelm chart only
Choose whenstatic installs and upgrades with no runtime logic
Avoid whenday-2 tasks such as failover must be automated
OptionManaged service
Choose whenan RDS, Cloud SQL or HANA Cloud instance meets the need
Avoid whenyou must stay in the cluster or avoid vendor lock-in
OptionCustom operator
Choose whenno operator exists and the logic is truly specific to you
Avoid whenan existing, well maintained operator already does it
44.4

Anatomy of a controller-runtime reconciler

In plain words

controller-runtime is the Go library behind Kubebuilder and Operator SDK. You write one Reconcile function that receives a name and namespace and returns whether to requeue.

The problem it solves

Writing informers, caches, leader election, metrics and webhooks from scratch is a lot of error-prone plumbing.

What it does

  • Reconcile(ctx, req): fetch the object by req.NamespacedName; if not found, return (it was deleted). Compare to desired child objects, create or update them, update status.
  • ctrl.NewControllerManagedBy(mgr).For(&Database{}).Owns(&appsv1.StatefulSet{}) makes changes to owned children trigger a reconcile of the parent.
  • The manager provides the cache, clients, leader election (only one active replica), health probes and metrics.
  • controllerutil.CreateOrUpdate and SetControllerReference make child management concise.
  • Return ctrl.Result{RequeueAfter: d} for periodic checks, or an error for retry with backoff.

A trimmed reconciler in Go

godatabase_controller.go
func (r *DatabaseReconciler) Reconcile(ctx context.Context, req ctrl.Request) (ctrl.Result, error) {
	var db datav1.Database
	if err := r.Get(ctx, req.NamespacedName, &db); err != nil {
		return ctrl.Result{}, client.IgnoreNotFound(err) // deleted, nothing to do
	}

	sts := &appsv1.StatefulSet{ObjectMeta: metav1.ObjectMeta{Name: db.Name, Namespace: db.Namespace}}
	_, err := controllerutil.CreateOrUpdate(ctx, r.Client, sts, func() error {
		sts.Spec = buildStatefulSetSpec(&db)                  // desired state from spec
		return controllerutil.SetControllerReference(&db, sts, r.Scheme)
	})
	if err != nil {
		return ctrl.Result{}, err                             // retried with backoff
	}

	db.Status.Phase = "Ready"
	db.Status.ObservedGeneration = db.Generation
	if err := r.Status().Update(ctx, &db); err != nil {
		return ctrl.Result{}, err
	}
	return ctrl.Result{RequeueAfter: time.Minute}, nil
}

func (r *DatabaseReconciler) SetupWithManager(mgr ctrl.Manager) error {
	return ctrl.NewControllerManagedBy(mgr).
		For(&datav1.Database{}).
		Owns(&appsv1.StatefulSet{}).
		Complete(r)
}
44.5

Status, conditions and generations

In plain words

A controller reports progress in status, using standard conditions, and records which version of the spec it has processed in observedGeneration.

The problem it solves

Users and automation need to know whether a custom resource is ready, stuck or failed, and whether the status reflects their latest change.

What it does

  • metadata.generation increases on every spec change; status.observedGeneration equals it once the controller has handled that change. If they differ, status is stale.
  • Conditions follow a standard shape: type (Ready), status (True/False/Unknown), reason (CamelCase), message, lastTransitionTime.
  • kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready and GitOps health checks depend on this convention.
  • Keep status derived and rebuildable; never store the only copy of important data there.

A status with conditions

yamlstatus-example.yaml
apiVersion: data.example.com/v1
kind: Database
metadata:
  name: orders
  namespace: shop
  generation: 4
status:
  observedGeneration: 4
  phase: Ready
  conditions:
    - type: Ready
      status: "True"
      reason: AllReplicasAvailable
      message: 3 of 3 instances are ready
      lastTransitionTime: "2026-10-31T10:15:00Z"
bashWait on conditions
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready database/orders -n shop --timeout=300s
kubectl get database orders -n shop -o jsonpath='{.metadata.generation} {.status.observedGeneration}{"\n"}'
44.6

Building operators and RBAC

In plain words

Frameworks scaffold the project: Kubebuilder and Operator SDK (Go), Kopf (Python), and Java Operator SDK. Whatever the language, the operator runs as a Deployment with a ServiceAccount and RBAC.

The problem it solves

Teams build operators with far too broad permissions, no leader election, and no metrics, then run them as cluster-admin.

What it does

  • Kubebuilder generates CRD manifests from Go type markers (make manifests), and RBAC rules from //+kubebuilder:rbac comments.
  • Run two replicas with leader election for availability; only the leader reconciles.
  • Give least-privilege RBAC: only the verbs and resources needed, namespaced where possible.
  • Expose metrics and health endpoints, and set resource requests. Test with envtest (a real API server and etcd binaries) before shipping.

Least privilege RBAC for the operator

yamloperator-rbac.yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: database-operator
rules:
  - apiGroups: ["data.example.com"]
    resources: ["databases", "databases/status", "databases/finalizers"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "update", "patch"]
  - apiGroups: ["apps"]
    resources: ["statefulsets"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch", "delete"]
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["services", "secrets", "events"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch"]
  - apiGroups: ["coordination.k8s.io"]
    resources: ["leases"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch"]

Section 45 of 65

Owner references, finalizers and garbage collection

5 concepts · about 40 minutes

Deleting an object is a process, not an instant. Kubernetes tracks who owns what and lets controllers block deletion until they have cleaned up. Understanding this is the key to fixing everything that is stuck in Terminating.

Goals
  • Use owner references so child objects are cleaned up automatically
  • Use finalizers to run cleanup for external resources before deletion
  • Unstick objects that stay Terminating without causing damage
45.1

Owner references

In plain words

An object can list its owner in metadata.ownerReferences. When the owner is deleted, the garbage collector deletes the dependants.

The problem it solves

A controller that creates child objects must clean them up when the parent goes away, even if the controller was down at that moment.

What it does

  • A ReplicaSet owns its Pods, a Deployment owns its ReplicaSets, a Job owns its Pods. Operators set the same for their children.
  • controller: true marks the managing owner; blockOwnerDeletion: true makes foreground deletion wait for the child.
  • Owner and dependant must be in the same namespace (or the owner cluster-scoped). Cross-namespace owners are not allowed.
  • kubectl get pod POD -o jsonpath='{.metadata.ownerReferences}' shows the chain.

Inspect owners

bashWho owns this
kubectl get pod web-7d9f8c-x2k4p -n shop -o jsonpath='{range .metadata.ownerReferences[*]}{.kind}{"/"}{.name}{" controller="}{.controller}{"\n"}{end}'
kubectl get rs -n shop -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,OWNER:.metadata.ownerReferences[0].name
kubectl tree deployment web -n shop        # needs the kubectl-tree plugin (krew)
45.2

Garbage collection and deletion propagation

In plain words

When you delete an object you choose what happens to its dependants: delete them in the background, wait for them first (foreground), or leave them behind (orphan).

The problem it solves

Sometimes you want to remove a Deployment but keep its Pods running while you replace it. Other times deletion must not return until everything is gone.

What it does

  • Background (default): the owner disappears at once; the garbage collector removes dependants afterwards.
  • Foreground: the owner gets a foregroundDeletion finalizer and stays visible until all dependants with blockOwnerDeletion are gone.
  • Orphan: dependants are kept and their owner reference is removed (--cascade=orphan).
  • Set with kubectl delete --cascade=background|foreground|orphan, or propagationPolicy in the API.

Commands

bashChoose how deletion cascades
kubectl delete deploy web -n shop --cascade=orphan          # Pods keep running without owner
kubectl delete deploy web -n shop --cascade=foreground      # wait for ReplicaSets and Pods
kubectl get rs,pods -n shop
45.3

Finalizers

In plain words

A finalizer is a string in metadata.finalizers that tells the API server "do not remove this object yet". Deletion sets deletionTimestamp, and the object stays until every finalizer has been removed by its controller.

The problem it solves

Some deletions need cleanup the API server cannot do: removing a cloud load balancer, deregistering from DNS, deleting a database in an external system. If the object vanished immediately, the cleanup would be lost.

What it does

  • The controller adds its finalizer when it first reconciles the object. On deletion, it sees deletionTimestamp, performs cleanup, removes its finalizer, and the API server then deletes the object.
  • Built-in examples: kubernetes.io/pvc-protection, foregroundDeletion, and namespace finalizers.
  • If the controller is gone, broken or cannot reach the external system, the object stays Terminating forever.
  • Always make cleanup idempotent, and remove the finalizer even when the external resource is already gone.

Finalizer handling in a reconciler

gofinalizer.go
const dbFinalizer = "data.example.com/cleanup"

if db.DeletionTimestamp.IsZero() {
	// object is live: make sure our finalizer is present
	if controllerutil.AddFinalizer(&db, dbFinalizer) {
		if err := r.Update(ctx, &db); err != nil {
			return ctrl.Result{}, err
		}
	}
} else if controllerutil.ContainsFinalizer(&db, dbFinalizer) {
	// object is being deleted: clean up, then release it
	if err := r.deleteExternalDatabase(ctx, &db); err != nil {
		return ctrl.Result{}, err // retry; the object stays Terminating
	}
	controllerutil.RemoveFinalizer(&db, dbFinalizer)
	if err := r.Update(ctx, &db); err != nil {
		return ctrl.Result{}, err
	}
	return ctrl.Result{}, nil
}
45.4

Objects stuck in Terminating

In plain words

An object with a deletionTimestamp that never disappears is waiting for a finalizer. Find out which one before you remove it.

The problem it solves

A namespace cannot be deleted, a PVC stays Terminating, or a custom resource blocks a Helm uninstall. Pipelines hang.

What it does

  • Look at metadata.finalizers and the owning controller. Is the controller running? Does its log show errors?
  • Namespaces: check kubectl get ns NAME -o yaml conditions (NamespaceContentRemaining, NamespaceFinalizersRemaining, NamespaceDeletionDiscoveryFailure). Typical cause: a CRD was removed first, leaving CRs without a controller, or an unavailable aggregated API (metrics-server).
  • Fix the cause first: restore the controller or the CRD, or fix the external dependency, and the object will finish itself.
  • Last resort: patch the finalizer away. This skips the cleanup, and can leave cloud resources (disks, load balancers) behind that cost money.

Commands

bashDiagnose before forcing
kubectl get ns shop -o jsonpath='{range .status.conditions[*]}{.type}{": "}{.message}{"\n"}{end}'
kubectl api-resources --verbs=list --namespaced -o name | xargs -n1 kubectl get --show-kind --ignore-not-found -n shop
kubectl get database orders -n shop -o jsonpath='{.metadata.finalizers}{" "}{.metadata.deletionTimestamp}{"\n"}'
kubectl logs -n database-system deploy/database-operator --tail=30
# last resort, accepting that cleanup will be skipped
kubectl patch database orders -n shop --type=merge -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":null}}'
Danger

Never "finalize" a namespace through /finalize or strip finalizers in bulk as a routine fix. It leaves orphaned external resources and hides the real fault. Record what you skipped and clean it up by hand.

Check yourself
What does the API server do when you delete an object that has a finalizer?

It sets deletionTimestamp and keeps the object until every finalizer is removed by its controller.

Name a safer first step than removing a finalizer.

Find the controller that owns the finalizer and restore it (or its CRD or dependency) so it can finish cleanup.

45.5

Server-side apply and field ownership

In plain words

With server-side apply (SSA), the API server tracks which manager owns each field (metadata.managedFields) and reports conflicts when two managers change the same field.

The problem it solves

GitOps, an operator, an HPA and a human may all edit the same object. With client-side apply, they overwrite each other silently or produce confusing diffs.

What it does

  • kubectl apply --server-side --field-manager=NAME claims fields your manifest sets. Fields you omit are left to other managers.
  • A conflict is returned when another manager owns a field you try to change; --force-conflicts takes ownership.
  • Example: the HPA owns spec.replicas, so your manifest should omit replicas for HPA-managed Deployments.
  • Operators should use SSA (client.Apply patches) to own only their fields.

Commands

bashSee and resolve ownership
kubectl get deploy web -n shop -o yaml --show-managed-fields | sed -n '/managedFields/,$p' | head -30
kubectl apply --server-side --field-manager=gitops -f deploy.yaml
kubectl apply --server-side --field-manager=gitops --force-conflicts -f deploy.yaml
kubectl diff --server-side -f deploy.yaml
← PreviousNext →
Section 46 of 65

Admission and conversion webhooks

6 concepts · about 45 minutes

Webhooks let external services take part in API requests. They power policy engines, sidecar injection and CRD version conversion. They are also a leading cause of cluster-wide outages when badly configured.

Goals
  • Place mutating and validating webhooks in the admission chain
  • Configure a webhook safely with failure policy, selectors and timeouts
  • Use ValidatingAdmissionPolicy and conversion webhooks, and debug webhook outages
46.1

The admission chain

In plain words

After a request is authenticated and authorised, it passes through admission. Mutating admission can change the object; validating admission can only accept or reject. Then the object is stored.

The problem it solves

RBAC says who may create a Pod, not what the Pod may contain. You need a place to enforce rules (no latest tags, required labels) and to inject defaults (sidecars, resource limits).

What it does

  • Order: authentication, authorisation, mutating admission (plugins, then webhooks), schema validation, validating admission (plugins, webhooks, ValidatingAdmissionPolicy), persist to etcd.
  • Admission applies to create, update, delete and connect operations, not to reads.
  • Built-in plugins include LimitRanger, ResourceQuota, ServiceAccount, PodSecurity and NodeRestriction.
  • Mutating webhooks may run more than once if another one changes the object (reinvocation); keep them idempotent.

Which webhooks are installed

bashInspect the chain
kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfigurations
kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations
kubectl get validatingadmissionpolicies,validatingadmissionpolicybindings
kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration istio-sidecar-injector -o jsonpath='{.webhooks[*].failurePolicy}{"\n"}'
46.2

Writing a validating webhook configuration

In plain words

A webhook configuration tells the API server which requests to send to which HTTPS endpoint, and what to do if it cannot be reached.

The problem it solves

A webhook that matches too much, or fails closed while its Pod is down, can block all Pod creation, including the Pods needed to fix the webhook.

What it does

  • rules select operations, API groups and resources. namespaceSelector and objectSelector narrow the scope. Exclude kube-system and the webhook's own namespace.
  • failurePolicy: Fail rejects when the webhook errors or times out (safe but risky); Ignore lets requests through (available but unenforced).
  • timeoutSeconds (1 to 30, default 10) caps the delay added to every matching request.
  • sideEffects must be None or NoneOnDryRun for dry-run to work. matchConditions (CEL) filter requests before the call, reducing load.
  • TLS: the API server needs a CA bundle (caBundle) for the service certificate; cert-manager can inject it.

A configuration with guardrails

yamlvalidating-webhook.yaml
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingWebhookConfiguration
metadata:
  name: policy-check
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/inject-ca-from: policy-system/policy-webhook-cert
webhooks:
  - name: pods.policy.example.com
    admissionReviewVersions: ["v1"]
    sideEffects: None
    timeoutSeconds: 5
    failurePolicy: Fail
    clientConfig:
      service:
        name: policy-webhook
        namespace: policy-system
        path: /validate-pods
    rules:
      - apiGroups: [""]
        apiVersions: ["v1"]
        operations: ["CREATE"]
        resources: ["pods"]
    namespaceSelector:
      matchExpressions:
        - key: kubernetes.io/metadata.name
          operator: NotIn
          values: ["kube-system", "policy-system"]
    matchConditions:
      - name: skip-system-pods
        expression: "!object.metadata.name.startsWith('kube-')"
46.3

The AdmissionReview exchange

In plain words

The API server POSTs an AdmissionReview JSON document containing the object and request details. The webhook answers with an AdmissionReview response with allowed true or false, and for mutation a JSON Patch.

The problem it solves

You need to know the contract to write, test and debug a webhook without a framework hiding it.

What it does

  • Request contains uid, kind, operation, userInfo, object and oldObject.
  • The response must echo the same uid. Rejection includes status.message, which the user sees in the error.
  • Mutation returns patchType: JSONPatch and a base64 encoded patch.
  • Webhook servers should respond fast and be stateless, run with several replicas, spread across nodes, and have a PodDisruptionBudget.

Response shapes

jsonadmission-response.json
{
  "apiVersion": "admission.k8s.io/v1",
  "kind": "AdmissionReview",
  "response": {
    "uid": "705ab4f5-6393-11e8-b7cc-42010a800002",
    "allowed": false,
    "status": {
      "code": 403,
      "message": "image must not use the latest tag"
    }
  }
}
46.4

ValidatingAdmissionPolicy with CEL

In plain words

ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (VAP) lets you write validation rules in CEL that run inside the API server, with no webhook service to host. A binding says where the policy applies.

The problem it solves

Webhooks need a running service, certificates and careful failure handling. For many simple rules that is more infrastructure than the rule is worth.

What it does

  • Stable (GA) since 1.30. A policy defines matchConstraints, optional paramKind, variables and validations; a ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding selects namespaces and sets validationActions (Deny, Warn, Audit).
  • Use Warn and Audit first to see what would be blocked, then switch to Deny.
  • Mutating counterpart MutatingAdmissionPolicy is newer; check its status in your Kubernetes version before relying on it.
  • Kyverno and OPA Gatekeeper still add richer features: mutation, generation, external data, reporting.

Disallow latest tags

yamlno-latest.yaml
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
metadata:
  name: no-latest-tag
spec:
  failurePolicy: Fail
  matchConstraints:
    resourceRules:
      - apiGroups: ["apps"]
        apiVersions: ["v1"]
        operations: ["CREATE", "UPDATE"]
        resources: ["deployments"]
  validations:
    - expression: "object.spec.template.spec.containers.all(c, !c.image.endsWith(':latest') && c.image.contains(':'))"
      message: "images must have an explicit tag and not use latest"
---
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding
metadata:
  name: no-latest-tag
spec:
  policyName: no-latest-tag
  validationActions: ["Warn", "Audit"]
  matchResources:
    namespaceSelector:
      matchLabels:
        env: prod
46.5

Conversion webhooks

In plain words

A conversion webhook converts a custom resource between versions when a client asks for a version that differs from the stored one. It is the CRD counterpart of admission webhooks.

The problem it solves

When v1 renames spec.size to spec.storageGB, old clients still read and write v1beta1. The API server needs a way to translate both ways without losing data.

What it does

  • Set spec.conversion.strategy: Webhook in the CRD with the service and conversionReviewVersions.
  • The webhook receives a ConversionReview with a list of objects and a desiredAPIVersion, and returns the converted list.
  • Conversions must be lossless and round-trip safe: converting there and back gives the original. Use annotations to hold fields that older versions cannot represent.
  • The webhook becomes a dependency of reads and writes for that CRD; if it is down, requests for that type fail. controller-runtime supports a hub and spoke model: every version converts to and from one hub version.

CRD conversion section

yamlcrd-conversion.yaml
spec:
  conversion:
    strategy: Webhook
    webhook:
      conversionReviewVersions: ["v1"]
      clientConfig:
        service:
          name: database-operator-webhook
          namespace: database-system
          path: /convert
Check yourself
What happens to reads of a custom resource if its conversion webhook is down?

Requests that need conversion fail, because the API server cannot translate between the stored and requested versions.

46.6

Debugging and hardening webhooks

In plain words

Webhook failures show up as odd API errors: timeouts when creating Pods, failed calling webhook, or Helm installs that hang. Know the symptoms and the emergency exit.

The problem it solves

A broken policy webhook can block Pod creation cluster-wide, including the controllers that would repair it, and the fix itself requires creating Pods.

What it does

  • Typical errors: failed calling webhook "...": context deadline exceeded (slow or unreachable), x509: certificate signed by unknown authority (bad caBundle), no endpoints available for service (webhook Pods down).
  • Emergency: delete or patch the failurePolicy of the configuration with kubectl; this works because API requests for webhook configurations themselves are not sent to webhooks.
  • Hardening: replicas of 2 or more with anti-affinity, PDB, a priority class, namespace exclusions, short timeouts, and matchConditions.
  • On EKS the control plane must reach the webhook Pod: security groups must allow the control plane to the webhook port (commonly 8443, 9443). Gardener and Kyma usually run webhooks within the cluster network without extra rules.
  • Observe: apiserver_admission_webhook_rejection_count and apiserver_admission_webhook_admission_duration_seconds metrics.

Commands

bashTriage and emergency steps
kubectl get endpoints policy-webhook -n policy-system
kubectl logs -n policy-system deploy/policy-webhook --tail=30
kubectl get validatingwebhookconfiguration policy-check -o jsonpath='{.webhooks[*].failurePolicy}{"\n"}'
# emergency: stop blocking the cluster, then fix and revert
kubectl patch validatingwebhookconfiguration policy-check --type=json \
  -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/webhooks/0/failurePolicy","value":"Ignore"}]'
kubectl get --raw /metrics | grep apiserver_admission_webhook_rejection_count | head
Careful

Remember to set failurePolicy back after the incident, and add a PDB and exclusions so it cannot happen again. An Ignore left in place silently disables your policy.
