Section 47 of 65

The Kubernetes API in depth

8 concepts · about 60 minutes

Every kubectl command, controller and operator is a client of one REST API. Knowing how that API is organised, versioned and protected under load makes upgrades, controllers and incidents far easier to reason about.

Goals
  • Read API groups, versions and discovery documents with confidence
  • Use server-side apply and field managers to share ownership of objects
  • Explain watch, resourceVersion, API priority and fairness and aggregated APIs
47.1

API groups, versions and resources

In plain words

Resources are organised into groups such as apps, batch and networking.k8s.io. Each group has one or more versions such as v1. The old core group has no name and is written v1.

The problem it solves

A single flat list of all object types could not evolve. Groups let teams ship and version their types independently, and let CRDs add their own.

What it does

  • A full path looks like /apis/apps/v1/namespaces/shop/deployments. The core group lives under /api/v1.
  • apiVersion in a manifest is group/version, and kind names the type.
  • A resource also has subresources such as pods/log, deployments/scale and pods/eviction, which RBAC treats separately.
  • kubectl api-resources lists resources, kubectl explain shows schemas.

Explore the API from kubectl

bashDiscover groups, resources and schemas
kubectl api-resources --api-group=apps -o wide
kubectl api-versions | sort | head -20
kubectl explain deployment.spec.strategy --api-version=apps/v1
kubectl get --raw /apis/apps/v1 | head -c 400
Check yourself
What is the group of Pods and Services?

The core group, which has no name. Its apiVersion is just v1 and its path starts with /api/v1.

47.2

Versions, stability levels and deprecation

In plain words

A version suffix tells you how stable an API is. v1 is stable, v1beta1 is a beta that may change, and v1alpha1 is experimental and off by default.

The problem it solves

Without clear levels, clusters would break on every upgrade and teams would not know which APIs are safe to depend on.

What it does

  • Stable APIs follow a deprecation policy. A GA API is supported for at least 12 months or 3 releases after it is deprecated, whichever is longer. Check the current policy page for the exact numbers.
  • Beta APIs are usually no longer enabled by default for new beta features since 1.24, though existing ones continue until removed.
  • Removed versions return 404. Stored objects are migrated by the API server, but your manifests and Helm charts are not.
  • The metric apiserver_requested_deprecated_apis shows who still calls deprecated endpoints.

Find deprecated usage before upgrading

bashDeprecated API usage
kubectl get --raw /metrics | grep apiserver_requested_deprecated_apis | head
kubectl get events -A --field-selector reason=FailedCreate | head
kubectl convert --help | head -3   # kubectl-convert is a separate plugin
Tip

Tools such as kubent or pluto scan manifests and Helm releases for removed APIs. Run one in CI before every minor upgrade. See the upgrade page in this track.

47.3

Discovery and OpenAPI

In plain words

The API server publishes what it serves. Clients read this at runtime so that kubectl can work with CRDs it has never seen.

The problem it solves

Hard-coding resource lists into clients would break whenever a cluster adds a CRD or aggregated API.

What it does

  • /api and /apis list groups and versions. Aggregated discovery (stable in recent releases) returns this in one or two calls instead of dozens.
  • /openapi/v3 serves schemas per group version. kubectl explain and IDE validation use it.
  • kubectl caches discovery in ~/.kube/cache/discovery. A stale cache can show missing resources after a CRD install.
  • kubectl get --raw reads any path directly, including /healthz, /readyz and /livez.

Reading discovery

bashDiscovery and health endpoints
kubectl get --raw /readyz?verbose | head -20
kubectl get --raw /openapi/v3 | head -c 300
rm -rf ~/.kube/cache/discovery   # force a refresh if resources look missing
47.4

Aggregated APIs and APIService

In plain words

An aggregated API lets another server join the main API under a group such as metrics.k8s.io. The kube-apiserver proxies matching requests to it.

The problem it solves

CRDs store plain data in etcd. Some features need custom logic, other storage or live data, such as metrics that are never stored in etcd.

What it does

  • You register an APIService object that names a group, a version and the Service that hosts the extension server.
  • The metrics-server uses this for kubectl top. If it is down, kubectl get apiservices shows False (MissingEndpoints) and namespace deletion can hang, since discovery fails.
  • Authentication is delegated: the aggregator authenticates the user and forwards identity in headers.
  • Prefer CRDs unless you need custom storage, subresource logic or non-etcd data.

Check APIService health

bashAPIService status
kubectl get apiservices | grep -v 'Local'
kubectl describe apiservice v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io | tail -15
yamlAPIService registration (shape)
apiVersion: apiregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: APIService
metadata:
  name: v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io
spec:
  group: metrics.k8s.io
  version: v1beta1
  groupPriorityMinimum: 100
  versionPriority: 100
  service:
    name: metrics-server
    namespace: kube-system
Check yourself
Why can a broken metrics-server block namespace deletion?

The namespace controller discovers all APIs. An unavailable aggregated API makes discovery fail, so it cannot confirm that the namespace is empty.

47.5

Server-side apply

In plain words

With server-side apply (SSA) you send your desired fields and the API server merges them into the live object and records who owns each field.

The problem it solves

Client-side kubectl apply stores the last config in an annotation and computes a patch on your laptop. Two writers such as a controller and a pipeline easily overwrite each other without noticing.

What it does

  • kubectl apply --server-side sends a PATCH of type application/apply-patch+yaml.
  • The server tracks ownership in metadata.managedFields. If another manager owns a field you set to a different value, you get a conflict 409.
  • --force-conflicts takes ownership. Use it deliberately, since the other manager may then fight back.
  • Fields you omit are left alone unless you previously owned them, in which case they are removed. This makes it safe to share objects.
  • Flux and Argo CD both support server-side apply, which also avoids the 262144 byte annotation limit hit by large CRDs.

Try SSA

bashServer-side apply with a dry run
cat > /tmp/cm.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: ssa-demo
data:
  mode: blue
EOF
kubectl apply --server-side --field-manager=team-a -f /tmp/cm.yaml --dry-run=server -o yaml | head -20
Careful

Do not set spec.replicas in a manifest that an HPA also manages. Remove the field from Git so that the HPA keeps ownership.

47.6

Field managers and managedFields

In plain words

Each writer has a manager name. managedFields lists which manager set which fields, with the operation (Apply or Update) and a timestamp.

The problem it solves

When a value keeps changing back, you need to know which tool is changing it.

What it does

  • kubectl sets the manager from the command: kubectl-client-side-apply, kubectl-edit, and so on. Use --field-manager to name your pipeline.
  • Controllers usually write as Update with their own names, for example kube-controller-manager or cluster-autoscaler.
  • kubectl get -o yaml --show-managed-fields prints the data; by default kubectl hides it.
  • Moving a field between managers: apply with the new manager and --force-conflicts, then stop the old one.

Find the owner of a field

bashWho changed it
kubectl get deploy api -n shop -o yaml --show-managed-fields | grep -E 'manager:|operation:|f:replicas' | head -20
kubectl get deploy api -n shop --show-managed-fields -o jsonpath='{range .metadata.managedFields[*]}{.manager}{" "}{.operation}{"\n"}{end}'
Check yourself
What does a 409 conflict on apply tell you?

Another field manager owns a field you tried to set to a different value. Decide who should own it, then drop the field or force.

47.7

Watch, resourceVersion and informers

In plain words

A watch is a long-lived HTTP stream of changes. Every object carries a resourceVersion that marks its place in etcd history, so a client can resume from a known point.

The problem it solves

Polling the API for changes would overload it. Controllers need cheap, ordered and resumable notifications.

What it does

  • GET ...?watch=true&resourceVersion=N streams ADDED, MODIFIED, DELETED and BOOKMARK events after N.
  • If N is too old (etcd compacted it) the server returns 410 Gone, and the client must list again. This is called a relist.
  • Treat resourceVersion as opaque. Never compare numbers; only pass them back.
  • Informers in client-go list once, then watch, and keep a local cache. Controllers read the cache and use work queues, so they rarely call the API directly.
  • Optimistic concurrency: an update with an old resourceVersion fails with 409, and the client retries.
  • Streaming list (sendInitialEvents) in recent versions reduces list memory on the API server. Check the current docs for your version.

Watch from the command line

bashSee raw watch events
kubectl get pods -n shop --watch-only -o name &
sleep 5; kill %1
kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/namespaces/shop/pods?watch=true&timeoutSeconds=5" | head -c 600
Check yourself
What should a client do after 410 Gone?

Perform a new LIST to obtain a fresh resourceVersion and then start a new watch.

47.8

API priority and fairness

In plain words

API Priority and Fairness (APF) is the API server's queueing system. It sorts requests into priority levels and flows so that one noisy client cannot starve the rest.

The problem it solves

A buggy controller listing all pods in a loop can make the API server slow for everyone, including the kubelets and the scheduler.

What it does

  • A FlowSchema matches requests by user, group, verb and resource, and assigns them to a PriorityLevelConfiguration.
  • Each level has concurrency shares and queues. Requests are spread by flow (typically per user and namespace) using shuffle sharding.
  • Overloaded levels return 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After. Exempt and system levels protect leader election and node traffic.
  • Metrics: apiserver_flowcontrol_rejected_requests_total and apiserver_flowcontrol_current_inqueue_requests.
  • Managed control planes such as EKS and Gardener shoots may restrict what you can change, so check which objects are writable.

Inspect and add a schema

bashLook at APF objects
kubectl get flowschemas
kubectl get prioritylevelconfigurations
kubectl get --raw /debug/api_priority_and_fairness/dump_priority_levels | head -20
yamlGive a batch controller its own flow
apiVersion: flowcontrol.apiserver.k8s.io/v1
kind: FlowSchema
metadata:
  name: batch-controller
spec:
  matchingPrecedence: 800
  priorityLevelConfiguration:
    name: workload-low
  distinguisherMethod:
    type: ByUser
  rules:
    - subjects:
        - kind: ServiceAccount
          serviceAccount:
            name: batch-controller
            namespace: batch
      resourceRules:
        - verbs: ["list", "watch"]
          apiGroups: ["*"]
          resources: ["*"]
          namespaces: ["*"]
Note

flowcontrol.apiserver.k8s.io/v1 is GA from 1.29. On older clusters use v1beta3. Check your version first.

← PreviousNext →
Section 48 of 65

kubectl mastery

8 concepts · about 55 minutes

kubectl is the main tool of every Kubernetes engineer. A few advanced features turn long pipelines of grep and awk into single reliable commands and make work on many clusters safer.

Goals
  • Extract exactly the fields you need with jsonpath and custom columns
  • Debug Pods and nodes with kubectl debug and ephemeral containers
  • Extend kubectl with plugins and krew and manage many contexts safely
48.1

Output formats and server-side printing

In plain words

-o changes how kubectl prints an object. Besides yaml and json, there are wide, name, jsonpath, custom-columns and go-template.

The problem it solves

Default tables hide fields you need, and scraping them with awk breaks when columns change.

What it does

  • -o wide adds node, IP and image columns. -o name prints kind/name, ideal for loops.
  • kubectl get asks the server for a Table, so columns can include custom printer columns of CRDs.
  • --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp sorts using a jsonpath. --no-headers helps scripts.
  • -l filters by label and --field-selector by a few supported fields, such as status.phase or spec.nodeName.

Everyday forms

bashSorting, selecting, naming
kubectl get pods -A -o wide --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp | tail -5
kubectl get pods -A --field-selector=status.phase!=Running,status.phase!=Succeeded
kubectl get deploy -n shop -o name
kubectl get pods -n shop -l app=api,tier=backend --show-labels
48.2

JSONPath

In plain words

JSONPath is a small query language over the object JSON. kubectl wraps it in braces: {.metadata.name}.

The problem it solves

You need one value, such as every image in the cluster or a node's internal IP, without parsing a table.

What it does

  • {.items[*].metadata.name} takes a field from all items. {range .items[*]}...{end} loops and lets you add newlines with {"\n"}.
  • Filters: {.items[?(@.status.phase=="Running")].metadata.name}.
  • Dots in keys are escaped: {.data.tls\.crt} reads the key tls.crt of a Secret.
  • kubectl's jsonpath has no regex or arithmetic. For more power use -o json | jq.

Useful queries

bashImages in use and a decoded secret key
kubectl get pods -A -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.namespace}{"\t"}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.spec.containers[*].image}{"\n"}{end}' | head
kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{" "}{.status.addresses[?(@.type=="InternalIP")].address}{"\n"}{end}'
kubectl get secret tls-cert -n shop -o jsonpath='{.data.tls\.crt}' | base64 -d | openssl x509 -noout -enddate
Check yourself
How do you read a Secret key named tls.crt in jsonpath?

Escape the dot, {.data.tls\.crt}, and base64-decode the result.

48.3

Custom columns and templates

In plain words

-o custom-columns=HEADER:path,... makes a tidy table from any fields. go-template gives loops and conditions when jsonpath is not enough.

The problem it solves

Operations reports need a stable, readable layout such as Pod name, node and restarts, and ad hoc scripts drift over time.

What it does

  • Each column is NAME:.json.path. Use [*] to join list values with commas.
  • custom-columns-file=cols.txt stores a layout for reuse in a team repository.
  • go-template supports if, range, printf and the index function for keys with dots.

Examples

bashReadable tables
kubectl get pods -n shop -o custom-columns=POD:.metadata.name,NODE:.spec.nodeName,RESTARTS:.status.containerStatuses[*].restartCount,IMAGE:.spec.containers[*].image
kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,CPU:.status.allocatable.cpu,MEM:.status.allocatable.memory,TAINTS:.spec.taints[*].key
kubectl get pods -n shop -o go-template='{{range .items}}{{.metadata.name}}{{"\n"}}{{end}}'
48.4

kubectl debug and ephemeral containers

In plain words

kubectl debug adds a temporary container with debugging tools to a running Pod, or copies a Pod, or starts a privileged Pod on a node.

The problem it solves

Production images are minimal or distroless and have no shell, so kubectl exec cannot help.

What it does

  • Ephemeral container: kubectl debug -it POD --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=app shares the process namespace of the target container. They cannot be removed, and the Pod keeps them until it is recreated.
  • Copy: --copy-to=NAME creates a clone, where you can change the image or command (--set-image) without touching the original.
  • Node: kubectl debug node/NODE -it --image=busybox starts a Pod in the host namespaces with the node filesystem at /host.
  • RBAC needs pods/ephemeralcontainers update permission; Pod Security may block privileged node debugging. Newer releases add debugging profiles (--profile); check the current docs.

Commands

bashDebug without changing the app
kubectl debug -it POD -n shop --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=api -- bash
kubectl debug POD -n shop -it --copy-to=api-dbg --set-image=api=busybox:1.36 -- sh
kubectl debug node/NODE -it --image=busybox:1.36 -- chroot /host sh
kubectl delete pod api-dbg -n shop
Careful

Node debugging gives root on the host. In Gardener or Kyma clusters follow your team's access policy and delete the debug Pod afterwards.

48.5

Contexts, kubeconfig and safe switching

In plain words

A kubeconfig holds clusters, users and contexts. A context is a named triple of cluster, user and default namespace.

The problem it solves

With Kyma, EKS and Gardener clusters at once, one command in the wrong context can change production.

What it does

  • KUBECONFIG=a.yaml:b.yaml merges files for one session; kubectl config view --flatten --minify exports one context.
  • Prefer one kubeconfig per cluster and an environment variable per terminal, rather than a global current-context.
  • kubectx and kubens switch quickly. Show the context in your shell prompt.
  • Always pass --context in scripts. Use kubectl auth whoami (recent versions) and kubectl auth can-i to confirm identity and rights.
  • Exec credential plugins (aws eks get-token, kubelogin for OIDC) fetch short lived tokens, so kubeconfig files hold no long-lived secret.

Commands

bashWork safely with contexts
kubectl config get-contexts
kubectl --context=prod-eks get ns | head -3
kubectl config view --minify --flatten > /tmp/one-cluster.yaml
KUBECONFIG=/tmp/one-cluster.yaml kubectl auth can-i delete deploy -n shop
Check yourself
Why pass --context in scripts?

The current-context can change between runs or terminals, and an explicit context prevents running against the wrong cluster.

48.6

kubectl plugins

In plain words

Any executable on your PATH named kubectl-NAME is a plugin and runs as kubectl NAME.

The problem it solves

Teams repeat the same multi-step commands and want them to look native.

What it does

  • Dashes in the file name become subcommands: kubectl-foo-bar runs with kubectl foo bar.
  • kubectl plugin list shows the discovered plugins and warns about shadowed ones.
  • Plugins can be bash, Go or Python. They read the same KUBECONFIG and receive the arguments.
  • Built-in commands cannot be overridden.

A tiny plugin

bashkubectl-restarts, top restarting Pods
cat > /tmp/kubectl-restarts <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
kubectl get pods "$@" --no-headers -o custom-columns=NS:.metadata.namespace,POD:.metadata.name,R:.status.containerStatuses[0].restartCount | sort -k3 -nr | head -10
EOF
chmod +x /tmp/kubectl-restarts
PATH=$PATH:/tmp kubectl restarts -A
48.7

krew and useful plugins

In plain words

krew is the plugin manager for kubectl. It installs community plugins from an index with kubectl krew install.

The problem it solves

Finding, installing and updating plugins by hand is slow and unsafe.

What it does

  • kubectl krew search, install, upgrade and list manage plugins in ~/.krew.
  • Popular ones: ctx, ns, neat (clean YAML), tree (owner hierarchy), who-can (RBAC), view-secret, stern style log tailing, resource-capacity, df-pv.
  • Plugins run with your credentials, so install only from trusted sources and review them in sensitive environments.
  • Check your organisation's policy on the default index.

Try it

bashInstall and use plugins
kubectl krew install ctx ns neat tree who-can
kubectl tree deployment api -n shop
kubectl who-can delete pods -n shop
kubectl get deploy api -n shop -o yaml | kubectl neat
48.8

Apply, diff, patch and wait

In plain words

Beyond apply, kubectl has verbs to preview, change a single field and wait for conditions, which make scripts and pipelines reliable.

The problem it solves

Pipelines that apply and immediately continue race against the cluster, and blind edits cause outages.

What it does

  • kubectl diff -f shows what would change; it exits with 1 if there are differences.
  • kubectl patch --type=merge|json|strategic edits fields. Strategic merge understands lists with keys; JSON patch uses op/path/value.
  • kubectl wait --for=condition=Available deploy/api --timeout=120s blocks until true; --for=delete and --for=jsonpath=... are also supported.
  • kubectl rollout status follows a rollout and fails on timeout.
  • --dry-run=server validates against admission without persisting.

Commands

bashSafe change sequence
kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml --dry-run=server
kubectl diff -f deploy.yaml || true
kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml
kubectl rollout status deploy/api -n shop --timeout=180s
kubectl wait --for=condition=Available deploy/api -n shop --timeout=60s
kubectl patch deploy api -n shop --type=json -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/replicas","value":3}]'
Check yourself
What does kubectl diff return when there are changes?

Exit code 1, so scripts can tell that a difference exists. Exit code above 1 means an error.

← PreviousNext →
Section 49 of 65

Gateway API in depth

7 concepts · about 55 minutes

Gateway API is the successor of Ingress. It is expressive, role based and portable across implementations such as Istio, Cilium, Envoy Gateway and the Kyma API Gateway module.

Goals
  • Explain the role-oriented model of GatewayClass, Gateway and routes
  • Configure HTTPRoute matching, traffic splitting, filters and cross-namespace access
  • Operate TLS, policy attachment and migration from Ingress
49.1

The role-oriented resource model

In plain words

Gateway API splits what Ingress mixed together. Infrastructure providers define a GatewayClass, cluster operators create Gateways, and app teams attach routes.

The problem it solves

One Ingress object forced platform and application owners to edit the same file, and annotations differed for every controller.

What it does

  • GatewayClass names a controller (like StorageClass).
  • Gateway declares listeners: port, protocol, hostname and TLS.
  • HTTPRoute, GRPCRoute, TLSRoute, TCPRoute and UDPRoute describe routing and attach to a Gateway through parentRefs. Route types beyond HTTPRoute vary in maturity; check the current support level.
  • Standard channel resources are GA (v1) for GatewayClass, Gateway, HTTPRoute and GRPCRoute. Experimental ones need the experimental CRD bundle.

Core objects

yamlGateway and HTTPRoute
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: public
  namespace: infra
spec:
  gatewayClassName: istio
  listeners:
    - name: https
      protocol: HTTPS
      port: 443
      hostname: "*.example.com"
      tls:
        mode: Terminate
        certificateRefs:
          - name: wildcard-example-com
      allowedRoutes:
        namespaces:
          from: Selector
          selector:
            matchLabels:
              gateway-access: "true"
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: api
  namespace: shop
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: public
      namespace: infra
  hostnames: ["api.example.com"]
  rules:
    - matches:
        - path: {type: PathPrefix, value: /v1}
      backendRefs:
        - name: api
          port: 8080
Check yourself
Which object does the application team normally own?

The route (HTTPRoute and similar). The Gateway belongs to the cluster operator, and the GatewayClass to the infrastructure provider.

49.2

Listeners, hostnames and allowedRoutes

In plain words

A listener is a port and protocol on a Gateway, optionally limited to a hostname. allowedRoutes decides which namespaces may attach routes to it.

The problem it solves

In a shared cluster, any team could claim any hostname or path on a shared entry point.

What it does

  • from: Same allows only the Gateway namespace, All any, Selector namespaces by label.
  • Routes whose hostnames do not intersect with the listener hostname are not accepted.
  • Status conditions on routes (Accepted, ResolvedRefs) tell you why attachment failed.
  • Conflicts on the same hostname and path are resolved by oldest creation time, then name.

Read the status

bashWhy was my route not accepted
kubectl get gateway -A
kubectl get httproute api -n shop -o jsonpath='{range .status.parents[*].conditions[*]}{.type}{"="}{.status}{" "}{.reason}{"\n"}{end}'
kubectl describe gateway public -n infra | tail -25
49.3

HTTPRoute matching and filters

In plain words

Each rule has matches (path, headers, query, method) and optional filters that change the request or response before it reaches the backend.

The problem it solves

Ingress annotations for redirects and rewrites were controller specific and not portable.

What it does

  • Path types: Exact, PathPrefix and RegularExpression (implementation specific).
  • Most specific match wins: exact over prefix, longer prefix first, then header and query matches.
  • Standard filters: RequestHeaderModifier, ResponseHeaderModifier, RequestRedirect, URLRewrite, RequestMirror. ExtensionRef points at custom filters.
  • Timeouts and retries have been added in newer releases; check support in your implementation.

Redirect and rewrite

yamlHTTP to HTTPS redirect and a path rewrite
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: redirect-http
  namespace: infra
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: public
      sectionName: http
  rules:
    - filters:
        - type: RequestRedirect
          requestRedirect:
            scheme: https
            statusCode: 301
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: legacy
  namespace: shop
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: public
      namespace: infra
  rules:
    - matches:
        - path: {type: PathPrefix, value: /old}
      filters:
        - type: URLRewrite
          urlRewrite:
            path: {type: ReplacePrefixMatch, replacePrefixMatch: /new}
      backendRefs:
        - name: api
          port: 8080
49.4

Traffic splitting and canary

In plain words

backendRefs accept a weight. Traffic is divided in proportion to the weights, so canary and blue-green releases need no extra tool.

The problem it solves

Gradual rollouts previously needed a mesh or controller-specific annotations.

What it does

  • Weights are relative integers, not percentages. 90 and 10 gives 90 and 10 percent.
  • A weight of 0 sends no traffic but keeps the backend defined.
  • Combine with header matches so testers reach the canary first.
  • Argo Rollouts and Flagger can drive these weights automatically.

Canary route

yaml90 / 10 split with a header override
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: api-canary
  namespace: shop
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: public
      namespace: infra
  rules:
    - matches:
        - headers:
            - name: x-canary
              value: "true"
      backendRefs:
        - name: api-canary
          port: 8080
    - backendRefs:
        - name: api-stable
          port: 8080
          weight: 90
        - name: api-canary
          port: 8080
          weight: 10
Check yourself
Are weights percentages?

No, they are relative shares. The share of a backend is its weight divided by the sum of weights.

49.5

TLS, certificates and cross-namespace references

In plain words

A Gateway listener terminates TLS using a Secret. If the Secret or a backend is in another namespace, a ReferenceGrant in the target namespace must allow it.

The problem it solves

Cross-namespace references would let any team read another team's Secrets or send traffic to its Services.

What it does

  • certificateRefs point at kubernetes.io/tls Secrets. cert-manager can create them from Gateway annotations or its Gateway support.
  • ReferenceGrant lists allowed from (kind and namespace) and to (kind, optionally name). Without it status shows RefNotPermitted.
  • TLS mode Passthrough forwards encrypted traffic to the backend by SNI using TLSRoute.
  • Backend TLS (gateway to Pod) is configured through BackendTLSPolicy, which is still maturing; check the current docs.

ReferenceGrant

yamlLet Gateways in infra use a Secret in certs
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: ReferenceGrant
metadata:
  name: allow-infra-gateway
  namespace: certs
spec:
  from:
    - group: gateway.networking.k8s.io
      kind: Gateway
      namespace: infra
  to:
    - group: ""
      kind: Secret
      name: wildcard-example-com
49.6

Policy attachment and implementations

In plain words

Policy attachment adds behaviour such as rate limits, retries or auth to a Gateway or Route by pointing a separate policy object at it using targetRefs.

The problem it solves

Not every feature fits into the core API, and putting it in annotations brings back the portability problem.

What it does

  • Implementations define their own policy CRDs: Istio AuthorizationPolicy and RequestAuthentication with targetRefs, Cilium and Envoy Gateway policy types, and so on.
  • Check the Gateway API implementations page for conformance level and features. Conformance is per feature, not all or nothing.
  • Kyma's API Gateway module exposes APIRule (v2) on Istio. Newer Kyma releases are adding Gateway API support, so confirm in the current Kyma docs which to use.
  • Always read status of GatewayClass for Accepted.

Istio policy bound to a Gateway

yamlRequire JWT on a Gateway (Istio)
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: RequestAuthentication
metadata:
  name: jwt
  namespace: infra
spec:
  targetRefs:
    - group: gateway.networking.k8s.io
      kind: Gateway
      name: public
  jwtRules:
    - issuer: https://ias.example.com
      jwksUri: https://ias.example.com/oauth2/certs
49.7

Migrating from Ingress

In plain words

Migration means translating Ingress rules and annotations into Gateways and routes, then moving traffic gradually.

The problem it solves

Ingress-NGINX is being retired (the Kubernetes project announced its end of maintenance in 2026; check the current announcement), and annotations do not carry over.

What it does

  • The ingress2gateway tool converts many Ingress resources, but annotations need manual review.
  • Run both side by side with different load balancers. Lower DNS TTLs, then shift records or weighted DNS.
  • Check each annotation: rewrite, auth, rate limits, body size, timeouts. Map to filters, policies or implementation CRDs.
  • Test with curl --resolve host:443:IP before changing DNS.

Commands

bashConvert and test
ingress2gateway print --providers ingress-nginx --namespace shop > /tmp/gw.yaml
kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f /tmp/gw.yaml
curl -sk --resolve api.example.com:443:203.0.113.10 https://api.example.com/healthz
Note

Flag names of ingress2gateway change between releases. Run ingress2gateway print --help first.

Check yourself
How can you test a new Gateway before changing DNS?

Call its address directly with curl --resolve host:port:IP so that the Host header and SNI still match.

Section 50 of 65

CNI deep dive, Cilium, Calico and eBPF

7 concepts · about 55 minutes

The network plugin decides how Pods get addresses, how they reach each other and how policy is enforced. Most hard production network problems are CNI problems.

Goals
  • Explain what a CNI plugin does when a Pod starts
  • Compare overlay, routed and eBPF dataplanes and choose between Cilium and Calico
  • Replace kube-proxy and observe traffic with Hubble
50.1

What a CNI plugin does

In plain words

The Container Network Interface is a small contract. When the runtime creates a Pod sandbox it calls the plugin with ADD, and the plugin creates the network interface and assigns an IP.

The problem it solves

Kubernetes defines the network model (every Pod can reach every Pod without NAT) but not how to build it. Plugins fill that gap in different ways.

What it does

  • The runtime reads config from /etc/cni/net.d and runs binaries from /opt/cni/bin.
  • Calls are ADD, DEL, CHECK and VERSION. IPAM (address management) is often a separate delegated plugin.
  • Most modern CNIs run an agent DaemonSet that programs routes, iptables or eBPF, and the binary only talks to that agent.
  • A node stays NotReady with "cni plugin not initialized" until a config file appears.

Look at a node

bashInspect CNI config on a node
kubectl debug node/NODE -it --image=busybox:1.36 -- sh -c 'ls /host/etc/cni/net.d /host/opt/cni/bin'
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o wide | grep -E 'cilium|calico|aws-node|flannel'
kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,PODCIDR:.spec.podCIDR
Check yourself
Why is a new node NotReady when the CNI is missing?

The kubelet reports the network plugin as not ready until a CNI config exists, so no Pods can get an interface.

50.2

Overlay, routed and native networking

In plain words

Pod traffic between nodes either travels inside a tunnel (overlay), is routed using the underlying network, or uses cloud-native addresses.

The problem it solves

Choosing wrongly gives extra overhead or IP exhaustion, or needs router changes you cannot make.

What it does

  • Overlay (VXLAN or Geneve): works anywhere, adds about 50 bytes of header, so watch the MTU.
  • Routed (BGP in Calico, or direct routes on one L2 network): no encapsulation, needs the fabric to carry or learn Pod routes.
  • Cloud native: AWS VPC CNI gives Pods real VPC addresses from ENIs, so security groups and flow logs work, but subnets can run out of IPs. Prefix delegation and custom networking reduce that pressure.
  • MTU mismatches show as large requests hanging while small ones work.

Check MTU

bashDetect MTU trouble
kubectl exec -n shop POD -- ping -M do -s 1400 -c 3 10.0.5.20
kubectl exec -n shop POD -- ip link show eth0 | head -2
Dataplane
OptionOverlay
Choose whenmixed networks and quick start
Avoid whenyou can route pod CIDRs and want lowest overhead
OptionBGP routed
Choose whenon-premises with BGP capable switches
Avoid whenthe network team cannot peer with nodes
OptionVPC native (EKS)
Choose whenyou need security groups per Pod and VPC visibility
Avoid whensubnets are small and IPs scarce
50.3

Calico

In plain words

Calico is a mature CNI known for routing with BGP and a rich policy engine. It can use iptables, nftables or an eBPF dataplane.

The problem it solves

Teams needing predictable routing, large scale and policy beyond standard NetworkPolicy.

What it does

  • Components: calico-node (Felix for policy, BIRD for BGP), Typha for large clusters, and the IPAM.
  • Modes: IP-in-IP, VXLAN or unencapsulated BGP.
  • Extra CRDs: GlobalNetworkPolicy, NetworkPolicy with ordering, deny rules and host endpoint protection.
  • calicoctl (or kubectl calico) inspects nodes and IP pools.

IP pool and global policy

yamlCalico pool and a default-deny policy
apiVersion: projectcalico.org/v3
kind: IPPool
metadata:
  name: default-pool
spec:
  cidr: 10.244.0.0/16
  ipipMode: Never
  vxlanMode: CrossSubnet
  natOutgoing: true
---
apiVersion: projectcalico.org/v3
kind: GlobalNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-app-namespaces
spec:
  selector: projectcalico.org/namespace starts with 'app-'
  types: [Ingress, Egress]
50.4

Cilium and eBPF

In plain words

Cilium uses eBPF, small verified programs that run inside the Linux kernel, to route, filter and observe traffic without long iptables chains.

The problem it solves

iptables rule lists grow linearly with Services, making updates slow and packet paths long in big clusters. Policy by IP breaks when Pods churn.

What it does

  • Identity based policy: Pods get a numeric identity from their labels, and policy matches identities, not IPs.
  • eBPF programs attach to the network device and socket layer for load balancing, policy and visibility.
  • Needs a modern kernel (see the Cilium requirements page). Managed offerings may restrict modes.
  • Extras: CiliumNetworkPolicy with L7 rules (HTTP, DNS, Kafka), transparent encryption (WireGuard or IPsec), Cluster Mesh, Gateway API and Hubble.

Install and verify

bashCilium CLI checks
cilium status --wait
cilium config view | grep -E 'kube-proxy-replacement|tunnel|routing-mode'
cilium connectivity test
Note

Settings and Helm values change between Cilium releases. Take the install values from the docs for your version.

Check yourself
What does identity based policy avoid?

Dependence on Pod IPs, which change constantly. Policy follows label-derived identities.

50.5

Replacing kube-proxy

In plain words

kube-proxy programs iptables or IPVS rules to turn Service addresses into Pod addresses. Cilium and Calico eBPF can do this in the kernel instead.

The problem it solves

Large Service counts make iptables updates slow, and DNAT with conntrack costs CPU and complicates source IPs.

What it does

  • Cilium: kubeProxyReplacement=true and k8sServiceHost/k8sServicePort, since there is no kube-proxy to reach the API on first start.
  • Gains: O(1) lookups, Maglev consistent hashing, direct server return, and preserving client source IP for NodePort.
  • Remove the kube-proxy DaemonSet and flush its leftovers (reboot nodes or clean iptables).
  • On managed clusters check whether kube-proxy can be disabled (EKS add-on can be removed, Gardener has a shoot setting).
  • The newer nftables mode of kube-proxy is another way to improve scale; check your Kubernetes version.

Helm values (shape)

yamlCilium values for kube-proxy replacement
kubeProxyReplacement: true
k8sServiceHost: api.cluster.example.com
k8sServicePort: 443
routingMode: tunnel
tunnelProtocol: vxlan
hubble:
  enabled: true
  relay:
    enabled: true
50.6

Observability with Hubble

In plain words

Hubble shows network flows between Pods, including which policy allowed or dropped them, using data from the eBPF dataplane.

The problem it solves

When NetworkPolicy blocks traffic, tcpdump on a node is slow and does not know Pod names or verdicts.

What it does

  • hubble observe streams flows filtered by namespace, Pod, verdict (FORWARDED, DROPPED) and protocol.
  • Shows DNS queries and HTTP when L7 visibility is enabled.
  • The UI draws a service map. Metrics export to Prometheus.
  • Flow data may contain sensitive endpoints, so protect access.

Commands

bashFind dropped flows
cilium hubble port-forward &
hubble observe --namespace shop --verdict DROPPED --last 20
hubble observe --from-pod shop/web --to-pod shop/api --protocol tcp
Check yourself
Which verdict shows a NetworkPolicy block?

DROPPED, along with the policy denial reason in the flow.

50.7

Choosing and migrating a CNI

In plain words

A CNI is a foundation decision. Changing it later usually means rebuilding nodes or clusters, so decide early and test upgrades.

The problem it solves

Wrong choice leads to IP exhaustion, missing policy features or lack of support from your platform.

What it does

  • Use what your platform supports: EKS defaults to VPC CNI (Cilium can chain or replace it); Gardener lets you choose Calico or Cilium per shoot; Kyma on Gardener commonly uses the provider's default network setup.
  • Evaluate: policy features (L7, FQDN, host policy), observability, encryption, scale, kernel support, and operations skills.
  • Migration: new cluster and move workloads is safest. Cilium also documents node-by-node migration with overlapping Pod CIDRs; read it fully and rehearse.
  • Keep NetworkPolicy tests in CI so a CNI change can be verified.
CNI choice
OptionVPC CNI
Choose whenEKS with security groups per Pod
Avoid whenIPs are scarce and you need eBPF features
OptionCilium
Choose wheneBPF, L7 policy, Hubble, kube-proxy replacement
Avoid whenkernels are old or the platform does not allow it
OptionCalico
Choose whenBGP, mature policy model, mixed environments
Avoid whenyou want built-in L7 and flow observability

Section 51 of 65

Storage deep dive

7 concepts · about 60 minutes

Storage failures cause the longest incidents because data cannot be recreated. This page goes beyond PVC basics into the CSI machinery, snapshots, expansion and backups.

Goals
  • Describe how CSI drivers provision, attach, mount and snapshot volumes
  • Expand volumes and use topology aware binding safely
  • Use ephemeral volumes and back up applications with Velero
51.1

The CSI architecture

In plain words

The Container Storage Interface lets storage vendors ship a driver as Pods instead of code inside Kubernetes. A controller part talks to the storage API and a node part mounts volumes.

The problem it solves

In-tree volume plugins tied every storage system to the Kubernetes release cycle. CSI separates them.

What it does

  • Controller plugin (Deployment) handles create, delete, attach, snapshot, resize, using sidecars: external-provisioner, external-attacher, external-resizer, external-snapshotter.
  • Node plugin (DaemonSet) runs NodeStageVolume and NodePublishVolume to format and mount into the Pod path. It registers with the kubelet through node-driver-registrar.
  • CSIDriver object describes capabilities (attachRequired, fsGroupPolicy). CSINode lists drivers per node.
  • On EKS the EBS CSI driver is an add-on that needs IAM permissions (IRSA or Pod Identity).

Inspect drivers

bashCSI objects
kubectl get csidrivers
kubectl get csinodes
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/name=aws-ebs-csi-driver
kubectl get volumeattachments
Check yourself
Which part mounts a volume on the node?

The CSI node plugin DaemonSet, called by the kubelet through the NodeStage and NodePublish calls.

51.2

StorageClasses, binding modes and reclaim

In plain words

A StorageClass is a template for dynamic volumes: which driver, which parameters, when to bind and what happens after deletion.

The problem it solves

Wrong binding mode creates volumes in a zone where the Pod can never run. Wrong reclaim policy deletes data or leaves orphaned disks.

What it does

  • volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer delays creation until a Pod is scheduled, so the volume lands in the right zone.
  • reclaimPolicy: Delete removes the disk with the PVC; Retain keeps it for manual recovery.
  • allowVolumeExpansion: true is required to grow volumes later.
  • parameters are driver specific, for example EBS type: gp3, iops, encrypted.
  • Mark exactly one class default with an annotation.

Example class

yamlgp3 class with late binding
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: gp3-encrypted
provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com
parameters:
  type: gp3
  encrypted: "true"
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
allowVolumeExpansion: true
reclaimPolicy: Delete
51.3

Volume expansion

In plain words

You can grow a PVC by editing its requested size. The driver resizes the disk, and the filesystem grows, often without restarting the Pod.

The problem it solves

Disks fill up, and recreating a database volume by copying is risky.

What it does

  • Needs allowVolumeExpansion on the class and a driver that supports it.
  • Edit spec.resources.requests.storage to a larger value. Shrinking is not supported.
  • Conditions on the PVC: Resizing, FileSystemResizePending. Online expansion works for most CSI drivers.
  • Cloud limit: EBS allows one modification per volume about every 6 hours. Check provider limits.
  • StatefulSet templates cannot be edited, so patch each PVC and recreate the StatefulSet object with --cascade=orphan.

Commands

bashGrow a PVC
kubectl patch pvc data-db-0 -n shop -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"50Gi"}}}}'
kubectl get pvc data-db-0 -n shop -w
kubectl describe pvc data-db-0 -n shop | grep -A5 -i conditions
kubectl exec -n shop db-0 -- df -h /var/lib/postgresql/data
Check yourself
Can you shrink a PVC?

No. Kubernetes only supports growing. Restore into a smaller volume from a backup instead.

51.4

Snapshots and clones

In plain words

A VolumeSnapshot captures a volume at a point in time through the CSI driver. You can create a new PVC from it, or clone a PVC directly.

The problem it solves

Copying data by hand is slow and inconsistent. Snapshots are fast and storage side.

What it does

  • Needs the snapshot CRDs, the snapshot controller, and a VolumeSnapshotClass for the driver.
  • VolumeSnapshotContent is the cluster-wide counterpart, like PV for PVC.
  • Restore: a new PVC with dataSource of kind VolumeSnapshot.
  • Crash consistent only. For databases quiesce or use application tools. Snapshots on the same storage system are not a backup against account loss.

Snapshot and restore

yamlSnapshot, then restore into a new PVC
apiVersion: snapshot.storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: VolumeSnapshot
metadata:
  name: db-snap-1
  namespace: shop
spec:
  volumeSnapshotClassName: ebs-snap
  source:
    persistentVolumeClaimName: data-db-0
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: data-db-restore
  namespace: shop
spec:
  storageClassName: gp3-encrypted
  dataSource:
    name: db-snap-1
    kind: VolumeSnapshot
    apiGroup: snapshot.storage.k8s.io
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 50Gi
51.5

Topology and access modes

In plain words

Volumes live somewhere: a zone, a node or a rack. Topology rules keep Pods and data together. Access modes say who may mount at once.

The problem it solves

A zone outage or a Pod move can leave a RWO disk stranded in another zone.

What it does

  • Block volumes (EBS) are zonal and ReadWriteOnce. A Pod must run in the zone of its volume.
  • allowedTopologies in StorageClass restricts zones. PV nodeAffinity records where a volume can attach.
  • ReadWriteOncePod (GA in recent releases) guarantees one Pod only; ReadWriteMany needs a file system such as EFS or NFS.
  • Multi-attach errors after a node failure appear until the old attachment is gone; check VolumeAttachment objects.
  • Spread StatefulSet replicas across zones with topology spread constraints, each with its own volume.

Diagnose Multi-Attach

bashAttachment checks
kubectl describe pod POD -n shop | grep -i -A3 'multi-attach\|FailedAttach'
kubectl get volumeattachments -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,NODE:.spec.nodeName,PV:.spec.source.persistentVolumeName,ATTACHED:.status.attached
kubectl get pv PVNAME -o jsonpath='{.spec.nodeAffinity}{"\n"}'
51.6

Ephemeral volumes

In plain words

Some volumes live only as long as a Pod: emptyDir, ConfigMap and Secret volumes, and generic ephemeral volumes that use a real StorageClass.

The problem it solves

Scratch space such as caches or ML datasets can be large, and emptyDir uses the node root disk and can cause evictions.

What it does

  • emptyDir can use medium: Memory (counts toward memory limits) and has sizeLimit.
  • Generic ephemeral volume: a volumeClaimTemplate in the Pod spec. The PVC is created and deleted with the Pod, and can use any CSI class, snapshots and capacity tracking.
  • CSI ephemeral volumes are inline and driver defined, used by Secrets Store CSI for example.
  • Set ephemeral-storage requests so the scheduler accounts for it.

Example

yamlScratch volume from a StorageClass
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: scratch
spec:
  containers:
    - name: work
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: ["sleep", "3600"]
      volumeMounts:
        - {name: scratch, mountPath: /scratch}
      resources:
        requests: {ephemeral-storage: 1Gi}
  volumes:
    - name: scratch
      ephemeral:
        volumeClaimTemplate:
          spec:
            accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
            storageClassName: gp3-encrypted
            resources:
              requests:
                storage: 20Gi
Check yourself
What happens to a generic ephemeral volume when the Pod is deleted?

Its PVC is owned by the Pod and is deleted with it.

51.7

Backup and restore with Velero

In plain words

Velero backs up Kubernetes objects to object storage and can back up volume data through CSI snapshots or file-level copy (kopia).

The problem it solves

Snapshots live in the same account and region as the cluster. A backup of both manifests and data lets you recover from deletion, corruption or cluster loss.

What it does

  • Backup, Schedule and Restore are CRDs. Backup locations point at an S3 compatible bucket.
  • Volume data: CSI snapshot integration (data stays in cloud snapshots, optionally moved to the bucket with data mover) or file system backup with node agent.
  • Hooks run commands before and after backup (for example pg_dump or fsfreeze) for consistency.
  • Restore can map namespaces, storage classes, and skip existing objects.
  • A backup is only proven by a restore test in an empty cluster. Schedule drills.

Commands and schedule

bashBackup and restore drill
velero backup create shop-$(date +%F) --include-namespaces shop --snapshot-move-data
velero backup describe shop-$(date +%F) --details
velero restore create --from-backup shop-$(date +%F) --namespace-mappings shop:shop-restore
yamlNightly schedule
apiVersion: velero.io/v1
kind: Schedule
metadata:
  name: shop-nightly
  namespace: velero
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"
  template:
    includedNamespaces: [shop]
    ttl: 168h
    snapshotMoveData: true
Tip

Restore into a different namespace or cluster first. Watch for Secrets, PVCs and webhooks that conflict with the live copy.

← PreviousNext →
Section 52 of 65

Advanced scheduling

6 concepts · about 55 minutes

The default scheduler is good, but busy shared clusters need priorities, rebalancing and fair queues for batch work.

Goals
  • Use priority classes and preemption deliberately
  • Rebalance clusters with the descheduler and spread constraints
  • Queue batch work with Kueue and understand scheduler profiles
52.1

The scheduling cycle and plugins

In plain words

For each Pod the scheduler filters nodes that can run it, scores the rest, and binds the best. Every step is a plugin.

The problem it solves

To tune placement you must know which extension point does what, or you change the wrong thing.

What it does

  • Queue: PreEnqueue, QueueSort. Scheduling cycle: PreFilter, Filter, PostFilter (preemption), PreScore, Score, Reserve, Permit. Binding cycle: PreBind, Bind, PostBind.
  • Filter plugins: NodeResourcesFit, NodeAffinity, TaintToleration, PodTopologySpread, VolumeBinding.
  • Score plugins prefer for example least allocated or balanced resources.
  • percentageOfNodesToScore limits scoring in huge clusters.

Read scheduler decisions

bashWhy this node
kubectl get events -n shop --field-selector reason=Scheduled -o custom-columns=POD:.involvedObject.name,MSG:.message | head
kubectl describe pod POD -n shop | grep -A6 Events
52.2

Scheduler profiles and configuration

In plain words

A KubeSchedulerConfiguration can define several profiles in one scheduler, each with its own name and plugin set. A Pod picks one with schedulerName.

The problem it solves

Different workloads want different strategies, such as bin-packing for batch and spreading for web, without running separate schedulers.

What it does

  • Profile plugins enable or disable plugins; pluginConfig sets args, for example NodeResourcesFit with MostAllocated scoring.
  • Self-managed control planes pass the file through --config. Managed services (EKS, Gardener shoot) often expose limited settings or none, so check what your platform allows.
  • A second full scheduler Deployment is possible for experiments.

Config shape

yamlTwo profiles
apiVersion: kubescheduler.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: KubeSchedulerConfiguration
profiles:
  - schedulerName: default-scheduler
  - schedulerName: binpack-scheduler
    pluginConfig:
      - name: NodeResourcesFit
        args:
          scoringStrategy:
            type: MostAllocated
            resources:
              - {name: cpu, weight: 1}
              - {name: memory, weight: 1}
Check yourself
How does a Pod pick a profile?

With spec.schedulerName set to the profile name.

52.3

Priority and preemption

In plain words

A PriorityClass gives Pods an integer priority. When a high priority Pod cannot fit, the scheduler may evict lower priority Pods to make room (preemption).

The problem it solves

Critical services must run even when a cluster is full of batch jobs.

What it does

  • PriorityClass has value, globalDefault and preemptionPolicy (PreemptLowerPriority or Never).
  • System classes system-cluster-critical and system-node-critical are reserved for platform Pods.
  • Preemption respects PodDisruptionBudgets only on a best effort basis, and victims get their grace period.
  • Priority also orders the queue and node-pressure eviction. Do not give everything high priority.

Classes

yamlPriority classes for batch and critical
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: business-critical
value: 100000
globalDefault: false
description: Customer facing services
---
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: batch-low
value: 1000
preemptionPolicy: Never
description: Batch jobs that wait rather than preempt
52.4

Topology spread and affinity at scale

In plain words

topologySpreadConstraints keep replicas balanced across zones or nodes. Affinity and anti-affinity attract or repel Pods.

The problem it solves

All replicas on one node or zone defeat redundancy.

What it does

  • maxSkew, topologyKey, whenUnsatisfiable (DoNotSchedule or ScheduleAnyway) and labelSelector define the rule.
  • minDomains and matchLabelKeys (for per-revision spreading in rollouts) refine it; check availability in your version.
  • Required pod anti-affinity is expensive in large clusters; prefer spread constraints.
  • Spread is evaluated only at scheduling time, so later imbalance needs the descheduler.

Example

yamlSpread over zone and node
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  replicas: 4
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app: api}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: {app: api}
    spec:
      topologySpreadConstraints:
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
          labelSelector:
            matchLabels: {app: api}
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
          whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
          labelSelector:
            matchLabels: {app: api}
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: registry.example.com/shop/api:1.8.3
Check yourself
Why does imbalance appear after node failures even with spread rules?

Constraints are checked only when a Pod is scheduled. Existing Pods are not moved afterwards.

52.5

The descheduler

In plain words

The descheduler is a separate component that evicts Pods that are badly placed now, so the scheduler can place them again.

The problem it solves

Clusters drift: new nodes join empty, taints change, spread skews, and long-lived Pods stay where they were first put.

What it does

  • Strategies (plugins): LowNodeUtilization, HighNodeUtilization, RemoveDuplicates, RemovePodsViolatingTopologySpreadConstraint, RemovePodsViolatingNodeAffinity, RemovePodsHavingTooManyRestarts, PodLifeTime.
  • Runs as Job, CronJob or Deployment. Respects PDBs and does not evict static or DaemonSet Pods by default.
  • Evictions use the eviction API, so graceful shutdown applies. Always set PDBs and test in dry-run (dryRun: true).

Policy (shape)

yamlDescheduler policy
apiVersion: descheduler/v1alpha2
kind: DeschedulerPolicy
profiles:
  - name: rebalance
    pluginConfig:
      - name: DefaultEvictor
        args:
          nodeFit: true
      - name: RemovePodsViolatingTopologySpreadConstraint
      - name: LowNodeUtilization
        args:
          thresholds: {cpu: 20, memory: 20, pods: 20}
          targetThresholds: {cpu: 50, memory: 50, pods: 50}
    plugins:
      balance:
        enabled:
          - RemovePodsViolatingTopologySpreadConstraint
          - LowNodeUtilization
Careful

The policy API version changes between releases. Copy the example from the release you deploy.

52.6

Kueue and job queueing

In plain words

Kueue is a Kubernetes SIG project that adds quotas and queues for batch workloads. Jobs are suspended until their quota is admitted.

The problem it solves

Without admission control, many Jobs create Pods at once, fill the cluster and leave important work Pending in a partial state.

What it does

  • ClusterQueue holds quotas per resource flavor (for example on-demand versus spot, or GPU types) and can borrow unused quota between queues in a cohort.
  • LocalQueue in a namespace points to a ClusterQueue. Jobs opt in with the label kueue.x-k8s.io/queue-name.
  • Works with Job, JobSet, Kubeflow and Ray types. Supports priority, preemption and fair sharing.
  • Admission is all or nothing for the whole workload (with optional partial admission).

Queue and Job

yamlQueue objects and a queued Job
apiVersion: kueue.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: ResourceFlavor
metadata:
  name: default
---
apiVersion: kueue.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: ClusterQueue
metadata:
  name: team-a
spec:
  namespaceSelector: {}
  resourceGroups:
    - coveredResources: [cpu, memory]
      flavors:
        - name: default
          resources:
            - {name: cpu, nominalQuota: 40}
            - {name: memory, nominalQuota: 160Gi}
---
apiVersion: kueue.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: LocalQueue
metadata:
  name: main
  namespace: batch
spec:
  clusterQueue: team-a
---
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: report
  namespace: batch
  labels:
    kueue.x-k8s.io/queue-name: main
spec:
  suspend: true
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: r
          image: busybox:1.36
          command: ["sleep", "30"]
          resources:
            requests: {cpu: "2", memory: 4Gi}
Check yourself
Why is a Kueue Job created suspended?

Kueue unsuspends it only when quota is available, so Pods are not created before admission.

Section 53 of 65

Stateful workloads, databases and operators

7 concepts · about 55 minutes

Kubernetes can run databases well when an operator encodes the operational knowledge. Without one, a StatefulSet alone leaves failover, backup and upgrades to you.

Goals
  • Decide when a database belongs on Kubernetes and when it does not
  • Run PostgreSQL with CloudNativePG and Kafka with Strimzi
  • Plan backups, failover, upgrades and storage for stateful systems
53.1

Should this database run on Kubernetes

In plain words

Running state on Kubernetes is a trade-off between portability and operational effort. A managed service moves the work to the provider.

The problem it solves

Teams either move every database into the cluster and drown in operations, or avoid it and lose the benefits for dev, test and edge cases.

What it does

  • Good fit: dev and test, many small databases per team, Kafka and caches close to apps, platforms that already have strong storage and backup.
  • Weaker fit: a single critical database with no one on call who knows it, or needs beyond what your storage offers (IOPS, cross-region replication).
  • Managed options (RDS, SAP HANA Cloud, BTP service instances) give backups, patching and SLAs.
  • In Kyma, consuming a BTP service through service bindings is often the supported path.
Where to run
OptionManaged service
Choose whenproduction data and a small team
Avoid whenyou need a feature the service does not offer
OptionOperator on Kubernetes
Choose whenmany instances, GitOps, portability
Avoid whenstorage or backups are not proven
OptionStatefulSet by hand
Choose whenlearning and throwaway tests
Avoid whenanything you would be paged for
53.2

StatefulSet guarantees and limits

In plain words

A StatefulSet gives each replica a stable name, stable network identity and its own PVC. It starts and stops replicas in order.

The problem it solves

Replicated databases need a fixed identity for peers and their own data directory.

What it does

  • Pods are db-0, db-1 with DNS names via a headless Service: db-0.db.shop.svc.
  • volumeClaimTemplates create one PVC per Pod, kept when scaling down or deleting the set (check persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy).
  • podManagementPolicy: Parallel removes ordering; updateStrategy.rollingUpdate.partition lets you stage upgrades.
  • It does not know about replication roles, failover or backups. That is the operator's job.

Commands

bashStaged update with a partition
kubectl patch sts db -n shop -p '{"spec":{"updateStrategy":{"rollingUpdate":{"partition":2}}}}'
kubectl rollout status sts/db -n shop
kubectl get pods -n shop -l app=db -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,REV:.metadata.labels.controller-revision-hash
Check yourself
What happens to PVCs when you scale a StatefulSet to zero?

They stay by default, so data survives and returns when you scale up, unless a retention policy says otherwise.

53.3

The operator pattern for databases

In plain words

An operator is a controller plus CRDs that encodes what a human DBA does: create a cluster, fail over, back up, upgrade and rotate certificates.

The problem it solves

Doing these steps by script or runbook is error-prone, especially at 3 am.

What it does

  • You declare kind: Cluster (CloudNativePG) or kind: Kafka (Strimzi) and the operator creates StatefulSets or Pods, Services, Secrets and PVCs.
  • It reconciles continuously: it replaces a lost replica, promotes a standby and issues certificates.
  • Check maturity: activity, release notes, upgrade path, backup and restore documentation, and what happens when the operator is down (databases normally keep running).
  • Operators from vendors or CNCF projects (CloudNativePG, Zalando, Percona, Strimzi) differ in features.
53.4

PostgreSQL with CloudNativePG

In plain words

CloudNativePG manages PostgreSQL clusters with one primary and streaming replicas, using native Kubernetes objects and no external HA tool.

The problem it solves

Automatic failover and backups for Postgres need many moving parts when built by hand.

What it does

  • A Cluster with instances: 3 creates a primary and two replicas, services -rw, -ro and -r.
  • Failover: if the primary fails, the most advanced replica is promoted and the -rw service switches.
  • Backups use Barman Cloud to object storage with WAL archiving, enabling point in time recovery. Scheduled with ScheduledBackup.
  • Rolling upgrades of minor versions and switchover supported. Check the current docs for how backup plugins are configured, as this has changed between releases.

Cluster manifest

yamlThree instance Postgres cluster
apiVersion: postgresql.cnpg.io/v1
kind: Cluster
metadata:
  name: shop-db
  namespace: shop
spec:
  instances: 3
  imageName: ghcr.io/cloudnative-pg/postgresql:17
  storage:
    size: 50Gi
    storageClass: gp3-encrypted
  walStorage:
    size: 10Gi
  affinity:
    topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
  resources:
    requests: {cpu: "1", memory: 4Gi}
    limits: {memory: 4Gi}
  backup:
    retentionPolicy: 14d
    barmanObjectStore:
      destinationPath: s3://shop-db-backups/
      s3Credentials:
        inheritFromIAMRole: true
bashOperate
kubectl cnpg status shop-db -n shop
kubectl cnpg promote shop-db shop-db-2 -n shop
kubectl get svc -n shop | grep shop-db
53.5

Kafka with Strimzi

In plain words

Strimzi runs Apache Kafka on Kubernetes with CRDs for clusters, topics, users and connectors.

The problem it solves

Kafka needs careful configuration of brokers, storage, listeners, TLS and rolling restarts.

What it does

  • Resources: Kafka, KafkaNodePool, KafkaTopic, KafkaUser, KafkaConnect. Recent Strimzi versions use KRaft mode without ZooKeeper; check the version notes for your release.
  • Node pools set roles (controller, broker), storage and replicas separately.
  • The Cluster Operator performs safe rolling updates, one broker at a time, checking in-sync replicas.
  • Users and ACLs are declared as resources, with generated Secrets for credentials.
  • Use rack awareness over zones so replicas are in different zones.

Topic as code

yamlTopic resource
apiVersion: kafka.strimzi.io/v1beta2
kind: KafkaTopic
metadata:
  name: orders
  namespace: kafka
  labels:
    strimzi.io/cluster: main
spec:
  partitions: 12
  replicas: 3
  config:
    retention.ms: 604800000
    min.insync.replicas: 2
Check yourself
Why set min.insync.replicas to 2 with replicas 3?

Writes with acks=all need two copies, so one broker can fail without losing data or availability.

53.6

Backup, restore and disaster recovery

In plain words

Replication protects against node loss. Backups protect against mistakes and corruption. Both are needed.

The problem it solves

A DROP TABLE replicates to all replicas within milliseconds.

What it does

  • Define RPO (how much data you can lose) and RTO (how long recovery may take) first.
  • Logical (pg_dump) is portable but slow; physical base backups plus WAL archive allow point in time recovery.
  • Store backups outside the cluster and the account, with retention and encryption.
  • Practise restoring into a new cluster, for example CNPG bootstrap.recovery from the object store, and measure the time.
  • Cross-region DR: replica clusters or storage-level replication, depending on the operator.

Recovery manifest

yamlRecover to a point in time
apiVersion: postgresql.cnpg.io/v1
kind: Cluster
metadata:
  name: shop-db-restored
  namespace: shop
spec:
  instances: 1
  storage:
    size: 50Gi
  bootstrap:
    recovery:
      source: shop-db
      recoveryTarget:
        targetTime: "2026-10-30 09:15:00+00"
  externalClusters:
    - name: shop-db
      barmanObjectStore:
        destinationPath: s3://shop-db-backups/
        s3Credentials:
          inheritFromIAMRole: true
53.7

Operating stateful workloads safely

In plain words

Day-two work: upgrades, node drains, disk growth, monitoring and protecting data from accidental deletion.

The problem it solves

Routine platform actions such as node upgrades can break quorum if they are not coordinated with the database.

What it does

  • PodDisruptionBudgets so a drain never takes two members of a quorum. Most operators create them.
  • Anti-affinity or spread constraints across nodes and zones.
  • Monitor replication lag, disk use, WAL growth, and under-replicated partitions, with alerts before the disk fills.
  • Protect PVCs: reclaimPolicy: Retain for important classes, RBAC that limits who can delete CRs, and finalizers or admission policies.
  • Upgrade in order: test restore, minor version first, operator before database version when the docs say so.

PDB example

yamlKeep quorum during drains
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: kafka-brokers
  namespace: kafka
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      strimzi.io/name: main-kafka
Check yourself
Which risk does a PDB address?

Voluntary disruptions such as drains. It does not protect from node crashes or data deletion.

← PreviousNext →
Section 54 of 65

Batch and ML on Kubernetes

6 concepts · about 50 minutes

Batch and machine learning workloads are bursty, resource hungry and often need special hardware. Kubernetes handles them well with the right primitives.

Goals
  • Design reliable Jobs and indexed parallel processing
  • Run GPU workloads with the device plugin model and node pools
  • Orchestrate multi-step and distributed training jobs
54.1

Jobs, completions and failure handling

In plain words

A Job runs Pods until a number of them finish successfully. It retries failed Pods up to a limit.

The problem it solves

Plain Pods are not rescheduled after completion or failure semantics are unclear. Deployments restart finished processes forever.

What it does

  • completions and parallelism define total and concurrent Pods. backoffLimit caps retries, activeDeadlineSeconds caps total runtime.
  • restartPolicy must be Never or OnFailure.
  • ttlSecondsAfterFinished removes finished Jobs. Without it they accumulate.
  • podFailurePolicy lets you fail fast on certain exit codes or ignore disruptions (preemption, drain).
  • backoffLimitPerIndex (for indexed jobs) isolates failures to individual indexes; check the current docs for status in your version.

Example

yamlJob with failure policy
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: nightly-report
  namespace: batch
spec:
  backoffLimit: 4
  activeDeadlineSeconds: 3600
  ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 86400
  podFailurePolicy:
    rules:
      - action: FailJob
        onExitCodes:
          containerName: report
          operator: In
          values: [42]
      - action: Ignore
        onPodConditions:
          - type: DisruptionTarget
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: report
          image: registry.example.com/batch/report:2.1
          resources:
            requests: {cpu: "1", memory: 2Gi}
Check yourself
Why use the Ignore action for DisruptionTarget?

Evictions and preemption are not application faults, so they should not consume the retry budget.

54.2

Indexed Jobs and work queues

In plain words

Indexed completion mode gives every Pod a number in JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX. Each Pod processes its own slice of the data.

The problem it solves

Splitting a big task needs a coordinator or message queue, which adds components.

What it does

  • completionMode: Indexed with completions: 100 and parallelism: 10 runs 100 indexes, 10 at once.
  • The Pod reads the index from the env var or annotation and picks its shard, for example file number or key range.
  • For dynamic work, use a queue (SQS, RabbitMQ, Redis) with workers and KEDA scaling on queue depth.
  • Make tasks idempotent so retries are safe.

Example

yamlIndexed job
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: thumbnail
spec:
  completionMode: Indexed
  completions: 20
  parallelism: 5
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: worker
          image: busybox:1.36
          command: ["sh", "-c", "echo processing shard $JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX"]
54.3

CronJobs done properly

In plain words

A CronJob creates Jobs on a schedule. It has settings that control overlap, missed runs and history.

The problem it solves

Default settings can run overlapping jobs, silently skip runs, or fill the namespace with old Jobs.

What it does

  • concurrencyPolicy: Allow, Forbid or Replace. Use Forbid for most data jobs.
  • startingDeadlineSeconds bounds how late a missed run may still start. If more than 100 runs are missed the controller stops scheduling.
  • timeZone (GA) sets the zone; otherwise the controller's local time (usually UTC).
  • successfulJobsHistoryLimit and failedJobsHistoryLimit keep a few for debugging.
  • suspend: true pauses it, useful during incidents.

Example

yamlSafe CronJob
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: cleanup
  namespace: batch
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"
  timeZone: Asia/Kolkata
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
  startingDeadlineSeconds: 600
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  failedJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      backoffLimit: 2
      template:
        spec:
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
          containers:
            - name: cleanup
              image: busybox:1.36
              command: ["sh", "-c", "echo cleaning"]
Check yourself
Which concurrencyPolicy avoids two overlapping runs?

Forbid skips a new run while the previous one is still active.

54.4

GPUs and device plugins

In plain words

GPUs are exposed to Kubernetes as extended resources such as nvidia.com/gpu by a device plugin. Pods request them in limits.

The problem it solves

The scheduler knows only CPU and memory natively. Special hardware must be advertised and allocated exclusively.

What it does

  • The NVIDIA GPU Operator installs drivers, container toolkit, device plugin and DCGM exporter. Managed offerings (EKS accelerated AMIs, GKE) may include some parts.
  • Whole GPUs are not shared by default. Sharing options: time slicing, MIG (partitions on supported cards), MPS. Check vendor docs.
  • Use dedicated node pools with taints (nvidia.com/gpu:NoSchedule) so that non-GPU Pods avoid expensive nodes.
  • Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) is the newer, more flexible API for devices; check its status in your version.

Request a GPU

yamlGPU Pod
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: gpu-check
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  tolerations:
    - key: nvidia.com/gpu
      operator: Exists
      effect: NoSchedule
  containers:
    - name: smi
      image: nvidia/cuda:12.4.1-base-ubuntu22.04
      command: ["nvidia-smi"]
      resources:
        limits:
          nvidia.com/gpu: 1
54.5

Distributed training and JobSet

In plain words

Training across many Pods needs them to start together and find each other. Operators and JobSet provide this.

The problem it solves

A plain Job may start 3 of 8 workers and the cluster fills with Pods that wait forever (partial allocation deadlock).

What it does

  • JobSet (Kubernetes SIG) models groups of Jobs, such as one driver plus many workers, with startup order and failure policy.
  • Kubeflow Training Operator offers PyTorchJob, TFJob and others; KubeRay manages Ray clusters and jobs.
  • Gang scheduling comes from Kueue (all or nothing admission) or schedulers such as Volcano.
  • Use topology-aware placement and fast networking (EFA on AWS) for large jobs.
  • Checkpoint to object storage so a preempted job can resume.

Shape

yamlJobSet with driver and workers
apiVersion: jobset.x-k8s.io/v1alpha2
kind: JobSet
metadata:
  name: train
spec:
  replicatedJobs:
    - name: workers
      replicas: 1
      template:
        spec:
          parallelism: 4
          completions: 4
          template:
            spec:
              restartPolicy: Never
              containers:
                - name: trainer
                  image: registry.example.com/ml/train:1.0
                  resources:
                    limits:
                      nvidia.com/gpu: 1
Check yourself
What problem does gang scheduling solve?

Jobs that need all workers at once otherwise hold partial resources and may never start.

54.6

Cost and capacity for batch

In plain words

Batch is the best candidate for spot or preemptible capacity, scale-to-zero node pools and bin-packing.

The problem it solves

Idle GPU or large nodes cost a lot. Batch runs at night should not need always-on capacity.

What it does

  • Use node autoscaling (Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter) with separate pools; scale to zero when no Jobs run.
  • Tolerate spot interruptions: retries, checkpoints, podFailurePolicy ignoring disruptions.
  • Priority classes: batch below services with preemptionPolicy: Never.
  • Set realistic requests; measure with kubectl top, Prometheus and cost tools (OpenCost).
  • Use ResourceQuota per namespace to cap runaway fan-out.

Karpenter pool for batch (shape)

yamlNodePool for batch on spot
apiVersion: karpenter.sh/v1
kind: NodePool
metadata:
  name: batch-spot
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      requirements:
        - key: karpenter.sh/capacity-type
          operator: In
          values: ["spot"]
      taints:
        - key: workload
          value: batch
          effect: NoSchedule
      nodeClassRef:
        group: karpenter.k8s.aws
        kind: EC2NodeClass
        name: default
  disruption:
    consolidationPolicy: WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized
    consolidateAfter: 1m
  limits:
    cpu: "400"
