Section 55 of 65

Security hardening

7 concepts · about 60 minutes

Hardening is a set of layers. Each layer assumes the previous one can fail. This page covers the controls that sit around the cluster, the node and the workload.

Goals
  • Audit a cluster against the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark
  • Apply seccomp, AppArmor and runtime detection with Falco
  • Enforce supply chain admission, encrypt secrets at rest and enable audit logging
55.1

CIS Benchmark and kube-bench

In plain words

The CIS Kubernetes Benchmark is a checklist of secure settings for the control plane, etcd, kubelet and policies. kube-bench runs the checks automatically.

The problem it solves

Hundreds of flags and file permissions are easy to get wrong and hard to review by hand.

What it does

  • kube-bench runs as a Job on a node and reports PASS, FAIL, WARN with remediation text per check.
  • Pick the benchmark that matches your platform (generic, EKS, GKE, AKS) with --benchmark.
  • On managed control planes (EKS, Gardener) you can only check what you own: worker nodes, kubelet and workloads. The provider covers the rest.
  • Treat findings as input, not as absolute truth. Record accepted risks.

Run it

bashkube-bench as a Job
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aquasecurity/kube-bench/main/job.yaml
kubectl logs job/kube-bench | grep -E '^\[(FAIL|WARN)\]' | head -20
kubectl delete job kube-bench
Note

The job manifest depends on the platform. Use the variant for EKS or others from the kube-bench repository.

55.2

Node and kubelet hardening

In plain words

The kubelet exposes an API on each node. Closing it down and keeping nodes minimal limits what an attacker can do after reaching a node.

The problem it solves

An open kubelet read-write port or anonymous access can lead to code execution in any Pod on the node.

What it does

  • Kubelet settings: authentication.anonymous.enabled: false, authorization.mode: Webhook, readOnlyPort: 0, protectKernelDefaults: true, rotateCertificates: true.
  • Use a minimal, immutable node OS (Bottlerocket, Flatcar, Garden Linux in Gardener) and no SSH where possible.
  • IMDS on AWS: require IMDSv2 and a hop limit of 1 so Pods cannot reach node credentials; use IRSA or Pod Identity instead.
  • Patch nodes by replacing them, not in place.

Kubelet configuration

yamlHardened KubeletConfiguration
apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: KubeletConfiguration
authentication:
  anonymous:
    enabled: false
  webhook:
    enabled: true
authorization:
  mode: Webhook
readOnlyPort: 0
protectKernelDefaults: true
rotateCertificates: true
serverTLSBootstrap: true
Check yourself
Why limit the IMDS hop limit to 1?

A Pod network adds a hop, so Pods cannot reach node credentials while the node itself still can.

55.3

Seccomp and AppArmor

In plain words

Seccomp filters which Linux system calls a container may make. AppArmor restricts file, network and capability access by profile.

The problem it solves

By default a container may call hundreds of syscalls, many unneeded and some used in kernel exploits.

What it does

  • securityContext.seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault applies the container runtime default profile. It is required by the Pod Security restricted level.
  • Localhost uses a custom profile stored on the node; the Security Profiles Operator can distribute and record profiles.
  • AppArmor: since Kubernetes 1.30 use the securityContext.appArmorProfile field (older versions used annotations). Requires AppArmor on the node OS. On SELinux hosts use seLinuxOptions.
  • Roll out in stages, test for denied syscalls in staging first.

Pod example

yamlPod with seccomp and AppArmor
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: hardened
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 10001
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: registry.example.com/shop/api:1.8.3
      securityContext:
        allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
        readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
        capabilities:
          drop: ["ALL"]
        appArmorProfile:
          type: RuntimeDefault
55.4

Runtime security with Falco

In plain words

Falco watches system calls and Kubernetes audit events and raises alerts when behaviour matches a rule, such as a shell opened inside a container.

The problem it solves

Admission checks stop bad configuration, not a running exploited process. You need detection at runtime.

What it does

  • Uses a kernel driver (modern eBPF probe) to observe events with container and Pod metadata.
  • Default rules: shell in container, write below /etc, reading sensitive files, unexpected outbound connections, privilege escalation.
  • Falcosidekick forwards alerts to Slack, SIEM, webhooks. Falco Talon can respond (for example label or delete the Pod).
  • Tune rules for noise; start in alert-only mode. Alternatives with similar goals: Tetragon, Tracee.

Install and rule

bashInstall with Helm
helm repo add falcosecurity https://falcosecurity.github.io/charts
helm upgrade --install falco falcosecurity/falco -n falco --create-namespace --set driver.kind=modern_ebpf
kubectl logs -n falco -l app.kubernetes.io/name=falco --tail=5
yamlCustom Falco rule
- rule: Shell in shop namespace
  desc: Interactive shell in a shop Pod
  condition: spawned_process and container and k8s.ns.name = "shop" and proc.name in (sh, bash)
  output: "Shell in %k8s.ns.name/%k8s.pod.name (user=%user.name cmd=%proc.cmdline)"
  priority: WARNING
Check yourself
What does Falco add that admission policy does not?

Detection of what processes actually do after start, not only the Pod configuration at creation.

55.5

Supply chain admission

In plain words

Admission policies can require that images come from approved registries, are signed, and have attestations such as an SBOM, before they may run.

The problem it solves

A compromised or unknown image runs with whatever rights the Pod has.

What it does

  • Sign images with cosign in CI (keyless via OIDC or a key). Verify at admission with Kyverno verifyImages, Sigstore policy-controller or Ratify.
  • Pin by digest. Block latest. Restrict registries with ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (CEL) which needs no webhook.
  • Scan images for CVEs in CI and continuously in the registry or cluster (Trivy Operator).
  • Start in audit mode (Audit or validationFailureAction: Audit) to see impact.

Policies

yamlAllow only the company registry (CEL)
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
metadata:
  name: approved-registry
spec:
  failurePolicy: Fail
  matchConstraints:
    resourceRules:
      - apiGroups: [""]
        apiVersions: ["v1"]
        operations: ["CREATE", "UPDATE"]
        resources: ["pods"]
  validations:
    - expression: "object.spec.containers.all(c, c.image.startsWith('registry.example.com/'))"
      message: "Images must come from registry.example.com"
---
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding
metadata:
  name: approved-registry
spec:
  policyName: approved-registry
  validationActions: ["Audit", "Warn"]
  matchResources:
    namespaceSelector:
      matchLabels:
        env: prod
55.6

Encrypting Secrets at rest

In plain words

By default Secrets are only base64 encoded in etcd. Encryption at rest makes the API server encrypt them before writing.

The problem it solves

Anyone with etcd or backup access reads every Secret in clear text.

What it does

  • An EncryptionConfiguration lists resources and providers in order. The first provider encrypts; all are tried for reading.
  • Providers: aescbc, secretbox, aesgcm with local keys, and kms v2 which wraps data keys using an external KMS (AWS KMS and others). KMS is the recommended choice.
  • After enabling, rewrite old data: kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -.
  • EKS: enable envelope encryption with a KMS key at cluster creation or later. Gardener supports encryption of Secrets and other resources through shoot configuration; check the current docs.
  • Encryption protects etcd and backups, not users who may read Secrets through the API (use RBAC).

Config

yamlEncryptionConfiguration with KMS v2
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: EncryptionConfiguration
resources:
  - resources: ["secrets"]
    providers:
      - kms:
          apiVersion: v2
          name: aws-kms
          endpoint: unix:///var/run/kmsplugin/socket.sock
          timeout: 3s
      - identity: {}
Check yourself
Why keep identity last in the provider list?

It lets the server still read old unencrypted data during migration, but new writes use the first provider.

55.7

Audit logging

In plain words

Audit logs record who did what to which object and when. The API server writes them according to an audit policy.

The problem it solves

After an incident you must answer who deleted the Deployment or read a Secret. Without audit logs there is no answer.

What it does

  • Levels per rule: None, Metadata, Request, RequestResponse. Use Metadata for Secrets to avoid logging their contents.
  • Stages include RequestReceived (often omitted) and ResponseComplete.
  • Output to a file with rotation or a webhook backend. On EKS enable the audit control plane log type to CloudWatch; Gardener and Kyma operators can configure audit policy through the shoot.
  • Ship to a log system and alert on exec, secrets reads by unusual users, RBAC changes, and anonymous access.

Policy

yamlAudit policy
apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1
kind: Policy
omitStages: ["RequestReceived"]
rules:
  - level: None
    users: ["system:kube-proxy"]
    verbs: ["watch"]
  - level: Metadata
    resources:
      - group: ""
        resources: ["secrets", "configmaps", "tokenreviews"]
  - level: RequestResponse
    resources:
      - group: "rbac.authorization.k8s.io"
  - level: Request
    verbs: ["create", "update", "patch", "delete"]
  - level: Metadata

Section 56 of 65

Bootstrapping with kubeadm, the hard way

7 concepts · about 55 minutes

Building a cluster by hand once removes the mystery. Even if you never run kubeadm in production, you learn what managed control planes provide and where failures come from.

Goals
  • Explain every component and certificate needed to build a cluster
  • Bootstrap a control plane and join workers with kubeadm
  • Understand what managed services such as EKS and Gardener do for you
56.1

What a cluster is made of

In plain words

A cluster is a handful of programs plus certificates that let them trust one another: etcd, kube-apiserver, kube-controller-manager, kube-scheduler on the control plane and kubelet, container runtime and CNI on each node.

The problem it solves

When a managed cluster misbehaves you must know which part is involved.

What it does

  • Control plane components usually run as static Pods defined in /etc/kubernetes/manifests and watched by the kubelet.
  • Everything talks to the API server; only the API server talks to etcd.
  • Cluster state: PKI in /etc/kubernetes/pki, kubeconfig files for admin, controller manager, scheduler and kubelet.
  • Add-ons: CoreDNS and kube-proxy (or a replacement) plus a CNI.

Look at an existing control plane

bashStatic Pod manifests (on a control plane node)
ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests /etc/kubernetes/pki
sudo crictl ps | head
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o wide
56.2

Prepare nodes

In plain words

Before kubeadm runs, each machine needs a supported OS, a container runtime, the kubelet, kubeadm and kubectl, and a few kernel settings.

The problem it solves

Most failed installs come from missing prerequisites such as swap, cgroup driver mismatch or blocked ports.

What it does

  • Disable swap (or configure the kubelet to tolerate it deliberately) and load overlay and br_netfilter; set net.ipv4.ip_forward=1.
  • Install containerd with SystemdCgroup = true to match the kubelet's systemd cgroup driver.
  • Install kubelet, kubeadm, kubectl from the pkgs.k8s.io repository for your minor version, and hold the packages.
  • Open ports: 6443 API, 2379-2380 etcd, 10250 kubelet, plus CNI ports. Unique hostnames and MAC addresses.

Commands

bashPrepare an Ubuntu node (outline)
sudo swapoff -a && sudo sed -i '/ swap / s/^/#/' /etc/fstab
printf 'overlay\nbr_netfilter\n' | sudo tee /etc/modules-load.d/k8s.conf
sudo modprobe overlay br_netfilter
echo 'net.ipv4.ip_forward=1' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/k8s.conf && sudo sysctl --system
sudo apt-get install -y containerd kubelet kubeadm kubectl
sudo apt-mark hold kubelet kubeadm kubectl
Check yourself
Which cgroup driver should containerd and kubelet share?

systemd on systemd-based hosts. A mismatch causes unstable Pods and kubelet errors.

56.3

kubeadm init, phase by phase

In plain words

kubeadm init runs ordered phases: preflight checks, certificates, kubeconfigs, static Pod manifests, wait for the control plane, upload config, bootstrap tokens and add-ons.

The problem it solves

Knowing the phases lets you debug a failed init and repeat a single step.

What it does

  • Use a config file for repeatability: kubeadm init --config kubeadm.yaml.
  • controlPlaneEndpoint should be a stable DNS name or load balancer for HA later.
  • podSubnet must match your CNI configuration; serviceSubnet must not overlap with networks.
  • kubeadm init phase NAME runs individual phases; kubeadm reset cleans up a failed attempt.
  • Output includes the admin kubeconfig and the join command with token and CA cert hash.

Config file

yamlkubeadm.yaml
apiVersion: kubeadm.k8s.io/v1beta4
kind: ClusterConfiguration
kubernetesVersion: v1.37.2
controlPlaneEndpoint: api.lab.example.com:6443
networking:
  podSubnet: 10.244.0.0/16
  serviceSubnet: 10.96.0.0/12
apiServer:
  certSANs: ["api.lab.example.com"]
---
apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: KubeletConfiguration
cgroupDriver: systemd
Note

Use the kubeadm config API version that your kubeadm release documents (kubeadm config print init-defaults).

56.4

Certificates and PKI

In plain words

Components authenticate with X.509 client certificates signed by cluster CAs. kubeadm creates a cluster CA, an etcd CA and a front-proxy CA.

The problem it solves

kubeadm certificates expire after one year. An expired certificate takes the API server down with confusing errors.

What it does

  • CA certificates last 10 years; leaf certificates (apiserver, kubelet client, etcd) 1 year and are renewed automatically during kubeadm upgrade.
  • kubeadm certs check-expiration shows dates. kubeadm certs renew all renews them; then restart the static Pods.
  • Kubelet client and server certificates can rotate automatically (rotateCertificates, serverTLSBootstrap with approved CSRs).
  • Inspect with openssl x509 -in file -noout -text.

Commands

bashCheck and renew
sudo kubeadm certs check-expiration
sudo kubeadm certs renew all
sudo openssl x509 -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/apiserver.crt -noout -subject -enddate
Check yourself
What happens when the API server certificate expires?

Clients and components fail TLS verification and the cluster appears down until certificates are renewed and Pods restarted.

56.5

Joining workers and extra control planes

In plain words

Nodes join using a bootstrap token and the hash of the cluster CA. The kubelet then requests its own certificate.

The problem it solves

Without a safe join protocol an attacker could join a rogue node or impersonate the API server.

What it does

  • kubeadm join ENDPOINT --token T --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:H for workers.
  • Tokens expire after 24 hours; kubeadm token create --print-join-command makes a new one.
  • Extra control plane nodes add --control-plane --certificate-key K, where the key decrypts certificates uploaded with kubeadm init --upload-certs (valid 2 hours).
  • Without a CNI, nodes join but stay NotReady.

Commands

bashJoin
kubeadm token create --print-join-command
kubectl get nodes -o wide
kubectl get csr
56.6

Install the CNI and verify

In plain words

After init, install a CNI so that Pods get IPs and CoreDNS can start. Then verify with a small workload.

The problem it solves

A cluster that shows Ready nodes can still have broken DNS or Pod-to-Pod traffic.

What it does

  • Apply the CNI manifest or Helm chart with the Pod CIDR you set at init.
  • Check kubectl get pods -n kube-system until all are Running.
  • Test: DNS lookup, Pod to Pod across nodes, Service access, NodePort.
  • Run kubectl get --raw /readyz?verbose and conformance tools such as sonobuoy for a deeper check.

Smoke tests

bashCluster smoke test
kubectl create deploy web --image=nginx:1.27 --replicas=3
kubectl expose deploy web --port=80
kubectl run t --rm -it --restart=Never --image=busybox:1.36 -- wget -qO- http://web
kubectl run d --rm -it --restart=Never --image=busybox:1.36 -- nslookup kubernetes.default
kubectl delete deploy,svc web
Check yourself
Why are nodes NotReady right after init?

No CNI is installed yet, so the kubelet reports the network as not ready.

56.7

What managed services do for you

In plain words

EKS and Gardener run and patch the control plane, etcd and certificates. You manage nodes (or let the service manage them), add-ons and workloads.

The problem it solves

Without this comparison you may assume a managed cluster protects things it does not.

What it does

  • EKS: managed API servers and etcd across AZs, control plane upgrades by API call, managed node groups, add-ons (CoreDNS, VPC CNI, kube-proxy, EBS CSI). You own node AMIs, IAM mapping, add-on upgrades.
  • Gardener: a seed cluster hosts each shoot's control plane as Pods; worker pools are defined in the Shoot; maintenance windows apply updates.
  • You cannot SSH into the control plane, so debugging relies on events, metrics and provider logs.
  • Self-managed gives full control but you own etcd backups, certificate renewal and upgrades.
← PreviousNext →
Section 57 of 65

High availability control plane and etcd drills

6 concepts · about 55 minutes

The control plane is only as available as etcd and the endpoint in front of the API servers. These drills turn theory into muscle memory.

Goals
  • Design a three node control plane with a stable API endpoint
  • Back up and restore etcd and rehearse failures
  • Monitor etcd health and handle member replacement
57.1

HA topologies

In plain words

A highly available control plane runs at least three API servers and three etcd members, behind one stable address.

The problem it solves

A single control plane node is a single point of failure for scheduling, scaling and deployments (running Pods continue, but nothing changes).

What it does

  • Stacked etcd: etcd runs on the same nodes as the control plane. Simpler, fewer machines.
  • External etcd: separate etcd nodes. More machines, isolates failure and resources.
  • API servers are stateless and are placed behind a load balancer or virtual IP (kube-vip, HAProxy, cloud LB).
  • Spread across failure zones. Managed services do this for you.
Check yourself
Why use a load balancer address as controlPlaneEndpoint?

Nodes and users keep working when one API server fails or is replaced, and certificates stay valid.

57.2

Raft quorum and failure math

In plain words

etcd uses the Raft algorithm. A write needs agreement from a majority (quorum) of members.

The problem it solves

Wrong member counts give no extra safety, or leave the cluster read-only after a failure.

What it does

  • Quorum is floor(n/2)+1. For 3 members quorum is 2 (tolerates 1 failure). For 5 it is 3 (tolerates 2). Even numbers add cost without tolerance.
  • Losing quorum makes etcd unavailable for writes; the API server then fails requests.
  • More members slows writes slightly. Three or five is the practical range.
  • Disk latency is the main risk: slow fsync causes leader elections and "etcdserver: request timed out".

Verify the numbers

pythonQuorum table
for n in range(1, 8):
    quorum = n // 2 + 1
    print(n, "members, quorum", quorum, ", tolerates", n - quorum)
57.3

Taking an etcd snapshot

In plain words

etcdctl snapshot save writes a consistent copy of the whole etcd database to a file.

The problem it solves

Without a recent snapshot, losing quorum or corrupting data means rebuilding the cluster and redeploying everything.

What it does

  • Needs endpoint and client certificates: --endpoints, --cacert, --cert, --key (kubeadm paths under /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd).
  • Verify with etcdutl snapshot status (older versions: etcdctl snapshot status).
  • Copy off the node to object storage. Encrypt, since snapshots contain Secrets. Automate with a CronJob or a systemd timer, and retain several days.
  • Managed control planes (EKS, Gardener) take backups for you; you cannot access etcd directly. Gardener backs up each shoot's etcd to object storage automatically.

Commands

bashSnapshot (on a kubeadm control plane node)
sudo ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  snapshot save /var/backups/etcd-$(date +%F).db
sudo etcdutl snapshot status /var/backups/etcd-$(date +%F).db -w table
Check yourself
Why encrypt etcd snapshots?

They contain all cluster data including Secrets in readable form unless encryption at rest was enabled.

57.4

Restoring etcd, the drill

In plain words

Restore creates a new data directory from a snapshot. All members then start from the same state with new cluster identity.

The problem it solves

Restores are done rarely and under pressure. Rehearsal avoids mistakes such as restoring only one member.

What it does

  • Stop the API servers and etcd (move static Pod manifests away on kubeadm).
  • Single member: etcdutl snapshot restore snap.db --data-dir /var/lib/etcd-restore, then point the etcd manifest at the new dir.
  • Multi member: restore on each node with --name, --initial-cluster, --initial-advertise-peer-urls and a new --initial-cluster-token.
  • Restart and check etcdctl endpoint status and kubectl get nodes.
  • Objects created after the snapshot are lost; controllers will reconcile what remains. Lease and node state catch up.

Commands

bashRestore single member
sudo mv /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml /tmp/
sudo mv /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml /tmp/
sudo etcdutl snapshot restore /var/backups/etcd-2026-10-30.db --data-dir /var/lib/etcd-restore
sudo sed -i 's#/var/lib/etcd$#/var/lib/etcd-restore#' /tmp/etcd.yaml
sudo mv /tmp/etcd.yaml /tmp/kube-apiserver.yaml /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
Careful

Never restore on only some members of a multi-member cluster. Stop, restore and start all of them with the same snapshot.

57.5

Failure drills

In plain words

A drill is a planned experiment: break one thing in a test cluster, observe, recover, and write down the steps and the time taken.

The problem it solves

Untested recovery plans fail on the day: wrong certificates, missing backups, expired tokens.

What it does

  • Drill 1: stop one control plane node. Expect API available through the LB, etcd still healthy.
  • Drill 2: stop two nodes. Expect writes to fail; restore quorum by bringing one back.
  • Drill 3: replace a member: etcdctl member remove, then member add, and start the new node with --initial-cluster-state existing.
  • Drill 4: full restore from snapshot into new machines.
  • Drill 5: expire certificates in a lab (set clock or use short lifetimes) and renew.

Member commands

bashMember health and replacement
ETCD="etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key"
sudo $ETCD member list -w table
sudo $ETCD endpoint status --cluster -w table
sudo $ETCD endpoint health --cluster
Check yourself
What happens to the API when two of three etcd members are down?

Quorum is lost. Reads may fail and writes are rejected until one member returns.

57.6

etcd performance, defrag and monitoring

In plain words

etcd keeps history of changes, and its database file grows. Compaction removes old revisions and defragmentation returns space to the disk.

The problem it solves

When the database hits its quota (2 GiB by default) etcd raises an alarm and becomes read-only: "mvcc: database space exceeded".

What it does

  • The API server compacts automatically (every 5 minutes by default); defragment members one at a time during quiet hours.
  • Clear alarms with etcdctl alarm disarm after freeing space.
  • Monitor etcd_server_has_leader, etcd_server_leader_changes_seen_total, etcd_disk_wal_fsync_duration_seconds (p99 under 10 ms is the guidance), etcd_mvcc_db_total_size_in_bytes.
  • Use fast local SSD or NVMe disks. Avoid noisy neighbours. Large numbers of Events or CRD objects inflate the database.

Commands

bashDefragment
ETCD="etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key"
sudo $ETCD endpoint status --cluster -w table
sudo $ETCD defrag
sudo $ETCD alarm list
← PreviousNext →
Section 58 of 65

Cluster API and fleet management

7 concepts · about 50 minutes

Once you run more than a few clusters, clicking in consoles does not scale. Fleet management treats clusters themselves as declarative objects.

Goals
  • Explain how Cluster API manages clusters as Kubernetes objects
  • Roll out upgrades and node pools declaratively across providers
  • Operate a fleet of clusters with GitOps and consistent policy
58.1

Why manage clusters declaratively

In plain words

Instead of scripts that create clusters, you describe each cluster in YAML in Git and a controller makes it real and keeps it that way.

The problem it solves

Hand-built clusters drift, upgrades are unrepeatable and nobody knows what is running where.

What it does

  • A management cluster runs controllers that create and upgrade workload clusters.
  • Git is the source of truth; pull requests are the change process.
  • The same model can describe EKS, Gardener shoots, vSphere or bare metal.
  • Tools: Cluster API, Crossplane, Terraform with pipelines, Gardener (its own model), vendor consoles.
Cluster provisioning
OptionCluster API
Choose whenmany clusters on varied infrastructure
Avoid whenone managed cluster is enough
OptionTerraform pipeline
Choose whenyou already use it for the rest of the cloud
Avoid whenyou need continuous drift correction
OptionGardener
Choose whenmany conformant clusters with a central team
Avoid whenyou need a single small cluster
58.2

Cluster API objects

In plain words

Cluster API (CAPI) is a Kubernetes SIG project. It defines CRDs such as Cluster, Machine, MachineDeployment and MachineSet, similar to Pod, Deployment and ReplicaSet but for nodes.

The problem it solves

Each cloud has different APIs for creating machines and control planes.

What it does

  • Cluster ties together a control plane object and an infrastructure object (for example AWSCluster).
  • KubeadmControlPlane (or a managed variant such as AWSManagedControlPlane for EKS) handles control plane replicas and upgrades.
  • MachineDeployment creates worker Machine objects from a MachineTemplate and a bootstrap config; rolling updates replace machines.
  • MachineHealthCheck replaces unhealthy nodes automatically.

Inspect with clusterctl

bashclusterctl basics
clusterctl init --infrastructure aws
clusterctl describe cluster prod-eu
kubectl get machines,machinedeployments -A
clusterctl get kubeconfig prod-eu > /tmp/prod-eu.kubeconfig
Check yourself
Which CAPI object replaces broken nodes automatically?

A MachineHealthCheck, which deletes machines that fail its conditions so the MachineSet creates new ones.

58.3

Upgrades and node pools with CAPI

In plain words

You change the Kubernetes version or machine template in YAML. CAPI performs a rolling replacement of control plane then workers.

The problem it solves

In-place upgrades of nodes are risky and slow to roll back.

What it does

  • Control plane first: update KubeadmControlPlane.spec.version; it adds new machines then removes old ones.
  • Workers: new MachineTemplate (immutable, so create a new one) referenced from the MachineDeployment, with rollingUpdate maxSurge and maxUnavailable.
  • Respect version skew: workers may lag the control plane by a few minors (check the current skew policy).
  • Pair with PodDisruptionBudgets so drains keep services up.

MachineDeployment (shape)

yamlWorker pool
apiVersion: cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: MachineDeployment
metadata:
  name: prod-eu-workers
spec:
  clusterName: prod-eu
  replicas: 5
  strategy:
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0
  selector:
    matchLabels: {}
  template:
    spec:
      clusterName: prod-eu
      version: v1.37.2
      bootstrap:
        configRef:
          apiVersion: bootstrap.cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
          kind: KubeadmConfigTemplate
          name: prod-eu-workers-v2
      infrastructureRef:
        apiVersion: infrastructure.cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta2
        kind: AWSMachineTemplate
        name: prod-eu-workers-v2
Note

CAPI API versions move. Generate templates with clusterctl generate cluster for your installed providers.

58.4

ClusterClass and topology

In plain words

ClusterClass is a reusable blueprint. A Cluster then says "use this class, with these variables" instead of repeating every object.

The problem it solves

Dozens of nearly identical clusters mean dozens of copied manifests that drift apart.

What it does

  • The class defines templates for control plane, infrastructure and worker classes, plus patches driven by variables.
  • A Cluster with spec.topology sets class, version, replicas and variables.
  • Upgrading the class or version rolls out through all clusters that use it, in a controlled way.
  • Good for platform teams who offer a few "flavours" of cluster.
58.5

Fleet GitOps with Argo CD or Flux

In plain words

A fleet needs the same add-ons (ingress, monitoring, policy) on every cluster, with per-cluster differences. GitOps tools do this from one repository.

The problem it solves

Installing add-ons manually on each cluster guarantees inconsistency.

What it does

  • Argo CD ApplicationSet generators (cluster, list, git) create one Application per registered cluster or folder.
  • Flux uses Kustomization per cluster with a shared base and overlays, or a hub controlling remote clusters through kubeconfig secrets.
  • Keep add-on versions in one place; promote through dev, staging, prod folders.
  • Secrets via External Secrets or SOPS, never in plain YAML.

ApplicationSet by cluster label

yamlInstall monitoring on every prod cluster
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: ApplicationSet
metadata:
  name: monitoring
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  generators:
    - clusters:
        selector:
          matchLabels:
            env: prod
  template:
    metadata:
      name: "monitoring-{{name}}"
    spec:
      project: platform
      source:
        repoURL: https://git.example.com/platform/addons.git
        targetRevision: main
        path: monitoring/overlays/prod
      destination:
        server: "{{server}}"
        namespace: monitoring
      syncPolicy:
        automated: {prune: true, selfHeal: true}
Check yourself
How does ApplicationSet know which clusters exist?

Argo CD cluster secrets are the inventory. The cluster generator creates one app per matching registered cluster.

58.6

Crossplane and composition

In plain words

Crossplane turns cloud resources into Kubernetes objects and lets platform teams publish simple custom APIs built from them.

The problem it solves

Developers need a database or a bucket, but should not learn every cloud option or hold cloud credentials.

What it does

  • Providers add managed resources (RDS, S3, VPC). Compositions map your own CRD (a PostgreSQLInstance claim) to several managed resources.
  • The platform team owns the composition; teams request with a few fields.
  • Overlaps with Terraform; Crossplane suits continuous reconciliation and self service through the Kubernetes API.
  • Check current API versions (Composition functions and pipelines replaced older patch-and-transform styles).
58.7

Fleet policy, inventory and upgrades at scale

In plain words

At scale the questions change: what versions are running, which clusters are out of date, which violate policy.

The problem it solves

A fleet with 40 clusters on 5 different Kubernetes versions cannot be patched safely or audited.

What it does

  • Keep an inventory (CMDB or a Git file): cluster, owner, environment, version, region. This is also useful in your own CLUSTERS.md.
  • Standardise versions: at most two minors in use; upgrade dev first, then staging, then production with soak time.
  • Policy as code (Kyverno, Gatekeeper, ValidatingAdmissionPolicy) distributed through GitOps.
  • Central observability: Prometheus remote write or Thanos, central log store, one dashboard per cluster label.
  • Automate end-of-life tracking from the Kubernetes release calendar and provider support dates.

Version report

bashServer version of every context
for c in $(kubectl config get-contexts -o name); do
  v=$(kubectl --context "$c" version -o json 2>/dev/null | python3 -c 'import sys,json; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["serverVersion"]["gitVersion"])' 2>/dev/null)
  echo "$c ${v:-unreachable}"
done

Section 59 of 65

Gardener and Kyma concepts

6 concepts · about 55 minutes

SAP BTP Kyma runtime is a Kubernetes cluster managed with Gardener, with Kyma modules installed on top. Knowing both layers helps you decide where a problem belongs.

Goals
  • Explain gardens, seeds and shoots and how a shoot control plane is hosted
  • Read a Shoot specification and understand maintenance and hibernation
  • Describe how Kyma sits on a Gardener cluster and what the module model is
59.1

Garden, seed and shoot

In plain words

Gardener is a Kubernetes extension that manages Kubernetes clusters at scale. It uses Kubernetes to run Kubernetes.

The problem it solves

Providing hundreds of conformant clusters with consistent upgrades needs a control layer that is itself cloud neutral.

What it does

  • Garden cluster: runs the Gardener API (Shoot, Seed, Project, CloudProfile objects).
  • Seed cluster: a Kubernetes cluster that hosts the control planes (kube-apiserver, etcd, controllers) of many shoots as Pods in per-shoot namespaces.
  • Shoot cluster: the end user cluster. Its worker nodes run in the customer's cloud account (or the provider's), while the control plane is in the seed.
  • Soil: the initial seed that hosts the garden itself.
Check yourself
Where does a shoot's kube-apiserver run?

As a Pod in a namespace of the seed cluster, not on the shoot's own worker nodes.

59.2

Reading a Shoot specification

In plain words

A Shoot object describes the cluster: provider, region, Kubernetes version, networking, worker pools, maintenance and hibernation.

The problem it solves

Cluster configuration must be reviewable and repeatable like any other code.

What it does

  • spec.provider.workers[]: pool name, machine type and image, minimum, maximum, zones, taints, labels.
  • spec.kubernetes.version, and optional kube-apiserver, kubelet and audit settings.
  • spec.networking: type (calico or cilium), pods, services and nodes CIDRs.
  • spec.maintenance: time window and whether to auto update Kubernetes patch version and machine image.
  • spec.hibernation schedules to stop worker nodes for savings. Fields differ per Gardener version and landscape; check your landscape's docs.

Excerpt

yamlShoot excerpt
apiVersion: core.gardener.cloud/v1beta1
kind: Shoot
metadata:
  name: dev-eu
  namespace: garden-myproject
spec:
  region: eu-central-1
  kubernetes:
    version: 1.37.2
  networking:
    type: calico
    nodes: 10.250.0.0/16
  provider:
    type: aws
    workers:
      - name: pool-a
        machine: {type: m5.xlarge, image: {name: gardenlinux}}
        minimum: 2
        maximum: 6
        zones: [eu-central-1a, eu-central-1b]
  maintenance:
    timeWindow: {begin: 220000+0000, end: 230000+0000}
    autoUpdate:
      kubernetesVersion: true
      machineImageVersion: true
59.3

Maintenance, updates and hibernation

In plain words

Gardener updates clusters in a maintenance window and can hibernate them, which stops workers while keeping the cluster definition and data.

The problem it solves

Patching many clusters by hand is slow, and idle dev clusters waste money.

What it does

  • Patch version and machine image updates can happen automatically in the window. Minor Kubernetes upgrades are normally your decision and must be done stepwise (one minor at a time).
  • Rolling node replacement drains nodes respecting PDBs. Pods without PDBs or with long shutdowns may be disrupted; set them properly.
  • Hibernation scales workers to zero on a schedule; PVC data persists but Pods stop.
  • Be aware of the drain and cordon lesson from earlier: after manual maintenance, check that nodes are uncordoned since reconciliation may interfere.

Check from kubectl

bashAfter maintenance
kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,VERSION:.status.nodeInfo.kubeletVersion,SCHEDULABLE:.spec.unschedulable,OS:.status.nodeInfo.osImage
kubectl get pdb -A
kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -15
Check yourself
Why define PDBs for Gardener maintenance?

Node replacement drains nodes. PDBs limit how many replicas of a service are evicted at once.

59.4

Gardener extensions and operations

In plain words

Gardener keeps cloud specifics out of its core. Extensions (provider, OS, network, DNS, certificates) handle each environment.

The problem it solves

Supporting AWS, Azure, GCP, OpenStack and others in one codebase would be unmaintainable.

What it does

  • Extension CRDs such as Infrastructure, Worker, ControlPlane, Network and OperatingSystemConfig are reconciled by provider extensions in the seed.
  • Shoot lifecycle shows in status.lastOperation and status.conditions (APIServerAvailable, ControlPlaneHealthy, EveryNodeReady, SystemComponentsHealthy).
  • Shoots get a shoot-info ConfigMap in kube-system and managed components in kube-system.
  • Operators use gardenctl to target gardens and obtain shoot kubeconfigs; credentials are short lived via the gardenlogin plugin.

Operator commands

bashgardenctl workflow
gardenctl target --garden mylandscape --project myproject --shoot dev-eu
gardenctl kubectl-env bash > /tmp/env.sh && source /tmp/env.sh
kubectl get nodes
kubectl -n kube-system get cm shoot-info -o yaml | head -20
Note

Commands depend on your landscape's setup. Follow your team's gardenctl configuration guide.

59.5

Kyma runtime on top of Gardener

In plain words

SAP BTP, Kyma runtime provides a Gardener shoot already prepared with Kyma. You get a kubeconfig, a managed set of modules and BTP integration.

The problem it solves

Teams want Kubernetes and BTP services together, without installing and wiring the platform pieces themselves.

What it does

  • Kyma runs in a BTP subaccount and is created via BTP cockpit, CLI or service instance. The cluster is a Gardener shoot managed by SAP.
  • Access is by OIDC through the BTP identity provider (SAP IAS), commonly with the kubelogin plugin and a downloaded kubeconfig.
  • Cluster add-ons (Istio, API Gateway, Serverless, Telemetry, etc.) are provided as Kyma modules managed via the Kyma custom resource, with release channels.
  • SAP is responsible for the control plane and the modules' lifecycle; you own namespaces and applications.

First contact

bashCheck a Kyma cluster
kubectl get kyma -n kyma-system -o jsonpath='{.items[0].status.state}{"\n"}'
kubectl get modules -A 2>/dev/null | head
kubectl get nodes -L topology.kubernetes.io/zone
59.6

The Kyma custom resource and release channels

In plain words

The Kyma resource in kyma-system lists enabled modules and their channel. Lifecycle Manager reads it and installs or upgrades the modules.

The problem it solves

Choosing and upgrading features needs a simple declarative handle.

What it does

  • Each module entry has name, optional channel (regular, fast) or a fixed version, and optional custom resource policy.
  • kubectl get kyma default -n kyma-system -o yaml shows each module's state (Ready, Processing, Error, Warning) and the installed version.
  • Each module has its own CR (for example Istio, APIGateway, Telemetry) holding module configuration.
  • Removing a module deletes its CR and may remove workloads, so read the module's deletion notes first.
  • Module names and fields change over releases; check the current Kyma docs.

Enable a module

yamlKyma resource with modules
apiVersion: operator.kyma-project.io/v1beta2
kind: Kyma
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: kyma-system
spec:
  channel: regular
  modules:
    - name: istio
    - name: api-gateway
    - name: serverless
    - name: telemetry
bashStatus of modules
kubectl get kyma default -n kyma-system -o jsonpath='{range .status.modules[*]}{.name}{" "}{.state}{" "}{.version}{"\n"}{end}'
Check yourself
Where do you enable or disable a Kyma module?

In the Kyma custom resource (or the BTP cockpit, which edits it).
